  8 May 1945); 1944–1945 (women's vote); 1958 (Ve République); Mai 68; 1999–2002 (the euro:
  1 € = 6,55957 F).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Him, her, it, them: direct object pronouns
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 gave you the tools to tell a story in the past. This module is about the small words
that make French sound natural: the pronouns that replace a noun you have just mentioned. In
English you say "Do you know Marc? Yes, I know him." French does the same, but the pronoun
goes in a different place, and that is the part that takes practice.

You have already met a few: *Je le prends* (I'll take it) when shopping, and *Tu l'as trouvé ?*
(Did you find it?) in French A1, and the reflexive *me* of *Je viens de me lever* in lesson 4. This lesson sets out the
whole system for the first group, the **[[direct object pronouns]]**, and the theme is people: love,
friendship and couples. Lesson 6 adds the indirect pronouns (to him, to them), lesson 7 *y* and
*en*, and lesson 8 puts all of them into the passé composé.

## What a direct object is

The **[[direct object]]** is the person or thing that the verb acts on, with no preposition in
between. Ask "who?" or "what?" after the verb:

- *Paul aime Julie.* — Paul loves Julie. (Paul loves whom? Julie.)
- *Je regarde le film.* — I'm watching the film. (I'm watching what? The film.)
- *Nous invitons nos voisins.* — We're inviting our neighbours.

If there is a preposition before the person, as in *Je parle à Julie*, it is not a direct
object: that is lesson 6.

## The direct object pronouns

| subject | direct object pronoun | example | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | me (m') | *Il m'aime.* | He loves me. |
| tu | te (t') | *Je t'attends.* | I'm waiting for you. |
| il | le (l') | *Je le connais.* | I know him / it. |
| elle | la (l') | *Je la connais.* | I know her / it. |
| nous | nous | *Elle nous invite.* | She's inviting us. |
| vous | vous | *Je vous écoute.* | I'm listening to you. |
| ils, elles | les | *Je les aime bien.* | I like them. |

Points to notice:

- *Le* and *la* replace things as well as people, and they follow the noun's gender, not the
  English word "it": *Le film ? Je le regarde ce soir. La voiture ? Je la prends.*
- *Les* is for all plurals, people or things, masculine or feminine: *Tes clés ? Je les
  cherche.*
- *Me, te, le, la* lose their vowel before a vowel or a mute *h*: *Je l'aime. Il m'écoute. Je
  t'invite.* *Nous, vous* and *les* never change in writing; before a vowel their *s* is spoken as a
  z: *Je les_invite. Elle nous_aime.*
- These pronouns look like the articles *le, la, les*, but an article stands before a noun and
  a pronoun usually stands before a verb: *Je regarde le film* (article) / *Je le regarde*
  (pronoun).

## Where the pronoun goes

This is the big difference from English. All the object pronouns in this module (direct,
indirect, *y* and *en*) follow the same four position rules.

![Three rows of word boxes showing where a pronoun goes. Row one, a single verb: "Je la connais." with the pronoun la in a coloured box before the verb connais, and the negative "Je ne la connais pas." with ne and pas around the pair. Row two, verb plus infinitive: "Je vais la voir." with la before the infinitive voir, not before vais, and the negative "Je ne vais pas la voir." Row three, the affirmative command "Regarde-le !" with le after the verb and joined by a hyphen, and the negative command "Ne le regarde pas !" with le back before the verb.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 1. Before the conjugated verb

In the present (and in every one-word tense, such as the
imparfait), the pronoun goes straight before the verb:

- *Tu connais Marc ? — Oui, je le connais.* — Do you know Marc? — Yes, I know him.
- *Son quartier ? Elle l'aimait beaucoup.* — Her neighbourhood? She loved it a lot.

In the negative, *ne … pas* goes around the pronoun and the verb together:

- *Je ne le connais pas.* — I don't know him.
- *Tu ne m'écoutes pas !* — You're not listening to me!

In questions the pronoun stays glued to the verb: *Tu la vois ? Est-ce que tu la vois ? La
vois-tu ?*

### 2. Before an infinitive

When a verb is followed by an infinitive (*aller, vouloir, pouvoir,
devoir* + infinitive), the pronoun goes before the infinitive, because it is the object of
that verb. (A few verbs, such as *faire* + infinitive, work differently: *Je le fais réparer*, I'm
having it repaired. You will meet them later.)

- *Je vais la voir samedi.* — I'm going to see her on Saturday.
- *Je veux le faire.* — I want to do it.
- *Tu peux m'aider ?* — Can you help me?
- *Je ne vais pas les inviter.* — I'm not going to invite them.

The same goes for the chunks from lesson 4: *Je viens de la voir* (I've just seen her), *Je suis
en train de le lire* (I'm reading it right now).

### 3. After the verb in an affirmative command

In the imperative (French A1, lesson 20) the
pronoun moves after the verb and is joined to it with a hyphen. *Me* and *te* become *moi* and
*toi*:

- *Regarde-le !* — Look at him / it!
- *Aide-moi !* — Help me!
- *Écoutez-moi, s'il vous plaît.* — Listen to me, please.
- *Invitons-les !* — Let's invite them!

You know this pattern already from reflexive commands: *Lève-toi !*

### 4. Before the verb in a negative command

With *ne … pas*, the pronoun goes back to its
usual place, without a hyphen, and *me* stays *me*:

- *Ne le regarde pas !* — Don't look at him!
- *Ne m'attends pas.* — Don't wait for me.

### Voici and voilà

*Voici* and *voilà* take the pronoun in front, like a verb: *Le voilà !* (There he is! There it
is!), *Les voilà !* (There they are!), *Me voici.* (Here I am.)

## English preposition, French direct object

Some verbs have a preposition in English but take a direct object in French, with nothing in
between. So they take *le, la, les*:

| French | English |
|---|---|
| attendre quelqu'un | to wait for someone |
| chercher quelque chose | to look for something |
| écouter quelqu'un | to listen to someone |
| regarder quelque chose | to look at something |
| payer quelque chose | to pay for something |

- *J'attends Sophie. Je l'attends depuis vingt minutes.* — I've been waiting for her for twenty
  minutes.
- *Tu cherches tes lunettes ? — Oui, je les cherche partout.* — Yes, I'm looking for them
  everywhere.

The verb *quitter* (to leave a person or a place) is another: *Elle quitte Paul. Elle le quitte.*
It needs an object; to say "she's leaving" with no object, use *partir*: *Elle part.* (The one
everyday exception is on the phone: *Ne quittez pas !* — Hold the line!)

## Each other: reciprocal se

When two people do something to each other, French uses *se* (and *nous, vous* for "we" and
"you"), the same pronouns as the reflexive verbs from French A1, lesson 17. A verb used this
way is a **[[reciprocal verb]]**:

- *Ils s'aiment.* — They love each other.
- *Léa et Tom se regardent.* — Léa and Tom look at each other.
- *Nous nous connaissons depuis dix ans.* — We've known each other for ten years.
- *Vous vous voyez souvent ?* — Do you see each other often?
- *On se voit demain ?* — Shall we meet tomorrow? (literally, "Do we see each other tomorrow?")

![Two panels. Left: one person looks into a mirror, with curved arrows going from the person to the mirror and back; caption "Il se regarde. He looks at himself." Right: two people face each other, with one arrow from each to the other; caption "Ils se regardent. They look at each other."](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

With one subject, *se* is reflexive (himself, herself); with two or more people it is usually
reciprocal (each other). Out of context *Ils se regardent* could mean either, but the situation
almost always makes it clear.

*On se voit* is one of the most common things friends say. With *on* the verb is singular, as
always: *on se voit, on s'appelle*.

Several relationship verbs are used with *se* in this way:

- *se disputer (avec quelqu'un)* — to argue, quarrel: *Ils se disputent tout le temps.*
- *se réconcilier* — to make up: *Après une dispute, ils se réconcilient vite.*
- *se séparer* — to split up: *Mes voisins se séparent.*
- *s'entendre (bien / mal) avec quelqu'un* — to get on (well / badly): *Je m'entends bien avec
  mes voisins.* (*S'entendre* is *entendre* + *se*, so it is a regular -re verb: *je
  m'entends, nous nous entendons*.)

Notice that *se disputer, se séparer* and *s'entendre* also work with one subject and *avec*:
*Je me dispute avec mon frère. Elle s'entend bien avec lui.* The passé composé of these verbs
(*ils se sont séparés*) is in lesson 8h2.

## Love and friendship: the words

Most of this lesson's words are easy to guess (*l'amour, l'amitié, le couple, la relation, le
sentiment, jaloux, fidèle*). A few need a note:

- *tomber amoureux / amoureuse de quelqu'un* — to fall in love with someone; *sortir avec
  quelqu'un* — to go out with someone (to date): *Elle sort avec Hugo depuis mars.*
- *le petit ami, la petite amie* — boyfriend, girlfriend; *un copain, une copine* (lesson 1) is
  more informal. *Célibataire* means single.
- *embrasser* — to kiss, and also to hug. At the end of a letter *Je t'embrasse* is "love"
  (lesson 23).
- *faire confiance à quelqu'un* — to trust someone: *Tu peux me faire confiance.* (In the third
  person it takes *lui* and *leur*, the indirect pronouns of lesson 6.)

### Aimer or aimer bien?

With people, *aimer* is strong. *Je t'aime* means "I love you". Add *bien* and it becomes weaker:
*Je t'aime bien* means "I like you", the thing you say to a friend. With things there is no such
difference: *J'aime le chocolat* and *J'aime bien le chocolat* both mean "I like chocolate".
(*Aimer beaucoup* a person also means "to like a lot", not "to love a lot".)

### The verb croire

| croire (to believe) | |
|---|---|
| je crois | nous croyons |
| tu crois | vous croyez |
| il / elle / on croit | ils / elles croient |
| participle: cru (*j'ai cru*) | imparfait: *je croyais* |

The *i* of the singular becomes *y* before a spoken ending, as in *voir* (*nous voyons*). *Je
crois que …* means "I think that …": *Je crois qu'il est amoureux.*

## Dialogue: Sarah and Inès talk about Léa

> Sarah : Tu connais Hugo, le nouveau copain de Léa ?
>
> Inès : Oui, je le connais un peu. Je le trouve sympa. Ils sortent ensemble depuis quand ?
>
> Sarah : Depuis le mois de mai. Elle est très amoureuse. Mais ils se disputent souvent.
>
> Inès : Ah bon ? Pourquoi ?
>
> Sarah : Il est un peu jaloux. Quand elle voit ses amis, il l'appelle toutes les heures.
>
> Inès : Elle ne va pas le quitter, quand même ?
>
> Sarah : Non, je ne crois pas. Ils se réconcilient toujours. Et elle lui fait confiance.
>
> Inès : Bon. Tu les vois samedi ?
>
> Sarah : Oui ! On se voit tous au café à huit heures. Viens avec nous ! Ils vont être contents de te voir.
>
> Inès : D'accord. Attendez-moi, je finis à huit heures et quart.

Translation:

> Sarah: Do you know Hugo, Léa's new boyfriend?
>
> Inès: Yes, I know him a bit. I think he's nice. How long have they been going out?
>
> Sarah: Since May. She's very much in love. But they often argue.
>
> Inès: Really? Why?
>
> Sarah: He's a bit jealous. When she sees her friends, he phones her every hour.
>
> Inès: She's not going to leave him, is she?
>
> Sarah: No, I don't think so. They always make up. And she trusts him.
>
> Inès: All right. Are you seeing them on Saturday?
>
> Sarah: Yes! We're all meeting at the café at eight. Come with us! They'll be happy to see you.
>
> Inès: OK. Wait for me, I finish at quarter past eight.

Notes: *Je le trouve sympa* is "I find him nice". *Il l'appelle*: *appeler* takes a direct
object, so *l'* = her. *Elle lui fait confiance* uses *lui* (to him) because the verb has *à*
(lesson 6). *Quand même* in this question means "surely not?" (lesson 21).

## Pronunciation

- *Le* in *Regarde-le !* is stressed, so it is pronounced fully, a little like the *eu* of *deux*.
  In *Je le vois* it is light and often almost swallowed: "zhuhl vwa".
- *Je l'aime* [ʒə lɛm] and *Je les aime* [ʒə le zɛm]: the plural has a whole extra syllable,
  *les* [le], linked to the verb with a z. Listen for "lay-z": that is how you hear the plural.
- *Nous nous aimons*: one liaison, after the second *nous*: [nu nu zɛmɔ̃].
- *Croient* sounds exactly like *crois, croit*: [kʁwa]. Only *croyons, croyez* sound different.

## Common mistakes

- English word order. Not ~~Je vois le~~ but *Je le vois*. Not ~~Je connais la pas~~ but *Je ne la
  connais pas*.
- Putting the pronoun before *aller* or *vouloir*. Not ~~Je la vais voir~~ but *Je vais la
  voir*. (You may meet *Je le veux faire* in old books; today it is *Je veux le faire*.)
- *Me* in an affirmative command. Not ~~Regarde-me~~ but *Regarde-moi !*
- Adding the English preposition. Not ~~J'attends pour le bus~~ or ~~Je cherche pour mes clés~~
  but *J'attends le bus, je cherche mes clés*, and so *Je l'attends, je les cherche*.
- Forgetting to elide. Not ~~Je le aime~~ but *Je l'aime*.
- *Je t'aime* to a friend. It means "I love you"; to a friend say *Je t'aime bien* or *Je t'adore*
  (lighter than it sounds in English).

## Key points

- Direct object pronouns: *me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les* (*m', t', l'* before a vowel). *Le,
  la* follow the noun's gender, people or things.
- They go before the conjugated verb (*je la connais, je ne la connais pas*), before an
  infinitive (*je vais la voir*), and after an affirmative command with a hyphen
  (*Regarde-le ! Aide-moi !*), but before a negative command (*Ne le regarde pas !*).
- *Attendre, chercher, écouter, regarder, payer, quitter* take a direct object: *Je l'attends.*
- Reciprocal *se* means "each other": *Ils s'aiment. On se voit demain ?*
- *Je t'aime* = I love you; *Je t'aime bien* = I like you.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson. The object pronoun reference sheet has every pronoun of this module in one place.

lessons.title: To him, to them: indirect object pronouns
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 5 you replaced a direct object with *le, la, les*: *Je connais Marc → Je le connais.*
But many verbs reach the person through the little word *à*: you speak to someone, you give
something to someone, you phone someone (*téléphoner à quelqu'un*). For these French has a
second set of pronouns, the **[[indirect object pronouns]]**. Two of them are new, *lui* and *leur*, and the hard part is knowing which
verbs take them. The theme is gifts, keeping in touch and the phone.

## What an indirect object is

An **[[indirect object]]** is a person reached through *à*:

- *Je parle à Marie.* — I'm speaking to Marie.
- *Il écrit à ses parents.* — He writes to his parents.
- *Nous offrons des fleurs à notre grand-mère.* — We're giving our grandmother flowers.

The last example has both kinds of object: *des fleurs* is the direct object (what we give), and
*à notre grand-mère* is the indirect object (who receives it). English often hides the "to"
("we're giving our grandmother flowers"), but French always has *à* before the person.

## The indirect object pronouns

| subject | indirect object pronoun | example | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | me (m') | *Tu me téléphones ?* | Will you phone me? |
| tu | te (t') | *Je t'écris demain.* | I'll write to you tomorrow. |
| il, elle | lui | *Je lui parle.* | I'm speaking to him / to her. |
| nous | nous | *Elle nous répond.* | She answers us. |
| vous | vous | *Je vous donne mon numéro.* | I'll give you my number. |
| ils, elles | leur | *Je leur envoie un message.* | I'm sending them a message. |

Compare with the direct pronouns of lesson 5: *me, te, nous, vous* are the same in both sets.
Only the third person is different: *le, la, les* become *lui* and *leur*.

![A chart with two columns of pronouns side by side. The left column, direct object, lists me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les. The right column, indirect object (à + person), lists me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur. Me, te, nous and vous are shaded the same colour in both columns because they don't change; le and la point to lui, and les points to leur. Under the chart: "Je l'appelle" for the direct column and "Je lui téléphone" for the indirect one.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Two things to remember:

- *Lui* means "to him" and also "to her": *Je lui téléphone* can be about Paul or about Marie.
  Context tells you which.
- *Leur* (to them) never takes an *s*. Don't confuse it with the possessive *leur, leurs*
  (their, French A1, lesson 6), which agrees with its noun. In *Je leur donne leurs cadeaux* (I
  give them their presents), the first *leur* is the pronoun, the second is the possessive.

## Verbs with à + person

These common verbs take *à* before the person, so they take *lui* and *leur*. Many of them also
have a direct object (a thing): *donner quelque chose à quelqu'un*.

| verb | pattern | example with a pronoun |
|---|---|---|
| parler | parler à qqn | *Je lui parle tous les jours.* |
| téléphoner | téléphoner à qqn | *Tu leur téléphones ce soir ?* |
| répondre | répondre à qqn | *Elle ne me répond pas.* |
| écrire, envoyer | écrire / envoyer qqch à qqn | *Je t'envoie une photo.* |
| donner, offrir, prêter, rendre | donner qqch à qqn | *On lui offre un bijou.* |
| dire, demander | dire / demander qqch à qqn | *Je vais lui demander son adresse.* |
| montrer | montrer qqch à qqn | *Montre-moi tes photos !* |
| conseiller, promettre | conseiller / promettre qqch à qqn | *Je te promets une surprise.* |
| sourire, plaire | sourire / plaire à qqn | *Le bébé nous sourit.* |

(*qqn* = *quelqu'un*, someone; *qqch* = *quelque chose*, something. Dictionaries use these
abbreviations.)

A few verbs to note:

- *Offrir* is to give as a present (also to offer). It is irregular but easy: it has -er endings
  in the present like *ouvrir* (French A1, lesson 21): *j'offre, tu offres, il offre, nous
  offrons, vous offrez, ils offrent*; participle *offert*. *Donner* is the general verb "to give".
- *Rendre* is to give back: *Je te rends ton livre demain.* It is a regular -re verb like
  *vendre*. *Prêter* (to lend) and *rendre* go together.
- *Promettre* is conjugated like *mettre*: *je promets, nous promettons*; participle *promis*. *Une
  promesse* is a promise.
- *Demander* is to ask (for): *Il me demande l'heure.* (He asks me the time.) It is not "to demand".
- *Conseiller* is to advise; *un conseil* is a piece of advice: *Je peux te donner un conseil ?*
- *Sourire* (to smile) is irregular: *je souris, tu souris, il sourit, nous sourions, vous
  souriez, ils sourient*; participle *souri*. *Le sourire* is a smile.
- *Remercier* (to thank) is a trap: it takes a direct object, with no *à*. *Je remercie Marie → Je la
  remercie.* (But *dire merci à* takes *à*: *Je lui dis merci*.)

## Direct or indirect?

Ask whether the verb puts *à* before the person. English is no help: "I'm calling her" and "I'm
phoning her" look alike, but in French one verb is direct and the other indirect.

| direct: le, la, les | indirect: lui, leur |
|---|---|
| appeler qqn: *Je l'appelle.* | téléphoner à qqn: *Je lui téléphone.* |
| aider qqn: *Je l'aide.* | répondre à qqn: *Je lui réponds.* |
| attendre qqn: *Je les attends.* | parler à qqn: *Je leur parle.* |
| remercier qqn: *Je la remercie.* | dire merci à qqn: *Je lui dis merci.* |
| inviter qqn: *Je les invite.* | écrire à qqn: *Je leur écris.* |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Direct or indirect object pronoun?
  accDescr: Start with the person you want to replace. If it is me, you, us or you plural, use me, te, nous or vous: they are the same in both sets. Otherwise ask whether the verb puts à before the person. If not, as in appeler Marie, use le, la or les: je l'appelle. If yes, as in téléphoner à Marie, use lui for one person or leur for several: je lui téléphone.
  A["Which person?"] -- "me, you, us, you all" --> B["me, te, nous, vous (same in both sets)"]
  A -- "him, her, them" --> C{"Does the verb put à before the person?"}
  C -- "no: appeler Marie" --> D["le, la, les: je l'appelle"]
  C -- "yes: téléphoner à Marie" --> E["lui (one), leur (several): je lui téléphone"]
```

*Lui* and *leur* are for people (and animals). For *à* + a thing or place, French uses *y*:
that is lesson 7.

## Where the pronoun goes

Exactly where the direct pronouns go (lesson 5):

- Before the verb: *Je lui écris.* Negative: *Je ne lui écris pas.*
- Before an infinitive: *Je vais leur téléphoner.* *Tu peux me répondre ?*
- After an affirmative command, with a hyphen: *Téléphone-lui ! Écris-leur ! Réponds-moi !
  Dites-moi !*
- Before a negative command: *Ne lui dis rien ! Ne leur réponds pas.*

## Penser à: a stressed pronoun instead

A few verbs with *à* don't take *lui* or *leur* for people. The two you need are *penser à* (to
think about) and *s'intéresser à* (to be interested in). With them you keep *à* and use a
stressed pronoun (*moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles*, French A1):

- *Je pense à toi.* — I'm thinking of you.
- *Il pense souvent à elle.* — He often thinks about her.
- *Elle s'intéresse à lui.* — She's interested in him.

Not ~~Je lui pense~~. *Penser* without *à* means "to think" in general: *Je pense que c'est une
bonne idée.*

## Plaire: the verb that works backwards

*Plaire à* means "to please", and French uses it where English says "to like". The thing you
like is the subject, and the person who likes it is the indirect object:

- *Ce film me plaît.* — I like this film. (literally: this film pleases me)
- *Ces chaussures lui plaisent ?* — Does he / she like these shoes?
- *Ça te plaît ?* — Do you like it?
- *Tu me plais.* — I like you, I find you attractive. (between two people, it is about
  attraction)

| plaire | |
|---|---|
| je plais | nous plaisons |
| tu plais | vous plaisez |
| il / elle plaît | ils / elles plaisent |
| participle: plu | |

*Il plaît* has a circumflex on the *i* (the 1990 spelling *plait* is also correct). *Ça me plaît*
is a set phrase worth learning whole. In the passé composé, just to recognise for now: *Le film
t'a plu ?* — Did you like the film?

## On the phone

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *le portable* | mobile phone, cell phone |
| *décrocher* | to pick up (answer) |
| *raccrocher* | to hang up |
| *C'est occupé.* | It's engaged / busy. (*Je suis occupé* = I'm busy.) |
| *le répondeur* | voicemail, answering machine |
| *laisser un message* | to leave a message |
| *rappeler qqn* | to call someone back |

*Rappeler* is *appeler* + *re-*, with the same spelling change: *je rappelle, tu rappelles, il
rappelle, nous rappelons, vous rappelez, ils rappellent*. It takes a direct object: *Je te
rappelle* (I'll call you back), *Rappelle-moi !*, *Je la rappelle ce soir.*

*Laisser* means to leave (something somewhere) and also to let: *Laisse-moi un message* (leave
me a message), *Laisse-moi parler !* (let me speak!).

![Two mobile phone screens side by side. Left: an incoming call from Maman, with a red button labelled raccrocher (hang up) and a green button labelled décrocher (pick up). Right: the screen after the call was missed: "Appels manqués: Maman (2)", a green button "Rappeler" (call back), and a voicemail notice "1 nouveau message" with the voicemail symbol, labelled le répondeur.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: a present for Mum

Lucas and his sister Chloé are planning a birthday present.

> Chloé : C'est l'anniversaire de maman samedi. Qu'est-ce qu'on lui offre ?
>
> Lucas : Un parfum ? Elle adore ça.
>
> Chloé : On lui a offert un parfum l'année dernière. Moi, je préfère un bijou. Une jolie bague, par exemple.
>
> Lucas : Bonne idée. Et on peut demander à papa de nous aider.
>
> Chloé : Je lui téléphone tout de suite… Ça sonne. Il ne décroche pas.
>
> Lucas : Laisse-lui un message.
>
> Chloé : « Papa, c'est Chloé. Rappelle-moi, s'il te plaît, c'est pour la surprise de maman. Et ne
> lui dis rien ! »
>
> Lucas : Tu crois que la bague va lui plaire ?
>
> Chloé : J'en suis sûre. Et je te promets une chose : cette fois, je ne lui dis rien avant samedi !

Translation:

> Chloé: It's Mum's birthday on Saturday. What shall we give her?
>
> Lucas: Perfume? She loves that.
>
> Chloé: We gave her perfume last year. I'd prefer a piece of jewellery. A nice ring, for example.
>
> Lucas: Good idea. And we can ask Dad to help us.
>
> Chloé: I'll phone him straight away… It's ringing. He's not picking up.
>
> Lucas: Leave him a message.
>
> Chloé: "Dad, it's Chloé. Call me back, please, it's about Mum's surprise. And don't tell her
> anything!"
>
> Lucas: Do you think she'll like the ring?
>
> Chloé: I'm sure. And I promise you one thing: this time I won't tell her anything before Saturday!

Notes: *Qu'est-ce qu'on lui offre ?* (What shall we give her?) is the usual way to discuss a
present. *On lui a offert* puts the pronoun before the auxiliary in the passé composé; lesson 8
explains it. *Demander à quelqu'un de faire quelque chose* is "to ask someone to do something".
*Ne lui dis rien* is "don't tell her anything". *Une bague* is a ring. *J'en suis sûre* (I'm sure
of it) uses *en*, which is lesson 7.

## Pronunciation

- *Lui* is one syllable, [lɥi]: the *u* glides quickly into *i*, like the *u* of *huit*. Not
  "loo-ee".
- *Leur* sounds like *l'heure* [lœʁ]. *Leur* and *leurs* sound the same, except that the *s* of
  the possessive links to a vowel (*leurs_enfants*). The pronoun never links with an *s*: *Je
  leur ai dit*.
- *Plaît* rhymes with *lait* [plɛ]; *plu* is [ply].
- *Sourire* has two r's: [suʁiʁ]. *Il sourit* drops the second one: [suʁi].

## Common mistakes

- *Lui* with a direct verb. Not ~~Je lui appelle~~ but *Je l'appelle*; not ~~Je lui remercie~~
  but *Je le / la remercie*.
- *Le, la* with an indirect verb. Not ~~Je la téléphone~~ but *Je lui téléphone*; not ~~Je les
  réponds~~ but *Je leur réponds*.
- An *s* on the pronoun. Not ~~Je leurs écris~~ but *Je leur écris*.
- *Lui* with *penser à*. Not ~~Je lui pense~~ but *Je pense à lui / à elle*.
- *Plaire* the English way round. Not ~~Je plais ce film~~ but *Ce film me plaît*.
- *Me* in an affirmative command. Not ~~Téléphone-me~~ but *Téléphone-moi !*

## Key points

- Indirect object = *à* + person. Pronouns: *me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur*.
- *Lui* = to him or to her; *leur* = to them, never with *-s*.
- Verbs with *à* + person: *parler, téléphoner, répondre, écrire, envoyer, donner, offrir,
  prêter, rendre, dire, demander, montrer, conseiller, promettre, sourire, plaire*.
- Direct, not indirect: *appeler, aider, attendre, remercier, inviter, rappeler*.
- Same positions as lesson 5: *Je lui téléphone. Je vais lui téléphoner. Téléphone-lui !*
- *Penser à, s'intéresser à* + stressed pronoun: *Je pense à elle.*
- *Ça me plaît* = I like it: the thing is the subject.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson. The verb *donner* (to give) is added here too: it is in no earlier word list.

lessons.title: Y and en
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 5 and 6 replaced people: *Je la connais, je lui téléphone.* Two more pronouns replace
things and places, and they are among the most frequent words in spoken French: **[[y]]** and **[[en]]**.
You have heard them for a long time in fixed phrases (*il y a, on y va*). This
lesson shows how they work, so you can use them in any sentence. The theme is cooking: recipes,
ingredients and quantities, where *en* is everywhere.

Good news first: *y* and *en* never change. They have no masculine or feminine, no singular or
plural.

## Y: there, and à + a thing

*Y* replaces a place you have just mentioned. In English it is usually "there":

- *Tu vas à Lyon ? — Oui, j'y vais demain.* — Are you going to Lyon? — Yes, I'm going there
  tomorrow.
- *Elle habite en Bretagne ? — Oui, elle y habite depuis dix ans.*
- *Les clés sont dans le tiroir ? — Oui, elles y sont.* — Are the keys in the drawer? — Yes,
  they're in there.
- *Tu es chez toi ce soir ? — Non, je n'y suis pas.* — Are you at home tonight? — No, I won't
  be.

So *y* stands for *à* + a place, but also for a place after *en, dans, chez, sur, sous* and the
like.

With *aller*, French needs the *y* even where English can stop: "Are you going to the market?
— Yes, I'm going." is *Oui, j'y vais*, never just ~~Oui, je vais~~.

*Y* also replaces *à* + a thing (an idea, an object, an activity) after verbs that take *à*:

- *Tu penses à ton examen ? — Oui, j'y pense tout le temps.* — I think about it all the time.
- *Tu joues au tennis ? — Oui, j'y joue le samedi.*
- *Il s'intéresse à la cuisine ? — Oui, il s'y intéresse beaucoup.*
- *Tu réponds à ce message ? — Oui, j'y réponds tout de suite.*

### Y is not for people

For *à* + a person, use *lui, leur* (lesson 6), or a stressed pronoun after *penser à* and
*s'intéresser à*. (In casual speech you will sometimes hear *j'y pense* about a person, but
careful French avoids it, and so should you.)

| à + thing → y | à + person → lui, leur or à + stressed pronoun |
|---|---|
| *Je réponds à la lettre. → J'y réponds.* | *Je réponds à Paul. → Je lui réponds.* |
| *Je pense à mon voyage. → J'y pense.* | *Je pense à ma mère. → Je pense à elle.* |

### Y in set phrases

- *Il y a* (there is, there are): *Il y a du pain ?*
- *On y va !* — Let's go! / Here we go!
- *Vas-y ! Allez-y !* — Go on! Go ahead! You say it to encourage someone, or to let them go
  first. *Va* gets its *s* back before *y*: *vas-y*, never ~~va-y~~.
- *Ça y est !* — That's it! Done! (something is finished or has finally happened)

## En: some, of it, of them

*En* replaces a noun introduced by *de*, in its different forms.

### 1. The partitive and des

The **[[partitive]]** is *du, de la, de l'* before a noun you can't count (*du pain, de la farine*:
"some" bread, "some" flour), as in French A1, lesson 9. *Des* is the plural (*des œufs*: some
eggs). *En* replaces the article and the noun together:

- *Tu veux du café ? — Oui, j'en veux bien.* — Do you want some coffee? — Yes, I'd like some.
- *Il y a de la crème ? — Oui, il y en a.* — Is there any cream? — Yes, there is (some).
- *Tu achètes des fraises ? — Non, je n'en achète pas.* — No, I'm not buying any.

English can often leave the pronoun out ("Yes, I'd like some", "Yes, there is"), but French
can't: the verb needs *en*.

### 2. A number or a quantity

When the noun follows a number or a quantity word, *en* replaces the noun and the number or
quantity stays, after the verb:

- *Tu as combien d'œufs ? — J'en ai six.* — I've got six (of them).
- *Il faut beaucoup de farine ? — Il en faut deux cents grammes.* — You need two hundred grams.
- *Tu as une voiture ? — Oui, j'en ai une.* — Yes, I've got one.
- *Il reste du gâteau ? — Oui, il en reste la moitié.* — Yes, there's half of it left.
- *Tu veux combien de tranches de pain ? — J'en veux deux.*

The negative of *J'en ai un / une* is just *Je n'en ai pas* (I haven't got one): *Tu as une
voiture ? — Non, je n'en ai pas.*

### 3. De + a thing or a place

*En* also replaces *de* + a thing after verbs and phrases with *de*, and *de* + a place with
*venir de, revenir de, sortir de*:

- *Tu parles de ton projet ? — Oui, j'en parle demain.* — Yes, I'm talking about it tomorrow.
- *Tu as besoin de sel ? — Non, je n'en ai pas besoin.* — No, I don't need any (it).
- *Tu viens de la boulangerie ? — Oui, j'en viens.* — Yes, I've just come from there.

(*Avoir besoin de*, "to need", is a lesson 14 phrase; you can use it already.) Careful: *venir
de* + infinitive (lesson 4) means "to have just done": *Je viens de manger.* That *de* is not
replaced by *en*.

### Il y a → il y en a

*Il y a* + *en* gives a phrase you will use every day:

- *Il y a des œufs ? — Oui, il y en a.* — Are there any eggs? — Yes, there are (some).
- *Il y a combien de personnes ? — Il y en a douze.* — There are twelve.
- *Il n'y en a plus.* — There isn't any left. (*ne … plus*, no more: lesson 17)
- *Il n'y en a pas.* — There isn't any. / There aren't any.

![A chart of what y and en replace. On the left, y replaces "à + a place" (Tu vas à Lyon ? J'y vais.), "a place with en, dans, chez, sur" (Elle est chez elle ? Elle y est.) and "à + a thing" (Tu penses à ton examen ? J'y pense.). On the right, en replaces "du, de la, des + noun" (Tu veux du pain ? J'en veux.), "a number or quantity + noun, keeping the number" (Tu as des œufs ? J'en ai six.) and "de + a thing or place" (Tu viens de la gare ? J'en viens.). A note at the bottom: for people, use lui, leur or a stressed pronoun.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Where y and en go

The same four rules as the other pronouns (lesson 5):

| sentence | y | en |
|---|---|---|
| one verb | *J'y vais.* | *J'en prends.* |
| negative | *Je n'y vais pas.* | *Je n'en prends pas.* |
| verb + infinitive | *Je vais y aller.* | *Je vais en prendre.* |
| affirmative command | *Vas-y !* | *Prends-en !* |
| negative command | *N'y va pas !* | *N'en prends pas !* |

In the negative, *ne* becomes *n'* before *y* and *en*, which start with a vowel sound: *Je n'y
vais pas. Je n'en veux pas.*

In an affirmative command, a *tu* form that ends in a vowel (all -er verbs, *aller*, *offrir*)
gets its *s* back before *y* and *en*, so that the two vowels link with a z sound: *Manges-en !* (Eat some!), *Achètes-en
deux.* (Buy two.), *Penses-y !* (Think about it!), *Vas-y !* Without *y* or *en* there is no *s*:
*Mange ! Achète du pain. Va au marché !*

## In the kitchen: recipes and quantities

French recipes give instructions in the *vous* imperative (*Coupez les carottes*) or in the
infinitive (*Couper les carottes*). Here is an original recipe card:

![A recipe card titled "Soupe de carottes au citron, pour 4 personnes". Ingredients: 600 g de carottes, 1 oignon, 1 gousse d'ail, 2 cuillères à soupe d'huile, 1 litre d'eau, 10 cl de crème, le jus d'un demi-citron, sel, poivre. Steps: 1. Coupez les carottes en tranches et l'oignon en morceaux. 2. Faites cuire l'oignon et l'ail dans l'huile, 5 minutes. 3. Ajoutez les carottes et l'eau. Faites cuire 25 minutes. 4. Mixez, puis ajoutez la crème et le jus de citron. 5. Salez, poivrez et mélangez.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(*Une gousse d'ail* is a clove of garlic, *une cuillère à soupe* a tablespoon; *mixez* means
"blend", and *salez, poivrez* "add salt, add pepper".) Words for the steps:

- *couper* — to cut: *Coupez le pain en tranches.* (*Une tranche*: a slice.)
- *ajouter* — to add: *Ajoutez du sel.* *J'en ajoute un peu ?* (Shall I add a bit?)
- *verser* — to pour: *Versez la soupe dans les bols.*
- *mélanger* — to mix, to stir: *Mélangez bien.* Like *manger*, it keeps an *e* before *o*: *nous
  mélangeons*.
- *cuire* — to cook (what food does): *Le riz cuit vingt minutes.* (The rice cooks for twenty
  minutes.) To say what the cook does, French usually says *faire cuire*: *Je fais cuire le
  riz.* *Cuisiner* (lesson 4) is to cook in general, to make meals: *J'aime cuisiner.*

| cuire | |
|---|---|
| je cuis | nous cuisons |
| tu cuis | vous cuisez |
| il / elle cuit | ils / elles cuisent |
| participle: cuit | |

*Cuit* is also an adjective: *bien cuit* (well done), *pas assez cuit* (undercooked).

*La moitié* (half) is a noun, so it takes *de*: *la moitié du gâteau, la moitié des invités.*
*Demi* is used in compounds and after a number: *un demi-citron* (half a lemon), *une heure et
demie*.

![A kitchen counter with labelled things: a saucepan on the hob (la casserole), a frying pan beside it (la poêle), a bag of flour (la farine), a bottle of oil (l'huile), a salt cellar (le sel), a lemon (le citron), an onion (l'oignon) and a head of garlic (l'ail).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: crêpes on Sunday

Emma and her flatmate Yanis want to make crêpes.

> Emma : On fait des crêpes ? J'ai une recette de ma grand-mère.
>
> Yanis : Bonne idée ! Il faut quoi ?
>
> Emma : De la farine, des œufs, du lait, du sucre et un peu d'huile. Tu as de la farine ?
>
> Yanis : Oui, j'en ai, mais pas beaucoup. Il en faut combien ?
>
> Emma : Deux cent cinquante grammes.
>
> Yanis : Ça va, il y en a assez. Des œufs, on en a quatre. Et du lait… il n'y en a pas.
>
> Emma : Je vais au supermarché, alors. Tu veux des fraises pour les crêpes ?
>
> Yanis : Oui, prends-en une barquette. Et du citron, pour moi.
>
> Emma : D'accord. J'y vais tout de suite.
>
> Yanis : Vas-y. Pendant ce temps, je mélange la farine et les œufs.

Translation:

> Emma: Shall we make crêpes? I've got a recipe from my grandmother.
>
> Yanis: Good idea! What do we need?
>
> Emma: Flour, eggs, milk, sugar and a bit of oil. Have you got any flour?
>
> Yanis: Yes, I have, but not much. How much do we need?
>
> Emma: Two hundred and fifty grams.
>
> Yanis: That's fine, there's enough. Eggs, we've got four. And milk… there isn't any.
>
> Emma: I'll go to the supermarket, then. Do you want strawberries for the crêpes?
>
> Yanis: Yes, get a punnet. And some lemon, for me.
>
> Emma: OK. I'll go right away.
>
> Yanis: Go on. Meanwhile I'll mix the flour and the eggs.

Notes: *Il faut quoi ?* is the casual way to ask "What do we need?". *Il en faut combien ?* — How
much (of it) do we need? *Une barquette* is the little tray that strawberries are sold in. *Pendant
ce temps* is "meanwhile".

## Pronunciation

- *En* links to a following vowel with an n sound: *j'en_ai* [ʒɑ̃ ne], *il y en_a* [il jɑ̃ na],
  often just [jɑ̃ na] in speech. *Prends-en* links with a z: [pʁɑ̃ zɑ̃]. *Vas-y* is [va zi].
- *Y* is just the sound [i]: *j'y vais* [ʒi vɛ].
- *La poêle* (frying pan) is said [pwal], exactly like *le poil* (hair): the *ê* is not
  pronounced as a separate vowel.
- *L'oignon* is [ɔɲɔ̃]: the *i* is silent. That is why the 1990 spelling *ognon* exists.
- *L'ail* is [aj], like "eye".

## Common mistakes

- Dropping the number. "I've got two" is *J'en ai deux*, with both *en* and the number, not
  ~~J'ai deux~~ or ~~J'en ai~~.
- Keeping *de* with *en*. Not ~~J'en ai deux d'œufs~~ but *J'en ai deux*.
- Using *y* for a person. For your mother, say *Je pense à elle*, not *J'y pense* (heard in casual
  speech, but avoided in careful French).
- Saying the noun twice. Not ~~J'y vais à Lyon~~ but *J'y vais* or *Je vais à Lyon*.
- Order in *il y en a*. Not ~~Il y a en~~ or ~~Il en y a~~ but *Il y en a*.
- *Va-y*. The command is *Vas-y !*
- Using *cuire* for "I cook dinner". Say *Je fais à manger* or *Je cuisine*; *cuire* is what the
  food does, or *faire cuire*.

## Key points

- *Y* replaces *à* + a thing, and a place (*à, en, dans, chez…* + place): *J'y vais. J'y pense.*
  Not for people in careful French.
- *En* replaces *du, de la, des* + noun, *de* + a thing or place, and a noun after a number or
  quantity, which stays: *J'en veux. J'en ai deux. Il en faut beaucoup.*
- *Il y a* → *il y en a*, *il n'y en a pas*.
- Same positions as the other pronouns: *Je n'y vais pas. Je vais en prendre. Prends-en !*
- Commands: *Vas-y ! Manges-en ! Penses-y !* (the *s* comes back before *y* and *en*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Pronouns in the past and with two verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You now have every object pronoun: *me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les* (lesson 5), *lui, leur*
(lesson 6), *y* and *en* (lesson 7). So far you have used them with one verb in the present, with
an infinitive and in commands. This lesson puts them into the passé composé, the tense you need
to say what happened: *I lost it, I found it, I told him*. It also covers the one real spelling
trap of this module, the agreement of the past participle. The theme is losing things, finding
them and getting them repaired.

## The pronoun goes before avoir or être

In the passé composé the conjugated verb is the auxiliary (*avoir* or *être*), so the pronoun goes
before the auxiliary, not before the participle:

- *Tu as vu le film ? — Oui, je l'ai vu.* — Yes, I've seen it.
- *Tu as parlé à Paul ? — Oui, je lui ai parlé hier.* — Yes, I spoke to him yesterday.
- *Vous êtes allés à Nice ? — Oui, nous y sommes allés en mai.* — Yes, we went there in May.
- *Tu as acheté du pain ? — Oui, j'en ai acheté.* — Yes, I bought some.
- *Mes parents m'ont téléphoné.* — My parents phoned me.

*Le* and *la* become *l'* before *ai, as, a, avons, avez, ont* (all start with a vowel): *je l'ai, tu
l'as, il l'a, ils l'ont*. *Les* stays *les*, with a z sound: *je les_ai, ils les_ont*.

### Negatives and questions

In the negative, *ne* comes before the pronoun and *pas* after the auxiliary. The participle comes
last, as in French A1:

- *Je ne l'ai pas vu.* — I didn't see it / him.
- *Je ne lui ai pas parlé.* — I didn't speak to him / her.
- *Nous n'y sommes pas allés.* — We didn't go (there).
- *Je n'en ai pas acheté.* — I didn't buy any.

Think of the pronoun and the auxiliary as one block that *ne … pas* wraps around.

![The sentence "Je ne l'ai pas vu." split into six word boxes: Je, ne, l', ai, pas, vu. A bracket over ne … pas and a dashed frame around l' and ai show that ne … pas wraps the pronoun and the auxiliary together, and the participle vu comes last. Labels under the boxes name the parts: subject, object pronoun, auxiliary (avoir), past participle.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In questions, the pronoun stays in front of the auxiliary:

- *Tu l'as trouvé ?* / *Est-ce que tu l'as trouvé ?* — Did you find it?
- *L'as-tu trouvé ?* — the same, with inversion (careful or written French).
- *Tu lui as répondu ?* — Did you answer him / her?

## Two verbs: the pronoun goes with the infinitive

When a conjugated verb is followed by an infinitive (*aller, pouvoir, vouloir, devoir* +
infinitive), the pronoun goes before the infinitive, as in lesson 5. That stays true when the
first verb is in the passé composé:

- *Je peux le faire.* — I can do it.
- *Je vais lui téléphoner.* — I'm going to phone him / her.
- *Tu dois y aller.* — You must go (there).
- *Je veux en acheter deux.* — I want to buy two.
- *Je n'ai pas pu le réparer.* — I couldn't repair it.
- *J'ai voulu lui parler.* — I wanted to talk to him.

(Again, *faire* + infinitive is different: *Je l'ai fait réparer*, I had it repaired, has the
pronoun before the auxiliary. That pattern is for later.)

So compare:

| one verb in the passé composé | conjugated verb + infinitive |
|---|---|
| *Je l'ai fait.* — I did it. | *Je vais le faire.* — I'm going to do it. |
| *Je lui ai écrit.* — I wrote to her. | *Je dois lui écrire.* — I have to write to her. |
| *J'y suis allé.* — I went there. | *Je veux y aller.* — I want to go there. |

Ask: which verb is the pronoun the object of? In *Je vais le faire*, you are going to *do it*,
so *le* goes with *faire*.

## Past participle agreement with avoir

French A1 taught that with *être* the participle agrees with the subject (*elle est partie*),
and that with *avoir* it does not (*elle a mangé*). There is one exception to the second rule,
and it comes with pronouns.

**[[Past participle agreement]]** with *avoir*: the participle agrees with the direct object when
that object comes before the verb. A direct object pronoun (*me, te, le, la, l', nous, vous,
les*) always comes before, so it is a **[[preceding direct object]]**, and the participle takes *-e*
for feminine and *-s* for plural, like an adjective:

- *J'ai perdu la clé.* — the object comes after: no agreement.
- *La clé ? Je l'ai perdue.* — *l'* = *la clé*, feminine, before the verb: *perdue*.
- *Les photos ? Je les ai mises sur le site.* — *les* = *les photos*, feminine plural: *mises*.
- *Mes papiers ? Je les ai retrouvés.* — masculine plural: *retrouvés*.
- *Le portefeuille ? Je l'ai rapporté.* — masculine singular: no change.

With *me, te, nous, vous* the participle agrees with the person they mean:

- *Marie, je t'ai vue au marché !* — Marie, I saw you at the market! (*t'* = Marie)
- *Nos amis nous ont invités.* — Our friends invited us. (*invitées* if "we" are all women)

![The two sentences "J'ai perdu la clé." and "La clé ? Je l'ai perdue." In the second one an arrow goes from "La clé" to the pronoun l' and on to the participle perdue, whose final e is highlighted: the object came first, so the participle agrees. Below, "Les photos ? Je les ai mises sur le site." with an arrow from les photos to les and to mises, its es highlighted.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### No agreement with lui, leur, en and y

Only a direct object counts. *Lui* and *leur* are indirect, and *en* and *y* are not direct
objects either, so the participle doesn't change:

- *Ma sœur ? Je lui ai parlé.* — not ~~parlée~~.
- *Mes voisins ? Je leur ai téléphoné.* — not ~~téléphonés~~.
- *Des pommes ? J'en ai acheté.* — not ~~achetées~~ (that is the usual rule; you may see agreement
  with *en* in older books).
- *La France ? J'y ai habité.* — not ~~habitée~~.

### A note on verbs with se

Lesson 2 showed *Elle s'est blessée* but *Elle s'est cassé la jambe*. The same idea explains
it. In *Elle s'est blessée* (she hurt herself), *se* is the direct object, it comes before the
verb, so the participle agrees. In *Elle s'est cassé la jambe* (she broke her leg), the direct
object is *la jambe*, which comes after the verb, so there is no agreement. Most verbs with *se*
simply agree with the subject (*elle s'est levée*); the honors lesson 8h2 looks at the
exceptions with reciprocal verbs (*ils se sont parlé*).

### Can you hear it?

Most of the time, no: *perdu, perdue, perdus, perdues* all sound the same, so the agreement only
shows in writing. You hear it only when the masculine participle ends in a silent consonant, which is then
spoken in the feminine:

| masculine | feminine | example |
|---|---|---|
| mis [mi] | mise [miz] | *La table ? Je l'ai mise.* |
| pris [pʁi] | prise [pʁiz] | *Ta voiture ? Je l'ai prise.* |
| fait [fɛ] | faite [fɛt] | *La vaisselle ? Je l'ai faite.* |
| ouvert [uvɛʁ] | ouverte [uvɛʁt] | *La porte ? Je l'ai ouverte.* |
| écrit [ekʁi] | écrite [ekʁit] | *La lettre ? Je l'ai écrite.* |

Others follow the same pattern: *dit → dite, offert → offerte, promis → promise, cuit → cuite*.
In relaxed speech you will sometimes hear the masculine (*la porte, je l'ai ouvert*), but write
the agreement and say it when you speak carefully. Agreement after the relative *que* (*les
photos que j'ai prises*) is lesson 10.

## Lost, found and repaired

Some useful words for when things go wrong:

- *perdre, retrouver* — to lose, to find again: *J'ai perdu mes écouteurs. Je les ai retrouvés
  sous le lit.* *Trouver* (French A1) is to find; *retrouver* (to find again) stresses that you had lost
  it. For lost things both are common: *J'ai trouvé / retrouvé mes clés.*
- *rapporter* — to bring back, to return (an item): *Un passager a rapporté mon portefeuille.*
- *déclarer la perte ou le vol* — to report the loss or the theft: *J'ai déclaré le vol à la
  police.* *Le vol* means theft (from *voler*, to steal) and also a flight.
- *les objets trouvés* — lost property: *Je suis allé aux objets trouvés.*
- *mes papiers* — my identity documents: *la carte d'identité, le passeport, le permis (de
  conduire)*. In this sense *les papiers* is always plural.
- *le portefeuille* — wallet (for cards and notes); *le porte-monnaie* — purse (for coins).
- *cassé* (broken), *abîmé* (damaged): *L'écran est cassé. Le sac est un peu abîmé.*
- *réparer, la réparation* — to repair, a repair. *Fonctionner* (to work, for a machine): *Ma
  montre ne fonctionne pas.* In everyday speech *marcher* (French A1) means the same: *Ça ne
  marche pas.*
- *le reçu, la facture, la garantie* — receipt, invoice or bill, guarantee: *Elle est encore sous
  garantie.*
- *récupérer* — to get back, to collect: *Vous pouvez la récupérer jeudi.* It changes *é → è* like
  *préférer*: *je récupère, nous récupérons*.
- *remarquer* — to notice: *Je n'ai rien remarqué.*
- *tout de suite* — straight away.

![A lost-property office under the sign "Objets trouvés". On the shelf: a passport (le passeport), a bunch of keys (les clés) and earbuds in their case (les écouteurs). On the counter: a wallet (le portefeuille), a coin purse (le porte-monnaie) and a watch (la montre).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: at the lost-property office

Thomas lost his wallet on the tram.

> Thomas : Bonjour. J'ai perdu mon portefeuille hier soir, dans le tram de la ligne 2.
>
> L'agent : Vous avez déjà déclaré la perte ?
>
> Thomas : Non, pas encore. Je l'ai cherché partout, et ce matin je suis venu directement ici.
>
> L'agent : Il est comment ?
>
> Thomas : Noir, en cuir, un peu abîmé. Il y a mes papiers dedans : ma carte d'identité et mon
> permis.
>
> L'agent : Attendez… Oui ! Une dame l'a rapporté hier à vingt-deux heures. Vous pouvez me
> montrer une pièce d'identité ?
>
> Thomas : Euh… ma carte d'identité est dans le portefeuille ! Mais j'ai mon passeport.
>
> L'agent : Parfait. Voilà votre portefeuille. Vérifiez tout de suite qu'il ne manque rien.
>
> Thomas : Les cartes… l'argent… Tout est là. La dame, vous lui avez parlé ? Je voudrais la
> remercier.
>
> L'agent : Non, désolé, elle n'a pas laissé son nom.

Translation:

> Thomas: Hello. I lost my wallet last night on the number 2 tram.
>
> Officer: Have you already reported the loss?
>
> Thomas: No, not yet. I looked for it everywhere, and this morning I came straight here.
>
> Officer: What does it look like?
>
> Thomas: Black, leather, a bit worn. My papers are in it: my identity card and my driving
> licence.
>
> Officer: Wait… Yes! A lady brought it in yesterday at ten p.m. Can you show me some ID?
>
> Thomas: Er… my identity card is in the wallet! But I've got my passport.
>
> Officer: Perfect. Here's your wallet. Check straight away that nothing is missing.
>
> Thomas: The cards… the money… It's all there. The lady, did you speak to her? I'd like to thank
> her.
>
> Officer: No, sorry, she didn't leave her name.

Notes: *Le tram* is the tram (streetcar). *Il est comment ?* asks what something looks like;
*dedans* means "inside (it)". *Il ne manque rien* is "nothing is missing". *Une pièce d'identité*
is any document that proves who you are (it is a lesson 19 word). Look at the pronouns: *Je l'ai
cherché, Une dame l'a rapporté*: *l'* is *le portefeuille*, masculine, so
there is no agreement. *Vous lui avez parlé* has *lui*: no agreement either. *Je voudrais la
remercier*: *remercier* takes a direct object (lesson 6), and the pronoun goes before the
infinitive.

## Pronunciation

- *Je l'ai* [ʒə le] and *je les ai* [ʒə le ze]: only the z of the liaison tells you it's plural.
- *Je l'ai mise* [ʒə le miz] — the z sound is the agreement. *Je l'ai mis* [ʒə le mi] is about a
  masculine thing.
- *Portefeuille* ends in the sound of *feuille* [pɔʁtəfœj]. *Porte-monnaie* is [pɔʁtmɔnɛ].
- *Le reçu* is [ʁəsy]: the cedilla makes the *c* an s sound before *u*.

## Common mistakes

- The pronoun before the participle. Not ~~J'ai le vu~~ but *Je l'ai vu*.
- *Pas* in the wrong place. Not ~~Je n'ai le pas vu~~ or ~~Je ne l'ai vu pas~~ but *Je ne l'ai pas
  vu*.
- The pronoun before the wrong verb. Not ~~Je le vais faire~~ but *Je vais le faire*.
- Agreeing with *lui* or *en*. Not ~~Je lui ai parlée~~ but *Je lui ai parlé*.
- Agreeing when the object comes after. Not ~~J'ai perdue la clé~~ but *J'ai perdu la clé*.
- Agreeing with the subject after *avoir*. Not ~~Elle a mangée~~ but *Elle a mangé*.
- In speech you will hear *Je l'ai pas vu*, with no *ne*. That is everyday spoken French; write
  *Je ne l'ai pas vu*.

## Key points

- Passé composé: the pronoun goes before *avoir / être*: *Je l'ai vu. Je lui ai parlé. J'y suis
  allé. J'en ai acheté.*
- Negative: *ne* + pronoun + auxiliary + *pas* + participle: *Je ne l'ai pas vu.*
- With a second verb, the pronoun goes before the infinitive: *Je vais le faire. Je n'ai pas pu
  le réparer.*
- With *avoir*, the participle agrees with a direct object that comes before it: *La clé ? Je l'ai
  perdue. Les photos ? Je les ai mises sur le site.*
- No agreement with *lui, leur, en, y*, and none when the object comes after the verb.
- You hear the agreement only in a few participles: *mise, prise, faite, ouverte, écrite*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: two pronouns at once
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lessons 5 to 8 each sentence had one object pronoun: *Je le donne. Je lui donne le livre.* But
real conversations often replace both objects at once. "Can you lend me your bike? — Yes, I'll
lend it to you." French does this too: *Oui, je te le prête.* Two pronouns sit side by side
before the verb, in a fixed order.

This lesson shows that order, how it works in the passé composé and with an infinitive, the
different order in affirmative commands, and what people really say in casual speech. It is at
the upper edge of A2: you will understand it much more often than you need to produce it, so
don't worry if it takes time. The setting is a flatshare, *une colocation*, where people are
always lending each other things.

## The order before the verb

When two object pronouns come before the verb, they always follow this **[[pronoun order]]**:

| 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| me, te, se, nous, vous | le, la, les | lui, leur | y | en |

Read the table from left to right, and take the two pronouns in the order of their columns:

- *Paul me prête son vélo. → Il me le prête.* — He lends it to me. (column 1, then 2)
- *Je donne les clés à Inès. → Je les lui donne.* — I give them to her. (2, then 3)
- *Je montre la photo à mes parents. → Je la leur montre.* — I show it to them. (2, then 3)
- *Il y a du café ? → Il y en a.* — There is some. (4, then 5)
- *Tu parles du problème à tes colocataires ? → Tu leur en parles ?* (3, then 5)

![The five columns of the pronoun order: column 1 me, te, se, nous, vous; column 2 le, la, les; column 3 lui, leur; column 4 y; column 5 en. Under them, three example sentences whose pronouns are coloured like their columns: "Il me le prête" (1 and 2), "Je les lui donne" (2 and 3), "Il y en a" (4 and 5). A note: lui and leur come after le, la, les, but me, te, nous, vous come before them.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A memory hook: in the first two columns, the person comes before the thing (*me le, te la, nous
les*). In the third column it is the other way round, the thing before the person (*le lui, la
leur*). So *lui* and *leur* are the odd ones out: they come after *le, la, les*.

Two combinations are not possible: *me, te, nous, vous* never go with *lui* or *leur*. You will
not need those at A2 (French uses *à* + a stressed pronoun instead: *Je te présente à elle*).

### Example 1: lending in the flat

Karim asks his flatmate Julie for her hair dryer. Build Julie's answer step by step.

*Karim : Tu me prêtes ton sèche-cheveux ?*

1. Find the two objects in *Je te prête mon sèche-cheveux*: the thing (*mon sèche-cheveux*,
   direct, masculine: *le*) and the person (*te*, already a pronoun).
2. Find the columns: *te* is column 1, *le* is column 2.
3. Put them before the verb in that order: *Je te le prête.*
4. Add anything around them: *Oui, je te le prête, mais rends-le-moi ce soir !*

Julie's answer: *Oui, je te le prête.* — Yes, I'll lend it to you.

## In the negative, the passé composé and with an infinitive

The pair of pronouns behaves like a single pronoun: it stays together, in the same place.

- Negative: *ne* before the pair, *pas* after the verb: *Je ne te le prête pas.* — I'm not lending
  it to you.
- Passé composé: the pair goes before the auxiliary: *Je le lui ai dit.* — I told him (it). *Il
  me l'a rendu.* — He gave it back to me.
- Negative passé composé: *Je ne le lui ai pas dit.* — I didn't tell him.
- With an infinitive: the pair goes before the infinitive: *Je vais te le montrer.* — I'm going to
  show it to you. *Tu peux me la prêter ?* — Can you lend it to me?

The agreement rule of lesson 8 still applies: the participle agrees with a direct object pronoun
that comes before it, even when another pronoun stands between them:

- *Les clés ? Je te les ai données.* — I gave them to you. (*les* = *les clés*, feminine plural)
- *La perceuse ? Il me l'a rendue hier.* — He gave it back to me yesterday.

### Example 2: who took the corkscrew?

Read the exchange and explain each pronoun pair.

> Julie : Karim, tu as vu le tire-bouchon ?
>
> Karim : Oui, je l'ai prêté à Max hier soir. Il ne te l'a pas rendu ?
>
> Julie : Non ! Et ma perceuse ? Tu la lui as prêtée aussi ?
>
> Karim : Non, ta perceuse, je ne la lui ai pas prêtée. Je l'ai rangée dans le placard.

1. *Je l'ai prêté à Max*: one pronoun, *l'* = *le tire-bouchon* (masculine): no agreement.
2. *Il ne te l'a pas rendu ?*: *te* (column 1) + *l'* (column 2) before *a*; *ne … pas* around the
   block; *rendu* agrees with *le* (masculine), so no change.
3. *Tu la lui as prêtée ?*: *la* (2) + *lui* (3); *la* = *la perceuse*, feminine and before the
   verb, so *prêtée*.
4. *Je ne la lui ai pas prêtée*: the same pair in the negative.
5. *Je l'ai rangée*: *ranger* (to put away, lesson 4); *l'* = *la perceuse*, so *rangée*.

(*Le placard* is a cupboard.)

## Commands: a different order

In an affirmative command the pronouns go after the verb, joined by hyphens, and the order
changes: the direct object comes first, then the person.

| statement | affirmative command |
|---|---|
| *Tu me le donnes.* | *Donne-le-moi !* — Give it to me! |
| *Tu nous les montres.* | *Montre-les-nous !* — Show them to us! |
| *Vous la lui rendez.* | *Rendez-la-lui !* — Give it back to him / her! |
| *Tu leur en achètes.* | *Achète-leur-en !* — Buy them some! |
| *Vous m'en donnez.* | *Donnez-m'en !* — Give me some! |

Rules for affirmative commands:

- Direct object (*le, la, les*) first, then *moi, toi, lui, nous, vous, leur*.
- *En* (and *y*) always come last.
- *Moi* and *toi* become *m'* and *t'* before *en*: *Donnez-m'en. Va-t'en !* (Go away!, a set
  phrase).

Negative commands go back to the normal order, before the verb, with no hyphens: *Ne me le donne
pas ! Ne la lui rendez pas ! Ne m'en donnez pas.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which order for two pronouns?
  accDescr: First ask whether the sentence is an affirmative command. If no, which covers statements, questions and negative commands, put both pronouns before the verb in the order me te se nous vous, then le la les, then lui leur, then y, then en: Je te le donne, Ne me le donne pas. If yes, put them after the verb with hyphens: the direct object le la les first, then moi toi lui nous vous leur, and en last: Donne-le-moi, Donnez-m'en.
  A{"Affirmative command?"} -- "no: statement, question, negative command" --> B["Before the verb: me/te/se/nous/vous, le/la/les, lui/leur, y, en"]
  B --> C["Je te le donne. Ne me le donne pas."]
  A -- "yes" --> D["After the verb, with hyphens: le/la/les, then moi/toi/lui/nous/vous/leur, then en"]
  D --> E["Donne-le-moi ! Donnez-m'en !"]
```

### Example 3: the flatshare rules

The flatmates write rules on the fridge. Turn each request into a command with two pronouns.

1. *Rendez les outils à Karim.* → the direct object *les outils* = *les*; the person *à Karim* =
   *lui*; command order: direct first. → *Rendez-les-lui.*
2. *Ne prêtez pas les clés aux voisins.* → *les* + *leur*; negative, so before the verb in the
   statement order (column 2, then 3). → *Ne les leur prêtez pas.*
3. *Donnez-moi du sel, s'il vous plaît.* → *du sel* = *en*; *moi* before *en* becomes *m'*. →
   *Donnez-m'en, s'il vous plaît.*
4. *Montre la facture à tes colocataires.* → *la* + *leur*. → *Montre-la-leur.*

## What people really say

The full forms above are correct French, in speech and in writing. In relaxed conversation you
will also hear some shortcuts. Recognise them, but don't write them:

- With *le, la, les* + *lui, leur*, the first pronoun is often dropped: *Je lui ai dit* for *Je le
  lui ai dit* (I told him). *Tu lui donnes ?* for *Tu le lui donnes ?* This is very common, and
  often the context makes the missing *le* obvious. (Informal.)
- In commands some speakers say *Donne-moi-le* instead of *Donne-le-moi*. It is heard but counted
  as a mistake; say *Donne-le-moi*. (Informal, non-standard.)
- *Il y en a* is said "y en a" [jɑ̃na] in quick speech: *Y en a plus !* (There's none left!).
  (Informal.)

When in doubt, use one pronoun and keep the other object as a noun: *Je lui prête mon vélo* or
*Je le prête à Inès*. That is always correct and natural.

## Words for the flatshare

- *la colocation* (informal *la coloc*) — flatshare, house share; *le colocataire* (informal *le
  coloc*) — flatmate, roommate.
- *partager* — to share: *On partage la cuisine.* Like *manger*: *nous partageons*.
- *rendre service à qqn* — to do someone a favour: *Tu peux me rendre service ?*
- *garder* — to keep, to look after: *Garde-le, je n'en ai pas besoin.*
- *confier qqch à qqn* — to entrust something to someone, to leave in someone's care: *Je te confie
  mes clés pendant les vacances.*
- *Tiens ! / Tenez !* — Here you are! (handing something over): *Tiens, je te le prête.*
- Objects: *l'outil* (tool), *la perceuse* (drill), *l'échelle* (ladder), *la rallonge*
  (extension lead), *le sèche-cheveux* (hair dryer), *le tire-bouchon* (corkscrew), *l'appareil
  photo* (camera).

## Common mistakes

- Wrong order before the verb. Not ~~Je lui le donne~~ but *Je le lui donne*; not ~~Je le te
  donne~~ but *Je te le donne*.
- Splitting the pair. Not ~~Je le ai lui donné~~ but *Je le lui ai donné*.
- *En* in the middle. Not ~~Il en y a~~ but *Il y en a*; not ~~Donnez-en-moi~~ but *Donnez-m'en*.
- The statement order in an affirmative command. Not ~~Me le donne !~~ but *Donne-le-moi !*
- Forgetting the agreement. *La clé ? Je te l'ai donnée*, with *-e*.

## Key points

- Before the verb: me/te/se/nous/vous → le/la/les → lui/leur → y → en. *Je te le donne. Je le lui
  dis. Il y en a.*
- The pair stays together: *Je ne le lui ai pas dit. Je vais te le montrer.*
- Affirmative commands: direct object first, *en* last: *Donne-le-moi ! Donnez-m'en !*
- Negative commands use the normal order: *Ne me le donne pas !*
- Casual speech often drops *le* before *lui*: *Je lui ai dit*. Recognise it; write the full form.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson. (*La colocation, le colocataire, partager, garder* and *l'outil* are in the word lists
of later honors lessons, so they aren't repeated here.)

lessons.title: Honors: Les familles d'aujourd'hui (families today)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

French A1 gave you the family: *le père, la mère, le frère, la sœur, les parents*. Families in
France, as elsewhere, are often more varied than that list: parents who have separated, new
partners, children from two couples, couples who marry and couples who sign a PACS. This lesson
gives you the words to describe a family like that, a few dated facts and figures from official
sources, and one grammar point that comes up in every love story: reciprocal verbs from lesson 5
(*ils se voient, ils se séparent*) in the passé composé, with their agreement.

The lesson describes; it doesn't judge. Every family in it is invented, and every figure comes
from INSEE, France's national statistics office, with its year.

## The family words

| French | English | note |
|---|---|---|
| *la famille recomposée* | blended family, stepfamily | a couple living with at least one child from an earlier relationship |
| *la famille monoparentale* | single-parent family | one parent living with the children |
| *le beau-père* | stepfather; father-in-law | plural *les beaux-pères* |
| *la belle-mère* | stepmother; mother-in-law | plural *les belles-mères* |
| *le demi-frère, la demi-sœur* | half-brother, half-sister | plural *les demi-frères, les demi-sœurs*: *demi* never changes |
| *le compagnon, la compagne* | partner (in a couple) | for a couple who aren't married |
| *le conjoint, la conjointe* | spouse, partner | the official word, on forms |
| *les grands-parents* | grandparents | *les petits-enfants*: grandchildren |
| *l'oncle, la tante* | uncle, aunt | |
| *le cousin, la cousine* | cousin | |
| *le neveu, la nièce* | nephew, niece | plural *les neveux* |

Two of these need care:

- *Beau-père* and *belle-mère* have two meanings. *Mon beau-père* can be my mother's husband
  (stepfather) or my wife's or husband's father (father-in-law). The situation tells you which.
  (*Belle-mère* has nothing to do with beauty here.)
- *Demi-frère* strictly means a brother who shares one parent with you. In everyday speech
  people also use it for a stepbrother, the son of your stepparent with no parent in common.
  A rarer, more precise word for that is *le quasi-frère*.

Some verbs and nouns that go with them:

- *élever* — to bring up, to raise: *Elle a élevé ses enfants seule.* It changes *e → è* like
  *acheter*: *j'élève, nous élevons*.
- *la garde* — custody: *la garde alternée* is shared custody, with the children living with each
  parent in turn (often one week each).
- *le foyer* — household, home: *un foyer de quatre personnes*.

### Example 1: describing Inès's family

![A family tree. At the top, Mamie and Papi, the grandparents, are joined by a line, and a line goes down to their daughter Claire. In the middle row, from left to right: Sophie and Antoine joined by a solid line (a couple), a dashed line from Antoine to Claire (separated), and Claire and Marc joined by a solid line. Three children in the bottom row: Zoé below Sophie and Antoine, Inès below Antoine and Claire, and Léo below Claire and Marc. Under each name is the relationship to Inès: Sophie la belle-mère, Antoine le père, Claire la mère, Marc le beau-père, Zoé la demi-sœur, Léo le demi-frère, and Mamie and Papi les grands-parents.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Inès is 15. Describe her family from her point of view, in French.

1. Start with the parents and say they are separated: *Mes parents sont séparés.*
2. Name the new partners. Marc lives with Inès's mother, so he is her stepfather: *Ma mère vit
   avec Marc, mon beau-père.* Sophie is her father's partner: *Mon père vit avec sa compagne,
   Sophie, ma belle-mère.*
3. The children: Léo has the same mother as Inès, and Zoé the same father, so both are half-
   siblings: *J'ai un demi-frère, Léo, et une demi-sœur, Zoé.*
4. Add custody and the grandparents: *Je suis en garde alternée : une semaine chez ma mère, une
   semaine chez mon père. Le dimanche, on voit souvent mes grands-parents.*

Result: *Mes parents sont séparés. Ma mère vit avec Marc, mon beau-père, et mon père vit avec sa
compagne, Sophie. J'ai un demi-frère, Léo, et une demi-sœur, Zoé. Je suis en garde alternée : une
semaine chez ma mère, une semaine chez mon père. Le dimanche, on voit souvent mes grands-parents.*

So Inès lives in two blended families. (*Vit* is from *vivre*, lesson 3.)

## Marriage, PACS, living together

French couples have three common ways of living together:

- *Le mariage* (marriage), at the town hall (*la mairie*). The civil wedding is the legal one; a
  religious ceremony, if there is one, must come after it. *Se marier* = to get
  married.
- *Le PACS* (*pacte civil de solidarité*, civil solidarity pact), created by the law of 15
  November 1999: a contract between two adults of the same sex or of different sexes, which
  organises their life together. Since 1 November 2017 it has been registered at the town hall or
  with a notary. *Se pacser* = to sign a PACS (an everyday verb made from the abbreviation).
- *L'union libre*, living together without either: *ils vivent en couple*.

Marriage has been open to couples of the same sex since the law of 17 May 2013. The first such
wedding took place in Montpellier on 29 May 2013.

In 2024 there were 248,174 marriages in France, 6,746 of them between two people of the same
sex, and 197,176 PACS (INSEE figures published in January 2026). So there are almost four PACS
for every five marriages.

## Families in figures

INSEE's census figures for 2020 (published in 2023) give this picture of families with at least one child under
18 in France:

| type of family | share of families (2020) | share of children under 18 (2020) |
|---|---|---|
| "traditional" (a couple and only their own children) | 66 % | 67 % |
| single-parent (*monoparentale*) | 25 % | 22 % |
| blended (*recomposée*) | 9 % | 11 % |

The share of single-parent families has doubled since 1990 (from 12 % to 25 %), while blended
families have stayed at about 9 % since 1999. In about four single-parent families out of five,
the parent living with the children is the mother.

### Example 2: reading the figures in French

Say what the table means, in simple French.

1. *Un quart* is a quarter: 25 % → *Un quart des familles sont monoparentales.* (With *un quart
   des* + plural, the verb is usually plural.)
2. 9 % is close to 10 %, one in ten: *Environ une famille sur dix est recomposée.* (*Une … sur
   dix* = one … in ten; *environ*, about, is a lesson 3 word.)
3. For the children: 11 % → *Environ un enfant sur neuf vit dans une famille recomposée.* (11 % is
   1 in 9.1, so "about one in nine".)
4. The trend: *La part des familles monoparentales a doublé depuis 1990.* (*La part* = the share.)

## Reciprocal verbs in the passé composé

Reciprocal verbs, like all verbs with *se*, take *être* in the passé composé (French A1, lesson
22). The pronoun comes first, as with every pronoun in lesson 8:

- *Ils se sont rencontrés en 2010.* — They met in 2010.
- *Nous nous sommes mariés en juin.* — We got married in June.
- *Elles se sont pacsées l'année dernière.* — They signed a PACS last year.
- *Ils ne se sont pas vus depuis Noël.* — They haven't seen each other since Christmas.

### When does the participle agree?

French A1 said that with a verb with *se*, the participle agrees with the subject: *elle s'est
levée*. For reciprocal verbs that is true most of the time, but here is the full rule, and it is
the rule of lesson 8 in disguise:

- The participle agrees when *se* is the direct object of the verb. Test it with the verb
  without *se*: *rencontrer quelqu'un* (direct), so *ils se sont rencontrés, elles se sont
  rencontrées*. The same goes for *voir, aimer, embrasser, quitter, appeler, retrouver*.
- It does not agree when *se* is an indirect object, because the verb takes *à* + person:
  *parler à quelqu'un*, so *ils se sont parlé* (they spoke to each other), *elles se sont parlé*.
  The same goes for *téléphoner, écrire, dire, sourire, plaire*: *Elles se sont téléphoné. Ils se
  sont écrit pendant un an. Ils se sont plu tout de suite.*
- *Se marier, se disputer, se séparer, se réconcilier* agree with the subject: *Elles se sont
  mariées. Ils se sont disputés.*

You hear the difference only in participles that end in a consonant, as in lesson 8: *Ils se
sont écrit* (no agreement) vs *Les lettres qu'ils se sont écrites* (that is the *que* agreement of
lesson 10, a preview).

| se = direct (agrees) | se = indirect (no agreement) |
|---|---|
| *Elles se sont vues.* (voir qqn) | *Elles se sont parlé.* (parler à qqn) |
| *Ils se sont aimés.* (aimer qqn) | *Ils se sont souri.* (sourire à qqn) |
| *Elles se sont quittées.* (quitter qqn) | *Elles se sont écrit.* (écrire à qqn) |

### Example 3: a love story in the past

Léa tells how she and Sami became a couple. Put the verbs in the passé composé, with the right
agreement (Léa is a woman, Sami a man, so "we" is masculine plural).

1. *nous / se rencontrer / à la fac* → *rencontrer qqn* is direct: *Nous nous sommes rencontrés à
   la fac.*
2. *nous / se plaire / tout de suite* → *plaire à qqn*, indirect; *plu* never agrees anyway: *Nous
   nous sommes plu tout de suite.*
3. *pendant les vacances, nous / s'écrire / tous les jours* → *écrire à qqn*, indirect: *Pendant
   les vacances, nous nous sommes écrit tous les jours.*
4. *nous / se pacser / en 2019, puis se marier / en 2023* → both agree: *Nous nous sommes pacsés en
   2019, puis nous nous sommes mariés en 2023.*

## Common mistakes

- *Beau-père* always as "father-in-law". Look at the situation: *ma mère et mon beau-père* is a
  stepfather.
- An *s* on *demi*. Not ~~des demis-frères~~ but *des demi-frères*.
- *Avoir* with a reciprocal verb. Not ~~Ils ont se rencontré~~ but *Ils se sont rencontrés*.
- Agreement with an indirect *se*. Not ~~Elles se sont téléphonées~~ but *Elles se sont
  téléphoné*.
- Forgetting the agreement with a direct *se*. Not ~~Elles se sont vu~~ but *Elles se sont vues*.

## Key points

- *La famille recomposée, monoparentale; le beau-père, la belle-mère* (step- or in-law); *le
  demi-frère, la demi-sœur* (half-, and in speech also step-).
- The PACS: law of 15 November 1999, for two adults of the same or different sexes. Marriage for
  same-sex couples: law of 17 May 2013.
- INSEE, 2020: of families with children under 18, about 25 % are single-parent and 9 % blended.
- Reciprocal verbs take *être*. The participle agrees when *se* is direct (*ils se sont
  rencontrés*), not when it is indirect (*ils se sont parlé*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Comparing: plus, moins, aussi … que and the best
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Modules 1 and 2 gave you the past and the pronouns. Module 3 is about describing things and
comparing them, which you do all the time: *Is the city more expensive than the country? Which
neighbourhood is the quietest? Who cooks better?* This lesson teaches the **[[comparative]]** (more,
less, as … as) and the **[[superlative]]** (the most, the least, the best), with the words you need
to compare places: town and suburbs, farm and valley.

You already know the adjectives *grand, petit, cher, beau, bon, mauvais* and the stressed
pronouns *moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles* (French A1). Both come back here.

## More, less, as: plus, moins, aussi + adjective + que

French compares two things with three small words before the adjective and *que* (than, as)
after it:

| | pattern | example |
|---|---|---|
| more … than | *plus* + adjective + *que* | *Paris est plus grand que Lyon.* — Paris is bigger than Lyon. |
| less … than | *moins* + adjective + *que* | *Le village est moins cher que la ville.* — The village is less expensive than the town. |
| as … as | *aussi* + adjective + *que* | *Ma rue est aussi bruyante que la place du marché.* — My street is as noisy as the market square. |

English has two ways ("bigger", "more expensive"); French has only one: *plus* + the adjective,
however short the adjective is (apart from a few irregular ones, below). *Plus grand* = bigger, *plus calme* = quieter, *plus moderne* =
more modern.

The adjective still agrees with the noun it describes, exactly as in A1:

- *La banlieue est plus calme que le centre.* — The suburbs are quieter than the centre.
- *Les rues de ce quartier sont moins propres que les rues du centre.* — The streets in this area are less clean than the streets in the centre.
- *Cette maison est aussi agréable que l'autre.* — This house is as pleasant as the other one.

*Que* becomes *qu'* before a vowel: *plus animé qu'avant* (livelier than before), *moins
dangereux qu'en ville* (less dangerous than in town).

After *que*, a pronoun is a stressed pronoun, as after a preposition: *Il est plus âgé que
moi.* — He's older than me. *Tu es aussi grand que lui.* Never *que je* or *que il* on their own here.

You can leave out the *que* part when it's obvious: *Le train, c'est plus pratique.* — The train
is more convenient.

![Three bar charts comparing a made-up town centre, suburb and village. Population: centre-ville 40,000, banlieue 15,000, village 800. Average rent: centre-ville 900 euros, banlieue 700 euros, village 500 euros. Noise, on a scale of 1 to 5: centre-ville 5, banlieue 3, village 1. Below: Le village est moins bruyant que le centre-ville. La banlieue est plus chère que le village.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The numbers in this chart are made up. Read it in French:

- *Le centre-ville a une population plus grande que la banlieue.*
- *Le loyer est moins cher au village qu'en banlieue.*
- *Le centre-ville est plus bruyant que le village. Le village est plus tranquille.*

## Comparing how: plus, moins, aussi + adverb + que

The same three words go before an adverb:

- *Le bus va moins vite que le métro.* — The bus goes less fast (more slowly) than the metro.
- *Je vais au marché plus souvent que toi.* — I go to the market more often than you.
- *Elle parle aussi lentement que son père.* — She speaks as slowly as her father.

## Comparing how much: plus de, moins de, autant de + noun

With a noun, you compare a quantity, and you add *de* (*d'* before a vowel), as after *beaucoup
de* (A1). No article after it:

| | pattern | example |
|---|---|---|
| more … than | *plus de* + noun + *que* | *Il y a plus de bruit en ville qu'à la campagne.* |
| less/fewer … than | *moins de* + noun + *que* | *Il y a moins de pollution ici.* |
| as much/many … as | *autant de* + noun + *que* | *Lyon n'a pas autant d'habitants que Paris.* |

Notice: with nouns, "as much / as many" is *autant de*, not *aussi*. *Aussi* goes with
adjectives and adverbs; *autant* goes with nouns and verbs.

## Comparing actions: verb + plus, moins, autant que

To compare how much people *do* something, put *plus, moins* or *autant* after the verb:

- *Mon frère travaille plus que moi.* — My brother works more than me.
- *Les enfants dorment moins que les bébés.* — Children sleep less than babies.
- *Tu manges autant que lui !* — You eat as much as he does!

In the passé composé they usually go between *avoir* and the participle: *J'ai plus dormi que toi.*
(*J'ai dormi plus que toi* is also heard.)

### Saying plus

*Plus* has three pronunciations, and they help you understand it:

- before a consonant, the *s* is silent: *plus grand* "plu grahn";
- before a vowel or mute h, a z sound links it: *plus_agréable* "plu-za-gray-abl";
- when it means "more" on its own, at the end or after a verb, the *s* is usually said:
  *Il travaille plus.* "ploos".

## Good, better, best: meilleur and mieux

Two comparatives have their own words, just as English "good, better" doesn't say "gooder":

| | basic | comparative | superlative |
|---|---|---|---|
| adjective: good | *bon, bonne* | *meilleur, meilleure* | *le meilleur, la meilleure* |
| adverb: well | *bien* | *mieux* | *le mieux* |
| adjective: bad | *mauvais, mauvaise* | *pire* or *plus mauvais(e)* | *le pire* or *le plus mauvais* |
| adverb: badly | *mal* | *plus mal* | *le plus mal* |

- *Ce gâteau est meilleur que l'autre.* — This cake is better than the other one. (good → better)
- *Elle chante mieux que moi.* — She sings better than me. (well → better)
- *Ce film est pire que l'autre.* — This film is worse than the other one.

To choose, ask what English "better" replaces. If it replaces "good" (a quality of a thing or
person), use *meilleur*, which agrees: *une meilleure idée, les meilleurs restaurants*. If it
replaces "well" (how you do something), use *mieux*, which never changes: *Ils parlent mieux
français.*

*Plus bon* is the classic mistake: as a comparative it doesn't exist. (*Moins bon*, less good,
is fine.) *Plus bien* doesn't exist either.

*C'est mieux* is very common: it compares situations. *C'est mieux de prendre le train.* — It's
better to take the train. *C'est meilleur* is usually about taste or quality: *Avec du sel, c'est meilleur.*

*Pire* and *plus mauvais* both mean worse. *Pire* is the usual choice for things that are bad
