already (*La pollution est pire en été*); *plus mauvais* is common for taste or quality (*Ce
café est plus mauvais que l'autre*).

## The superlative: le plus, la moins … de

The **[[superlative]]** says "the most" or "the least". Put *le, la* or *les* before *plus* or
*moins*, and agree with the noun:

- *C'est la rue la plus animée de la ville.* — It's the liveliest street in the town.
- *Ce sont les quartiers les moins chers.* — They're the cheapest (least expensive) areas.

Where does the adjective go? In its usual place (A1):

| adjective's usual place | superlative | |
|---|---|---|
| before the noun (*grand, petit, beau, bon, jeune, vieux* …) | *la plus grande ville* | one article |
| after the noun (most adjectives) | *la ville la plus animée* | the article comes twice |

The second article is easy to forget: *le quartier le plus calme*, *la vallée la plus
tranquille*, *les immeubles les plus modernes*.

"In" after a superlative is normally *de* (with *du, de la, des* as usual), not *dans* or *en*:

- *C'est le plus grand musée de France.* — It's the biggest museum in France.
- *Lucas est l'élève le plus bavard de la classe.* — Lucas is the most talkative pupil in the class.

The irregular ones: *le meilleur, la meilleure, les meilleurs* (the best, adjective), *le
mieux* (the best, adverb), *le pire* (the worst):

- *C'est le meilleur restaurant du quartier.* — It's the best restaurant in the area.
- *C'est Inès qui cuisine le mieux.* — Inès is the one who cooks best.

With an adverb or a verb, the superlative is always *le* (it never agrees): *C'est elle qui
parle le plus vite.* With a noun, it's *le plus de* / *le moins de*: *C'est Paris qui a le plus
d'habitants.*

![A podium with three steps. On the top step, number 1: le meilleur, le plus grand. On the left, number 2: plus grand que le n° 3. On the right, number 3: le moins grand. Underneath: le meilleur = the best (adjective), le mieux = the best (adverb), le pire = the worst.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Town and country

![A landscape: on the left a town with tall blocks of flats and, around it, smaller houses of the suburbs; in the middle a river running down a green valley between two hills; on the right a farm with a red-roofed house and a barn, and a field of wheat, with some trees.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| la ville | la campagne |
|---|---|
| *l'immeuble* (m) — block of flats | *la ferme* — farm |
| *la banlieue* — suburbs | *l'agriculteur, l'agricultrice* — farmer |
| *la population* — population | *le champ* — field |
| *la pollution* — pollution | *l'arbre* (m) — tree |
| *bruyant* — noisy; *animé* — lively | *la rivière* — river |
| *pollué* — polluted; *sale* — dirty | *la vallée* — valley; *la colline* — hill |
| *moderne* — modern; *pratique* — handy | *calme, tranquille* — quiet, peaceful |

A few notes:

- *Propre* means "clean" after the noun (*une rue propre*), and "own" before it (*ma propre
  chambre*, my own room).
- *Sûr* means "safe" for a place (*un quartier sûr*) and "sure" for a person (*Tu es sûr ?*).
- *L'espace* is space or room: *Il y a plus d'espace à la campagne.* A room in a house is *une
  pièce*.
- *Une rivière* is a river that flows into another river; *un fleuve* (A1) flows into the sea,
  like the Seine or the Rhône. In everyday speech many people say *rivière* for both.
- *La banlieue* is singular in French where English often says "the suburbs": *J'habite en
  banlieue.* — I live in the suburbs.

## Dialogue: La ville ou la campagne ?

Inès lives in the suburbs of Lyon. She is visiting her cousin Hugo, who is a farmer.

> Hugo : Alors, la vie à Lyon, c'est comment ?
>
> Inès : J'habite en banlieue, dans un immeuble moderne. C'est plus pratique pour le travail, mais c'est moins calme qu'ici. Il y a plus de bruit et plus de pollution.
>
> Hugo : Ici, à la ferme, c'est sûr, c'est plus tranquille ! Mais je travaille plus que toi.
>
> Inès : Ça, ce n'est pas sûr ! Moi aussi, je travaille beaucoup. Mais j'aime la ville : c'est plus animé, et il y a les meilleurs restaurants de la région.
>
> Hugo : Les meilleurs restaurants ? Ma mère fait la meilleure cuisine du monde !
>
> Inès : C'est vrai. Et ici, l'air est plus propre, il y a plus d'espace… Ta vallée est la plus belle de la région.
>
> Hugo : Alors, viens habiter ici ! On a des champs, des arbres, une rivière, deux collines…
>
> Inès : Non merci ! Le matin, je me lève à sept heures. Toi, tu te lèves à cinq heures. C'est pire !

In English:

> Hugo: So, what's life like in Lyon?
>
> Inès: I live in the suburbs, in a modern block of flats. It's more convenient for work, but it's less quiet than here. There's more noise and more pollution.
>
> Hugo: Here on the farm it's certainly more peaceful! But I work more than you.
>
> Inès: That's not certain! I work a lot too. But I love the city: it's livelier, and it has the best restaurants in the region.
>
> Hugo: The best restaurants? My mother makes the best food in the world!
>
> Inès: That's true. And here the air is cleaner, there's more space… Your valley is the most beautiful in the region.
>
> Hugo: Then come and live here! We've got fields, trees, a river, two hills…
>
> Inès: No thanks! I get up at seven in the morning. You get up at five. That's worse!

Find the comparatives (*plus pratique, moins calme qu'ici, plus de bruit, plus que toi*), the
superlatives (*les meilleurs restaurants de la région, la meilleure cuisine du monde, la plus
belle de la région*) and *pire*.

## Pronunciation

- *meilleur*: "meh-YUR"; *mieux*: "myuh", one syllable.
- *pire*: "peer".
- *bruyant*: "brwee-YAHN"; *tranquille*: "trahn-KEEL" (the *ll* is said *l*, as in *ville*).
- *le champ*: "shahn" (the *p* is silent); *la ferme*: "fairm".
- *l'agriculteur*: "lah-gree-kül-TUR", with the French *u* of *tu*.
- *autant*: "oh-TAHN".

## Common mistakes

- *plus bon* → *meilleur*: *Ce vin est meilleur.* *Plus bien* → *mieux*: *Je dors mieux.*
- *Il chante meilleur que moi* → *Il chante mieux que moi* (how he sings: an adverb).
- *Elle est plus grande que je* → *que moi*: a stressed pronoun after *que*.
- *Il y a plus bruit* → *plus de bruit*: *de* before a noun.
- *Il y a aussi de bruit* → *autant de bruit*: with a noun, *autant de*.
- *la ville plus animée* → *la ville la plus animée*: repeat the article when the adjective
  follows the noun.
- *le plus grand musée en France* → *de France*: "in" after a superlative is *de*.

## Key points

- *plus / moins / aussi* + adjective or adverb + *que*: *plus calme que, moins vite que, aussi
  cher que*. The adjective agrees.
- With nouns: *plus de / moins de / autant de* + noun (+ *que*). With verbs: verb + *plus /
  moins / autant* (+ *que*).
- After *que*: *moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles*.
- *bon → meilleur* (agrees), *bien → mieux* (never changes), *mauvais → pire* or *plus
  mauvais*. *C'est mieux* = it's better (a situation).
- Superlative: *le/la/les plus* + adjective; the article twice after the noun (*la ville la plus
  animée*); "in" = *de* (*le plus grand de France*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The person who, the thing that: qui, que and où
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far your French sentences have been short: *J'ai une appli. Elle marche bien.* Real French
joins them: *J'ai une appli qui marche bien.* — I've got an app that works well. The joining
words are **[[relative pronouns]]**, and this lesson teaches the three you need at A2: *qui*, *que*
and *où*. They also let you describe a thing whose name you don't know, which is a lifesaver in
a shop or on the phone: *C'est un truc qui sert à …* — It's a thing that's used for …

The theme is technology: computers, phones, apps and the internet.

## Joining two sentences

Look at what happens in each pair. The second sentence talks about a noun from the first, and
the relative pronoun replaces that noun and joins the sentences:

| two sentences | one sentence |
|---|---|
| *J'ai une tablette. Elle est très légère.* | *J'ai une tablette qui est très légère.* |
| *C'est le site. J'utilise ce site tous les jours.* | *C'est le site que j'utilise tous les jours.* |
| *C'est la ville. J'habite dans cette ville.* | *C'est la ville où j'habite.* |

*Elle* became *qui*, *ce site* became *que*, and *dans cette ville* became *où*.

The part that starts with *qui, que* or *où* is a **[[relative clause]]**. The noun it describes
(*une tablette, le site, la ville*) is its **[[antecedent]]**: the word that "goes before". The
relative clause comes straight after its antecedent, even in the middle of a sentence:

*L'ordinateur que j'utilise au bureau est très lent.* — The computer (that) I use at work is very
slow.

## qui: the subject

Use *qui* when the antecedent is the subject of the next verb: the person or thing that does
it. So *qui* is followed directly by a verb (or by a pronoun + verb, like *qui me plaît*):

- *J'ai une amie qui travaille dans une banque.* — I've got a friend who works in a bank.
- *C'est une appli qui explique la grammaire.* — It's an app that explains grammar.
- *Je n'aime pas les écrans qui sont trop petits.* — I don't like screens that are too small.

Two things English speakers don't expect:

- *Qui* is for both people and things. It isn't only "who": *le portable qui est sur la table* =
  the phone that is on the table.
- *Qui* never becomes *qu'*: *l'appli qui est gratuite, un ami qui habite ici.* (So in a relative clause,
  a *qu'* in front of a vowel is always *que*.)

The verb after *qui* agrees with the antecedent: *les sites qui marchent bien* (plural), *C'est
toi qui as le chargeur ?* (*toi* → *as*).

(*Marcher* is "to walk", but for a machine or an idea it means "to work": *Mon imprimante ne
marche pas.*)

## que: the object

Use *que* when the antecedent is the object of the next verb: the thing or person that
someone does it to. So *que* is followed by a subject and then a verb:

- *C'est le mot de passe que j'utilise partout.* — It's the password (that) I use everywhere.
- *La vidéo que tu m'as envoyée est super.* — The video (that) you sent me is great.
- *Le collègue que je préfère, c'est Karim.* — The colleague I like best is Karim.

*Que* becomes *qu'* before a vowel: *le fichier qu'il a téléchargé, l'appli qu'elle utilise.*

English can drop "that" (the film I saw); French never drops *que*: *le film que j'ai vu*, never
*le film j'ai vu*.

### que and the passé composé

Lesson 8 showed that the participle after *avoir* agrees with a direct object that comes before
it. *Que* is a direct object that comes before, so the participle agrees with the antecedent:

- *les photos que j'ai prises* — the photos (that) I took (*les photos*: feminine plural)
- *la vidéo que tu as faite* — the video (that) you made
- *les fichiers que j'ai enregistrés* — the files (that) I saved

You mostly see this agreement rather than hear it: *enregistré, enregistrés* sound the same. You
hear it with participles that end in a consonant: *prise, mise, faite, écrite, ouverte*.

## où: place and time

Use *où* after a place, where English says "where" or "in which":

- *C'est le café où on travaille le samedi.* — It's the café where we work on Saturdays.
- *Le site où j'ai acheté ma tablette est très pratique.* — The website where I bought my tablet is very handy.

And after a time word, where English says "when" (or nothing):

- *le jour où je suis arrivé* — the day (when) I arrived
- *l'année où on s'est rencontrés* — the year we met
- *au moment où le téléphone a sonné* — at the moment (when) the phone rang

After a time noun, French uses *où*, not *quand*: *le jour où*, never *le jour quand*.

Careful: a place noun doesn't always take *où*. *Où* replaces "in it, there". If the place is the
subject or object of the next verb, use *qui* or *que*: *C'est une ville qui me plaît* (it pleases
me), *C'est une ville que j'adore* (I love it), *C'est la ville où je suis né* (I was born there).

## How to choose

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing qui, que or où
  accDescr: First ask whether the second part says where or when something happens, about the noun. If yes, use où, as in la ville où j'habite. If not, look at what follows the gap. A verb means the noun is the subject, so use qui, as in l'appli qui marche. A subject and a verb mean the noun is the object, so use que, or qu' before a vowel, as in le site que j'utilise.
  A["The noun, then a gap: la ville ___ …"] --> B{"Does the rest say WHERE or WHEN, about that noun?"}
  B -- "yes: in it, there, then" --> C["où: la ville où j'habite"]
  B -- "no" --> D{"What comes right after the gap?"}
  D -- "a verb" --> E["qui: l'appli qui marche"]
  D -- "a subject + a verb" --> F["que / qu': le site que j'utilise"]
```

A quick test for *qui* or *que*: cover the relative pronoun and look to the right. *___ marche
bien*: a verb, so *qui*. *___ j'utilise*: *je*, a subject, so *que*.

## C'est … qui, c'est … que: pointing at one thing

You will often hear *c'est … qui* and *c'est … que* to put one part of a sentence in the
spotlight. This is just a preview: understand it and use it in simple sentences.

- *C'est Léa qui a le mot de passe.* — It's Léa who has the password. (not someone else)
- *C'est ce site que j'utilise.* — This is the site I use. (not another one)
- *C'est moi qui paie !* — I'm paying! (literally: it's me who pays)

## Describing a thing you can't name

When you don't know a word, describe it with a relative clause. This is a real skill at A2, and
exactly what you need in a speaking test when a word escapes you.

- *C'est un truc qui sert à ouvrir les bouteilles.* — It's a thing for opening bottles.
- *C'est une machine qu'on utilise pour imprimer.* — It's a machine you use to print.
- *C'est l'endroit où on met les fichiers.* — It's the place where you put the files. (*l'endroit*, m = the place)

*Ça sert à quoi ?* (What's it for?) asks the question. *Ça sert à* + infinitive answers it: *Ça
sert à charger le portable.* — It's for charging the phone. *Le truc* is informal and very common
in speech; in writing use *l'objet* (the object) or *la chose* (the thing).

## At the computer

![A desk with a screen, a keyboard, a mouse, a printer, a tablet and a phone plugged into its charger. The screen shows a website with an address bar, a password box and a link.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *l'ordinateur portable* (m) | laptop (often just *le portable*, which also means a mobile phone) |
| *la tablette, l'écran* (m) | tablet, screen |
| *le clavier, la souris* | keyboard, mouse (*les souris*: no -s) |
| *l'imprimante* (f), *imprimer* | printer, to print |
| *la batterie, le chargeur, charger* | battery, charger, to charge |
| *l'application / l'appli* (f), *le site* | app, website |
| *internet* (m, usually no article) | internet: *sur internet* |
| *le réseau social* | social network (*les réseaux sociaux*) |
| *en ligne, se connecter* | online, to log in |
| *le mot de passe, le lien, le fichier* | password, link, file |
| *cliquer (sur), télécharger, enregistrer* | to click (on), to download, to save |

*Télécharger* and *charger* keep an *e* in the *nous* form like *manger*: *nous téléchargeons,
nous chargeons*. *Enregistrer* also means "to record" (a song, a message). *Utiliser* is "to use":
*J'utilise une appli pour apprendre le français.*

## Dialogue: Allô, Camille ?

Léo phones his sister Camille, who is good with computers.

> Léo : Allô, Camille ? Tu as cinq minutes ? J'ai un problème avec l'ordinateur portable que j'ai acheté la semaine dernière.
>
> Camille : Oui, je suis au café où on va le samedi. Qu'est-ce qui se passe ?
>
> Léo : Je n'arrive pas à me connecter au site de ma banque. Le mot de passe que j'utilise d'habitude ne marche pas.
>
> Camille : Tu as cliqué sur « Mot de passe oublié » ? Ils envoient un lien qui sert à changer le mot de passe.
>
> Léo : Ah, d'accord. Autre chose : l'imprimante que tu m'as donnée n'imprime rien.
>
> Camille : Tu as l'application qui va avec ? Tu la télécharges, et c'est tout.
>
> Léo : Quelle application ?
>
> Camille : Regarde sur la boîte : c'est l'appli qui a le nom de l'imprimante !
>
> Léo : Merci ! Tu es la seule personne qui comprend les ordinateurs dans la famille.

In English:

> Léo: Hello, Camille? Have you got five minutes? I've got a problem with the laptop I bought last week.
>
> Camille: Yes, I'm at the café where we go on Saturdays. What's happening?
>
> Léo: I can't log in to my bank's website. The password I usually use doesn't work.
>
> Camille: Did you click on "Forgotten password"? They send a link that you use to change the password.
>
> Léo: Oh, OK. Something else: the printer you gave me doesn't print anything.
>
> Camille: Have you got the app that goes with it? You download it, and that's it.
>
> Léo: What app?
>
> Camille: Look on the box: it's the app that has the printer's name!
>
> Léo: Thanks! You're the only person in the family who understands computers.

(*n'arrive pas à* = can't manage to; *oublié* = forgotten; *seul(e)* before a noun = only.)
Find *que* (*l'ordinateur portable que j'ai acheté, le mot de
passe que j'utilise, l'imprimante que tu m'as donnée* — with agreement), *qui* (*un lien qui sert
à, l'application qui va avec, l'appli qui a le nom, la seule personne qui comprend*) and *où* (*le café où on va*).

## Pronunciation

- *qui* "kee", *que* "kuh", *où* "oo". Don't let *qui* and *que* sound the same: one is "ee", the
  other a short "uh".
- *internet*: "an-tair-NET", with a nasal *in* and the final *t* said.
- *le site*: "seet". *L'appli*: "lah-PLEE".
- *le clavier*: "kla-VYAY"; *la souris*: "soo-REE" (silent *s*).
- *télécharger*: "tay-lay-shar-ZHAY"; *l'imprimante*: "lan-pree-MAHNT".
- *le réseau social*: "ray-ZOH so-SYAL"; plural *les réseaux sociaux* "so-SYOH".

## Common mistakes

- *l'appli que marche* → *qui marche*: a verb follows, so *qui*.
- *le site qui j'utilise* → *que j'utilise*: a subject follows, so *que*.
- *l'ami qu'habite à Lyon* → *qui habite*: *qui* never elides.
- *le film j'ai vu* → *le film que j'ai vu*: never leave *que* out.
- *le jour quand je suis arrivé* → *le jour où*.
- *les photos que j'ai pris* → *prises*: after *que*, the participle agrees with the antecedent.

## Key points

- *qui* + verb (subject), for people and things; never *qu'*.
- *que / qu'* + subject + verb (object); never left out.
- *où* for places (where, in which) and times (when): *la ville où, le jour où*.
- Test: cover the pronoun; a verb next → *qui*; a subject next → *que*.
- After *que* in the passé composé, the participle agrees: *les photos que j'ai prises*.
- *C'est … qui / que* points at one part. *C'est un truc qui sert à …, Ça sert à quoi ?* to describe
  what you can't name.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: This one, mine: celui, celle and le mien
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In a shop you don't repeat the noun every time: *Which bag? This one or that one? Not mine, the
leather one.* French does the same with two sets of pronouns. **[[Demonstrative pronouns]]**
(*celui, celle, ceux, celles*) mean "the one(s)"; **[[possessive pronouns]]** (*le mien, la tienne,
les nôtres* …) mean "mine, yours, ours". Both replace a noun you've already mentioned, and both
agree with that noun, the way *ce, cette* and *mon, ma* do (A1).

You'll also learn to say what things are made of (*en bois, en cuir, en or*) and what shape and
weight they are.

## celui, celle, ceux, celles: the one, the ones

The pronoun takes the gender and number of the noun it replaces:

| | masculine | feminine |
|---|---|---|
| singular | *celui* | *celle* |
| plural | *ceux* | *celles* |

- *Quel sac ? — Celui-ci.* (le sac → celui)
- *Quelle veste ? — Celle-là.* (la veste → celle)
- *Tu préfères quels gâteaux ? — Ceux de Julie.* (les gâteaux → ceux)

These pronouns never stand alone: something always follows them. At A2 you need three ways to
finish them.

![A chart of the demonstrative pronouns. In the middle, a grid: celui (masculine singular), celle (feminine singular), ceux (masculine plural), celles (feminine plural). Around it, three ways to finish them: plus -ci or -là (celui-ci, celle-là), plus de and a noun (celle de Paul), plus qui or que (ceux qui sont en cuir, celle que j'ai achetée).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### + -ci or -là: this one, that one

*Celui-ci* is "this one" (nearer) and *celui-là* "that one" (further). In everyday speech
*celui-là* is often used for both, and *-ci* mostly appears when you contrast two things:

- *Je prends celle-ci ou celle-là ?* — Shall I take this one or that one?
- *Ces chaussures sont jolies, mais je préfère celles-là.* — I prefer those.

### + de: the one of, …'s

French has no *'s*. *La voiture de Paul* becomes *celle de Paul* (Paul's):

- *Ce n'est pas ma clé, c'est celle de Julie.* — It's not my key, it's Julie's.
- *Mes notes sont meilleures que celles de mon frère.* — My marks are better than my brother's.

### + qui or que: the one that

This links back to lesson 10:

- *Prends le pull bleu, celui qui est sur la chaise.* — Take the blue jumper, the one that's on the chair.
- *Les gâteaux ? Ceux que j'ai achetés sont sur la table.* — The ones I bought are on the table.

(Notice the agreement *achetés*: *que* stands for *ceux*, masculine plural.)

## ça, cela, ceci: when there's no noun

When you point at something you can't or don't name, or at an idea, there is no gender to agree
with, so you use *ça*:

- *C'est quoi, ça ?* — What's that?
- *Je voudrais ça, s'il vous plaît.* — I'd like that, please. (pointing)
- *Ça me plaît.* — I like it. *Ça, c'est une bonne idée !*

*Cela* is the same word in careful speech and in writing (*ça* is a shortened *cela*): *Cela ne
me surprend pas.* — That doesn't surprise me. *Ceci* (this) is rare in speech; you see it in
writing and set phrases. René Magritte's famous painting of a pipe is captioned *Ceci n'est pas
une pipe* — This is not a pipe.

So: a noun in mind → *celui, celle* …; no noun → *ça*. *Tu veux quel gâteau ? — Celui-là.* but
*Tu veux quoi ? — Ça.*

## le mien, la tienne: possessive pronouns

A possessive pronoun replaces "my bag", "your keys" and so on with "mine", "yours". It has an
article, and it agrees with the thing owned, never with the owner:

| owner | the thing is masc. sing. | fem. sing. | masc. plural | fem. plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| je | *le mien* | *la mienne* | *les miens* | *les miennes* |
| tu | *le tien* | *la tienne* | *les tiens* | *les tiennes* |
| il / elle | *le sien* | *la sienne* | *les siens* | *les siennes* |
| nous | *le nôtre* | *la nôtre* | *les nôtres* | *les nôtres* |
| vous | *le vôtre* | *la vôtre* | *les vôtres* | *les vôtres* |
| ils / elles | *le leur* | *la leur* | *les leurs* | *les leurs* |

![A grid of possessive pronouns with the owner on the left (je, tu, il or elle, nous, vous, ils or elles) and the thing owned across the top (masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, feminine plural). Arrows show that mon sac becomes le mien and ma clé becomes la mienne: the pronoun agrees with the thing, not the owner.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *C'est ton portable ? — Oui, c'est le mien.* — Is that your phone? — Yes, it's mine.
- *Ma valise est grise. La tienne est de quelle couleur ?* — Mine is grey. What colour is yours?
- *J'ai oublié mes clés. Tu as les tiennes ?* — I forgot my keys. Have you got yours?

The thing decides, as with *son, sa, ses*, so *le sien* can be "his" or "hers":

- *Paul cherche sa clé. — La sienne ? Elle est sur la table.* — His? It's on the table. (*clé* is
  feminine, so *la sienne*, even though Paul is a man.)
- *Léa cherche son sac. — Le sien ? Il est dans la voiture.* — Hers? It's in the car. (*sac* is
  masculine, so *le sien*, even though Léa is a woman.)

Four details:

- *Le nôtre, le vôtre* have a circumflex and a closed *o* ("noht", "voht"). The determiners
  *notre, votre* (*notre maison*) have neither (open *o*, as in *note*).
- *Le leur* has *-s* only in the plural: *les leurs*. Don't confuse it with *leur*, the
  indirect object pronoun of lesson 6 (*je leur parle*), which never has *-s*.
- The article joins with *à* and *de* as usual: *Je pense au mien* (à + le mien). *Je parle des
  leurs* (de + les leurs).
- After a comparative: *Ta voiture est plus rapide que la mienne.* — Your car is faster than mine.

### C'est à qui ? C'est à moi.

In everyday speech, the simplest way to say who something belongs to is *être à* + a person or
a stressed pronoun:

- *C'est à qui, ce sac ? — C'est à moi.* — Whose bag is this? — It's mine.
- *Ces lunettes sont à Paul.* — These glasses are Paul's.

*C'est à moi* and *c'est le mien* both mean "it's mine". *C'est à moi* answers "whose is it?";
*c'est le mien* is more natural when you're telling apart two things of the same kind: *Ce n'est
pas ton parapluie, c'est le mien !*

## Lequel ? Which one?

A1 taught *lequel ?* (which one?). It agrees too: *lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles*. The
answer is often a demonstrative:

- *Tu veux une tasse ? — Laquelle ? — Celle qui est rouge.*
- *J'ai deux chargeurs. Tu veux lequel ? — Celui de la tablette.*

## What's it made of? Materials and shapes

French uses *en* + material, with no article: *un sac en cuir* (a leather bag), *une table en
bois* (a wooden table). (*De* is also possible, *un sac de cuir*, but *en* is the everyday
choice.)

![A shop shelf with six objects: a wooden bowl, a metal box, a plastic bottle, a leather bag, a wool jumper and a gold ring.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| material | example |
|---|---|
| *le bois* (wood) | *une cuillère en bois* |
| *le métal* (metal; plural *les métaux*) | *une boîte en métal* |
| *le plastique* (plastic) | *une bouteille en plastique* |
| *le cuir* (leather) | *une veste en cuir* |
| *le coton* (cotton) | *un tee-shirt en coton* |
| *la laine* (wool) | *un pull en laine* |
| *l'or* (m) (gold) | *un bijou en or* |
| *l'argent* (silver) | *une bague en argent* (a silver ring) |
| *le verre* (glass, the material) | *un vase en verre* |

Two A1 words have a second meaning here: *l'argent* is money, but also silver; *le verre* is a
drinking glass, but also glass the material. *Une bouteille en verre* is a glass bottle.

Shape, weight and feel:

- *la forme* (shape): *Il est de quelle forme ? — Il est rond.* (round); *carré* (square).
- *lourd* (heavy) and *léger, légère* (light): *Ma valise est trop lourde. — Prends la mienne, elle
  est plus légère.*
- *doux, douce* (soft; also gentle, mild): *La laine est douce.* *dur* (hard): *Ce pain est dur !*
- *la marque* (brand): *C'est de quelle marque ?* — What brand is it?

## Dialogue: Au marché

Sarah and her friend Malik are at a market stall that sells bags.

> Le vendeur : Bonjour ! Vous cherchez quelque chose ?
>
> Sarah : Oui, un sac pour le travail. Je peux voir celui-là, en cuir ?
>
> Le vendeur : Bien sûr. Il est très beau, mais il est un peu lourd. Celui-ci est en coton : il est plus léger, et moins cher.
>
> Sarah : Hmm. Malik, ton sac est de quelle marque ? Le tien est très pratique.
>
> Malik : Le mien ? Il n'a pas de marque. C'est celui de mon frère !
>
> Sarah : Il me plaît, ce sac en coton, mais la couleur… Vous avez celui-ci en vert ?
>
> Le vendeur : En vert, non. J'ai ceux qui sont sur la table, en bleu et en noir.
>
> Sarah : Je prends le bleu. Et ça, c'est quoi ? C'est en or ?
>
> Le vendeur : Non, madame, c'est du métal. Un bijou en or à ce prix-là, ça n'existe pas !

In English:

> Seller: Hello! Are you looking for something?
>
> Sarah: Yes, a bag for work. Can I see that one, the leather one?
>
> Seller: Of course. It's very nice, but it's a bit heavy. This one is cotton: it's lighter, and cheaper.
>
> Sarah: Hmm. Malik, what brand is your bag? Yours is very practical.
>
> Malik: Mine? It hasn't got a brand. It's my brother's!
>
> Sarah: I like this cotton bag, but the colour… Have you got this one in green?
>
> Seller: Not in green. I've got the ones that are on the table, in blue and in black.
>
> Sarah: I'll take the blue one. And that, what is it? Is it gold?
>
> Seller: No, madam, it's metal. A gold piece of jewellery at that price doesn't exist!

(*le vendeur* = the seller; *exister* = to exist.) For "the blue one", French usually just puts
the article before the colour: *le bleu, la verte, les noirs*.

## Pronunciation

- *celui* "suh-LWEE"; *celle, celles* both "sel"; *ceux* "suh", like *deux* without the d.
- *le mien* "myan" (nasal); *la mienne* "myen" (the n is said). The same for *tien / tienne*,
  *sien / sienne*.
- *le nôtre* "noht" (closed, like *beau*) but *notre* "notr" (open, like *note*).
- *le cuir* "kweer", one syllable. *La laine* "len". *L'or* "lor".
- *léger* "lay-ZHAY", *légère* "lay-ZHAIR".

## Common mistakes

- *Je prends celui.* → *celui-ci* or *celui-là*: the pronoun never stands alone.
- *Paul cherche sa clé ; j'ai le sien.* → *la sienne*: agree with *clé*, not with Paul.
- *C'est le notre.* → *le nôtre*, with a circumflex.
- *les leur* → *les leurs* (but *je leur parle*, no -s).
- *Je voudrais celui.* (pointing at a thing you can't name) → *Je voudrais ça.*
- *un sac en le cuir* → *un sac en cuir*: no article after *en*.

## Key points

- *celui, celle, ceux, celles* + *-ci / -là*, + *de* (*celle de Paul*), or + *qui / que*
  (*celui qui …*). Never alone.
- *ça* (everyday), *cela* (careful), *ceci* (rare): for things with no noun.
- *le mien, le tien, le sien, le nôtre, le vôtre, le leur*: agree with the thing owned.
  *Nôtre, vôtre* with a circumflex.
- *C'est à moi / à Paul* is the everyday "it's mine / Paul's".
- Materials: *en bois, en métal, en plastique, en cuir, en coton, en laine, en or, en argent, en
  verre*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: How you do it: adverbs in -ment; character and feelings
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 9 compared things; this lesson describes how people do things and what they're like. An
**[[adverb]]** tells you how, when or how much something happens: *Elle parle doucement* (she speaks
softly), *Il travaille sérieusement* (he works seriously). Many English adverbs end in *-ly*;
many French ones end in *-ment*, and you can build them yourself from adjectives you already
know. You met two in A1: *lentement* (slowly) and *heureusement* (fortunately).

The second half of the lesson gives you words for character (*patient, paresseux, généreux*)
and feelings (*content, triste, inquiet*), so you can describe people properly.

## Adjective or adverb?

An adjective describes a noun and agrees with it. An adverb describes a verb (or an adjective,
or a whole sentence) and never changes:

| adjective (agrees) | adverb (never changes) |
|---|---|
| *Elle est lente.* — She is slow. | *Elle marche lentement.* — She walks slowly. |
| *une réponse sérieuse* — a serious answer | *Il répond sérieusement.* — He answers seriously. |
| *Ce gâteau est bon.* — This cake is good. | *Il cuisine bien.* — He cooks well. |
| *C'est un mauvais film.* — It's a bad film. | *Il chante mal.* — He sings badly. |

*Bon / bien* and *mauvais / mal* are the pairs English speakers mix up most. Ask: "good" or
"well"? *Il parle bon français* is wrong; *Il parle bien français* is right. (After *c'est*,
both exist with different meanings: *C'est bon* = it tastes good, or OK, that's fine; *C'est
bien* = that's good, well done.)

## Making adverbs in -ment

Most *-ment* adverbs are **[[adverbs of manner]]**: they answer *comment ?* (how?), like *lentement*
or *poliment*.

![A flow chart for making adverbs. Start with the masculine adjective. If it ends in a vowel (vrai, poli, facile, rapide), add -ment to it: vraiment, poliment, facilement, rapidement. If it ends in -ant or -ent, change the ending to -amment or -emment, both said amment: courant gives couramment, évident gives évidemment. Otherwise, take the feminine and add -ment: doux, douce, doucement; sérieux, sérieuse, sérieusement; complet, complète, complètement.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Rule 1: feminine + -ment

For most adjectives, take the feminine form and add *-ment*:

| masculine | feminine | adverb |
|---|---|---|
| *doux* | *douce* | *doucement* — gently, softly, slowly |
| *sérieux* | *sérieuse* | *sérieusement* — seriously |
| *complet* | *complète* | *complètement* — completely |
| *heureux* | *heureuse* | *heureusement* — fortunately |
| *fier* | *fière* | *fièrement* — proudly |
| *lent* | *lente* | *lentement* — slowly |

The accent of the feminine stays: *complète → complètement, fière → fièrement*.

### Rule 2: a vowel at the end → masculine + -ment

If the masculine already ends in a vowel, add *-ment* to it. This includes adjectives in *-e*,
which are the same in both genders:

| adjective | adverb |
|---|---|
| *vrai* | *vraiment* — really |
| *poli* | *poliment* — politely |
| *facile* | *facilement* — easily |
| *rapide* | *rapidement* — quickly |
| *honnête* | *honnêtement* — honestly |

### Rule 3: -ant → -amment, -ent → -emment

Most adjectives ending in *-ant* or *-ent* swap that ending for *-amment* or *-emment*. Both endings
are said the same way, "a-MAHN":

| adjective | adverb |
|---|---|
| *courant* (current, everyday) | *couramment* — fluently |
| *évident* (obvious) | *évidemment* — obviously, of course |
| *patient* | *patiemment* — patiently |
| *récent* | *récemment* — recently |

One-syllable *lent* follows rule 1: *lentement*.

### A few to learn by heart

- *gentil → gentiment* (kindly); *précis → précisément*, *énorme → énormément* (with *é*).
- *bon → bien*, *mauvais → mal*, and their comparatives *mieux* (better) and *plus mal* (lesson 9).
- *vite* is already an adverb (fast, quickly): *Viens vite !* The adjective is *rapide*. *Il est
  vite* is wrong; say *Il est rapide* or *Il va vite*. *Vite* is the everyday word; *rapidement*
  is a little more formal.

*Seulement* (only) comes from *seul* (alone): *J'ai seulement dix euros.* — I've only got ten
euros. (Lesson 17 shows another way: *Je n'ai que dix euros.*)

## Where adverbs go

In the present, an adverb usually goes straight after the verb:

- *Il parle couramment anglais.* — He speaks English fluently.
- *Je comprends vraiment.* — I really understand.

Before an adjective or another adverb, it goes in front, as in English: *vraiment sympa*
(really nice), *complètement différent* (completely different), *très facilement*.

In the passé composé, it depends on the adverb:

- Short, very common adverbs usually go between *avoir / être* and the participle: *J'ai bien
  dormi. Il a vraiment aimé le film. Tu as déjà mangé ?* Several common *-ment* adverbs often go
  there too: *J'ai complètement oublié. Elle a rapidement compris.*
- Longer *-ment* adverbs, especially ones that say how something was done, usually go after the
  participle: *Il a parlé lentement. Elle a répondu poliment.*

If you're not sure, put a *-ment* adverb that says how something was done after the participle.

At the start of a sentence, adverbs that comment on the whole sentence are common, with a
comma: *Évidemment, il est en retard. Heureusement, il a pris le train.*

## Character: what people are like

| quality | the opposite, or a related word |
|---|---|
| *patient* — patient | *Il attend patiemment.* |
| *travailleur, travailleuse* — hard-working | *paresseux, paresseuse* — lazy |
| *sérieux, sérieuse* — serious, reliable | *Elle travaille sérieusement.* |
| *généreux, généreuse* — generous | *égoïste* — selfish |
| *honnête* — honest | *Honnêtement, …* |
| *curieux, curieuse* — curious | *Il pose beaucoup de questions.* |

*Sérieux* is a compliment in French when you talk about work: *un collègue sérieux* is a reliable
colleague, not a gloomy one. *Curieux* can mean "curious, interested in everything" (good) or
"nosy" (less good), as in English.

## Feelings: how people feel

![Five faces, each with a different feeling: one smiling, one sad with a tear, one angry with frowning eyebrows and a red face, one worried with raised eyebrows and a drop of sweat, and one proud with its chin up and a medal.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| feeling | example |
|---|---|
| *content* — pleased, happy | *Je suis content de te voir !* — I'm pleased to see you! |
| *triste* — sad | *Elle est triste parce que son chat est malade.* |
| *fier, fière* — proud | *Je suis fière de toi.* — I'm proud of you. |
| *en colère* — angry | *Le voisin est en colère.* (no agreement: *en colère* is a phrase) |
| *énervé* — annoyed | *Il est énervé : le bus est en retard.* |
| *inquiet, inquiète* — worried | *Ma mère est inquiète : il est minuit.* |
| *s'ennuyer* — to be bored | *Je m'ennuie. Les enfants s'ennuient.* |
| *la joie, le bonheur* — joy, happiness | *C'est une grande joie. L'argent ne fait pas le bonheur.* |

*Content* is lighter than *heureux* (A1): you're *content* about something specific (*content de
ton travail*); *heureux* is deeper happiness (*une vie heureuse*). *L'argent ne fait pas le
bonheur* is a proverb: money doesn't buy happiness.

*S'ennuyer* changes *y* to *i* before a silent ending, like *nettoyer* (and *payer*, which may also keep the *y*): *je m'ennuie,
tu t'ennuies, il s'ennuie, nous nous ennuyons, vous vous ennuyez, ils s'ennuient*. Careful: "I'm
bored" is *je m'ennuie*. *Je suis ennuyeux* means "I'm boring" (*ennuyeux* is a lesson 22 word).

*Énervé* is "annoyed, wound up"; *en colère* is "angry", a little stronger.

## Dialogue: La réunion avec la maîtresse

Mr and Mrs Martin meet their son's teacher at the end of the first term.

> La maîtresse : Bonjour ! Alors, Lucas… C'est un élève très curieux. Il pose beaucoup de questions, et il lit vraiment bien.
>
> Mme Martin : Ah, tant mieux ! Et en anglais ?
>
> La maîtresse : Il parle presque couramment ! Évidemment, son père est anglais, c'est plus facile. Mais il est un peu paresseux en maths : il fait ses exercices trop vite.
>
> M. Martin : Oui, à la maison aussi. Il dit qu'il s'ennuie.
>
> La maîtresse : C'est normal, il comprend facilement. Mais il doit travailler plus sérieusement. Et il est généreux : il aide les autres élèves patiemment.
>
> Mme Martin : Nous sommes contents. Il est parfois triste le soir, il dit que ses copains se moquent de lui…
>
> La maîtresse : Je n'ai rien remarqué, mais je vais faire attention. Honnêtement, ne soyez pas inquiets : c'est un enfant heureux, et vous pouvez être fiers de lui.

In English:

> Teacher: Hello! So, Lucas… He's a very curious pupil. He asks a lot of questions, and he reads really well.
>
> Mrs Martin: Oh, good! And in English?
>
> Teacher: He speaks almost fluently! Of course, his father is English, which makes it easier. But he's a bit lazy in maths: he does his exercises too fast.
>
> Mr Martin: Yes, at home too. He says he's bored.
>
> Teacher: That's normal, he understands easily. But he has to work more seriously. And he's generous: he helps the other pupils patiently.
>
> Mrs Martin: We're pleased. He's sometimes sad in the evening; he says his friends make fun of him…
>
> Teacher: I haven't noticed anything, but I'll pay attention. Honestly, don't worry: he's a happy child, and you can be proud of him.

(*tant mieux* = good, so much the better; *presque* = almost; *se moquer de* = to make fun of;
*faire attention* = to pay attention; *ne soyez pas* = don't be, the imperative of *être*.)

## Pronunciation

- *-amment* and *-emment* are both "a-MAHN": *évidemment* "ay-vee-da-MAHN", *couramment*
  "koo-ra-MAHN", *patiemment* "pa-sya-MAHN".
- *patient* "pa-SYAHN": the *ti* is said "sy", as in *la patience*.
- *vraiment* "vray-MAHN"; *complètement* "kohn-plet-MAHN".
- *inquiet* "an-KYEH", *inquiète* "an-KYET". *Fier* "fyair" (the r is said).
- *s'ennuyer* "sahn-nwee-YAY"; *je m'ennuie* "zhuh mahn-NWEE".
- *égoïste* "ay-go-EEST": the two dots on *ï* tell you to say *o* and *i* separately.
- *honnête* "o-NET": the *h* is silent, so *un_honnête homme* has a liaison.

## Common mistakes

- *Il parle bon français.* → *Il parle bien français.* (how he speaks: an adverb)
- *Il est vite.* → *Il est rapide* or *Il va vite*.
- *doucment, sérieuxment* → *doucement, sérieusement*: start from the feminine.
- *évidentment, courantment* → *évidemment, couramment*.
- *Je suis ennuyeux* (when you mean "I'm bored") → *Je m'ennuie*.
- *Elle est en colèrée* → *en colère* never changes.
- *J'ai dormi bien* → *J'ai bien dormi*: *bien* goes between *avoir* and the participle.

## Key points

- Adverbs never agree. *bon / mauvais* are adjectives; *bien / mal* are adverbs.
- Feminine + *-ment* (*doucement, sérieusement, complètement*); after a vowel, masculine + *-ment*
  (*vraiment, poliment, facilement*); *-ant → -amment*, *-ent → -emment* (*couramment,
  évidemment*), both said "a-MAHN".
- *vite* is an adverb; *rapide* is the adjective. *gentiment, précisément, énormément* are
  exceptions.
- Position: after the verb in the present; in the passé composé, short common adverbs before
  the participle (*j'ai bien dormi*), most *-ment* adverbs of manner after it (*il a parlé
  lentement*).
- *Je m'ennuie* = I'm bored. *Content* is lighter than *heureux*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: More relatives: dont, ce qui, ce que
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 10 gave you *qui, que* and *où*. They cover most sentences, but you'll quickly hear three
more relatives that French speakers use all the time: *dont* (of which, whose, about which), *ce
qui* and *ce que* (what, the thing that). This lesson is a B1 preview: learn to recognise
them and try them in simple sentences. Nothing here is needed for the DELF A2, and you'll study
them properly at B1.

The theme is objects with a story: things you keep, inherit, use and remember.

## Why qui and que aren't always enough

Lesson 10's test was: a verb after the gap → *qui*; a subject after the gap → *que*. That works
when the noun is the subject or the direct object. But many French verbs take *de* before their
object:

| verb + de | example |
|---|---|
| *parler de* — to talk about | *Je parle de ce livre.* |
| *avoir besoin de* — to need | *J'ai besoin de cet outil.* |
| *se souvenir de* — to remember | *Je me souviens de ce jour.* |
| *avoir peur de* — to be afraid of | *Il a peur du grenier.* |
| *être fier de* — to be proud of | *Elle est fière de sa bague.* |
| *se servir de* — to use, make use of | *Je me sers de ce couteau.* |
| *se passer de* — to do without | *Je ne peux pas me passer de mon portable.* |
| *se moquer de* — to make fun of | *Ils se moquent de lui.* |
| *avoir honte de* — to be ashamed of | *Il a honte de sa voiture.* |
| *profiter de* — to make the most of | *On profite du soleil.* |
| *hériter de* — to inherit | *J'ai hérité de cette montre.* |

You can't join these with *que*, because *ce livre* isn't the direct object of *parler*: the verb
needs *de* in front of it (*de ce livre*). French has a special relative for *de* + noun: *dont*.

## dont: replacing de + a noun

*Dont* replaces *de* + the antecedent. It works for people and things:

- *Je parle de ce livre.* → *C'est le livre dont je parle.* — It's the book I'm talking about.
- *J'ai besoin de cet outil.* → *Voici l'outil dont j'ai besoin.* — Here's the tool I need.
- *Je me souviens de ce jour.* → *C'est un jour dont je me souviens.* — It's a day I remember.
- *Ils se moquent de ce garçon.* → *C'est le garçon dont ils se moquent.* — the boy they make fun of.

Notice that English often leaves the preposition at the end ("the book I'm talking about").
French moves it to the front, inside *dont*.

### dont + a noun: whose

*Dont* also replaces *de* in front of a noun, where English says "whose" or "of which":

- *J'ai un ami. Le père de cet ami est pilote.* → *J'ai un ami dont le père est pilote.* — I've
  got a friend whose father is a pilot.
- *C'est un roman. J'ai oublié le titre de ce roman.* → *C'est un roman dont j'ai oublié le
  titre.* — It's a novel whose title I've forgotten.

The word order after *dont* is the normal order: subject, verb, object. *dont j'ai oublié le
titre*, never *dont le titre j'ai oublié*.

### Example 1: joining two sentences with dont

*Join: "Voici la bague. Ma grand-mère était très fière de cette bague."*

1. Find the shared noun: *la bague* / *cette bague*.
2. Look at how it's used in the second sentence: *fière de cette bague*. There is *de*, so
   the relative is *dont*.
3. Put *dont* straight after the antecedent and keep the rest in normal order: *Voici la bague
   dont ma grand-mère était très fière.*

Result: *Voici la bague dont ma grand-mère était très fière.* — Here's the ring my grandmother
was very proud of.

A second one: *"C'est un outil. Mon grand-père se servait de cet outil."* → *de cet outil* →
*C'est un outil dont mon grand-père se servait.* — It's a tool my grandfather used.

Check yourself with the verb: *aimer quelque chose* takes no preposition, so *le livre que
j'aime*; *parler de quelque chose* takes *de*, so *le livre dont je parle*. The verb decides, not
the noun.

## ce qui, ce que: what, the thing that

Sometimes there's no noun to describe: you mean "what" in the sense of "the thing that". French
puts *ce* (the thing) in front of *qui* or *que*, and the choice works exactly as in lesson 10:

| | followed by | example |
|---|---|---|
| *ce qui* | a verb (*ce* is the subject) | *Ce qui me plaît, c'est le calme.* — What I like is the quiet. |
| *ce que / ce qu'* | a subject + verb (*ce* is the object) | *Ce que j'aime, c'est la mer.* — What I love is the sea. |

Both are very common at the start of a sentence, followed by *c'est*: it's how French puts
something in the spotlight.

- *Ce qui est difficile, c'est la grammaire.* — What's difficult is the grammar.
- *Ce que je préfère, c'est le dimanche matin.* — What I like best is Sunday morning.
- *Je ne comprends pas ce qu'il dit.* — I don't understand what he's saying.
- *Prends ce que tu veux.* — Take what(ever) you want.
- *Tout ce qui brille n'est pas or.* — All that glitters is not gold. (a proverb; *briller* = to shine)

*Ce dont* exists too, for verbs with *de*: *Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est d'un café.* — What I need
is a coffee.

You will meet *ce que* and *ce qui* again in lesson 19, in indirect questions (*Dites-moi ce que
vous voulez*). The words are the same; there they report a question.

### Example 2: ce qui or ce que?

*Complete: "___ m'intéresse, c'est l'histoire." and "___ je cherche, c'est un cadeau."*

1. Cover the gap and look right. *___ m'intéresse*: after the gap comes *m'intéresse*, a pronoun
   and a verb. There is no subject, so "the thing" is the subject: *ce qui*.
2. *___ je cherche*: after the gap comes *je*, a subject. "The thing" is the object of *chercher*:
   *ce que*.

Results: *Ce qui m'intéresse, c'est l'histoire.* — What interests me is history. *Ce que je
cherche, c'est un cadeau.* — What I'm looking for is a present.

The trap: *me, te, le, lui …* before a verb are object pronouns, not subjects. *Ce qui me plaît*:
the subject is *ce*; *me* is "to me".

## Reading: Le grenier de ma grand-mère

> L'été dernier, nous avons vidé la maison de ma grand-mère. Le grenier, c'était l'endroit dont j'avais peur quand j'étais petite : il était sombre et plein de vieux cartons. Mais cette fois, j'y ai trouvé des trésors.
>
> D'abord, une boîte d'outils. Ce sont les outils dont mon grand-père se servait pour tout réparer : les vélos, les chaises, la radio… Mon frère les a gardés, parce qu'il adore bricoler.
>
> Ensuite, un roman dont j'avais oublié le titre, mais dont je me souvenais très bien. Ma grand-mère me le lisait le soir. Le personnage principal est une petite fille dont les autres enfants se moquent, mais qui devient très courageuse. Ce que j'aimais dans cette histoire, c'était la fin.
>
> Enfin, au fond d'un tiroir, une bague en or : la bague dont ma grand-mère était si fière. C'était un cadeau de son père. Ce n'est pas un objet très précieux, mais c'est moi qui en ai hérité, et je ne vais jamais la vendre.
>
> Ce qui me touche, quand je regarde ces objets, c'est qu'ils racontent une vie. Ma grand-mère n'avait pas beaucoup d'argent, mais elle savait profiter de tout. Elle n'avait jamais honte de sa vieille cuisine. Elle disait : « On peut se passer de beaucoup de choses, mais pas de ses amis. »

Glosses: *vider* = to empty; *sombre* = dark; *plein de* = full of; *le carton* = cardboard box;
*le trésor* = treasure; *le titre* = title; *principal* = main; *devenir* = to become;
*courageux* = brave; *au fond de* = at the back of; *le tiroir* = drawer; *la bague* = ring; *si*
= so; *j'en ai hérité* = I inherited it (*en* = *de cette bague*); *toucher* = to touch, to move
(emotionally); *raconter* = to tell; *savoir* + infinitive = to know how to.

In English:

> Last summer we emptied my grandmother's house. The attic was the place I was afraid of when I was little: it was dark and full of old boxes. But this time I found treasures there.
>
> First, a box of tools. They're the tools my grandfather used to repair everything: bikes, chairs, the radio… My brother kept them, because he loves DIY.
>
> Then a novel whose title I'd forgotten, but which I remembered very well. My grandmother used to read it to me in the evenings. The main character is a little girl the other children make fun of, but who becomes very brave. What I loved in that story was the ending.
>
> Finally, at the back of a drawer, a gold ring: the ring my grandmother was so proud of. It was a present from her father. It isn't a very valuable object, but I'm the one who inherited it, and I'm never going to sell it.
>
> What moves me, when I look at these objects, is that they tell the story of a life. My grandmother didn't have much money, but she knew how to make the most of everything. She was never ashamed of her old kitchen. She used to say: "You can do without lots of things, but not without your friends."

Every *dont* in the text replaces *de* + a noun: *avoir peur de l'endroit, se servir des outils,
le titre du roman, se souvenir du roman, se moquer de la fille, être fière de la bague*.

### Example 3: qui, que, où or dont?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing qui, que, où or dont
  accDescr: Look at how the noun is used in the second sentence. If it is the place or time where or when something happens, use où. If the verb takes de before it, use dont. If it is the subject, so a verb follows the gap, use qui. If it is the direct object, so a subject follows the gap, use que.
  A["How is the noun used in the second sentence?"] --> B["a place or a time: in it, then"]
  A --> C["after de: parler de, avoir besoin de"]
  A --> D["the subject: a verb follows"]
  A --> E["the direct object: a subject follows"]
  B --> F["où"]
  C --> G["dont"]
  D --> H["qui"]
  E --> I["que / qu'"]
```


*Choose the relative: "C'est la maison ___ j'ai grandi." / "C'est la maison ___ je rêve." / "C'est
la maison ___ mes parents ont achetée." / "C'est la maison ___ est au bout de la rue."*

1. *grandir dans la maison* → a place, "in it": *où*. *C'est la maison où j'ai grandi.*
2. *rêver de la maison* → *de*: *dont*. *C'est la maison dont je rêve.* — the house I dream of.
3. *acheter la maison* → direct object, subject *mes parents* follows: *que*. *C'est la maison
   que mes parents ont achetée* (agreement after *que*, lesson 10).
4. *la maison est au bout de la rue* → subject, a verb follows: *qui*. *C'est la maison qui est
   au bout de la rue.*

### Beyond: lequel after a preposition

After other prepositions (*avec, sur, dans, pour* …), French usually uses *qui* for people and
*lequel* (*laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles*) for things: *l'ami avec qui je travaille, la table sur
laquelle j'écris*. This is B1 material: recognise it when you read, but you don't need to make
it yet. At A2, *où* often does the job for places: *la boîte où je range mes photos*.

## Words for this lesson

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *le grenier* | attic (a word from honors lesson 04h1) |
| *l'outil* (m) | tool |
| *garder* | to keep |
| *précieux, précieuse* | precious, valuable |
| *le roman, le personnage* | novel, character (in a story) |
| *se servir de* | to use, to make use of |
| *se passer de* | to do without |
| *se moquer de* | to make fun of |
| *avoir honte (de)* | to be ashamed (of) |
| *profiter de* | to make the most of, to enjoy |
| *hériter (de)* | to inherit |

*Le roman* is a novel; a romance is *une histoire d'amour*. *Le caractère* (A1) is someone's
personality; *le personnage* is a character in a book or film.

## Common mistakes

- *le livre que je parle* → *le livre dont je parle* (*parler de*).
- *l'outil que j'ai besoin* → *l'outil dont j'ai besoin* (*avoir besoin de*).
- *un ami dont son père est pilote* → *dont le père*: *dont* already means "of whom", so no
  possessive.
- *le roman dont j'en parle* → *dont je parle*: *dont* already contains the *de*; don't add *en*.
- *Ce que me plaît* → *Ce qui me plaît*: *me* is not a subject.
- *Qu'est-ce que j'aime, c'est la mer* → *Ce que j'aime, c'est la mer*: *qu'est-ce que* asks a
  question.

## Key points

- *dont* = *de* + antecedent: *le livre dont je parle* (*parler de*), *l'outil dont j'ai besoin*.
- *dont* + noun = whose: *un ami dont le père est pilote*. Normal word order after it.
- The verb decides: no preposition → *que*; *de* → *dont*; place or time → *où*.
- *ce qui* + verb, *ce que* + subject = what (the thing that): *Ce qui me plaît, c'est …*; *Ce que
  j'aime, c'est …*.
- *lequel* after a preposition is B1: recognise it only.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Paris, Lyon, Marseille: comparing cities
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 9 taught you to compare: *plus grand que, la ville la plus animée, la meilleure cuisine*.
This lesson uses those patterns on real facts about France's three biggest cities, Paris,
Marseille and Lyon. You'll read a short travel guide, learn how French cities are organised
(*arrondissements*, *métropoles*), work with real population figures, and add a few ways to
make comparisons more precise: *deux fois plus*, *beaucoup moins*, *de loin*.

All the figures come from official French sources and are dated. Population figures change a
little every year, so always look at the date.

## Three cities on the map

![A simplified outline map of mainland France with four cities marked by dots: Paris in the north, Lyon in the east-centre, Marseille on the Mediterranean coast in the south-east, and Toulouse in the south-west. The Mediterranean Sea is shaded at the bottom right.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The three cities are far apart: Paris in the north, on the Seine; Lyon in the east, where the
Rhône and the Saône meet; Marseille in the south, on the Mediterranean.

## How many people? Reading the figures

France counts its people through INSEE, the national statistics office. The census (*le
recensement*) is now done a little every year, and each December INSEE publishes the official
population of every *commune* (town or city). The figures published in December 2025 describe
the population on 1 January 2023 and became the legal figures on 1 January 2026.

| city (commune) | population, 1 January 2023 | area | people per km² (rounded) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paris | 2 103 778 | 105.4 km² | about 20 000 |
| Marseille | 886 040 | 240.6 km² | about 3 700 |
| Lyon | 519 127 | 47.9 km² | about 10 800 |
| Toulouse | 514 819 | 118.3 km² | about 4 400 |

![A bar chart of the 2023 population of four French cities: Paris 2,103,778, Marseille 886,040, Lyon 519,127 and Toulouse 514,819. Source: INSEE, populations de référence au 1er janvier 2023.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

French writes big numbers with a space between groups of three (*2 103 778*) and a comma for
decimals (*105,4 km²*, said *cent cinq virgule quatre kilomètres carrés*). *Km²* is read
*kilomètres carrés*.

Two surprises in this table:

- Lyon is only just third. Toulouse has only about 4 300 fewer people, and between 2017 and
  2023 Toulouse grew much faster (INSEE: about 1.2 % a year, against 0.1 % for Lyon). Paris,
  meanwhile, lost people over the same years.
- Marseille is bigger than Paris on the map. The commune of Marseille covers more than twice
  the area of the commune of Paris, because it includes hills, beaches and the *calanques*
  (rocky inlets). So Paris is far more densely populated (*plus densément peuplé*).

These are the figures for the *commune* only, the city inside its official boundary. Around each
city there are suburbs (*la banlieue*) where many more people live.

## Arrondissements and métropoles

The three biggest cities are divided into numbered districts called *arrondissements*: *le 5e
arrondissement* (*le cinquième*), or just *le 5e*. Paris has 20, Marseille 16 and Lyon 9. In Lyon
each one has its own town hall (*mairie d'arrondissement*); in Marseille they are paired into eight
sectors, each with a town hall (*mairie de secteur*).

In Paris the numbers turn in a spiral, like a snail's shell, starting in the centre: the Louvre is
in the 1st, and the 20th is in the east. A 2017 law grouped the first four into one
sector, called *Paris Centre*, with one town hall; the others each have their own. Parisians often give their address by arrondissement: *J'habite
dans le 11e.* Postcodes show it too: *75011* is the 11th.

A *métropole* is a group of communes that work together on transport, housing, roads and so on.
The three cities each have one:

| métropole | created | size |
|---|---|---|
| *la Métropole de Lyon* | 1 January 2015 | about 1.4 million people; it also does the work of a *département* |
| *la Métropole du Grand Paris* | 1 January 2016 | 131 communes, more than 7 million people |
| *la Métropole d'Aix-Marseille-Provence* | 1 January 2016 | 92 communes, about 1.9 million people |

## Making comparisons more precise

Lesson 9's patterns become sharper with a few extra words. You need them to read numbers like
the ones above.

| French | English | example |
|---|---|---|
| *beaucoup plus / moins* | much more / less | *Paris est beaucoup plus peuplé que Marseille.* |
| *un peu plus / moins* | a bit more / less | *Lyon est un peu plus peuplé que Toulouse.* |
| *presque aussi … que* | almost as … as | *Toulouse est presque aussi peuplée que Lyon.* |
| *deux fois plus (de) … que* | twice as (many) … as | *Paris a deux fois plus d'habitants que Lyon.* |
| *de loin* | by far | *Paris est de loin la plus grande ville de France.* |

Paris has about four times as many people as Lyon, so *deux fois plus* is true but weak; *quatre
fois plus d'habitants* is more exact. In area it's the other way round: *Marseille est plus de deux
fois plus grande que Paris* (about 240 km² against 105 km²).

City names have no fixed gender. Paris and Lyon are usually masculine (*Paris est grand*); names
ending in *-e*, like Marseille and Toulouse, are often feminine (*Marseille est grande*). You'll
see both, and with *la ville* there's no doubt: *Paris est une ville chère*.

### Example 1: from figures to sentences

*Using the table, compare Paris and Marseille (population), then Marseille and Lyon.*

1. Paris: 2 103 778; Marseille: 886 040. Paris has more people: *Paris a plus d'habitants que
   Marseille.*
2. How many times more? 2 103 778 ÷ 886 040 ≈ 2.4. So more than twice as many: *Paris a plus de
   deux fois plus d'habitants que Marseille.*
3. Marseille: 886 040; Lyon: 519 127. 886 040 ÷ 519 127 ≈ 1.7. Not twice: *Marseille a beaucoup
   plus d'habitants que Lyon*, or *Lyon est moins peuplé que Marseille.*

Note *plus d'habitants* (a noun: *plus de*) but *plus peuplé* (an adjective: *plus*).

### Example 2: a superlative from a table

*Which city in the table is the most densely populated, and which the least?*

1. Compare the last column: Paris about 20 000 people per km², Lyon about 10 800, Toulouse about
   4 400, Marseille about 3 700.
2. The highest number: Paris. *Peuplé* follows the noun, so the article comes twice: *Paris est
   la ville la plus densément peuplée du tableau.*
3. The lowest: Marseille. *Marseille est la ville la moins densément peuplée du tableau.*
4. "In the table" is *du tableau* (*de* after a superlative, lesson 9).

(*densément* = densely, from *dense*: an exception with *é*, like *énormément* in lesson 12.)

## Reading: three cities in a few lines

This is an original short guide, written in the style of a travel website.

> *Paris, la Ville Lumière.* C'est la capitale et, de loin, la ville la plus peuplée de France. Ses monuments sont parmi les plus connus du monde. Paris est plus cher et plus stressant que les autres villes, disent ses visiteurs. Mais on y trouve des musées pour tous les goûts, et le soir, ses quartiers sont parmi les plus animés du pays.
>
> *Marseille, la cité phocéenne.* Marseille est la plus ancienne des trois : des marins grecs venus de Phocée l'ont fondée vers 600 avant Jésus-Christ, d'où son surnom. C'est un grand port sur la Méditerranée, beaucoup plus ensoleillé que Paris et, dit-on, plus détendu. Sur une colline, la basilique Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde, que les Marseillais appellent « la Bonne Mère », regarde la ville. Les supporters de foot remplissent le stade Vélodrome les soirs de match.
>
> *Lyon, entre Rhône et Saône.* Lyon est plus petit que Marseille, mais beaucoup plus dense. Le Rhône et la Saône s'y rejoignent. Son centre historique est inscrit au patrimoine mondial de l'UNESCO depuis 1998. Sur la colline de Fourvière, une autre basilique domine la ville. Pour beaucoup de Français, Lyon est la capitale de la gastronomie : on y mange dans les *bouchons*, de petits restaurants traditionnels. Et pour circuler, le tramway et le métro sont plus pratiques que la voiture.

Glosses: *la lumière* = light; *parmi* = among; *stressant* = stressful;
*pour tous les goûts* = for every taste; *le marin* = sailor; *grec* = Greek; *fonder* = to found; *d'où* = hence;
*dit-on* = people say; *détendu* = relaxed; *remplir* = to fill; *le match* = (football) match; *se rejoindre* = to meet
(rivers); *inscrit au patrimoine mondial* = listed as World Heritage; *dominer* = to overlook;
*circuler* = to get around.

Find the superlatives (*la ville la plus peuplée de France, parmi les plus connus du monde, parmi
les plus animés du pays, la plus ancienne des trois*) and the comparatives (*plus cher et plus
stressant que, beaucoup plus ensoleillé que, plus détendu, plus petit que, beaucoup plus dense,
plus pratiques que*).

The facts behind the text, checked: Marseille was founded around 600 BC by Greek sailors from
Phocaea (in today's Turkey), which is why it's nicknamed *la cité phocéenne* (Lyon was founded by
the Romans in 43 BC); Marseille had about 2 950 hours of sunshine in 2024 and Paris about 1 500
(Météo-France); and the Historic Site of Lyon was added to UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1998.
The other statements (*plus cher, plus stressant, plus détendu, la capitale de la gastronomie*)
are opinions and reputations, which the text marks with *disent ses visiteurs*, *dit-on* and *pour
beaucoup de Français*.

### Example 3: write your own comparison

*Write three sentences comparing two of the cities, with one figure, one superlative and one
opinion.*

1. A figure, with a comparative: *Lyon a moins d'habitants que Marseille (519 127 contre 886 040
   en 2023).* (*contre* = against, compared with.)
2. A superlative, with *de*: *Paris est la ville la plus peuplée de France.*
3. An opinion, marked as one: *À mon avis, Marseille est plus agréable en hiver, parce qu'il fait
   plus doux.* (*à mon avis* = in my opinion; lesson 21 teaches more ways.)

## Rivalries: a generalisation

The French like to tease each other about their cities, and the jokes are part of everyday
culture. These are stereotypes, not facts, and many people on all sides find them silly.

- Many people outside Paris joke that Parisians are always in a hurry, stressed and a bit snobbish.
  Parisians joke back that everything outside Paris is *la province*, a word that can sound
  condescending.
- Marseille has a reputation for exaggeration and big talk, often teased with a story about a
  sardine that blocked the port. People from Marseille reply that they simply enjoy life more.
- The football rivalry between Paris and Marseille is the most famous in France: matches between
  the two clubs are called *le Classique*.
- Lyon and Marseille argue about which is France's "second city". Counting the people in the
  commune, it's Marseille; many Lyonnais answer with their food.

Talking about rivalries is a good way to practise comparatives, but keep it light: *On dit que les
Parisiens sont plus pressés, mais ce n'est pas toujours vrai.* (*pressé* = in a hurry.)

## Words for this lesson

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *l'arrondissement* (m) | district (of Paris, Lyon or Marseille) |
| *la métropole* | metropolitan authority, big city |
| *le recensement* | census |
| *la superficie, le kilomètre carré* | area, square kilometre |
| *peuplé* | populated |
| *le port, le stade, le tramway* | port, stadium, tram |
| *le monument, la basilique* | monument, basilica |
| *historique, le patrimoine* | historic, heritage |
| *la gastronomie* | gastronomy, fine food |
| *connu* | well-known |
| *le surnom* | nickname |
| *la rivalité* | rivalry |

*Le surnom* is a false friend: it is a nickname, not a surname (*le nom de famille*).

## Common mistakes

- *Paris est la plus grande ville en France.* → *de France*.
- *Paris a plus habitants que Lyon.* → *plus d'habitants*.
- *Marseille est deux fois plus grande de Paris.* → *que Paris*.
- *Paris est plus peuplé de Marseille.* → *que Marseille*.
- *2,103,778* → *2 103 778* in French; *105.4* → *105,4*.
- *le 5ème* / *le 5e*: both are seen; the official abbreviation is *5e*.

## Key points

- Official populations come from INSEE's census (*le recensement*); the figures in force from 1
  January 2026 describe 1 January 2023: Paris 2 103 778, Marseille 886 040, Lyon 519 127.
- *Arrondissements*: Paris 20, Marseille 16, Lyon 9. *Métropoles*: Lyon (2015), Grand Paris and
  Aix-Marseille-Provence (2016).
- Sharper comparisons: *beaucoup plus, un peu moins, presque aussi … que, deux fois plus (de) …
  que, de loin*.
- Reputations and rivalries are generalisations: say so (*on dit que, pour beaucoup de Français*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: En marchant: the gérondif
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 12 showed how to say *how* you do something with an adverb: *Il travaille sérieusement.*
French has a second way, very common in speech and writing: *en* + a verb form ending in *-ant*.

- *Je travaille en écoutant de la musique.* — I work while listening to music.
- *On apprend une langue en la pratiquant.* — You learn a language by practising it.

This form is the **[[gérondif]]**. It sits on the line between A2 and B1: some A2 courses teach it,
others leave it for B1, and it isn't part of this course's core grammar. Learn to understand it
and to make it with common verbs; it is not drilled in this course.

The theme is learning a language: habits, methods, podcasts and subtitles.

## Making the present participle

The *-ant* form is the **[[present participle]]**. You build it like the imparfait (lesson 1): take
the *nous* form of the present, remove *-ons*, and add *-ant*.

| infinitive | nous present | present participle |
|---|---|---|
| *parler* | *nous parlons* | *parlant* |
| *finir* | *nous finissons* | *finissant* |
| *prendre* | *nous prenons* | *prenant* |
| *faire* | *nous faisons* | *faisant* |
| *lire* | *nous lisons* | *lisant* |
| *boire* | *nous buvons* | *buvant* |
| *conduire* | *nous conduisons* | *conduisant* |
| *manger* | *nous mangeons* | *mangeant* |
| *commencer* | *nous commençons* | *commençant* |

The *-ger* and *-cer* verbs keep their *e* and *ç* (*mangeant, commençant*), because *-ant*
starts with *a*, just as in *nous mangeons*.

Only three common verbs break the rule:

| infinitive | present participle |
|---|---|
| *être* | *étant* |
| *avoir* | *ayant* |
| *savoir* | *sachant* |

The present participle never changes in the gérondif: no agreement, no endings for persons.

### Example 1: building a gérondif

*Make the gérondif of "écrire", "voir" and "se lever" (with je).*

1. *écrire*: *nous écrivons* → remove *-ons*: *écriv-* → add *-ant*: *écrivant* → *en écrivant*.
2. *voir*: *nous voyons* → *voy-* → *voyant* → *en voyant*.
3. *se lever*: *nous nous levons* → *lev-* → *levant*. A reflexive verb keeps its pronoun, which
   matches the subject of the sentence: *je … en me levant*, *tu … en te levant*, *il … en se
   levant*.

So: *Je me suis fait mal en me levant.* — I hurt myself (while) getting up.

## The gérondif: en + present participle

Put *en* in front of the present participle. The gérondif always refers to the subject of the
main verb: the same person does both things.

![A timeline with two parallel arrows for the same person. The upper arrow, labelled the main verb, says Je prends mon petit-déjeuner. The lower arrow, labelled en plus the present participle, says en écoutant la radio. Both arrows run over the same stretch of time, showing that the two actions happen at once. Underneath: same subject, same time.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

It has three main jobs.

### 1. Two things at the same time

*En* + *-ant* says that the subject does something while doing something else:

- *Je prends mon petit-déjeuner en écoutant la radio.* — I have breakfast while listening to the radio.
- *Il siffle en travaillant.* — He whistles while he works.
- *Ne téléphone pas en conduisant !* — Don't phone while (you're) driving!

*Tout en* stresses that the two things happen together, often with a hint of contrast: *Elle
révise tout en regardant la télé.* — She revises while watching TV (at the same time).

### 2. How: by doing

The gérondif answers *comment ?* (how?), like an adverb:

- *On apprend en pratiquant.* — You learn by practising.
- *J'ai progressé en regardant des séries avec les sous-titres.* — I made progress by watching
  series with subtitles.
- *Elle est partie en pleurant.* — She left in tears (crying).

### 3. When: on doing, as you do

With verbs like *arriver, sortir, entrer, ouvrir*, the gérondif often means "when, as soon as":

- *En arrivant à la gare, j'ai vu que le train était parti.* — When I got to the station, I saw
  that the train had left.
- *En ouvrant la porte, il a trouvé un colis.* — On opening the door, he found a parcel.

(*était parti*, "had left", is the plus-que-parfait, a B1 tense: just recognise it.)

## Same subject, always

The gérondif and the main verb share their subject. This is the rule English speakers break most:

- *J'ai vu Paul en sortant du métro.* — I saw Paul as I came out of the metro. (I came out.)
- To say that *Paul* came out, use another structure: *J'ai vu Paul qui sortait du métro.*

A sentence like *En arrivant, le chien m'a sauté dessus* (*sauter dessus* = to jump on) means that the dog arrived. If you
arrived, say *Quand je suis arrivé, le chien m'a sauté dessus.* (A few old proverbs break the
rule, such as *L'appétit vient en mangeant*, "appetite comes with eating", but don't copy them.)

### Example 2: joining two sentences

*Join with a gérondif: "Je conduis. J'écoute des podcasts."* and *"Marie lit. Son frère fait la
cuisine."*

1. First pair: same subject (*je*). Choose the main action: *Je conduis*. Turn the other one into
   a gérondif: *écouter → nous écoutons → écoutant*. Result: *J'écoute des podcasts en
   conduisant* or *Je conduis en écoutant des podcasts.* Both are correct; the gérondif carries
   the background action.
2. Second pair: two subjects (*Marie, son frère*). A gérondif is impossible. Use *pendant que*
   (while, lesson 2): *Marie lit pendant que son frère fait la cuisine.*

## Not every English -ing is a gérondif

English uses *-ing* for many things. French uses the gérondif only for "while / by / on doing",
with the same subject. Elsewhere it uses other forms you already know:

| English | French | not |
|---|---|---|
| I am reading. | *Je lis.* (or *Je suis en train de lire*, lesson 4) | *Je suis lisant.* |
| I like reading. | *J'aime lire.* (infinitive) | *J'aime lisant.* |
| Swimming is good for you. | *Nager, c'est bon pour la santé.* | *Nageant est bon.* |
| before leaving | *avant de partir* | *avant partant* |
| without saying anything | *sans rien dire* (*sans* + infinitive) | *sans disant* |
| I'm thinking of moving. | *Je pense déménager.* (*déménager* = to move house) | *Je pense en déménageant.* |
| He learned by listening. | *Il a appris en écoutant.* | — this one is a gérondif |

The quick test: can you say "while" or "by" in English? If yes, the gérondif is likely. If the
*-ing* word is a subject, an object or follows a preposition other than "by / while / on",
French uses an infinitive or another verb form.

### Example 3: gérondif or not?

*Translate: (a) "She learned French by watching films." (b) "I hate waiting." (c) "He fell while
running." (d) "Thanks for helping me."*

1. (a) "by watching": the same subject, "by" → gérondif: *Elle a appris le français en regardant
   des films.*
2. (b) "waiting" is the object of "hate" → infinitive: *Je déteste attendre.*
3. (c) "while running", same subject → gérondif: *Il est tombé en courant.*
4. (d) "for helping": after *merci de*, French uses an infinitive (here the past infinitive is
   common, B1: *Merci de m'avoir aidé*). At A2, *Merci pour ton aide* says the same.

## Reading: Comment j'ai appris le français

Emma is from Leeds. She wrote this on a language-learning forum.

> J'ai commencé le français à 35 ans, sans professeur. Ma méthode ? Apprendre en faisant autre chose. Le matin, mon trajet en bus dure quarante minutes : j'écoute des podcasts en français avec mon casque. Au début, je ne comprenais rien ! Mais en écoutant tous les jours, j'ai progressé.
>
> Le soir, je regarde des séries françaises. D'abord, je mettais les sous-titres en anglais, puis en français. C'est la manière la plus efficace de mémoriser des mots : on les entend et on les voit à la fois.
>
> J'ai aussi pris une habitude un peu bizarre : je parle toute seule en faisant la cuisine. Je décris ce que je fais, en même temps que je le fais. Mon mari me trouve drôle, mais mon français s'améliore. Et le dimanche, je pratique avec une voisine française en promenant le chien.
>
> Mon conseil : n'attendez pas d'avoir le temps. On apprend une langue en la parlant, pas en la regardant dans un livre !

Glosses: *autre chose* = something else; *durer* = to last; *au début* = at first; *efficace* =
effective; *entendre* = to hear; *bizarre* = strange; *tout(e) seul(e)* = all alone; *décrire* =
to describe; *en même temps que* = at the same time as; *promener le chien* = to walk the dog;
*n'attendez pas d'avoir* = don't wait until you have.

In English:

> I started French at 35, without a teacher. My method? Learn while doing something else. In the morning my bus journey lasts forty minutes: I listen to French podcasts on my headphones. At first I didn't understand a thing! But by listening every day, I made progress.
>
> In the evening I watch French series. First I used to put the subtitles in English, then in French. It's the most effective way to memorise words: you hear them and see them at the same time.
>
> I've also got into a slightly strange habit: I talk to myself while cooking. I describe what I'm doing, at the same time as I'm doing it. My husband finds me funny, but my French is getting better. And on Sundays I practise with a French neighbour while walking the dog.
>
> My advice: don't wait until you have time. You learn a language by speaking it, not by looking at it in a book!

Find the six gérondifs (*en faisant autre chose, en écoutant tous les jours, en faisant la
cuisine, en promenant le chien, en la parlant, en la regardant*). *En même temps que* and *à la
fois* say "at the same time" without one, and *en français* is just the preposition *en*. Notice the
object pronoun goes between *en* and the participle: *en la parlant*.

## Words for this lesson

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *la méthode, la manière* | method, way (manner) |
| *l'habitude* (f) | habit (*d'habitude*, A1 = usually) |
| *progresser, s'améliorer* | to make progress, to get better |
| *pratiquer, mémoriser* | to practise, to memorise |
| *le trajet* | journey (the trip from A to B) |
| *le podcast, le casque* | podcast, headphones (also: helmet) |
| *les sous-titres* (m) | subtitles |
| *conduire, siffler* | to drive, to whistle |
| *en même temps, à la fois* | at the same time |

*Conduire* is irregular: *je conduis, nous conduisons, ils conduisent*; *j'ai conduit*.
*À la fois* also means "both": *C'est à la fois simple et efficace.*

## Common mistakes

- *En sortant, la pluie a commencé.* (if you mean that *you* went out) → *Quand je suis sorti, la
  pluie a commencé.* The gérondif needs the same subject as the main verb.
- *en étant* / *en ayant* / *en sachant*: not *en êtant*, *en avant*, *en savant*.
- *en mangant, en commencant* → *en mangeant, en commençant*.
- *Je suis lisant* → *Je lis*. French has no *être* + *-ant* tense.
- *J'aime en lisant* → *J'aime lire*.
- *en se levant* with *je* → *en me levant*: the reflexive pronoun matches the subject.

## Key points

- Present participle: *nous* present − *-ons* + *-ant* (*parlant, finissant, faisant,
  mangeant*). Irregular: *étant, ayant, sachant*.
- Gérondif = *en* + present participle: while (*en écoutant*), by (*en pratiquant*), on / when
  (*en arrivant*). *Tout en* stresses "at the same time".
- Same subject as the main verb, always. Two subjects → *pendant que* or *quand*.
- English *-ing* is often an infinitive in French (*j'aime lire, avant de partir, sans dire*).
- A2/B1 boundary: understand it, use it with common verbs; it isn't drilled.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: What will happen: the futur simple
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Since A1 you have talked about the future with *aller* + infinitive, the futur proche: *Je vais
partir.* Lesson 04 put it on a timeline next to *venir de* and *être en train de*. This module is
about plans, wishes and the future, and it starts with the second way French talks about what
will happen: the **[[futur simple]]** (*je partirai*, I will leave). It is one word, not two, and it
is the tense of predictions (*Il fera beau demain*), promises (*Je t'appellerai*) and plans
further ahead (*Un jour, j'aurai une maison*).

The futur simple also prepares lesson 14. The conditionnel (*je partirais*, I would leave) is built
on exactly the same stem, so every stem you learn here gives you two tenses.

## Building the futur simple

Take the infinitive and add the endings *-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont*. Verbs in *-re* drop
their final *e* first: *prendre → prendr-*.

| | parler | finir | prendre |
|---|---|---|---|
| je | parler*ai* | finir*ai* | prendr*ai* |
| tu | parler*as* | finir*as* | prendr*as* |
| il / elle / on | parler*a* | finir*a* | prendr*a* |
| nous | parler*ons* | finir*ons* | prendr*ons* |
| vous | parler*ez* | finir*ez* | prendr*ez* |
| ils / elles | parler*ont* | finir*ont* | prendr*ont* |

Two memory hooks:

- The endings are the present of *avoir*: *j'ai, tu as, il a, nous (av)ons, vous (av)ez, ils
  ont*.
