- Every futur form has an *r* just before the ending. That *r* is the sound of the future:
  *je parle* (now), *je parlerai* (later).

![A builder chart for the futur simple. On the left, three infinitives: parler, finir and prendre, with the final e of prendre crossed out. A plus sign, then the six endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont, with a note that they are the present of avoir. On the right, the results: je parlerai, tu finiras, il prendra, nous parlerons, vous finirez, ils prendront.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Je partirai à huit heures.* — I'll leave at eight.
- *Tu finiras ton travail après le dîner.* — You'll finish your work after dinner.
- *Nous prendrons le train de 9 h 15.* — We'll take the 9.15 train.
- *Mes parents dormiront à l'hôtel.* — My parents will sleep at the hotel.
- *Je me lèverai tôt demain.* — I'll get up early tomorrow. (Reflexive verbs keep their pronoun:
  *je me lèverai, nous nous lèverons*.)

The negative goes round the one verb, as in the present: *Je ne partirai pas. Il ne pleuvra
pas.*

## The irregular stems

A small group of very common verbs have an **[[irregular stem]]** in the futur. The endings never change:
only the stem is new, and every stem still ends in *r*.

| verb | future stem | futur (je) |
|---|---|---|
| être | ser- | je serai |
| avoir | aur- | j'aurai |
| aller | ir- | j'irai |
| faire | fer- | je ferai |
| venir, revenir, devenir | viendr-, reviendr-, deviendr- | je viendrai, je deviendrai |
| pouvoir | pourr- | je pourrai |
| vouloir | voudr- | je voudrai |
| devoir | devr- | je devrai |
| savoir | saur- | je saurai |
| voir | verr- | je verrai |
| envoyer | enverr- | j'enverrai |
| recevoir | recevr- | je recevrai |
| il faut (falloir) | faudr- | il faudra |
| il pleut (pleuvoir) | pleuvr- | il pleuvra |

*Mourir* (A1) also has a double *r*: *il mourra*.

![A wheel of irregular future stems. In the centre: same endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. Around it, twelve segments, each with an infinitive and its stem: être ser-, avoir aur-, aller ir-, faire fer-, venir viendr-, devenir deviendr-, pouvoir pourr-, vouloir voudr-, devoir devr-, savoir saur-, voir verr-, envoyer enverr-.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Grouping them helps:

- double *r*: *pourr-, verr-, enverr-* (and *mourr-*);
- *-dr-*: *viendr-, voudr-* (and *faudr-*);
- *-vr-*: *devr-, recevr-* (and *pleuvr-*);
- short and odd: *ser-, aur-, ir-, fer-, saur-*.

Examples:

- *Demain, il fera beau.* — Tomorrow the weather will be nice.
- *Je serai à la maison vers 18 heures.* — I'll be home around 6 p.m.
- *Samedi, nous irons à la plage.* — On Saturday we'll go to the beach.
- *Il faudra partir tôt.* — We'll have to leave early.
- *On verra !* — We'll see! (a very common answer when you don't want to decide yet)

## -er verbs that change their spelling

An *-er* verb that changes its spelling in the *je* form of the present (A1 lesson 15) usually keeps
that change in the whole futur (verbs with *é*, below, are the exception). The easiest way to get it right: take the *je* present and add *r* +
the ending.

| present (je) | futur |
|---|---|
| j'achète | j'achèterai, nous achèterons |
| j'appelle | j'appellerai, vous appellerez |
| je jette (*jeter*, to throw away, lesson 16) | je jetterai |
| je nettoie (*nettoyer*, lesson 04) | je nettoierai |
| je paie / je paye | je paierai / je payerai (both correct) |
| j'essaie / j'essaye | j'essaierai / j'essayerai (both correct) |

Verbs with *é* in the stem, like *préférer* and *espérer*, traditionally keep the *é*: *je
préférerai, j'espérerai*. The 1990 spelling reform allows *je préfèrerai*, which matches the
sound; both are accepted in this course.

Verbs in *-ger* and *-cer* need no change in the futur, because an *e* follows the *g* or *c*:
*je mangerai, je commencerai, je changerai*.

## Prévoir and devenir

*Prévoir* (to plan, to forecast, to expect) is built on *voir* in the present, but not in the
futur:

| | prévoir, present | prévoir, futur |
|---|---|---|
| je | prévois | prévoirai |
| nous | prévoyons | prévoirons |
| ils | prévoient | prévoiront |

- *La météo prévoit de la pluie pour demain.* — The forecast says rain for tomorrow.
- *Qu'est-ce que vous avez prévu pour le week-end ?* — What have you planned for the weekend?
- *Tout s'est passé comme prévu.* — Everything went as planned.

*Devenir* (to become) is conjugated like *venir*, with *être* in the passé composé: *je deviens,
ils deviennent; je suis devenu(e); je deviendrai*. Like *être*, it takes no article before a job:

- *Ma sœur est devenue infirmière.* — My sister became a nurse.
- *Un jour, tu deviendras pilote.* — One day you'll become a pilot.

## Futur simple or futur proche?

Both tenses talk about the future, and very often either one is correct. Native speakers use the
futur proche a lot in conversation. The difference is a matter of feel:

| futur proche: *aller* + infinitive | futur simple |
|---|---|
| something already decided or arranged | predictions (the weather, the future in general) |
| something about to happen, that you can see coming | promises |
| everyday conversation | plans further ahead or less certain |
| | writing, announcements, forecasts |
| *Ce soir, je vais voir un film.* | *Demain, il fera 25 degrés.* |
| *Attention, tu vas tomber !* | *Je t'appellerai demain, promis.* |
| *On va déménager en mai.* | *Un jour, nous vivrons à la campagne.* |

![A timeline that starts at "maintenant". Just after now, close to the start, the futur proche: je vais partir, ce soir, on va manger, with the note: decided, near, everyday speech. Further along the line, the futur simple: un jour, je serai médecin, il fera beau, je t'appellerai, with the note: predictions, promises, further ahead, writing. A shaded band in the middle says: often both are fine.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

If you choose "the wrong one", you'll still be understood and usually still be correct. Where
English uses "will" for a promise or a prediction, the futur simple is the safer choice.

Weather forecasts are a classic place for the futur simple (*Demain, il pleuvra en Bretagne*):
lesson 16 has a whole forecast.

## Quand + futur

After *quand* (when), if the action is in the future, French uses the futur where English uses
the present:

- *Quand je serai grand, je serai pilote.* — When I grow up, I'll be a pilot.
- *Quand tu arriveras à la gare, appelle-moi.* — When you get to the station, call me.
- *Je t'écrirai quand j'aurai le temps.* — I'll write to you when I have time.

*Dès que* (as soon as) works the same way: *Dès que je saurai, je te le dirai.* — As soon as I
know, I'll tell you.

But when *quand* means "every time" (a habit or a general truth), the present stays: *Quand il
pleut, je prends le bus.* — When it rains, I take the bus.

## How sure are you?

Time words for the future: *bientôt* (soon), *plus tard* (later), *un jour* (one day), *demain*,
*la semaine prochaine*, *l'année prochaine*, *dans deux ans* (in two years' time, lesson 03), *en
2030*.

Words that say how sure you are, from most to least certain:

| | |
|---|---|
| *certainement* | certainly, definitely |
| *sûrement* | very probably (despite its look, it usually means a little less than "for sure") |
| *probablement* | probably |
| *peut-être* | maybe, perhaps |

They usually go after the verb in the futur: *Il viendra sûrement. Elle sera probablement en
retard.* At the start of a sentence, say *peut-être que*: *Peut-être qu'il viendra.* (Written French
also has *Peut-être viendra-t-il*, with inversion.) Don't mix up *peut-être* (maybe) with *peut
être* without a hyphen (can be): *Ça peut être difficile.*

## Plans and dreams

- *Je pense souvent à mon avenir.* — I often think about my future. (*L'avenir* is the everyday
  word for the future; *le futur* is mostly the name of the tense.)
- *Tu as des projets pour l'été ?* — Have you got any plans for the summer?
- *Mon rêve, c'est de vivre au bord de la mer.* — My dream is to live by the sea.
- *Je rêve de voyager en Asie.* — I dream of travelling in Asia. (*rêver de* + infinitive or noun)
- *Mon objectif, c'est de parler couramment.* — My goal is to speak fluently. *Le but*, the aim or
  purpose, is close: *Quel est le but de ton voyage ?*
- *J'ai décidé de changer de travail.* — I've decided to change jobs. (*décider de* + infinitive;
  *changer de* + noun with no article; *prendre une décision*, to make a decision)
- *Elle a réalisé son rêve.* — She made her dream come true. (*Réaliser* means to achieve or carry
  out. For "realise" in the sense of understand, careful French says *se rendre compte*, though
  *réaliser* is often heard that way too.)
- *Elle fera carrière dans la musique.* — She'll make a career in music. (*la carrière*)
- *Ce sera un grand changement.* — It will be a big change. (*le changement*, from *changer*)
- *Quel est le programme pour samedi ?* — What's the plan for Saturday? (*le programme* = the plan
  of events, the schedule)
- *Qui s'occupera du chat ?* — Who'll look after the cat? (*s'occuper de*: *je m'occupe des
  enfants*)

## Dialogue: Et l'année prochaine ?

Léa and Samir are finishing their studies in Lyon.

> Samir : *Alors, Léa, quels sont tes projets pour l'année prochaine ?*
>
> Léa : *J'ai pris une décision : je partirai au Canada en septembre. Je travaillerai dans un
> hôtel à Montréal.*
>
> Samir : *Au Canada ! C'est ton rêve depuis longtemps, non ?*
>
> Léa : *Oui. Et toi ? Tu resteras à Lyon ?*
>
> Samir : *Probablement. Mon objectif, c'est de devenir professeur de musique. Mais d'abord, je
> devrai réussir mon examen en juin.*
>
> Léa : *Tu le réussiras, j'en suis sûre !*
>
> Samir : *Peut-être… Et un jour, j'aurai ma petite école de musique. Tu viendras me voir ?*
>
> Léa : *Bien sûr ! Quand je reviendrai en France, je viendrai à ton premier concert.*
>
> Samir : *Et qui s'occupera de ton chat quand tu seras à Montréal ?*
>
> Léa : *Devine !*
>
> Samir : *Ah non… Moi ?*

Translation:

> Samir: So, Léa, what are your plans for next year?
>
> Léa: I've made a decision: I'll go to Canada in September. I'll work in a hotel in Montreal.
>
> Samir: Canada! That's been your dream for a long time, hasn't it?
>
> Léa: Yes. And you? Will you stay in Lyon?
>
> Samir: Probably. My goal is to become a music teacher. But first I'll have to pass my exam in
> June.
>
> Léa: You'll pass it, I'm sure!
>
> Samir: Maybe… And one day I'll have my own little music school. Will you come and see me?
>
> Léa: Of course! When I come back to France, I'll come to your first concert.
>
> Samir: And who'll look after your cat when you're in Montreal?
>
> Léa: Guess!
>
> Samir: Oh no… Me?

Notice *quand je reviendrai* and *quand tu seras*: futur after *quand*, present in English. And
*j'en suis sûre*: *en* stands for *de ça* (lesson 07).

## Pronunciation

- In *-er* verbs, the *e* before the *r* is often hardly said: *je parlerai* sounds like
  "parl-ray", *nous regarderons* like "ruh-gard-ron".
- *Je ferai, nous ferons*: the *e* of *fer-* is the weak "uh" of *le*: "fuh-ray", "fuh-ron". The
  same goes for *je serai* "suh-ray".
- The double *rr* is said as a single *r*: *je pourrai* "poo-ray", *je verrai* "vay-ray".
- *Je parlerai* ends in an "ay" sound, *il parlera* in "a". Lesson 14 compares *-rai* with *-rais*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~je prendrerai~~ → *je prendrai* (the *e* of *-re* goes).
- ~~j'allerai~~ → *j'irai*; ~~je fairai~~ → *je ferai*; ~~je voirai~~ → *je verrai*.
- ~~je prévrai~~ → *je prévoirai*: *prévoir* is not like *voir* in the futur.
- ~~il pleuvera~~ → *il pleuvra*; ~~il fallera~~ → *il faudra*.
- ~~j'acheterai~~ → *j'achèterai* (keep the accent of *j'achète*).
- ~~ils serons~~ → *ils seront* (*nous* -ons, *ils* -ont).
- ~~Quand je suis grand, je serai pilote~~ → *Quand je serai grand* (futur after *quand* for the
  future).
- ~~Il deviendra un médecin~~ → *Il deviendra médecin* (no article before a job).

## Key points

- Futur simple = infinitive (*-re* verbs drop the *e*) + *-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont*.
- Irregular stems, same endings: *ser-, aur-, ir-, fer-, viendr-, deviendr-, pourr-, voudr-,
  devr-, saur-, verr-, enverr-, recevr-; il faudra, il pleuvra*. *Prévoir → je prévoirai.*
- Spelling-change *-er* verbs: *je* present + *r*: *j'achèterai, j'appellerai, je paierai /
  payerai*.
- Futur proche for what is decided or near; futur simple for predictions, promises, plans further
  ahead and writing. Often both are fine.
- *Quand* + futur for the future: *Quand j'aurai le temps, je t'écrirai.*
- *certainement > sûrement > probablement > peut-être*; *peut-être que* at the start.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Would you…? The conditionnel for requests, wishes and advice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Since A1 you have used *je voudrais*, *j'aimerais* and *pourriez-vous* as set phrases. They are
forms of the **[[conditionnel]]** (the conditional), the French "would" tense. This lesson shows how
it is built, and it is good news: you already know both halves. The stem is the future stem from
lesson 13, and the endings are the imparfait endings from lesson 01.

Then you'll use the conditionnel for four everyday jobs: polite requests, wishes, advice and
suggestions. The theme is travel: booking a hotel, a gîte or a youth hostel, asking at reception
and planning a holiday.

## Building the conditionnel

Future stem + *-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient*:

| | parler | finir | prendre | être |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| je | parler*ais* | finir*ais* | prendr*ais* | ser*ais* |
| tu | parler*ais* | finir*ais* | prendr*ais* | ser*ais* |
| il / elle / on | parler*ait* | finir*ait* | prendr*ait* | ser*ait* |
| nous | parler*ions* | finir*ions* | prendr*ions* | ser*ions* |
| vous | parler*iez* | finir*iez* | prendr*iez* | ser*iez* |
| ils / elles | parler*aient* | finir*aient* | prendr*aient* | ser*aient* |

Every irregular future stem works here too, with no exceptions:

- *vouloir → je voudrais* (I would like), *pouvoir → tu pourrais* (you could), *être → il
  serait* (he would be), *aimer → nous aimerions* (we would like), *devoir → vous devriez* (you
  should), *avoir → ils auraient* (they would have);
- *aller → j'irais, faire → je ferais, venir → je viendrais, savoir → je saurais, voir → je
  verrais, il faut → il faudrait*;
- spelling-change verbs as in the futur: *j'achèterais, j'appellerais, je paierais / payerais*.

![A builder chart for the conditionnel. The future stem fer- (from faire) is shown once. An arrow to the left adds the futur endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont and gives je ferai, I will do. An arrow to the right adds the imparfait endings -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient and gives je ferais, I would do. A note underneath says: same stem, the endings decide.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Polite requests

The conditionnel turns a demand into a **[[polite request]]**: it turns "I want" into "I'd like" and "can you" into "could
you", exactly as in English. *Je veux une chambre* is not rude in every situation, but at a hotel
desk *Je voudrais une chambre* sounds much better.

- *Pourriez-vous m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?* — Could you help me, please?
- *Vous pourriez parler plus lentement ?* — Could you speak more slowly? (the same request in
  everyday word order)
- *Est-ce que vous auriez une chambre pour ce soir ?* — Would you have a room for tonight?
- *Ce serait possible de payer par carte ?* — Would it be possible to pay by card?
- *Je voudrais réserver une table pour quatre.* — I'd like to book a table for four.
- *J'aimerais un renseignement.* — I'd like some information. (*le renseignement*, lesson 19)

With friends, use *tu*: *Tu pourrais m'appeler ce soir ?* — Could you call me tonight?

## Wishes

*J'aimerais* and *je voudrais* + infinitive or noun say what you would like:

- *J'aimerais bien voir la mer.* — I'd really like to see the sea. (*aimer bien* in the
  conditionnel = would really like)
- *Je voudrais être guide de montagne.* — I'd like to be a mountain guide.
- *Nous aimerions partir en Grèce cet été.* — We'd like to go to Greece this summer.
- *Ce serait super !* — That would be great!

## Advice

There are three common ways to give advice with the conditionnel:

- *tu devrais / vous devriez* + infinitive (you should): *Tu devrais réserver tôt.* — You should
  book early. *Vous devriez prendre un sac à dos.* — You should take a backpack.
- *à ta place / à votre place* (if I were you) + *je* + conditionnel: *À ta place, je partirais en
  juin.* — If I were you, I'd go in June.
- *il faudrait* + infinitive (you'd need to, we ought to): *Il faudrait arriver avant midi.* — We'd
  need to arrive before noon.

*Tu devrais* is gentler than *tu dois* (you must). Lesson 15 adds more ways to give advice and
talk about obligation.

## Suggestions

*On pourrait* (we could) + infinitive makes a suggestion:

- *On pourrait faire une excursion demain.* — We could go on a trip tomorrow.
- *On pourrait demander à l'office de tourisme.* — We could ask at the tourist office.
- *Vous pourriez visiter le château.* — You could visit the castle.

## Futur or conditionnel?

*Je ferai* (I will do) and *je ferais* (I would do) differ by one letter. In careful speech the
*-rai* of the futur ends in a closed "ay" (like *été*) and the *-rais* of the conditionnel in an
open "eh" (like *mère*), but many speakers today say them the same way. So in writing, check
the meaning:

- "will" → futur, *-rai*: *Demain, je ferai les courses.* — Tomorrow I'll do the shopping.
- "would" → conditionnel, *-rais*: *Je ferais bien une pause.* — I'd happily take a break.

A quick test: change *je* to *nous*. If *nous ferons* fits, write *je ferai*; if *nous ferions*
fits, write *je ferais*. With the other persons the difference is easy to see and hear:

| | futur | conditionnel |
|---|---|---|
| je | ferai | ferais |
| tu | feras | ferais |
| il | fera | ferait |
| nous | ferons | ferions |
| vous | ferez | feriez |
| ils | feront | feraient |

You'll also meet the conditionnel after a *si* clause in the imparfait: *Si j'avais le temps, je
voyagerais* (If I had time, I would travel). That pattern is B1 and comes later, in honors lesson
16h1. For now, use *si* only with the present (lesson 15).

## Where to stay

| | |
|---|---|
| *l'hôtel* (A1) | a hotel; you go to *la réception* (the front desk) |
| *l'auberge de jeunesse* | a youth hostel: cheap, often with shared rooms |
| *le gîte* | a holiday cottage or flat in the country, often rented by the week |
| *le camping* (A1) | a campsite |
| *la location* | a rental (a flat, a house, a car); not "a location", which is *un endroit* |

For the stay itself: *le séjour* (stay; *Bon séjour !* = Enjoy your stay!), *la réservation*
(booking), *le tarif* (rate, fare: *le tarif réduit*, the reduced rate). A room or a date can be
*disponible* (available) or *complet* (fully booked; feminine *complète*). Breakfast may be
*compris* (included). You can *confirmer* (confirm) or *annuler* (cancel) a booking. At
reception you can leave *les bagages* (luggage, masculine plural; one piece is *un bagage*):
*Vous pouvez laisser vos bagages ici jusqu'à midi.*

![A hotel reception desk. Behind the desk a receptionist stands under a sign reading Réception. On the desk lie a key with a small tag and an open guidebook. In front of the desk stand a suitcase and a backpack. On the wall to the right is an air-conditioning unit, and a window shows a view of the sea with a sailing boat. Labels name la réception, la clé, le guide, la valise, le sac à dos, la climatisation and la vue.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

On holiday you might go to *l'agence de voyages* (travel agency) before you leave, then to
*l'office de tourisme* (tourist office) when you arrive, to book *une visite guidée* (a guided
tour) or *une excursion* (a day trip). *Le guide* is a guidebook, or a guide; *le touriste* (*la
touriste*) is a tourist. At the beach, don't forget *le maillot de bain* (swimsuit) and *la crème
solaire* (sun cream, lesson 15), and you can *bronzer* (sunbathe).

Two words to keep apart: *visiter* (A1) is for places (*visiter un musée*); for people, French says
*rendre visite à* (*rendre visite à ma tante*). And *avoir besoin de* means to need: *J'ai besoin
d'une chambre. Tu as besoin d'aide ?*

## Reading a booking page

![An original booking page for an invented hotel, Hôtel des Trois Mouettes in Saint-Malo, for 14 to 16 August, 2 nights, 2 adults. Three rooms: a double room with sea view, 98 euros a night, disponible; a family room, 135 euros a night, complet; a single room, 72 euros a night, disponible. Notes: petit-déjeuner compris, climatisation, Wi-Fi gratuit, annulation gratuite jusqu'à 48 h avant l'arrivée. Two buttons: Réserver and Annuler.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The page says *petit-déjeuner compris* (breakfast included) and *annulation gratuite jusqu'à 48 h
avant l'arrivée* (free cancellation up to 48 hours before arrival). The family room is
*complet*; the two others are *disponibles*. Two nights in the double room cost 2 × 98 = 196 €.

## Dialogue: Au téléphone avec l'hôtel

Thomas calls the hotel on the booking page.

> La réceptionniste : *Hôtel des Trois Mouettes, bonjour !*
>
> Thomas : *Bonjour, madame. Je voudrais réserver une chambre double du 14 au 16 août. Est-ce que
> vous auriez une chambre avec vue sur la mer ?*
>
> La réceptionniste : *Je regarde… Oui, elle est disponible. C'est 98 euros la nuit, petit-déjeuner
> compris.*
>
> Thomas : *Parfait. Et est-ce qu'il y a la climatisation ?*
>
> La réceptionniste : *Oui, toutes nos chambres ont la clim.*
>
> Thomas : *Ce serait possible d'annuler plus tard ?*
>
> La réceptionniste : *Oui, sans frais jusqu'à 48 heures avant votre arrivée. Pourriez-vous me
> donner votre nom et votre adresse e-mail ? Je vous enverrai une confirmation.*
>
> Thomas : *Thomas Bernard. Et nous aurons une voiture : vous auriez une place de parking ?*
>
> La réceptionniste : *Bien sûr. Je vous souhaite un bon séjour à Saint-Malo !*

Translation:

> Receptionist: Hôtel des Trois Mouettes, hello!
>
> Thomas: Hello. I'd like to book a double room from 14 to 16 August. Would you have a room with a
> sea view?
>
> Receptionist: Let me look… Yes, it's available. It's 98 euros a night, breakfast included.
>
> Thomas: Perfect. And is there air conditioning?
>
> Receptionist: Yes, all our rooms have air conditioning.
>
> Thomas: Would it be possible to cancel later?
>
> Receptionist: Yes, free of charge up to 48 hours before you arrive. Could you give me your name
> and your email address? I'll send you a confirmation.
>
> Thomas: Thomas Bernard. And we'll have a car: would you have a parking space?
>
> Receptionist: Of course. I hope you have a lovely stay in Saint-Malo!

(*sans frais* = free of charge; *une place de parking* = a parking space.) Notice how both
tenses appear: the conditionnel for the polite questions (*vous auriez, ce serait, pourriez-vous*)
and the futur for facts about the future (*je vous enverrai, nous aurons*).

Later, Thomas's friend Inès asks for advice:

> Inès : *On part en Bretagne en août, mais on n'a pas beaucoup d'argent. Tu as une idée ?*
>
> Thomas : *À ta place, je prendrais une auberge de jeunesse, ou un gîte si vous êtes nombreux.
> Et tu devrais réserver maintenant : en août, tout est complet !*

(Inès: We're going to Brittany in August, but we haven't got much money. Any ideas? Thomas: If I
were you, I'd take a youth hostel, or a gîte if there are a lot of you. And you should book now:
in August everything's fully booked! — *si vous êtes nombreux* uses *si* + present, lesson 15.)

## Pronunciation

- *Nous parlerions* "par-luh-RYON", *vous parleriez* "par-luh-RYAY": the *-ions* and *-iez*
  endings add a "y" sound, so they are a syllable longer than the futur's *parlerons*,
  *parlerez*.
- *Je voudrais* "voo-DRAY", *j'aimerais* "zhem-RAY", *je pourrais* "poo-RAY" (one *r* sound).
- *Le gîte* "zheet", *la réception* "ray-sep-SYON".

## Common mistakes

- ~~Je voudrai un café~~ (that's the futur, "I will want") → *Je voudrais un café*.
- ~~Vous pourrez m'aider ?~~ as a polite request now (that means "will you be able to?") → *Pourriez-vous m'aider ?* / *Vous pourriez
  m'aider ?*
- ~~Tu devrais de réserver~~ → *Tu devrais réserver* (no *de* after *devoir*).
- ~~je ferrais~~ → *je ferais* (one *r*: only some stems have *rr*).
- ~~À ta place, je pars en juin~~ → *À ta place, je partirais en juin* (the conditionnel after *à
  ta place*).
- ~~une location~~ for "a place" → *un endroit*; *une location* is a rental.

## Key points

- Conditionnel = future stem + imparfait endings: *je voudrais, tu pourrais, il serait, nous
  aimerions, vous devriez, ils auraient*.
- Polite requests: *Pourriez-vous … ? Est-ce que vous auriez … ? Ce serait possible de … ?*
- Wishes: *J'aimerais (bien) … Je voudrais …*
- Advice: *Tu devrais* + infinitive; *À ta place, je* + conditionnel; *Il faudrait* + infinitive.
- Suggestions: *On pourrait* + infinitive.
- *-rai* = will (futur), *-rais* = would (conditionnel); test with *nous*: *ferons / ferions*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: If…: si + present, il faut and advice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 13 and 14 gave you the futur and the conditionnel. This lesson joins them to the word
*si* (if) to make **[[conditional sentences]]**: "If you're tired, rest", "If it's sunny, we'll go to
the beach". It also gathers the ways to say what someone must do, mustn't do, or had better do:
*il faut, devoir, tu devrais, il vaut mieux, conseiller de* and the imperative.

The theme is health and well-being: sleep, food, sport and stress. The advice in this lesson is
everyday common sense, not medical advice.

## Si + present

A conditional sentence has two parts: the **[[if-clause]]** with *si* + the condition, and the main
clause with the result. With a real, possible condition, the *si* clause is in the present,
and the main clause can be in three tenses:

| si-clause | main clause | use | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *si* + present | present | something generally true, or true now | *Si je dors mal, je suis fatigué.* — If I sleep badly, I'm tired. |
| *si* + present | futur (or futur proche) | a result in the future | *S'il fait beau, on ira à la plage.* — If it's nice, we'll go to the beach. |
| *si* + present | imperative | advice or an instruction | *Si tu es fatigué, repose-toi.* — If you're tired, have a rest. |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Si + present: which tense in the main clause?
  accDescr: A decision chart. Start with si plus the present tense, for example si tu es fatigué. Then ask what the main clause does. If it states something generally true or true now, use the present: tu travailles mal. If it gives a result in the future, use the futur simple or the futur proche: tu iras au lit tôt, or tu vas aller au lit. If it gives advice or an order, use the imperative: repose-toi. A note at the bottom: never the futur or the conditionnel in the si clause.
  A["si + present: Si tu es fatigué, ..."] --> B{"What does the main clause do?"}
  B -- "true in general or now" --> C["present: ... tu travailles mal."]
  B -- "result in the future" --> D["futur: ... tu iras au lit tôt."]
  B -- "advice or order" --> E["imperative: ... repose-toi !"]
  C --> F["Never futur or conditionnel after this si"]
  D --> F
  E --> F
```

Three rules to keep:

- No futur after *si* in this meaning, even when the condition is about the future: ~~S'il
  fera beau~~ → *S'il fait beau, on ira à la plage.* (The same goes for the conditionnel: ~~si
  j'aurais~~.)
- *Si* + *il* / *ils* → *s'il*, *s'ils*. Only *il* and *ils* make *si* drop its *i*: *si
  elle, si on, si un ami*.
- Either part can come first. With *si* first, put a comma: *Si tu veux, on peut sortir.*
  With *si* second, no comma: *On peut sortir si tu veux.*

Two notes so the rule doesn't become too strict:

- *Si* can also take the passé composé for something finished: *Si tu as fini, tu peux partir.* —
  If you've finished, you can go.
- When *si* means "whether" (an indirect question, lesson 19), the futur is fine: *Je ne sais pas
  s'il viendra.* — I don't know whether he'll come.

## Obligation: il faut, devoir, il ne faut pas

An **[[obligation]]** says what has to be done. French has two main tools:

- *il faut* + infinitive (A1): a general need, with no person named. *Il faut dormir au moins sept
  heures.* — You need to sleep at least seven hours. It works in every tense: *il fallait, il a
  fallu, il faudra, il faudrait*.
- *devoir* + infinitive: a particular person must. *Je dois aller chez le dentiste.* — I have to go
  to the dentist.

The negatives are a trap for English speakers:

| French | means | not |
|---|---|---|
| *Il ne faut pas fumer ici.* | You must not smoke here. | ~~You don't have to smoke.~~ |
| *Tu ne dois pas manger trop de sucre.* | You mustn't eat too much sugar. | |
| *Tu n'es pas obligé de venir.* | You don't have to come. | |
| *Ce n'est pas la peine de réserver.* | There's no need to book. | |

So "you don't have to" is *tu n'es pas obligé(e) de* + infinitive (*obligé*, obliged), or *ce
n'est pas la peine de* + infinitive. *Il ne faut pas* always forbids.

## Advice: from gentle to firm

| how firm | French | English |
|---|---|---|
| gentle | *Tu pourrais* + infinitive (lesson 14) | You could … |
| | *Tu devrais* + infinitive (lesson 14) | You should … |
| | *Il vaut mieux* + infinitive | It's better to … |
| | *Je te conseille de* + infinitive | I advise you to … |
| firm | imperative | Do …! |
| firmest | *Il faut* + infinitive / *Tu dois* + infinitive | You have to … |

- *Il vaut mieux* is impersonal like *il faut*: *Il vaut mieux bouger un peu tous les jours.* —
  It's better to move a little every day. With *ne pas* (both words together before the
  infinitive, lesson 17): *Il vaut mieux ne pas boire de café le soir.* — It's better not to
  drink coffee in the evening.
- *Conseiller* (lesson 06) takes *à* + person and *de* + infinitive: *Le médecin m'a conseillé de
  faire du sport.* — The doctor advised me to do some sport. *Je vous conseille de vous
  détendre.* — I advise you to relax.

## The imperative with pronouns: a review

Advice often uses the imperative. Lessons 05–07 placed the pronouns; here they are together:

| affirmative: pronoun after, with a hyphen | negative: pronoun before |
|---|---|
| *Prends-le.* — Take it. | *Ne le prends pas.* — Don't take it. |
| *Repose-toi.* — Have a rest. | *Ne te couche pas tard.* — Don't go to bed late. |
| *Entraîne-toi.* — Practise. | *Ne t'inquiète pas.* — Don't worry. |
| *Mets-en.* — Put some on. | *N'en mets pas trop.* — Don't put too much on. |
| *Détendez-vous.* — Relax. | *Ne vous levez pas.* — Don't get up. |

Remember: *te* becomes *toi* after the verb (*repose-toi*), and *me* becomes *moi* (*aide-moi*).

## Health words

- *La santé* (health): *Le sport, c'est bon pour la santé.* You are *en forme* (fit, well) or not.
- *Le sommeil* (sleep), *le stress* (stress); you can be *stressé(e)* and need to *se détendre*
  (relax: *je me détends, détends-toi*).
- *L'alimentation* (diet, what you eat) should be *équilibrée* (balanced) and *saine* (healthy).
  *Le régime* is a diet to lose weight: *être au régime*.
- *Maigrir* (to lose weight) and *grossir* (to put on weight) are *finir* verbs: *je maigris, nous
  maigrissons*. *Le poids* is weight.
- *Bouger* (to move, be active: *nous bougeons*), *s'entraîner* (to train: *je m'entraîne à la
  salle de sport*, at the gym).
- *Fumer* (to smoke), *la cigarette*, *l'alcool* (alcohol), *arrêter de* + infinitive (to stop):
  *J'ai arrêté de fumer.*
- *Se sentir* (to feel), conjugated like *partir*: *je me sens bien, il se sent mal, nous nous
  sentons fatigués*.
- *Le dentiste* (*la dentiste*); *la crème solaire* (sun cream); *grave* (serious): *Ce n'est pas
  grave* (It doesn't matter, it's not serious).

![A weekly planner from lundi to dimanche, with a small picture in each day: lundi, a moon and a bed (sleep); mardi, a dumbbell (the gym); mercredi, a plate with vegetables, fish and bread (a balanced meal); jeudi, a tooth (the dentist); vendredi, a cigarette crossed out (stop smoking); samedi, a tube of sun cream and a sun; dimanche, a person stretching on a mat (relax). Captions: dormir huit heures, la salle de sport, un repas équilibré, le dentiste, arrêter de fumer, la crème solaire, se détendre.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: Dix conseils pour être en forme

> *1. Si vous travaillez assis, levez-vous toutes les heures et bougez un peu.*
> *2. Il vaut mieux prendre l'escalier que l'ascenseur.*
> *3. Mangez des fruits et des légumes tous les jours : votre alimentation sera plus équilibrée.*
> *4. Ne sautez pas le petit-déjeuner.*
> *5. Si vous voulez maigrir, ne faites pas de régime trop strict : parlez-en à votre médecin.*
> *6. Buvez de l'eau, et pas trop d'alcool.*
> *7. Si vous fumez, essayez d'arrêter : demandez de l'aide, c'est plus facile.*
> *8. Il faut dormir assez : le sommeil, c'est la santé !*
> *9. Si vous êtes stressé, prenez dix minutes pour vous détendre.*
> *10. En été, mettez de la crème solaire, même s'il y a des nuages.*

Translation: 1. If you work sitting down, get up every hour and move a little. 2. It's better to
take the stairs than the lift. 3. Eat fruit and vegetables every day: your diet will be more
balanced. 4. Don't skip breakfast. 5. If you want to lose weight, don't go on too strict a diet:
talk to your doctor about it. 6. Drink water, and not too much alcohol. 7. If you smoke, try to
stop: ask for help, it's easier. 8. You need to sleep enough: sleep is health! 9. If you're
stressed, take ten minutes to relax. 10. In summer, put on sun cream, even if there are clouds.

(*l'escalier* = the stairs; *sauter* = to skip; *strict* = strict; *même si* = even if; *parlez-en*
= talk about it, with *en* from lesson 07.)

## Dialogue: Tu as l'air fatiguée

> Julien : *Ça va, Nora ? Tu as l'air fatiguée.*
>
> Nora : *Je ne me sens pas très bien. Je dors mal, je suis stressée à cause du travail…*
>
> Julien : *Tu bois du café le soir ?*
>
> Nora : *Oui, deux ou trois.*
>
> Julien : *Alors il vaut mieux arrêter le café après quatre heures. Et si tu fais un peu de sport,
> tu dormiras mieux.*
>
> Nora : *Je n'ai pas le temps d'aller à la salle de sport !*
>
> Julien : *Tu n'es pas obligée d'aller à la salle. Si tu rentres à pied, c'est déjà bien. Et
> détends-toi le soir : pas d'écran au lit !*
>
> Nora : *D'accord, docteur ! Et si ça ne va pas mieux ?*
>
> Julien : *Si ça ne va pas mieux dans quinze jours, prends rendez-vous chez le médecin. Ce n'est
> sûrement pas grave, mais il ne faut pas attendre trop longtemps.*

Translation:

> Julien: Are you all right, Nora? You look tired.
>
> Nora: I don't feel very well. I'm sleeping badly, I'm stressed because of work…
>
> Julien: Do you drink coffee in the evening?
>
> Nora: Yes, two or three.
>
> Julien: Then it's better to stop coffee after four o'clock. And if you do a bit of sport, you'll
> sleep better.
>
> Nora: I haven't got time to go to the gym!
>
> Julien: You don't have to go to the gym. If you walk home, that's already good. And relax in the
> evening: no screens in bed!
>
> Nora: OK, doctor! And if it doesn't get better?
>
> Julien: If it isn't better in a fortnight, make an appointment with the doctor. It's very
> probably nothing serious, but you shouldn't wait too long.

(*avoir l'air* + adjective = to look …; *à cause de* = because of, lesson 20; *quinze jours* = a
fortnight, two weeks; *l'écran* = the screen, lesson 10.)

## Pronunciation

- *S'il* "seel", *s'ils* "seel" too (before a vowel: *s'ils_ont* "seel-zon").
- *Il vaut mieux* "eel vo MYEU".
- *Le sommeil* "so-MAY", with a "y" glide at the end; *l'alcool* "al-KOL"; *sain* "san" (nasal),
  *saine* "sen".
- *Il faut* "eel fo", *il faudra* "eel fo-DRA".

## Common mistakes

- ~~S'il fera beau, on ira à la plage~~ → *S'il fait beau, on ira à la plage.*
- ~~Si il pleut~~ → *S'il pleut*; but ~~s'elle~~ → *si elle*.
- ~~Il ne faut pas venir~~ for "you don't have to come" → *Tu n'es pas obligé(e) de venir.*
- ~~Il vaut mieux de dormir~~ → *Il vaut mieux dormir* (no *de*).
- ~~Je te conseille dormir~~ → *Je te conseille de dormir.*
- ~~Reposes-toi~~ → *Repose-toi* (no *s* in the *tu* imperative of *-er* verbs; it only comes back
  before *en* or *y*: *manges-en, penses-y*).
- ~~Ne repose-toi pas~~ → *Ne te repose pas* (in the negative the pronoun goes before the verb).

## Key points

- *Si* + present → present, futur or imperative: *Si tu es fatigué, repose-toi. S'il fait beau, on
  ira à la plage.*
- Never the futur or the conditionnel after *si* (= if). *S'il, s'ils*, but *si elle, si on*.
- *Il faut* / *devoir* + infinitive = must; *il ne faut pas* = must not; "don't have to" = *tu n'es
  pas obligé(e) de*.
- Advice: *tu devrais, il vaut mieux* + infinitive, *conseiller à quelqu'un de* + infinitive, the
  imperative (*Prends-le. Ne le prends pas.*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Weather, nature and the environment: il est + adjective + de
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You now have five tenses: the present, the passé composé, the imparfait, the futur proche and
the futur simple. The weather is a perfect place to use them all, because its verbs are always in
the same person: *il pleut, il a plu, il pleuvait, il va pleuvoir, il pleuvra*. This lesson
puts the weather in every tense, then moves on to the environment: recycling, energy and the
future of the planet. On the way you'll learn a pattern you'll meet on signs, notices and in the
news: *il est important de …, il est interdit de …* + infinitive.

## The weather in every tense

Weather verbs are **[[impersonal verbs]]**: their subject *il* stands for nothing (like English "it" in
"it's raining"), and it never changes. Only the tense changes:

| | *il fait beau* | *il pleut* | *il neige* | *il y a du vent* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| present | il fait beau | il pleut | il neige | il y a du vent |
| passé composé | il a fait beau | il a plu | il a neigé | il y a eu du vent |
| imparfait | il faisait beau | il pleuvait | il neigeait | il y avait du vent |
| futur proche | il va faire beau | il va pleuvoir | il va neiger | il va y avoir du vent |
| futur simple | il fera beau | il pleuvra | il neigera | il y aura du vent |

The usual choice between the past tenses (lesson 02) applies: the imparfait sets the scene (*Il
faisait froid et il neigeait*), the passé composé sums up a finished period or an event (*Il a
plu toute la journée. Hier soir, il y a eu un orage.*).

More ways to describe the weather:

- *Le ciel est nuageux / ensoleillé.* — The sky is cloudy / sunny. (*nuageux, nuageuse*;
  *ensoleillé* also describes a day or a place: *une terrasse ensoleillée*)
- *L'air est humide / sec.* — The air is damp / dry. (*sec, sèche*)
- *Quelle chaleur !* — It's so hot! (*la chaleur* = heat)
- *Il fait 30 degrés.* — It's 30 degrees. *La température va baisser.* — The temperature is going
  to drop. (*baisser* = to go down; *monter* = to go up)
- *Il fait moins cinq.* — It's minus five (−5 °C).
- *Il y a eu des inondations.* — There were floods.

![A simplified map of France, not to scale, with forecast symbols for tomorrow: a sun over Marseille with 28 degrees, a cloud over Paris with 19 degrees, a storm cloud with lightning over Lyon with 24 degrees, a cloud with rain drops over Brest with 16 degrees, a cloud with snowflakes over the Alps with minus 2 degrees, and wind lines over Bordeaux with 21 degrees. A title reads: Demain. Each symbol is labelled: ensoleillé, nuageux, un orage, de la pluie, de la neige, du vent.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The map's forecast, in the futur simple:

> *Demain, il fera beau et chaud dans le sud : le ciel sera ensoleillé à Marseille, avec 28
> degrés. À Paris, le temps sera nuageux. Attention aux orages l'après-midi à Lyon. En Bretagne,
> il pleuvra toute la journée, et dans les Alpes, il neigera en montagne. Il y aura du vent sur
> la côte atlantique.*

Tomorrow it will be fine and hot in the south: the sky will be sunny in Marseille, at 28 degrees.
In Paris the weather will be cloudy. Watch out for storms in the afternoon in Lyon. In Brittany it
will rain all day, and in the Alps it will snow in the mountains. It will be windy on the
Atlantic coast. (*l'orage* = thunderstorm, lesson 02.)

## Impersonal expressions: il est + adjective + de + infinitive

Signs, notices and news reports use an **[[impersonal expression]]**: *il est* + adjective + *de* +
infinitive. As with the weather, *il* means nothing; the real subject is the infinitive.

- *Il est important de trier ses déchets.* — It's important to sort your rubbish.
- *Il est nécessaire de réserver.* — Booking is necessary.
- *Il est interdit de fumer.* — Smoking is forbidden.
- *Il est possible de recycler ce sac.* — This bag can be recycled.
- *Il est difficile de trouver un parking.* — It's hard to find a car park.
- *Il n'est pas nécessaire d'imprimer le billet.* — There's no need to print the ticket.

In everyday speech, people usually say *c'est* instead: *C'est important de trier. C'est interdit
de fumer ici.* Both are correct; *il est* sounds more written or formal.

When the adjective refers back to something already said, with nothing after it, only *c'est*
works:

- *Trier les déchets ? Oui, c'est important.* — Sorting rubbish? Yes, it's important.
- *Fumer ici ? Non, c'est interdit.* — Smoking here? No, it's not allowed.

On signs, the shortest form is common: *Interdit de fumer*, *Baignade interdite* (no swimming),
*Stationnement interdit* (no parking). *Interdit* agrees with the noun: *une baignade interdite*.

## On for rules and general statements

*On* (A1) often means "people in general" or "we, here". It's the usual way to state rules and
habits politely:

- *Ici, on ne jette pas le verre dans la poubelle.* — Here we don't throw glass in the bin.
- *En France, on trie les emballages.* — In France people sort their packaging.
- *On ne gaspille pas l'eau.* — We don't waste water.

## Pour + infinitive: saying why

*Pour* + infinitive says what something is for, the purpose (lesson 20 goes further):

- *On trie pour recycler.* — We sort in order to recycle.
- *J'éteins la lumière pour économiser l'électricité.* — I turn off the light to save electricity.
- *Je prends les transports en commun pour polluer moins.* — I use public transport so as to
  pollute less.

(*éteindre* = to turn off: *j'éteins*.)

## The environment

- *L'environnement* (environment), *la planète* (planet), *le climat* (climate), *l'énergie* (energy),
  *l'électricité* (electricity).
- *Protéger* (to protect) has two spelling changes: *je protège, nous protégeons*. Futur *je
  protégerai* (1990 spelling *je protègerai*).
- *Polluer* (to pollute), *gaspiller* (to waste), *économiser* (to save: energy, water, money),
  *recycler* (to recycle), *le recyclage* (recycling).
- *Trier* (to sort): *je trie, nous trions*; in the imparfait *nous triions*, with two *i*'s.
- *Jeter* (to throw away) doubles its *t* before a silent ending: *je jette, ils jettent*, but
  *nous jetons*; futur *je jetterai*.
- *Le déchet*, usually plural: *les déchets* (waste, rubbish).

Sorting your rubbish at home usually means several bins or containers. The colours are not the
same everywhere: each town or group of towns decides, so check your local rules (they are often
printed on the bin lid or on the town's website). A common set looks like this:

![Four bins side by side, with a note that colours and rules vary from town to town. A yellow bin labelled emballages et papiers, with a plastic bottle, a can and a cardboard box above it. A green bottle bank labelled verre, with a glass bottle and a jar. A brown bin labelled déchets de cuisine, with vegetable peelings and an apple core. A grey bin labelled ordures ménagères, for everything else.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Since 1 January 2023, across almost all of metropolitan France, all packaging (including
plastic pots, trays and films) can go in the yellow bin. Glass doesn't go in it: it usually goes
to a bottle bank (*la colonne à verre*). And since 1 January 2024, local councils must offer a way to
sort food waste (*les biodéchets*): a brown bin, a collection point or a compost bin. Honors
lesson 16h2 tells you more.

## The future of the planet

Talk about the future of the planet uses the futur simple for predictions:

- *Les étés seront plus chauds et plus secs.* — Summers will be hotter and drier.
- *Il y aura plus de vagues de chaleur.* — There will be more heatwaves. (*la vague* = wave)
- *Il pleuvra moins en été dans le sud.* — It will rain less in summer in the south.

These are not just guesses. In January 2026 the French government officially adopted a
"reference warming trajectory" (*la TRACC*) so that towns, companies and services all plan for
the same future: about +2.7 °C in 2050 and about +4 °C in 2100 for metropolitan France, compared
with the pre-industrial era.

## Reading: Notre immeuble devient plus vert

A notice on the wall of a block of flats:

> *Chers habitants,*
>
> *À partir du 1er mars, il y aura un nouveau bac marron dans la cour pour les déchets de
> cuisine. Il est important de bien trier : les emballages et le papier vont dans le bac jaune,
> le verre dans le conteneur de la rue.*
>
> *Il est interdit de laisser des cartons ou des meubles dans le hall. Pour les gros objets,
> on appelle la mairie.*
>
> *L'hiver dernier, nous avons gaspillé beaucoup d'énergie. Cette année, le chauffage sera à
> 19 degrés. Si vous avez froid, mettez un pull !*
>
> *Merci de protéger notre environnement. — Le conseil syndical*

Translation:

> Dear residents,
>
> From 1 March there will be a new brown bin in the courtyard for kitchen waste. It's important to
> sort properly: packaging and paper go in the yellow bin, glass in the container in the street.
>
> It's forbidden to leave cardboard boxes or furniture in the hall. For large items, we call the
> town hall.
>
> Last winter we wasted a lot of energy. This year the heating will be at 19 degrees. If you're
> cold, put on a jumper!
>
> Thank you for protecting our environment. — The owners' committee

(*le bac* = the bin, here; *les meubles* = furniture; *le chauffage* = heating; *le conseil
syndical* = the committee that represents the owners of a block of flats. *Le bac* also means
the school-leaving exam, lesson 18: the context tells you which.)

## Pronunciation

- *Il pleuvra* "eel pleu-VRA"; *il a plu* "eel a PLÜ", with the *u* of *tu*.
- *L'environnement* "lahn-vee-ron-MAHN"; *l'inondation* "lee-non-da-SYON".
- *Ensoleillé* "ahn-so-lay-YAY"; *nuageux* "nü-a-ZHEU".
- *Sec* "sek", *sèche* "sesh".
- *Je jette* "zhuh ZHET", *nous jetons* "noo zhuh-TON" (the first *e* is weak).

## Common mistakes

- ~~Il a pleuvé~~ → *Il a plu*; ~~il pleuvera~~ → *il pleuvra*.
- ~~Ils pleuvent~~ → *Il pleut*: weather verbs stay in the *il* form.
- ~~Il est important trier~~ → *Il est important de trier* (*de* before the infinitive).
- ~~Trier ? Oui, il est important.~~ → *Oui, c'est important* (nothing follows the adjective).
- ~~Je jete~~ → *Je jette*; ~~je protége~~ → *je protège*.
- ~~Le temps est soleil~~ → *Le temps est ensoleillé* / *Il y a du soleil*.

## Key points

- Weather verbs are impersonal: *il* never changes. *Il pleut / il a plu / il pleuvait / il va
  pleuvoir / il pleuvra*; *il fait / il a fait / il faisait / il fera beau*.
- *Il est* + adjective + *de* + infinitive: *Il est important de trier.* In speech: *C'est
  important de trier.* With nothing after the adjective: *C'est important.*
- *On* states rules and habits: *On ne jette pas le verre ici.*
- *Pour* + infinitive gives the purpose: *On trie pour recycler.*
- Bin colours and sorting rules depend on your town; check locally.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: If I won the lottery: si + imparfait + conditionnel
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 15 you made sentences with *si* + present about things that can really happen: *S'il
fait beau demain, on ira à la plage.* In lesson 14 you met the conditionnel and were told that
it also appears after *si* + imparfait, "later". This honors lesson is that "later".

French has a second kind of if-sentence, the **[[imaginary condition]]**, for situations you only
imagine: *Si je gagnais au
loto, j'achèterais un voilier.* — If I won the lottery, I'd buy a sailing boat. This is a B1
pattern, so treat this lesson as a preview: learn to recognise it and use it in a few set ways
(*si j'étais toi, si j'avais le temps*). You won't be drilled on it.

## Two kinds of if

| | real (lesson 15) | imaginary (this lesson) |
|---|---|---|
| the situation | could really happen | is not true now, or very unlikely |
| *si* + | present | imparfait |
| main clause | present, futur or imperative | conditionnel |
| example | *Si j'ai le temps, je viendrai.* | *Si j'avais le temps, je viendrais.* |
| meaning | If I have time, I'll come. (I might.) | If I had time, I'd come. (I don't.) |

![Two signposts side by side. The left one, labelled réel (real), shows si + présent, then présent, futur or impératif, with the example: S'il fait beau, on ira à la plage. The right one, labelled imaginaire (imaginary), shows si + imparfait, then conditionnel, with the example: Si j'étais riche, j'achèterais un voilier. A thought bubble over the right sign holds a small sailing boat.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

English works in a very similar way: "If I have …, I will …" against "If I had …, I would …".
French simply uses the imparfait where English uses its past tense ("had", "won", "were").

## The pattern: si + imparfait, conditionnel

You already know both tenses: the imparfait from lesson 01 (*nous parlons → je parlais*; *être →
j'étais*) and the conditionnel from lesson 14 (future stem + *-ais*).

| si-clause: imparfait | main clause: conditionnel |
|---|---|
| *Si j'étais riche,* | *j'aurais une maison à la mer.* |
| *Si tu habitais à Paris,* | *tu irais au musée tous les week-ends.* |
| *S'il faisait moins froid,* | *on sortirait.* |
| *Si nous avions une voiture,* | *nous pourrions partir en week-end.* |
| *Si vous parliez plus lentement,* | *je comprendrais mieux.* |
| *Si elles gagnaient au loto,* | *elles feraient le tour du monde.* |

Notice that the two halves end in the same letters in many persons (*-ais, -ait*). The difference
is in the stem: the imparfait uses the *nous* stem (*av-, habit-*; *ét-* for *être*), the conditionnel the future
stem (*aur-, ser-, ir-*), which always ends in *r*.

As with *si* + present, either half can come first, with a comma only when *si* comes first:
*J'achèterais un voilier si j'étais riche.*

## The golden rule: no conditionnel after si

The conditionnel goes in the main clause, never in the *si* clause:

- ~~Si j'aurais le temps, je viendrais.~~ → *Si j'avais le temps, je viendrais.*
- ~~Si tu serais là, …~~ → *Si tu étais là, …*

You will hear ~~si j'aurais~~ from some native speakers, but it is considered a mistake. A
memory trick used in French-speaking schools: *Les si n'aiment pas les -rais* ("si doesn't like
the -rais endings"), a pun that sounds like *les scies n'aiment pas les raies*, "saws don't like
rays".

## Set phrases you can use now

Some imaginary if-sentences are so common that you can learn them as chunks:

- *Si j'étais toi, …* (If I were you, …) + conditionnel: *Si j'étais toi, je prendrais le train.*
  It means the same as *à ta place* (lesson 14). Note *si j'étais toi*, not ~~si j'étais tu~~:
  after *être* here, French uses the stressed pronoun.
- *Si j'avais le temps, …* (If I had time, …): *Si j'avais le temps, j'apprendrais le piano.*
- *Si j'étais riche, …*: *Si j'étais riche, je ne travaillerais plus.*
- *Si seulement …* (If only …) + imparfait: *Si seulement il faisait beau !*
- *Ce serait génial !* (That would be great!): *Une semaine à Rome ? Ce serait génial !*

### Example 1: from real to imaginary

*Task.* Change the real condition *Si j'ai de l'argent, je ferai un voyage* into an imaginary
one.

1. Find the *si* clause: *si j'ai de l'argent* (present). Put *avoir* in the imparfait: *nous
   avons → av- → j'avais*. → *si j'avais de l'argent*.
2. Find the main clause: *je ferai un voyage* (futur). Keep the stem *fer-* and change the ending
   to the imparfait ending: *je ferais*.
3. Result: *Si j'avais de l'argent, je ferais un voyage.* — If I had money, I'd go on a trip.

The first sentence says "I might have money"; the second says "I don't have it, but imagine…".
In writing the main change in the main clause is one letter, *ferai → ferais*, so check it.

### Example 2: answering "What would you do if…?"

*Task.* Answer the classic question *Qu'est-ce que tu ferais si tu gagnais au loto ?* in three
sentences.

1. Keep the question's *si* clause and change the person: *si tu gagnais → si je gagnais*.
2. Put each thing you would do in the conditionnel. Choose verbs whose future stems you know:
   *acheter → j'achèterais*, *partir → je partirais*, *aider → j'aiderais*, *faire → je ferais*.
3. Vary the sentences: one with *si* first, one with *d'abord / ensuite* (first / then), one with a
   negative.

> *Si je gagnais au loto, d'abord, j'achèterais une petite maison à la campagne. Ensuite, je
> partirais six mois en Amérique du Sud avec ma sœur. Mais je ne démissionnerais pas : j'aime mon
> travail !*

If I won the lottery, first I'd buy a little house in the country. Then I'd go to South America
for six months with my sister. But I wouldn't quit my job: I like my work!

### Example 3: real or imaginary?

*Task.* Complete each sentence with *viendra* or *viendrait*.

| sentence | reasoning | answer |
|---|---|---|
| *S'il a le temps, il ___.* | *si* + present (*a*) → futur | *viendra* |
| *S'il avait le temps, il ___.* | *si* + imparfait (*avait*) → conditionnel | *viendrait* |
| *Si sa voiture marche demain, il ___.* | *marche*: present → futur | *viendra* |
| *Si elle n'habitait pas si loin, elle ___.* | *habitait*: imparfait → conditionnel | *viendrait* |

The tense in the *si* clause decides. You never need to look anywhere else.

## Classic "what if" questions

French conversation classes, magazines and friends love these questions. Answer them with the
conditionnel:

- *Imagine : tu es sur une île déserte. Qu'est-ce que tu emporterais ?* — Imagine you're on a
  desert island. What would you take? (*emporter* = to take with you) *J'emporterais un livre et
  une guitare.*
- *Si tu étais invisible pendant une journée, qu'est-ce que tu ferais ?* — If you were invisible
  for a day, what would you do? *J'irais partout sans payer !*
- *Si tu étais président(e), qu'est-ce que tu changerais ?* — If you were president, what would
  you change? *Je construirais des pistes cyclables partout.* (*construire* = to build)
- *Si tu avais une fortune, tu la partagerais ?* — If you had a fortune, would you share it?
  *Oui, je la partagerais avec ma famille.* (*la* = it, lesson 05)

The question itself uses *si* + imparfait for the imagined situation, and asks with the
conditionnel: *qu'est-ce que tu ferais ?* Copy the question's structure in your answer.

## Not the same thing: si on + imparfait

Lesson 22 teaches *Si on allait au cinéma ?* — How about going to the cinema? It looks like the
pattern of this lesson, but it is a suggestion on its own: there is no main clause and no
conditionnel. *Si on* + imparfait + question mark = "How about …?" or "Shall we …?"

| *Si on allait à la plage ?* | How about going to the beach? (a suggestion, lesson 22) |
|---|---|
| *Si on allait à la plage, on serait moins stressés.* | If we went to the beach, we'd be less stressed. (an imaginary condition) |

## Beyond A2: if it had happened

To imagine the past differently, French uses the plus-que-parfait (*j'avais su*, honors lesson
04h1) and the conditionnel passé (*je serais venu*): *Si j'avais su, je serais venu.* — If I had
known, I would have come. This is B1–B2 grammar: just recognise *si j'avais su* (if I'd known),
which people say all the time.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which kind of if-sentence?
  accDescr: A decision chart. Ask whether the situation could really happen. If yes, use si plus the present, then the present, the futur or the imperative, as in s'il fait beau, on ira à la plage. If no, because it is imaginary or not true now, use si plus the imparfait, then the conditionnel, as in si j'étais riche, j'achèterais un voilier. If it is about the past that did not happen, it is B1: si j'avais su, je serais venu. A separate box: si on plus imparfait with a question mark, and no main clause, is a suggestion: si on allait au cinéma ?
  A["An if-sentence"] --> B{"Could it really happen?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["si + present, then present, futur or imperative: S'il fait beau, on ira à la plage."]
  B -- "no, imaginary now" --> D["si + imparfait, then conditionnel: Si j'étais riche, j'achèterais un voilier."]
  B -- "about a past that didn't happen" --> E["B1: Si j'avais su, je serais venu."]
  F["si on + imparfait + ? with no main clause"] --> G["a suggestion: Si on allait au cinéma ?"]
```

## Reading: Et si vous gagniez au loto ?

A local radio station asked three people in the street what they would do with a fortune.

> *Martine, 64 ans : « Si je gagnais au loto ? Je partagerais avec mes enfants et mes
> petits-enfants. Et je ferais enfin le tour du monde en voilier. Mon mari a peur de l'eau, mais
> tant pis ! »*
>
> *Kevin, 23 ans : « Moi, si j'étais millionnaire, je démissionnerais tout de suite ! Non, je
> plaisante. J'aime mon métier. Mais j'achèterais un appartement pour mes parents. »*
>
> *Amina, 38 ans : « Je ne joue jamais, alors c'est une hypothèse… Si j'avais beaucoup d'argent, je
> créerais une association pour les enfants malades. Ce serait mon souhait. »*

Translation:

> Martine, 64: "If I won the lottery? I'd share with my children and grandchildren. And I'd finally
> sail round the world. My husband is scared of water, but never mind!"
>
> Kevin, 23: "Me, if I were a millionaire, I'd quit straight away! No, I'm joking. I like my job.
> But I'd buy a flat for my parents."
>
> Amina, 38: "I never play, so it's a hypothesis… If I had a lot of money, I'd start a charity for
> sick children. That would be my wish."

(*partager* = to share, honors lesson 16h3; *tant pis* = never mind; *plaisanter* = to joke; *le
métier* = job, lesson 17; *créer une association* = to set up a charity or non-profit.)

Amina is wise. The French national Loto asks you to choose 5 numbers out of 49 and one "lucky
number" (*le numéro Chance*) out of 10. There are 1,906,884 ways to choose 5 numbers out of 49,
and 10 lucky numbers, so the chance of winning the jackpot is 1 in 1,906,884 × 10 =
1 in 19,068,840, about one in 19 million (the figure the French personal-finance site *La
finance pour tous* gives). As Amina says, it's only *une hypothèse*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~Si j'aurais le temps~~ → *Si j'avais le temps* (no conditionnel after *si*).
- ~~Si j'avais le temps, je viendrai~~ → *je viendrais*: with *si* + imparfait, the main clause is
  conditionnel, not futur.
- ~~Si j'étais tu~~ → *Si j'étais toi*.
- ~~Si il était riche~~ → *S'il était riche* (*si* + *il* = *s'il*, as in lesson 15).
- ~~Si on allait au cinéma, ?~~: the suggestion has no comma and no main clause: *Si on allait au
  cinéma ?*
- Using this pattern for something likely: *S'il pleut demain, on restera à la maison* is the
  natural sentence for tomorrow's weather. *S'il pleuvait demain, on resterait …* is possible
  but sounds as if rain were unlikely.

## Key points

- Real condition: *si* + present → present / futur / imperative (lesson 15).
- Imaginary condition (B1 preview): *si* + imparfait → conditionnel: *Si j'étais riche,
  j'achèterais un voilier.*
- Never the conditionnel after *si*: *Les si n'aiment pas les -rais.*
- Useful chunks: *si j'étais toi* (= *à ta place*), *si j'avais le temps*, *si seulement …*, *Ce
  serait génial !*
- *Si on* + imparfait + ? alone is a suggestion (lesson 22), not a condition.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: L'écologie au quotidien: green habits in France
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 16 gave you the weather, the environment words and the pattern *il est important de* +
infinitive. This honors lesson looks at what "green" means in daily life in France: how people
sort their rubbish, why second-hand shopping is booming, how shared bikes changed French cities,
and what people eat. It ends with a short debate written in the futur and with *il faut*, the
kind of text you'll read in a local newspaper.

Every rule and date here was checked in an official or press source (listed in the course notes),
but rules change and differ from town to town: treat the details as a snapshot from late 2026.

## Le tri: what goes where

*Le tri* (sorting) is the noun for *trier*. French households usually sort their rubbish into
three to five streams:

| stream | French | what goes in |
|---|---|---|
| packaging and paper | *la poubelle jaune* (or *le bac jaune*) | *les emballages*: plastic bottles and pots, *les canettes* (cans), *les cartons*, *le papier*, newspapers |
| glass | *la colonne à verre* (bottle bank in the street) | bottles and jars, without their lids |
| food waste | *le compost*, or a brown bin | peelings, leftovers, coffee grounds |
| everything else | *les ordures ménagères* (grey or dark bin) | what can't be sorted |

Two national dates matter:

- Since 1 January 2023, the sorting rule is the same across almost all of metropolitan France:
  *tous les emballages* go in the yellow bin, including the plastic pots, trays and films that
  used to go in the general bin. Before that, the rule depended on the town.
- Since 1 January 2024, every local council must give households a way to sort *les
  biodéchets* (food and garden waste): a brown bin, collection points, or compost bins for
  homes and buildings.

The colours of the bins, however, still vary: the yellow bin is the most widespread, but some
towns use other colours, and many collect paper separately. Your town's *guide du tri* (sorting
guide), the bin lid, or the logo on the packaging (*le Triman* with its sorting instructions) will
tell you.

### Example 1: Où est-ce que ça va ?

*Task.* You have five things to throw away in a town that follows the common system: a yoghurt
pot, a jam jar, an apple core, a pizza box and a broken plate.

1. *Le pot de yaourt* is packaging. Since 2023, all packaging goes in the yellow bin → *dans la
   poubelle jaune*.
2. *Le pot de confiture* (jam jar) is glass packaging, and glass doesn't go in the yellow bin → *à
   la colonne à verre* (without the lid; a metal lid goes in the yellow bin).
3. *Le trognon de pomme* (apple core) is food waste → *au compost* or in the brown bin.
4. *Le carton de pizza*: cardboard is packaging → yellow bin. (Many guides ask you to put it in
   only if it isn't too greasy; check yours.)
5. *L'assiette cassée* (broken plate): china is not packaging and isn't recycled with glass → *dans
   les ordures ménagères*.

In French: *Le pot de yaourt va dans la poubelle jaune, le pot de confiture va au verre, le trognon
va au compost.* Notice *aller* with things: *Ça va où ?* — Where does this go?

## Réduire, réutiliser, recycler

Recycling is good, but French and European waste law puts it third. The best waste is the waste
you never produce; next best is using things again; recycling comes after that, and throwing away
comes last.

![A pyramid upside down, wide at the top and narrow at the bottom, with four levels. Top, widest and green: réduire (reduce), with a reusable water bottle. Second: réutiliser (reuse), with a bag used again. Third: recycler (recycle), with a recycling triangle. Bottom, narrowest and grey: jeter (throw away), with a bin. An arrow down the side says: du meilleur au moins bon (from best to least good).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Réduire* (to reduce; like *conduire*: *je réduis, nous réduisons, j'ai réduit*): *Nous voulons
  réduire nos déchets.* Many people now carry *une gourde* (a reusable water bottle) and their own
  bags.
- *Durable* means both lasting and sustainable: *un produit durable* (a product that lasts), *le
  développement durable* (sustainable development).
- *Réutiliser* (to reuse): *Je réutilise les pots de confiture pour mes épices.*
- Since 1 July 2016, shops in France may no longer give out single-use plastic carrier bags at
  the checkout; thin plastic bags for loose fruit and vegetables followed on 1 January 2017
  (compostable ones are allowed).
- The anti-waste law of 10 February 2020 (*la loi anti-gaspillage pour une économie
  circulaire*, often called *la loi AGEC*) bans the destruction of unsold new non-food products
  (from 2022 or the end of 2023, depending on the product), requires sorting instructions on
  products, and ended the automatic printing of till receipts. It also created the *bonus
  réparation*, a discount on your repair bill when a labelled repairer fixes an electrical
  appliance or, since a later extension, clothes and shoes.

## Acheter d'occasion

Buying *d'occasion* (second-hand) has become ordinary in France. *D'occasion* never changes: *un
vélo d'occasion, des livres d'occasion, une voiture d'occasion*.

- *Le vide-grenier* ("attic-emptier"; plural *les vide-greniers*): usually on a weekend day in spring
  or summer, a village or a district closes a street and people sell their old things on stalls.
  The British car-boot sale or the American yard sale is the closest idea. *La brocante* is
  similar, but usually with professional sellers.
- *La friperie*: a shop for second-hand (and often vintage) clothes.
- Websites and apps for second-hand goods are very popular for furniture, clothes, phones and
  children's things.

*J'ai acheté ce manteau dans une friperie : il coûtait douze euros !* — I bought this coat in a
second-hand clothes shop: it was twelve euros!

## Se déplacer autrement

- *Le vélo en libre-service* (self-service bike): you take a bike at a street station and leave it
  at another one. Lyon's *Vélo'v* opened in 2005 and was one of the first big schemes; Paris's
  *Vélib'* opened on 15 July 2007. Today most large French cities have one.
- *Le covoiturage* (car-sharing): you share a car, and the cost of the journey, with people going
  the same way, often found through an app. *On fera du covoiturage pour aller à Lyon.*
- *Les transports en commun* (lesson 16) and walking complete the picture. *Le vélo, c'est
  écologique et économique !* — Cycling is green and cheap!

## Manger local et de saison

- *Local* (feminine *locale*, masculine plural *locaux*): *des produits locaux*.
- *De saison* (in season): *Les fraises de saison arrivent en mai.*
- *Bio* (organic), short for *biologique*, usually doesn't change: *des légumes bio*.
- *Le gaspillage* (wasting) is the noun for *gaspiller*: *le gaspillage alimentaire* (food waste).
  Apps now sell shops' and bakeries' unsold food at the end of the day at low prices.

![A timeline of green milestones in France from 2005 to 2024. 2005: Vélo'v, shared bikes in Lyon. 15 July 2007: Vélib' in Paris. 1 July 2016: no more single-use plastic checkout bags. 10 February 2020: the anti-waste law (loi AGEC). 1 January 2023: all packaging in the yellow bin. 1 January 2024: food-waste sorting offered everywhere.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: un débat

A local newspaper asked two readers: *Faut-il interdire les voitures dans le centre-ville ?*
(Should cars be banned from the town centre?)

> *Pour — Claire, 41 ans, cycliste*
>
> *Oui ! Sans voitures, l'air sera plus propre et la ville sera moins bruyante. Les enfants
> pourront aller à l'école à vélo. Bien sûr, il faudra plus de bus et plus de pistes cyclables,
> mais dans dix ans, tout le monde trouvera ça normal. Il faut penser à l'avenir de nos enfants.*
>
> *Contre — Bernard, 67 ans, commerçant*
>
> *Non. Les clients ne viendront plus dans nos magasins s'ils ne peuvent pas se garer. Et les
> personnes âgées ? Elles ne pourront pas toutes prendre le vélo. Il faut protéger
> l'environnement, d'accord, mais il ne faut pas tuer le centre-ville. Il vaudrait mieux
> développer le covoiturage et les transports en commun.*

Translation:

> For — Claire, 41, cyclist: Yes! Without cars the air will be cleaner and the town will be less
> noisy. Children will be able to go to school by bike. Of course, we'll need more buses and more
> cycle lanes, but in ten years everyone will find it normal. We have to think about our
> children's future.
>
> Against — Bernard, 67, shopkeeper: No. Customers won't come to our shops any more if they can't
> park. And elderly people? They won't all be able to cycle. We have to protect the environment,
> fine, but we mustn't kill the town centre. It would be better to develop car-sharing and public
> transport.

(*la piste cyclable* = cycle lane; *le commerçant* = shopkeeper; *se garer* = to park; *les
personnes âgées* = elderly people; *tuer* = to kill; *bruyant* = noisy, lesson 09; *ne … plus* = no
longer, lesson 17.) Each writer uses the futur to predict (*l'air sera, les clients ne viendront
plus*), *il faut* / *il ne faut pas* for what must or mustn't be done, and *il faudra* / *il
vaudrait mieux* for what will be needed or would be better. That mix is typical of a short
argument in French.

### Example 2: eco resolutions for a flat share

*Task.* Write five lines to your flatmates proposing new green habits, using the futur, *il faut*
and *on*.

1. Start with a greeting and the reason: *Salut à tous ! Cette année, on va essayer de réduire
   nos déchets.*
2. Give two habits in the futur: *On achètera les légumes au marché. On prendra nos sacs.*
3. Add an obligation with *il faut* + infinitive and a prohibition with *il ne faut pas*: *Il faut
   trier les emballages. Il ne faut pas jeter le verre dans la poubelle jaune.*
4. Add a suggestion with *on pourrait* (lesson 14): *On pourrait aussi aller au vide-grenier
   dimanche.*
5. Close: *Qu'est-ce que vous en pensez ? Bises, Hugo.*

Check: *on* takes the *il* form (*on achètera*, never ~~on achèterons~~); *il faut* is followed
directly by the infinitive, with no *de*; and *achètera* keeps the *è* of *j'achète*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~des vêtements d'occasions~~ → *des vêtements d'occasion* (never plural).
- ~~des produits locals~~ → *des produits locaux*.
- ~~des légumes bios~~ → *des légumes bio* (usually invariable).
- ~~Je recycle le verre dans la poubelle jaune~~ → glass goes *à la colonne à verre*.
- ~~On achèterons~~ → *On achètera* (*on* takes the *il* form).
- ~~le gaspille~~ → *le gaspillage* (the noun); *gaspiller* is the verb.
- ~~réutilizer~~ → *réutiliser* (one *s*, said "z").

## Key points

- *Le tri*: all packaging in the yellow bin since 1 January 2023; a way to sort food waste offered
  everywhere since 1 January 2024; glass at the bottle bank. Colours vary: check locally.
- Reduce, reuse, recycle, in that order: *réduire, réutiliser, recycler*.
- *D'occasion* (invariable), *le vide-grenier, la friperie*; *local / locaux, de saison, bio*.
- *Le vélo en libre-service* (Vélo'v 2005, Vélib' 2007), *le covoiturage*.
- A short argument: futur to predict, *il faut / il ne faut pas* for duties, *il vaudrait mieux*
  to suggest.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Il faut que …: meeting the subjunctive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 15 you used *il faut* + infinitive: *Il faut dormir.* Sooner or later you will hear a
longer version: *Il faut que tu dormes.* — You need to sleep. That *dormes* is not a present
you know (*tu dors*). It is the **[[subjunctive]]**, a set of verb forms that French uses after
certain expressions: of necessity (*il faut que*), of wanting (*je veux que*), of feeling and of
doubt.

The subjunctive is B1 grammar. This honors lesson is a preview for recognition only: you will
learn what it is, how the regular forms are made, six common irregular ones, and, just as
important, how to avoid it while you are at A2. Nothing here is drilled. The setting is a flat
share (*une colocation*) and its rules.

## What is the subjunctive?

Grammar books call the subjunctive a **[[mood]]**, not a tense. The tenses you know (present,
passé composé, imparfait, futur) belong to the indicative mood, which states facts: *Tu fais la
vaisselle.* — You do the dishes. The subjunctive presents an action as something needed, wanted
or felt, not as a fact: *Il faut que tu fasses la vaisselle.* — You have to do the dishes (it
needs doing; it isn't done).

At A2 you only need to recognise it in two places:

- after *il faut que* (it is necessary that, you have to): *Il faut que je parte.* — I have to
  leave.
- after *vouloir que* (to want someone to): *Je veux que tu viennes.* — I want you to come. *Ma
  mère voudrait que je téléphone plus souvent.* — My mother would like me to phone more often.

The subjunctive almost always follows *que*, which is why tables often show it with *que*: *que
je parle, que tu parles …*

## Regular forms: start from ils

For most verbs, take the *ils* form of the present, remove *-ent*, and add *-e, -es, -e, -ions,
-iez, -ent*.

![A builder chart for the subjunctive. Start: the ils present, ils partent. Remove -ent to get the stem part-. Add the endings -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent. Results: que je parte, que tu partes, qu'il parte, que nous partions, que vous partiez, qu'ils partent. A note: the nous and vous forms look like the imparfait.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| | parler (ils parlent) | finir (ils finissent) | partir (ils partent) | prendre (ils prennent) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| que je | parle | finisse | parte | prenne |
| que tu | parles | finisses | partes | prennes |
| qu'il / elle / on | parle | finisse | parte | prenne |
| que nous | parlions | finissions | partions | prenions |
| que vous | parliez | finissiez | partiez | preniez |
| qu'ils / elles | parlent | finissent | partent | prennent |

Three things to notice:

- For *-er* verbs, the *je, tu, il* and *ils* forms look exactly like the present: *que je parle*
  = *je parle*. You can only tell them apart by what comes before (*il faut que …*).
- For most other verbs the singular sounds different from the present: *je pars* but *que je
  parte* (the *t* is heard); *je finis* but *que je finisse*.
- The *nous* and *vous* forms look like the imparfait: *que nous parlions* = *nous parlions*. Verbs
  that change their stem in the present keep two stems here too: *que je prenne* but *que nous
  prenions*; *que je vienne* but *que nous venions*.

## Six irregular verbs to recognise

These very common verbs have their own forms. Don't learn them to produce yet: learn to spot
them.

| | être | avoir | aller | faire | pouvoir | savoir |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| que je (j') | sois | aie | aille | fasse | puisse | sache |
| que tu | sois | aies | ailles | fasses | puisses | saches |
| qu'il | soit | ait | aille | fasse | puisse | sache |
| que nous | soyons | ayons | allions | fassions | puissions | sachions |
| que vous | soyez | ayez | alliez | fassiez | puissiez | sachiez |
| qu'ils | soient | aient | aillent | fassent | puissent | sachent |

Some of these look familiar: *sois, soyons, soyez*, *aie, ayons, ayez* and *sache, sachons,
sachez* are close to the imperatives you met in A1 (*Sois sage ! Sachez que …*). And *que j'aie*
sounds just like *j'ai* for most speakers.

## Il faut que and je veux que in context

- *Il faut que tu sois là à huit heures.* — You have to be there at eight.
- *Il faut qu'on fasse les courses.* — We need to do the shopping.
- *Il faut que vous ayez votre passeport.* — You must have your passport.
- *Je veux que tu saches la vérité.* — I want you to know the truth.
- *Mes parents veulent que j'aille à l'université.* — My parents want me to go to university.
- *Le propriétaire voudrait qu'on puisse visiter l'appartement samedi.* — The landlord would like
  people to be able to view the flat on Saturday.

Two important limits:

1. With *vouloir*, the subjunctive is only for wanting *someone else* to do something. If the
   person who wants is the person who does it, use the infinitive: *Je veux partir* (I want to
   leave), never ~~je veux que je parte~~.
2. With *il faut*, the infinitive is for a general need, or when the person is obvious: *Il faut
   partir* (we/you have to go). *Il faut que* + subjunctive names the person: *Il faut que Paul
   parte.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Do I need the subjunctive?
  accDescr: A decision chart for A2 learners. Start with a need or a wish. If it is general or the person is obvious, use il faut plus the infinitive, as in il faut partir. If you want to do something yourself, use vouloir plus the infinitive, as in je veux partir. If a different, named person must do it or you want someone else to do it, French uses il faut que or vouloir que plus the subjunctive, as in il faut que tu partes or je veux que tu partes. At A2 you can avoid this with devoir plus the infinitive: tu dois partir.
  A["A need or a wish"] --> B{"Who does the action?"}
  B -- "people in general, or obvious" --> C["il faut + infinitive: Il faut partir."]
  B -- "the person who wants it" --> D["vouloir + infinitive: Je veux partir."]
  B -- "someone else, named" --> E["il faut que / vouloir que + subjunctive: Il faut que tu partes."]
  E --> F["A2 way round it: Tu dois partir."]
```

## Words for living together

- *Vivre en colocation* = to share a flat; *le colocataire / la colocataire* (informally *le, la
  coloc*) = flatmate.
- *C'est ton tour de faire les courses.* — It's your turn to do the shopping. (*le tour*; *la tour*
  is a tower.) *On le fait à tour de rôle.* — We take turns.
- *Le propriétaire ne permet pas les animaux.* — The landlord doesn't allow pets. (*permettre*,
  like *mettre*: *il permet, ils permettent, il a permis*)
- *Il faut respecter les règles.* — You have to follow the rules.
- *On partage les tâches.* — We share the chores. (*nous partageons*; *la tâche* = task, with a
  circumflex: *la tache* is a stain)
- *Une bonne entente est indispensable.* — Getting on well is essential.
- *Ce n'est pas urgent : on en parlera dimanche.* — It isn't urgent: we'll talk about it on
  Sunday.

## How to avoid it at A2

While you are learning, you can say almost everything without the subjunctive:

| with the subjunctive (B1) | A2 alternative |
|---|---|
| *Il faut que tu fasses la vaisselle.* | *Tu dois faire la vaisselle.* / *Il faut faire la vaisselle.* |
| *Il faut que nous partions tôt.* | *Nous devons partir tôt.* / *Il faut partir tôt.* |
| *Je veux que tu viennes.* | *Viens, s'il te plaît !* / *Tu peux venir ?* / *J'aimerais bien te voir.* |
| *Il faut que je sois patient.* | *Je dois être patient.* |

These are natural and correct. The subjunctive is not "more correct"; it is the form that
follows these particular expressions.

## Reading: Les règles de la coloc

Chloé, Malik and Jade share a flat in Bordeaux. On the fridge, next to *le planning du ménage*
(the cleaning rota), there is a list.

> *Les règles de la coloc*
>
> *1. Il faut que chacun fasse sa vaisselle le jour même. Pas de désordre dans la cuisine !*
>
