> *2. On sort la poubelle à tour de rôle : c'est sur le planning.*
>
> *3. Si quelqu'un invite des amis, il faut qu'il prévienne les autres.*
>
> *4. Après 23 heures, on respecte le sommeil des colocataires et des voisins.*
>
> *5. On partage le frigo, mais on ne mange pas la nourriture des autres !*
>
> *6. Le loyer, c'est le 1er du mois. Le propriétaire exige qu'on ne soit jamais en retard.*
>
> *7. Chaque dimanche, il faut qu'on ait cinq minutes pour parler des tâches de la semaine.*

Translation:

> Flat-share rules: 1. Everyone has to do their own washing-up the same day. No mess in the
> kitchen! 2. We take out the bin in turn: it's on the rota. 3. If someone invites friends, they
> have to let the others know. 4. After 11 p.m. we respect our flatmates' and neighbours' sleep.
> 5. We share the fridge, but we don't eat other people's food! 6. The rent is due on the 1st of
> the month. The landlord insists that we're never late. 7. Every Sunday we need to have five minutes
> to talk about the week's chores.

(*chacun* = each one, lesson 18; *le jour même* = the same day; *prévienne* is the subjunctive of
*prévenir*, to let know, lesson 19; *la nourriture* = food; *le loyer* = rent, A1; *exiger que* also
takes the subjunctive.) Four rules use the subjunctive (*fasse, prévienne, soit, ait*), and the
others say the same kind of thing with *on* + present, which is how most French notices do it.

### Example 1: building que tu partes

*Task.* Find the subjunctive of *partir* for *tu*, as in *Il faut que tu ___ avant midi.*

1. Take the *ils* present: *ils partent*.
2. Remove *-ent*: *part-*.
3. Add the *tu* ending *-es*: *partes*.
4. Result: *Il faut que tu partes avant midi.* — You have to leave before noon. The *t*, silent in
   *tu pars*, is heard in *tu partes*.

The same steps give *que je dorme* (*ils dorment*), *qu'il écrive* (*ils écrivent*), *que tu
lises* (*ils lisent*).

### Example 2: spotting the subjunctive

*Task.* Malik sends a message. Which verbs are in the subjunctive, and how would you say them at
A2?

> *Jade, il faut que tu ailles chez le propriétaire demain, et il faut que tu prennes le
> chèque. Je veux que ce soit réglé avant vendredi !*

1. Look for *que* after a trigger: *il faut que tu ailles*, *il faut que tu prennes*, *je veux que
   ce soit*.
2. Identify the verbs: *ailles* (*aller*, irregular), *prennes* (*prendre*: *ils prennent →
   prenn- + -es*), *soit* (*être*).
3. An A2 version: *Jade, tu dois aller chez le propriétaire demain, et tu dois prendre le chèque.
   Ça doit être réglé avant vendredi !*

(*réglé* = sorted out, lesson 20.) Both versions mean the same: "Jade, you need to go to the
landlord's tomorrow and take the cheque. I want it sorted out before Friday!"

## Beyond this lesson

At B1 you will learn more triggers: feelings (*Je suis content que tu sois là*), doubt (*Je ne
pense pas que ce soit vrai*, lesson 21's note) and some conjunctions (*pour que, avant que, bien
que*). For now, when you see *que* after one of these expressions and a verb form you don't
recognise, think "subjunctive" and find the verb from its stem.

## Common mistakes

- ~~Je veux que je parte~~ → *Je veux partir* (same subject: infinitive).
- ~~Il faut que tu vas~~ → the subjunctive is *que tu ailles*; at A2, *Tu dois aller* is fine.
- ~~Il faut de partir~~ → *Il faut partir* (no *de* after *il faut*).
- Reading *que je parle* as a mistake: it is a correct subjunctive that looks like the present.
- Thinking the subjunctive is "more polite" or "more correct": it is simply the form after these
  expressions; *Tu dois …* is just as correct.

## Key points

- The subjunctive is a mood for actions that are needed or wanted, not stated as facts. It follows
  *que* after triggers such as *il faut que, vouloir que*.
- Regular: *ils* present minus *-ent* + *-e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent*: *que je parte, que nous
  partions*.
- Recognise *sois, aie, aille, fasse, puisse, sache*.
- Same subject → infinitive: *Je veux partir.*
- At A2, avoid it: *Il faut* + infinitive, *devoir* + infinitive.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Never, nothing, nobody, no longer: negation beyond ne … pas
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In French A1 you learned to say no with *ne … pas* (*Je ne travaille pas le lundi*), and you met
*ne … jamais* (never) and *ne … rien* (nothing). This lesson completes the set. You'll learn to say
"no longer", "nobody", "not a single", "nowhere" and "only", where each word goes in the passé
composé, and how to use *rien* and *personne* as the subject of a sentence.

The theme is work: job adverts, applying for a job and the interview. Job hunting is full of
negatives: *Je n'ai aucune expérience. Il n'y a plus de poste. Personne n'a répondu.*

## One pattern, many second words

All these expressions work like *ne … pas*: *ne* goes before the conjugated verb (*n'* before a
vowel or mute *h*), and a second word goes after it. A combination like this is called a
**[[negative expression]]**.

| expression | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *ne … pas* | not | *Je ne travaille pas le samedi.* — I don't work on Saturdays. |
| *ne … plus* | no longer, not any more | *Je ne travaille plus ici.* — I don't work here any more. |
| *ne … jamais* | never | *Il n'est jamais en retard.* — He's never late. |
| *ne … rien* | nothing, not anything | *Je ne comprends rien.* — I don't understand anything. |
| *ne … personne* | nobody, not anybody | *Je ne connais personne ici.* — I don't know anybody here. |
| *ne … aucun / aucune* + noun | no, not a single | *Je n'ai aucune idée.* — I have no idea. |
| *ne … nulle part* | nowhere, not anywhere | *Je ne trouve mon badge nulle part.* — I can't find my badge anywhere. |
| *ne … que* | only | *Je ne travaille que le matin.* — I only work in the mornings. |

The new pieces of each pair go in the same slot as *pas*, so you never use *pas* as well:
~~Je ne travaille pas plus ici~~ is wrong; *Je ne travaille plus ici.*

![A chart of French negation. Top row, the present: Je, ne, travaille, plus, ici, with ne and plus in red around the green verb. Middle row, the passé composé with the short words: Je, n', ai, then a red box listing pas, plus, jamais, rien, then vu: the second word sits between avoir and the participle. Bottom row: Je, n', ai, vu, then a red box listing personne, aucun client, que Paul: these words come after the participle.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Ne … plus: no longer

*Plus* here means "no more": something was true and has stopped.

- *Elle ne fume plus.* — She doesn't smoke any more.
- *Il n'y a plus de café.* — There's no more coffee.
- *Je ne suis plus au chômage : j'ai trouvé un emploi !* — I'm no longer unemployed: I've found a
  job!

In *ne … plus* the *s* of *plus* is silent: "ply". (When *plus* means "more", lesson 09, the *s* is
often said: *J'en veux plus* "plus" = I want more.)

### Ne … aucun: not a single one

*Aucun* is a determiner: it goes before a noun, in place of *un, une, des*, and agrees with it:
*aucun* before a masculine noun, *aucune* before a feminine one. The noun is normally singular.

- *Je n'ai aucun diplôme.* — I don't have a single qualification.
- *Il n'y a aucune offre d'emploi intéressante cette semaine.* — There isn't a single interesting
  job advert this week.
- *Aucun problème !* — No problem at all!

*Aucun* is stronger than *pas de*: *Je n'ai pas d'expérience* (I have no experience), *Je n'ai
aucune expérience* (I have no experience at all).

### Ne … que: only, a restriction

*Ne … que* looks like a negative but it isn't one: it means "only", like *seulement* (lesson 12).
It is a **[[restriction]]**: it limits what you say to one thing. *Que* goes right before the word it
limits, so it doesn't always come straight after the verb:

- *Je n'ai que dix euros.* — I only have ten euros.
- *Le magasin n'embauche que des étudiants.* — The shop only takes on students.
- *On ne travaille que le samedi.* — We only work on Saturdays.
- *Je ne l'ai vu qu'une fois.* — I've only seen him once.

Because *ne … que* is not a real negative, *un, une, des, du, de la* stay as they are: *Je n'ai que
du pain* (only bread), never ~~je n'ai que de pain~~.

## De after a negative

You know from A1 that *un, une, des, du, de la* become *de* (*d'*) after *ne … pas*: *Je n'ai pas
de voiture.* The same happens after *ne … plus* and *ne … jamais*:

- *Il n'y a plus de poste à temps plein.* — There are no more full-time positions.
- *Je ne bois jamais de café le soir.* — I never drink coffee in the evening.

Two exceptions, as in A1: after *être* (*Ce n'est pas un problème*), and after *ne … que*, which is
not a real negative (*Il n'y a que des stages*, there are only internships).

## In the passé composé: before or after the participle?

In the passé composé, *ne* goes before the auxiliary as usual. The second word goes in one of two
places:

| before the participle | after the participle |
|---|---|
| *pas, plus, jamais, rien* | *personne, aucun, que, nulle part* |
| *Je n'ai pas postulé.* | *Je n'ai vu personne.* |
| *Il n'a plus travaillé.* | *Je n'ai eu aucun problème.* |
| *Elle n'est jamais venue.* | *Il n'a gagné que mille euros.* |
| *Je n'ai rien compris.* | *Je ne l'ai trouvé nulle part.* |

A memory hook: *pas, plus, jamais* and *rien* are short words that squeeze in next to *avoir* or
*être*, just like *pas*; *personne, aucun, que* and *nulle part* take the place of the object, the
noun or the place (nobody, not a single X, only X, nowhere), so they go where that object or
place would go: after the participle.

With an object pronoun (lesson 08), the pronoun stays glued to the auxiliary, inside *ne*: *Je ne
l'ai jamais vu. Je ne lui ai rien dit.*

### With an infinitive

Before an infinitive, *ne pas, ne plus, ne jamais, ne rien* stay together in front of it. You see
this on signs and in instructions:

- *Merci de ne pas fumer.* — Thank you for not smoking.
- *J'ai décidé de ne plus travailler le dimanche.* — I've decided not to work on Sundays any more.
- *Il est important de ne rien oublier.* — It's important not to forget anything.

*Personne* goes after the infinitive: *Je préfère ne voir personne.* — I prefer not to see anyone.

## Rien and personne as the subject

*Rien* and *personne* can start the sentence as the subject. Then *ne* comes straight after them,
and there is no *pas*:

- *Personne n'a répondu à mon annonce.* — Nobody answered my advert.
- *Rien n'est simple.* — Nothing is simple.
- *Personne ne travaille ici le dimanche.* — Nobody works here on Sundays.
- *Aucun candidat n'est venu.* — Not a single candidate came.

The verb is singular, and *personne* (nobody) takes a masculine agreement: *Personne n'est venu.*

## Short answers

Most of the second words work alone as an answer:

- *Tu as déjà travaillé dans un restaurant ? — Jamais !* — Never!
- *Qui est au bureau ? — Personne.* — Nobody.
- *Tu as compris ? — Rien du tout.* — Nothing at all.
- *Vous avez des questions ? — Aucune.* — None.
- *Tu fumes encore ? — Non, plus maintenant.* — No, not any more.
- *Tu aimes ton travail ? — Pas du tout !* — Not at all!

## Personne or la personne?

Don't mix up the pronoun *personne* (nobody) and the noun *la personne* (a person):

| | *personne* (pronoun) | *la personne* (noun) |
|---|---|---|
| meaning | nobody, not anybody | a person |
| article | none | *la, une, les, des* |
| with *ne* | yes: *Personne n'est là.* | no: *Une personne est là.* |
| gender | masculine agreement | always feminine, even for a man |

*Personne n'est venu*, nobody came. *Une personne est venue*, a person came. *Il y a deux
personnes à l'accueil.* — There are two people at reception. *Ton collègue est une personne très
sympa.* — Your colleague is a very nice person.

## Working life: the words

Three words for "job":

- *le métier*: the trade or profession you have learned: *Quel est votre métier ? — Je suis
  infirmière.*
- *l'emploi* (masculine): a job as employment, something you have or look for: *chercher un emploi,
  une offre d'emploi*.
- *le poste*: one particular position in a company: *un poste de vendeur, un poste à temps
  partiel*. Careful: *le poste* is masculine; *la poste* is the post office.

And *le travail* (A1) is work in general: *J'ai beaucoup de travail.*

The job hunt, step by step:

1. *L'entreprise embauche.* — The company is hiring. It publishes *une offre d'emploi* (a job advert)
   for a job *à temps plein* (full-time) or *à temps partiel* (part-time), or for *un stage* (an
   internship).
2. *Je postule.* — I apply (*postuler à une offre, postuler pour un poste*). I send *mon CV* and a
   letter: that is *ma candidature*, my application.
3. *J'ai un entretien.* — I have an interview. They ask about *mon expérience*.
4. *Je travaille dans une équipe.* — I work in a team, with *des collègues*, *un patron* or *une
   patronne* (the boss or owner; for a manager in a big company the word is a little informal), and far too many *réunions* (meetings).
5. *Je gagne un salaire.* — I earn a salary. (*Gagner* also means to win: *gagner un match*.)

And if you have no job: *Je suis au chômage* (I'm unemployed; *le chômage*, unemployment).

## A job advert

Here is a small ad from a grocer's in Rennes. Notice *aucun* and *ne … que* doing real work.

![A job advert. Heading: Le Petit Marché, épicerie à Rennes, recrute. Then: Poste : vendeur / vendeuse. À temps partiel : 20 heures par semaine, du mardi au samedi. Salaire : 14 € brut de l'heure. Expérience : aucun diplôme demandé, mais un an d'expérience dans la vente. Candidature : CV et lettre avant le 30 novembre. At the bottom: Nous ne répondons qu'aux candidatures complètes.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Aucun diplôme demandé* = no qualification required. *Nous ne répondons qu'aux candidatures
complètes* = we only reply to complete applications. (*Brut* means before tax and social charges,
"gross".)

## Dialogue: L'entretien

Inès has an interview for the job in the advert.

> Patronne : Bonjour ! Asseyez-vous. Alors, vous avez déjà travaillé dans un magasin ?
>
> Inès : Oui, j'ai été vendeuse dans une boulangerie pendant un an. Mais je n'y travaille plus depuis septembre.
>
> Patronne : Pourquoi ?
>
> Inès : La boulangerie a fermé. Maintenant, je ne travaille que le dimanche, dans un café.
>
> Patronne : Vous avez un diplôme de commerce ?
>
> Inès : Non, je n'ai aucun diplôme de commerce. Mais j'apprends vite !
>
> Patronne : Ce n'est pas un problème. Ici, on travaille en équipe : personne ne reste seul en magasin. Vous êtes libre le samedi ?
>
> Inès : Oui, le samedi, je n'ai rien de prévu.
>
> Patronne : Parfait. Vous avez des questions ?
>
> Inès : Non, aucune… Ah si, une seule : quand est-ce que vous allez embaucher ?
>
> Patronne : Je vous appelle la semaine prochaine.

*Boss: Hello! Have a seat. So, have you worked in a shop before? — Inès: Yes, I was a sales assistant
in a bakery for a year. But I haven't worked there since September. — Boss: Why? — Inès: The bakery
closed. Now I only work on Sundays, in a café. — Boss: Do you have a business qualification? —
Inès: No, I haven't got any business qualification. But I learn fast! — Boss: That's not a problem.
Here we work as a team: nobody stays alone in the shop. Are you free on Saturdays? — Inès: Yes, on
Saturdays I don't have anything planned. — Boss: Perfect. Do you have any questions? — Inès: No, none… Oh yes, just
one: when are you going to hire someone? — Boss: I'll call you next week.*

*Asseyez-vous* is the imperative of *s'asseoir*, to sit down: just learn it as a phrase for now.
*Si* (A1) contradicts a negative: Inès has just said *aucune*, then changes her mind. *Rien de
prévu*, nothing planned: *rien* + *de* + adjective, which lesson 18 explains.

## Dropping ne in speech

In everyday speech, French people very often drop *ne* and keep only the second word:

- *J'ai rien compris.* = *Je n'ai rien compris.*
- *Je travaille plus ici.* = *Je ne travaille plus ici.*
- *Y a personne.* = *Il n'y a personne.*

Recognise this when you hear it, but write the full form, and use it in the DELF and anywhere
formal. One trap: without *ne*, *plus* can mean "more" or "no more", and only the *s* tells them
apart: *J'en veux plus* "ply" = I don't want any more; *J'en veux plus* "plus" = I want more.

One more expression you will meet: *ne … ni … ni* (neither … nor): *Je ne parle ni allemand ni
italien.* — I speak neither German nor Italian. Just recognise it for now.

## Pronunciation

- *ne … plus* "ply", with a silent *s*.
- *personne* "pair-SON", the same in the pronoun and the noun.
- *aucun* "oh-KUN" (nasal), *aucune* "oh-KÜN" (French *u* of *tu*, *n* said); before a vowel, liaison:
  *aucun_emploi* "oh-kuhn-nahn-plwa", with the *n* carried over.
- *le CV* "say-vay"; *l'emploi* "lahn-plwa".
- *nulle part* "nül par".

## Common mistakes

- *Je ne travaille pas plus ici.* One second word only: *Je ne travaille plus ici.*
- *Personne n'est pas venu.* With *personne* or *rien* as the subject, no *pas*: *Personne n'est
  venu.*
- *Je n'ai personne vu.* *Personne* goes after the participle: *Je n'ai vu personne.* (But *Je n'ai
  rien vu*, before it.)
- *Je n'ai aucuns diplômes.* *Aucun* normally takes a singular noun: *Je n'ai aucun diplôme.*
- *Je n'ai que d'eau.* After *ne … que* the article stays: *Je n'ai que de l'eau* (only water).
- Leaving out *ne* when you write. It's fine in casual speech, not in a letter or an exam.
- *La poste* for a job. A position is *le poste*.

## Key points

- *ne* + verb + *plus / jamais / rien / personne / aucun(e) + noun / nulle part / que*. Never with
  *pas* as well.
- *ne … que* = only (a restriction, not a negative): the article stays (*que du pain*).
- *de* after *pas, plus, jamais*: *Il n'y a plus de travail.*
- Passé composé: *pas, plus, jamais, rien* before the participle (*Je n'ai rien vu*); *personne,
  aucun, que, nulle part* after it (*Je n'ai vu personne*).
- *Personne n'est venu. Rien ne marche.* (subject: no *pas*).
- *Merci de ne pas fumer*: *ne pas* together before an infinitive.
- *personne* (nobody, no article) ≠ *la personne* (a person, always feminine).
- Work words: *le métier, l'emploi, le poste, l'entreprise, le salaire, l'entretien, le CV, postuler,
  embaucher, le stage, à temps plein / partiel*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Each, every, several, everyone: indefinite words
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 17 gave you the words for "nobody" and "nothing". This lesson gives you their opposites and
all the words in between: "each", "every", "all", "several", "a few", "some", "everyone",
"somewhere". Grammars call them indefinite words, because they talk about people and things
without saying exactly which ones or exactly how many.

They come in two kinds. An **[[indefinite determiner]]** goes in front of a noun, in the place of an
article: *chaque jour* (each day), *plusieurs fois* (several times). An **[[indefinite pronoun]]**
stands alone, in the place of a noun: *chacun* (each one), *tout le monde* (everyone). Many
mistakes come from using one kind where the other belongs, so this lesson keeps them side by
side.

The theme is studies: school subjects, university and training.

## Chaque and chacun

*Chaque* (each, every) is a determiner. It always comes before a singular noun and doesn't
change for masculine or feminine:

- *chaque jour, chaque semaine, chaque matière* — every day, every week, every subject
- *Chaque étudiant a un emploi du temps.* — Each student has a timetable.

*Chacun* (each one, everyone) is the pronoun: it stands alone. Its feminine is *chacune*. The verb
after it is singular:

- *Chacun a son emploi du temps.* — Everyone has their own timetable.
- *Les étudiantes ? Chacune a choisi une matière.* — The students? Each one chose a subject.
- *chacun de nous, chacune de mes sœurs* — each of us, each of my sisters

So: *chaque* + noun, *chacun* alone. ~~Chaque a son livre~~ is wrong; so is ~~chacun étudiant~~.

## Tout, toute, tous, toutes

You met *tout* in A1 (*Tout est prêt*, everything is ready). As a determiner, *tout* agrees with the
noun and is followed by an article (*le, la, les*), a possessive (*mon, ma, mes*) or a demonstrative
(*ce, cette, ces*). The singular and the plural say different things:

| | masculine | feminine | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| singular | *tout le temps* | *toute la journée* | the whole, all (the) |
| plural | *tous les jours* | *toutes les semaines* | every, all (the) |

- *J'ai étudié toute la journée.* — I studied all day (the whole day).
- *J'ai cours tous les jours.* — I have classes every day.
- *Toute ma famille est venue.* — My whole family came.
- *Tous mes amis font des études.* — All my friends are at university.

![A chart of indefinite words in two columns. Left, determiners, which go before a noun: chaque plus a singular noun, as in chaque jour; tout le, toute la, tous les, toutes les plus a noun, as in tous les jours and toute la journée; plusieurs plus a plural noun, as in plusieurs fois; quelques plus a plural noun, as in quelques amis. Right, pronouns, which stand alone: chacun, chacune, as in chacun a son livre; tous, toutes with the s of tous pronounced, as in ils sont tous là; plusieurs, as in j'en ai plusieurs; tout le monde with a singular verb, as in tout le monde est là; quelqu'un or quelque chose plus de and an adjective, as in quelque chose d'intéressant.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Tous as a pronoun: say the s

*Tous* and *toutes* can also stand alone, meaning "all of them":

- *Mes cours ? Ils sont tous intéressants.* — My classes? They're all interesting.
- *Les filles sont toutes là.* — The girls are all here.
- *Je les connais tous.* — I know all of them.

Here the *s* of *tous* is pronounced: "toos". As a determiner it is silent: *tous les jours* "too lay
zhoor". So *Ils sont tous là* "toos", but *tous les étudiants* "too lay-zay-tü-dyahn".

*Tout* alone (everything) goes before the participle in the passé composé, like *rien* in lesson 17:
*J'ai tout compris.* — I understood everything. *Je n'ai rien compris.* — I understood nothing.

### Tout le monde: everyone

*Tout le monde* means everyone. For "the whole world", French usually says *le monde entier*. It takes a
singular verb, like *chacun*:

- *Tout le monde est content.* — Everyone is pleased.
- *Tout le monde a réussi l'examen.* — Everyone passed the exam.

Never ~~tout le monde sont~~.

## Plusieurs, quelques, certains, d'autres

- *Plusieurs* (several) goes straight before a plural noun, with no article, and is the same for
  masculine and feminine: *plusieurs fois, plusieurs matières*. Never ~~des plusieurs~~. It can
  also stand alone, usually with *en*: *Des examens ? J'en ai plusieurs cette semaine.*
- *Quelques* (a few, some) also goes before a plural noun: *quelques jours, quelques amis*. It
  suggests a small number; *plusieurs* just means "more than one or two" and often sounds like
  rather more than *quelques*. Alone, it becomes
  *quelques-uns / quelques-unes*: *Il y a des exercices difficiles, mais quelques-uns sont faciles.*
- *Certains / certaines* (some, certain ones) picks out part of a group: *Certains étudiants
  travaillent le soir* (some students, not all). Alone: *Certains préfèrent la fac.* — Some
  (people) prefer uni. Careful: after the noun, *certain* means "sure": *un progrès certain*, a
  definite improvement.
- *D'autres* (others, other) is the plural of *un autre, une autre* (A1): *des* becomes *d'* before
  *autres*: *D'autres matières sont plus
  faciles. Certains aiment les maths, d'autres préfèrent l'histoire.*

## Something interesting, someone nice: de + adjective

After *quelque chose, quelqu'un, rien* and *personne*, an adjective needs *de* (*d'*) and stays
masculine singular:

- *J'ai appris quelque chose d'intéressant.* — I learned something interesting.
- *C'est quelqu'un de très sérieux.* — He's (she's) a very reliable person.
- *Rien de nouveau.* — Nothing new.
- *Je n'ai vu personne d'important.* — I didn't see anybody important.

English just says "something interesting"; French needs the *de*. And it stays masculine even
when you talk about a woman: *Ma prof de maths ? C'est quelqu'un de génial.*

## Somewhere, sometimes: the quelque family

| French | English | note |
|---|---|---|
| *quelqu'un* | someone | A1 |
| *quelque chose* | something | A1 |
| *quelque part* | somewhere | *J'ai laissé mon cahier quelque part.* |
| *quelquefois* | sometimes | = *parfois*; one word |
| *quelques* | a few | + plural noun |

*Quelquefois* means exactly the same as *parfois* (A1): *Quelquefois, je mange à la cantine.* Don't
confuse it with *quelques fois* (two words), "a few times": *Je suis allé à Lyon quelques fois.*

### A preview: n'importe qui, quoi, où

You'll often hear *n'importe* (literally "it doesn't matter") + a question word: *n'importe qui*
(anyone at all), *n'importe quoi* (anything at all), *n'importe où* (anywhere). *Tu peux t'asseoir
n'importe où.* — You can sit anywhere. *Il dit n'importe quoi !* — He's talking nonsense! Just
recognise these for now; they come back at B1.

## Studies in France

Lesson 01 took you through school: *l'école maternelle, l'école primaire, le collège* (ages 11 to
15) and *le lycée* (15 to 18). At the end of the lycée most pupils *passent le bac*, the
baccalaureate, the exam that ends secondary school. Careful with a false friend: *passer un
examen* means to *take* an exam; to pass it is *réussir un examen* (A1 *réussir*) or *avoir son
bac*.

With the bac you can go on to higher education, *faire des études* (to study, at university or
another school). The university degrees are counted in years after the bac:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The main path through French education
  accDescr: From le collège, ages 11 to 15, pupils go to le lycée, ages 15 to 18, which ends with the exam called le bac. After the bac there are two common paths. At the university, la fac, la licence takes 3 years, called bac plus 3; le master takes 2 more years, bac plus 5; le doctorat takes about 3 more years, bac plus 8. Alternatively, a BTS is a 2-year professional diploma, bac plus 2, usually taken in a lycée.
  A["le collège (11–15 ans)"] --> B["le lycée (15–18 ans)"]
  B --> C["le bac"]
  C --> D["la fac : la licence (bac + 3)"]
  C --> G["un BTS (bac + 2)"]
  D --> E["le master (bac + 5)"]
  E --> F["le doctorat (bac + 8)"]
```

- *la licence* — the bachelor's degree, three years at university: *une licence d'histoire*.
- *le master* — two more years: *un master de géographie*.
- *le doctorat* — the doctorate, about three more years.
- *un BTS* — a two-year professional diploma after the bac, usually taken in a lycée.

French people describe their level this way: *J'ai un bac + 3* means "I have three years of
higher education", usually a licence. (This is simplified: there are also selective *grandes
écoles*, many of them entered after two years of special preparatory classes.)

University is *l'université*, or informally *la fac*: *Je suis à la fac. Je vais à la fac.* Before
you start, you have to *s'inscrire* (to enrol, register): *Je me suis inscrit en licence de
maths.* *S'inscrire* is conjugated like *écrire*: *je m'inscris, nous nous inscrivons*; the
noun is *l'inscription*. *La formation* is training or a course of study: *une formation en
informatique* (a computer course), and on a CV, *Formation* is the section for your education.

## At school: subjects, timetable, homework

A school subject is *une matière*: *Quelle est ta matière préférée ?* Some subjects: *les maths*
(always plural; said "mat": the *t* is heard, the *h* and *s* are silent), *la géographie, l'histoire* (A1 "story", at school also
history; often together as *l'histoire-géo*), *le français, l'anglais, la musique, le sport*.

Your week of classes is *l'emploi du temps* (the timetable; not *l'horaire*, which is a bus or
train timetable). Here is the timetable of Léo, a pupil in a lycée:

![Léo's school timetable for lundi to vendredi, with five slots a day: 8 h to 10 h, 10 h to 12 h, lunch from 12 h to 13 h 30, 13 h 30 to 15 h 30 and 15 h 30 to 17 h 30. Each lesson has an icon and its name: les maths (a plus and an equals sign), l'anglais (a speech bubble saying Hello!), la géographie (a globe), le sport (a football), la musique (a musical note). Every lunch slot shows la cantine (a plate with a fork and knife), except on Wednesday. Monday: maths, anglais, cantine, géographie, sport. Tuesday: géographie, musique, cantine, sport, anglais. Wednesday: musique, anglais, then pas cours in the afternoon. Thursday: maths, géographie, cantine, anglais, musique. Friday: anglais, sport, cantine, géographie, musique.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Le mercredi après-midi, Léo n'a pas cours. Il a maths deux fois par semaine.* (*Avoir cours* = to
have class; *avoir maths* = to have maths: no article.) At lunchtime Léo eats *à la cantine*; at
university the canteen is *le resto U* (*le restaurant universitaire*).

After class there are *les devoirs* (homework, masculine plural: *J'ai beaucoup de devoirs*). Then
come *les résultats*. *Tu as réussi ?* (Did you pass?) *Non, j'ai raté mon examen* (informal) or
*j'ai échoué à mon examen* (more formal): two ways to say "I failed". *Il a échoué au bac.* *Rater*
also means to miss: *J'ai raté le bus.*

## Dialogue: Les inscriptions

Two friends meet in front of the university in September.

> Sofia : Salut, Hugo ! Tu fais quoi ici ?
>
> Hugo : Je viens m'inscrire. Chaque année, c'est la même chose : il y a plusieurs papiers à remplir, et tout le monde fait la queue !
>
> Sofia : Moi, je me suis inscrite en ligne. Tu es en quelle année ?
>
> Hugo : En deuxième année de licence d'histoire. Et toi ?
>
> Sofia : Je commence un master de géographie. J'ai quelques cours le matin, et je travaille à temps partiel l'après-midi.
>
> Hugo : Tous les jours ?
>
> Sofia : Non, seulement le mardi et le jeudi. Quelquefois le samedi aussi.
>
> Hugo : Et tes profs, ils sont sympas ?
>
> Sofia : Certains sont très sympas, d'autres sont plus stricts. Mais chacun a sa méthode. Bon, on mange ensemble à midi ? On va au resto U ?
>
> Hugo : D'accord. Je te retrouve quelque part ?
>
> Sofia : Devant la bibliothèque, à midi et demi !

*Sofia: Hi, Hugo! What are you doing here? — Hugo: I've come to enrol. Every year it's the same
thing: there are several papers to fill in, and everyone queues! — Sofia: I enrolled online. What
year are you in? — Hugo: Second year of a history degree. And you? — Sofia: I'm starting a master's in
geography. I have a few classes in the morning, and I work part-time in the afternoon. — Hugo: Every
day? — Sofia: No, only on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Sometimes on Saturdays too. — Hugo: And your
lecturers, are they nice? — Sofia: Some are very nice, others are stricter. But each one has their
own method. Right, shall we eat together at lunchtime? Shall we go to the university canteen? —
Hugo: OK. Shall I meet you somewhere? — Sofia: In front of the library, at half past twelve!*

*Je me suis inscrite*: the participle agrees with Sofia (pronominal verbs take *être*). *Le prof,
la prof* is the everyday word for *le professeur* (A1).

## Pronunciation

- *tous* as a pronoun "toos" (*ils sont tous là*); as a determiner "too" (*tous les jours*).
- *plusieurs* "plü-zyeur"; liaison before a vowel: *plusieurs_heures* "plü-zyeu-zeur".
- *quelques* "kel-kuh", liaison *quelques_amis* "kel-kuh-za-mee".
- *chaque* "shak"; *chacun* "sha-kun" (nasal).
- *les maths* "lay mat" (*t* said, *h* and *s* silent); *le bac* "bak".
- *l'emploi du temps* "lahn-plwa dü tahn".

## Common mistakes

- *chaque jours*, *chaques jours*. *Chaque* + singular: *chaque jour*. (Or *tous les jours*.)
- *Chaque a son livre.* Alone, use *chacun*: *Chacun a son livre.*
- *Tout le monde sont là.* Singular verb: *Tout le monde est là.*
- *des plusieurs livres*. No article: *plusieurs livres*.
- *tous le monde*. It's *tout le monde*.
- *quelque chose intéressant*, *quelque chose d'intéressante*. *De* + masculine: *quelque chose
  d'intéressant*.
- *Toute la semaine* for every week. *Toute la semaine* = the whole week; *toutes les semaines* =
  every week.
- *J'ai passé mon examen* to mean you passed. *Passer* = to take; *réussir* = to pass.
- Saying the *s* of *tous* in *tous les jours*, or not saying it in *ils sont tous là*.

## Key points

- Determiners (before a noun): *chaque* + singular; *tout le, toute la, tous les, toutes les*;
  *plusieurs, quelques, certains, d'autres* + plural.
- Pronouns (alone): *chacun(e)*, *tous / toutes* (s said: "toos"), *tout le monde* (+ singular verb),
  *plusieurs, quelques-uns, certains, d'autres*.
- *toute la journée* (the whole day) ≠ *tous les jours* (every day).
- *quelque chose / quelqu'un / rien / personne* + *de* + masculine adjective.
- *quelquefois* = *parfois*; *quelques fois* = a few times; *quelque part* = somewhere.
- Studies: *le bac*, *la fac*, *la licence* (bac + 3), *le master* (bac + 5); *s'inscrire*,
  *l'inscription*, *la formation*; *la matière, l'emploi du temps, les devoirs, les résultats*.
- *passer un examen* = to take it; *réussir* = to pass; *rater / échouer* = to fail.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: He says that…, I'm asking if…: reported speech and indirect questions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At the bank, the town hall or any office, you spend a lot of time passing on what someone said
(*The adviser says that my card is blocked*) and asking questions politely and indirectly (*I'd
like to know if the office is open on Saturdays*). This lesson teaches both:

- **[[reported speech]]** (also called indirect speech): telling someone what another person says,
  with *dire que …, répondre que …*;
- **[[indirect questions]]**: a question inside a sentence, with *si, où, quand, ce que …*

Everything here is in the present: *Il dit que … , Elle demande si …* Reporting in the past is a B1
topic; you'll see a short preview at the end.

## Reporting a statement: dire que

To report what someone says, use a verb such as *dire* (to say), *répondre* (to answer),
*expliquer* (to explain), *écrire* (to write) or *informer* (to inform), then *que* + the
sentence:

- « Le bureau est fermé. » → *L'agent dit que le bureau est fermé.* — The official says (that) the
  office is closed.
- « Il faut une pièce d'identité. » → *Elle explique qu'il faut une pièce d'identité.*

English can drop "that" (*He says the office is closed*). French never drops *que*: ~~Il dit le
bureau est fermé~~ is wrong. *Que* becomes *qu'* before a vowel: *Il dit qu'il est malade.* If
you report two things, repeat *que*: *Elle dit qu'elle est désolée et que ma carte est bloquée.*

### Pronouns and possessives change

When you report someone else's words, *je, me, mon* become whatever fits from your point of view,
just as in English:

| what Marc says | what you report |
|---|---|
| « Je suis malade. » | *Marc dit qu'il est malade.* |
| « Mon compte est vide. » | *Il dit que son compte est vide.* |
| « Nous avons un problème. » | *Ils disent qu'ils ont un problème.* |
| « Vous devez patienter. » (to you) | *Il dit que je dois patienter.* |
| « Votre dossier est complet. » (to you) | *Elle dit que mon dossier est complet.* |

The tense doesn't change when the reporting verb is in the present: *est* stays *est*.

![A chart of reported speech. Top: a speech bubble from a bank adviser saying « Je suis désolée, votre carte est bloquée. » An arrow leads down to the reported sentence: Elle dit qu'elle est désolée et que ma carte est bloquée. Coloured labels show the changes: je becomes elle, votre becomes ma, and que is added before each part. Below, a second example: the question « Est-ce que vous avez votre code ? » becomes Il me demande si j'ai mon code, with est-ce que becoming si and no question mark.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Reporting an instruction: dire de + infinitive

An order or request in the imperative is reported with *dire de* or *demander de* + infinitive:

- « Patientez ! » → *Il nous dit de patienter.* — He tells us to wait.
- « Remplissez ce formulaire. » → *Elle me demande de remplir ce formulaire.*
- « Ne quittez pas. » (on the phone) → *Il me dit de ne pas quitter.* — He tells me to hold the
  line. (*ne pas* + infinitive, lesson 17)

*Dire* and *demander* take *à* + the person, so the pronouns are *me, te, lui, nous, vous, leur*
(lesson 06): *Elle lui demande de signer.*

## Indirect questions

A direct question has a question mark: *Où est l'accueil ?* An indirect question is part of a
longer sentence that asks or wonders: *Je voudrais savoir où est l'accueil.* *Il demande quand la
banque ouvre.* It has statement word order and, unless the whole sentence is a question, no
question mark.

### Yes/no questions → si

A question that expects *oui* or *non* is reported with *si* (if, whether):

- « Tu viens ? » / « Est-ce que tu viens ? » → *Il demande si tu viens.*
- « Avez-vous votre code ? » → *Elle me demande si j'ai mon code.*

*Si* + *il* / *ils* becomes *s'il* / *s'ils*, but *si elle*, *si on* stay as they are: *Je me
demande s'il est là. Je me demande si elle est là.*

### Question words stay

*Où, quand, comment, combien, pourquoi, qui* and *quel* stay at the front of the indirect
question:

- « Où habitez-vous ? » → *Il demande où j'habite.*
- « Quand est-ce que le colis arrive ? » → *Je voudrais savoir quand le colis arrive.*
- « Combien coûte la carte ? » → *Elle demande combien coûte la carte* (or *combien la carte
  coûte*).
- « Quel est votre numéro de compte ? » → *Il me demande quel est mon numéro de compte.*

### Qu'est-ce que → ce que, qu'est-ce qui → ce qui

The question word "what" changes. *Qu'est-ce que* (and *que, quoi*) becomes *ce que*; *qu'est-ce
qui* becomes *ce qui*:

- « Qu'est-ce que vous voulez ? » → *Dites-moi ce que vous voulez.* — Tell me what you want.
- « Tu fais quoi ? » → *Il demande ce que tu fais.*
- « Qu'est-ce qui se passe ? » → *Je ne sais pas ce qui se passe.* — I don't know what's going on.

*Ce que* is "what" as an object (someone wants it, does it); *ce qui* is "what" as the subject
(it happens, it doesn't work). The same test as *qui / que* in lesson 10: is there a subject after
the gap? *ce que vous voulez* (yes: *vous*), *ce qui se passe* (no: *ce qui* is the subject).

### Word order: no est-ce que, no inversion

In an indirect question, *est-ce que* disappears and the subject pronoun doesn't swap with the
verb:

- « Où est-ce que tu travailles ? » / « Où travailles-tu ? » → *Il demande où tu travailles.*
  Never ~~où est-ce que tu travailles~~ or ~~où travailles-tu~~ inside the sentence.

With a noun subject and a short verb, the noun may come after the verb, as in *où est l'accueil*
or *combien coûte la carte*. That isn't a question inversion (no hyphen, no pronoun); it just sounds
better than ending the sentence on a short verb.

Here is the whole choice in one chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to turn a direct question into an indirect question
  accDescr: Start from the direct question. If it is a yes or no question, use si, which becomes s'il before il or ils. If it starts with qu'est-ce que, que or quoi, use ce que. If it starts with qu'est-ce qui, use ce qui. If it starts with où, quand, comment, combien, pourquoi, qui or quel, keep that word. In every case drop est-ce que, use statement word order with no inversion, and leave out the question mark unless the whole sentence is a question.
  A["Direct question"] --> B{"What kind?"}
  B -- "yes / no" --> C["si (s'il)"]
  B -- "qu'est-ce que, que, quoi" --> D["ce que"]
  B -- "qu'est-ce qui" --> E["ce qui"]
  B -- "où, quand, comment, combien, pourquoi, qui, quel" --> F["keep the word"]
  C --> G["Drop est-ce que, no inversion: Il demande si tu viens."]
  D --> G
  E --> G
  F --> G
```

### Polite questions at an office

Indirect questions are the polite way to ask for information in French. Start with one of these
and add the question:

- *Je voudrais savoir si …* — I'd like to know whether …
- *Pourriez-vous me dire où / quand …* — Could you tell me where / when … (lesson 14)
- *Savez-vous si …* — Do you know if …

*Pourriez-vous me dire où se trouve l'accueil ?* (Here the question mark is back, because the
whole sentence is a question.)

And when you ask yourself, use *se demander* (to wonder): *Je me demande si la banque est ouverte
le samedi.* — I wonder whether the bank is open on Saturdays.

## Bank and office words

At the bank you have *un compte* (an account) and *une carte bancaire* (a bank card, often called
*la carte bleue* or *la CB*). *Je retire de l'argent au distributeur* (I take out money at the
cash machine; in full *le distributeur de billets*): *je tape mon code* (I key in my PIN). *Mon
salaire arrive par virement* (my salary comes by transfer), and *ma conseillère* or *mon
conseiller* (my adviser) answers my questions.

In public offices, *l'administration* (the authorities) asks you to do *des démarches*
(formalities): *je fais une demande* (I make an application), *j'apporte les documents pour mon
dossier* (I bring the documents for my file), and I always need *une pièce d'identité* (ID). *Le délai* is the time
allowed: *Le délai est de deux semaines* means you have two weeks (it doesn't mean a delay, which is
*le retard*). Some documents are *obligatoires* (required).

To find out: *se renseigner* (*Je me renseigne à l'accueil*), *un renseignement* (a piece of
information; the sign *Renseignements* = Information). *Prévenir* (to let know, to warn) is
conjugated like *venir* but with *avoir*: *Préviens-moi ! Je vous ai prévenu.*

And before all that, there is usually a wait: *On fait la queue* (we queue) in *la file d'attente*
(the queue), and a sign says *Merci de patienter* (please wait).

![Inside a bank, with five things labelled. On the left, a cash machine in the wall with a screen and a keypad: le distributeur. In front of it, a large bank card: la carte bancaire. In the middle, a desk with a person behind it under a round information sign marked i: l'accueil. On the right, a counter with a glass window and a clerk behind it: le guichet. In front of the counter, three customers wait in a line: la file d'attente.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: À la banque

Laura has lost her bank card. She goes to her bank with her husband Tom, who stays a few steps back
and can't hear the conversation.

> Agent d'accueil : Bonjour, madame. Je vous écoute.
>
> Laura : Bonjour. J'ai perdu ma carte bancaire hier. Je voudrais savoir si vous pouvez la bloquer.
>
> Agent d'accueil : Bien sûr. Vous avez une pièce d'identité ?
>
> Laura : Oui, voilà mon passeport.
>
> Tom : Qu'est-ce qu'il dit ?
>
> Laura : Il demande si j'ai une pièce d'identité. … Pardon, monsieur, pourriez-vous me dire quand j'aurai une nouvelle carte ?
>
> Agent d'accueil : Le délai est d'une semaine, à peu près. Votre conseillère va vous prévenir par SMS.
>
> Laura : Et en attendant, comment est-ce que je retire de l'argent ?
>
> Agent d'accueil : Vous pouvez retirer de l'argent ici, au guichet, avec votre passeport.
>
> Tom : Alors ?
>
> Laura : Il dit que j'aurai une nouvelle carte dans une semaine et que je peux retirer de l'argent au guichet. Il explique aussi que ma conseillère va me prévenir.

*Reception officer: Hello, madam. How can I help? (literally: I'm listening to you) — Laura: Hello.
I lost my bank card yesterday. I'd like to know if you can block it. — Officer: Of course. Do you
have ID? — Laura: Yes, here's my passport. — Tom: What's he saying? — Laura: He's asking if I have
ID. … Excuse me, could you tell me when I'll get a new card? — Officer: It takes about a week. Your
adviser will let you know by text. — Laura: And in the meantime, how do I take out money? — Officer:
You can withdraw money here, at the counter, with your passport. — Tom: So? — Laura: He says I'll
get a new card in a week and that I can withdraw money at the counter. He also explains that my
adviser will let me know.*

Notice how Laura's reports change the pronouns: the agent's *Votre conseillère va vous prévenir*
becomes *ma conseillère va me prévenir*. *Le guichet* (A1, ticket office) is also a bank counter.

## A preview: reporting in the past

When the reporting verb is in the past (*Il a dit que …*), French usually shifts the tense, as
English does: « Je suis malade » → *Il a dit qu'il était malade* (he said he was ill). This is B1
material; for now, recognise it when you meet it, and keep your own reports in the present.

## Pronunciation

- *s'il* "seel"; *si elle* "see el" (no elision).
- *ce que* "suh-kuh"; *ce qui* "suh-kee".
- *le distributeur* "dee-stree-bü-teur"; *le virement* "veer-mahn" (the middle *e* is silent).
- *le renseignement* "rahn-sen-yuh-mahn"; *se renseigner* "rahn-sen-yay".
- *le conseiller* "kon-say-yay", *la conseillère* "kon-say-yair".

## Common mistakes

- *Il dit il est malade.* Never drop *que*: *Il dit qu'il est malade.*
- *Je me demande si il vient.* Elision: *s'il vient* (but *si elle vient*).
- *Il demande où est-ce que tu habites.* Drop *est-ce que*: *Il demande où tu habites.*
- *Je voudrais savoir quand ouvre-t-il.* No inversion: *quand il ouvre.*
- *Dites-moi qu'est-ce que vous voulez.* Use *ce que*: *Dites-moi ce que vous voulez.*
- *Il demande si tu viens ?* No question mark when the sentence is a statement.
- *Il me dit que je patiente* for an order. Use *de* + infinitive: *Il me dit de patienter.*
- *le délai* for a delay (a train, a parcel). That's *le retard*; *le délai* is the time allowed.

## Key points

- Reported speech: *dire / répondre / expliquer que* + sentence; *que* is never dropped and is
  repeated before each part.
- Pronouns and possessives change to fit the speaker: « Mon compte » → *son compte*.
- Orders: *dire / demander à quelqu'un de* + infinitive: *Il me dit de patienter.*
- Indirect questions: yes/no → *si* (*s'il*); *où, quand, comment, combien, pourquoi, qui, quel*
  stay; *qu'est-ce que* → *ce que*, *qu'est-ce qui* → *ce qui*.
- No *est-ce que*, no inversion, no question mark (unless the whole sentence asks).
- Polite: *Je voudrais savoir si … Pourriez-vous me dire où … ?* Wondering: *se demander si …*
- Bank and office: *le compte, la carte bancaire, le distributeur, retirer, le virement, le code;
  le dossier, la démarche, la demande, l'accueil, se renseigner, le délai, obligatoire, la pièce
  d'identité*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Why and what for: cause, consequence and purpose
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A parcel that doesn't arrive, a wrong item, a broken product: to sort it out you have to explain
why something happened, what happened as a result, and what you want. These are three
ideas with three sets of linking words:

- a **[[cause]]** answers "why?": *because, as, because of, thanks to*;
- a **[[consequence]]** says what follows: *so, that's why*;
- a **[[purpose]]** says what something is for, what you want to achieve: *(in order) to, for*.

You know *parce que, donc* and *alors* from A1, and you met *pour* + infinitive in lesson 16. This
lesson adds the rest, with the theme of orders, deliveries and complaints.

## Cause: parce que, car, comme

All three are followed by a full sentence (a subject and a verb).

*Parce que* (A1) is the everyday word, and the one that answers the question *Pourquoi ?*:

- *Pourquoi tu appelles ? — Parce que mon colis n'est pas arrivé.*
- *Je suis en retard parce que le bus est tombé en panne.*

*Car* means the same, but it belongs to writing and careful speech: letters, e-mails, the
news. It always comes after what it explains, usually in the middle between the two halves: you
can't put *car* + the cause first (that's the job of *comme*), and it is never used alone as an
answer to *Pourquoi ?*:

- *Je vous écris car ma commande n'est pas complète.* — I am writing to you because my order is
  incomplete.

*Comme* (as, since) gives the cause first, at the start of the sentence, and the result after
it. It's the natural way to begin an explanation:

- *Comme le magasin était fermé, je suis rentré.* — As the shop was closed, I went home.
- *Comme je n'ai pas reçu le colis, je demande un remboursement.* — As I haven't received the
  parcel, I'm asking for a refund.

So *Comme il pleuvait, on est restés à la maison* = *On est restés à la maison parce qu'il
pleuvait*: same meaning, different order. *Comme* also means "like" or "as" (*comme toi, comme
prévu*): the position tells you which.

## Cause with a noun: à cause de and grâce à

*Parce que, car* and *comme* need a verb. Before a noun or a pronoun, use *à cause de* or
*grâce à*:

| | meaning | with a noun | with a pronoun |
|---|---|---|---|
| *à cause de* | because of (usually something bad) | *à cause de la neige, à cause du retard* | *à cause de moi* |
| *grâce à* | thanks to (something good) | *grâce à votre aide, grâce au service client* | *grâce à toi* |

- *Le colis est en retard à cause de la grève.* — The parcel is late because of the strike.
- *Grâce au service client, le problème est réglé.* — Thanks to customer service, the problem is
  sorted out.

*De* and *à* contract with *le* and *les* as usual: *à cause du bruit, à cause des travaux, grâce
au vendeur, grâce aux clients*. The pronoun after them is the stressed one (*moi, toi, lui, elle,
nous, vous, eux, elles*).

Don't use *grâce à* for bad news: ~~grâce à la grève, mon train est annulé~~ sounds sarcastic.

## Explaining further: en effet

*En effet* confirms or explains what you have just said, a bit like "indeed" or "in fact":

- *Je suis très mécontent. En effet, j'attends ma commande depuis trois semaines.* — I am very
  unhappy. Indeed, I have been waiting for my order for three weeks.
- *Vous avez reçu un pull bleu ? — En effet.* — Yes, that's right.

It doesn't mean "in effect". It's common in formal letters.

## Consequence: donc, alors, c'est pourquoi

- *Donc* (so, therefore) can start the second half or follow the verb: *Le produit était cassé,
  donc je l'ai renvoyé. J'ai donc appelé le service client.*
- *Alors* (so, A1) is more spoken: *Personne ne répondait, alors j'ai écrit un e-mail.*
- *C'est pourquoi* (that's why) is more formal, typical of letters: *Le colis était abîmé, c'est
  pourquoi je vous écris.* In speech you'll hear *c'est pour ça que …*

Cause and consequence are two views of the same link:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Cause and consequence with the same two facts
  accDescr: Two facts: the parcel was damaged, and I am asking for a refund. To give the cause first, use comme at the start: Comme le colis était abîmé, je demande un remboursement. To give the result first and then the cause, use parce que in speech or car in writing: Je demande un remboursement parce que, or car, le colis était abîmé. To give the cause first and then the consequence, use donc, alors or c'est pourquoi: Le colis était abîmé, donc, alors, or c'est pourquoi, je demande un remboursement. With a noun instead of a sentence, use à cause de for a bad cause, as in à cause du colis abîmé, or grâce à for a good one.
  A["Cause: le colis était abîmé"] --> R["Result: je demande un remboursement"]
  R --- P1["Comme le colis était abîmé, je demande un remboursement."]
  R --- P2["Je demande un remboursement parce que (car) le colis était abîmé."]
  R --- P3["Le colis était abîmé, donc (c'est pourquoi) je demande un remboursement."]
  R --- P4["With a noun: à cause du colis abîmé (bad) / grâce à (good)"]
```

## Purpose: pour + infinitive

To say what you do something for, use *pour* + infinitive. Here the subject of the main verb also
does the action of the infinitive (I call, and I book):

- *J'appelle pour réserver une table.* — I'm calling (in order) to book a table.
- *Je vous écris pour demander un remboursement.* — I'm writing to you to ask for a refund.
- *Il travaille le soir pour payer ses études.* — He works in the evenings to pay for his studies.

*Pour* + a noun means "for": *C'est pour mon fils. J'appelle pour ma commande.*

A question with *Pourquoi ?* can be answered with a cause (*Parce que …*) or with a purpose (*Pour
…*): *Pourquoi tu appelles ? — Parce que j'ai un problème* (cause) / *Pour savoir où est mon colis*
(purpose).

When someone else does that action (*I'm calling so that you can …*), French uses *pour que* + a
verb form called the subjunctive: *Je vous appelle pour que vous puissiez vérifier.* That's B1;
just recognise *pour que* for now.

![A chart in three panels. Cause, why?: parce que, car (written) and comme (first) plus a sentence; à cause de (bad) and grâce à (good) plus a noun. Consequence, so: donc, alors, c'est pourquoi, and in speech c'est pour ça que. Purpose, what for?: pour plus an infinitive, as in pour demander un remboursement, and pour plus a noun, as in pour mon fils. Under them, an arrow pointing back is labelled looks back: the reason; an arrow pointing forward, looks forward: the result; and an arrow hitting a target, aims at a goal.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Avant de, sans, au lieu de + infinitive

Three more links take an infinitive, where English uses an "-ing" form:

- *avant de* + infinitive: *Vérifiez le colis avant de signer.* — Check the parcel before signing.
  (Before a noun, just *avant*: *avant la livraison*.)
- *sans* + infinitive (A1 *sans*): *Il est parti sans payer.* — He left without paying.
- *au lieu de* + infinitive or noun: *Au lieu de répondre, il a raccroché.* — Instead of answering,
  he hung up. *J'ai reçu un pull bleu au lieu du rouge.*

This is a big difference from English: after a preposition, French normally uses the infinitive:
*pour réserver, avant de partir, sans attendre*, never ~~avant de partant~~.

## Orders, deliveries and complaints: the words

- *passer une commande* (to place an order) on *le site* (lesson 10), *le numéro de commande*;
- *la livraison* (delivery), *livrer* (to deliver): *Le colis sera livré demain*;
- *le colis* (parcel; plural *les colis*), *le produit* (product);
- *le client, la cliente* (customer), *le service client* (customer service);
- *une erreur* (a mistake), *se tromper* (to make a mistake): *Vous vous êtes trompés de taille* (you got the wrong size).
  *Se tromper de* + noun = to get the wrong …: *se tromper d'adresse, de numéro*;
- *la faute* (fault, blame): *Ce n'est pas ma faute !* (It's not my fault.) Also a spelling
  mistake: *une faute d'orthographe*. A mistake in general is usually *une erreur*;
- *satisfait* / *mécontent* (satisfied / unhappy): *Je suis mécontent de la livraison*;
- *se plaindre (de)* (to complain about), conjugated *je me plains, nous nous plaignons*; *la
  réclamation* (a formal complaint): *faire une réclamation*;
- *remplacer* (to replace; *nous remplaçons*), *le remboursement* (refund; the verb *rembourser*
  is A1), *régler* (to sort out, to settle, to pay: *régler un problème, régler la facture*; *je
  règle, nous réglons*).

## A complaint e-mail

A short formal complaint follows a simple plan: what happened (the cause), why it's a problem,
what you want (the purpose), and a polite ending. Notice *en effet, comme* and *pour*.

![A complaint e-mail. Objet : Commande n° 48213, lampe cassée. Madame, Monsieur, Le 3 novembre, j'ai commandé une lampe sur votre site (commande n° 48213). Le colis est arrivé hier, mais la lampe était cassée. En effet, la boîte était très abîmée. Comme j'ai besoin de cette lampe pour mon bureau, je vous demande de la remplacer rapidement. Si ce n'est pas possible, je souhaite un remboursement. Vous trouverez une photo du produit en pièce jointe. Je vous remercie par avance. Cordialement, Julien Morel. A paperclip icon shows the attachment, lampe.jpg.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Subject: Order no. 48213, broken lamp. Dear Sir or Madam, On 3 November I ordered a lamp on your
website (order no. 48213). The parcel arrived yesterday, but the lamp was broken. Indeed, the box
was badly damaged. As I need this lamp for my office, I am asking you to replace it quickly. If
that isn't possible, I would like a refund. Please find a photo of the product attached. Thank you
in advance. Regards, Julien Morel.*

*Vous trouverez … en pièce jointe* (please find … attached) and *Je vous remercie par avance* (thank
you in advance) are set phrases worth learning as they are.

## Dialogue: Au service client

Julien calls customer service three days later.

> Conseillère : Service client, bonjour ! Je vous écoute.
>
> Julien : Bonjour, madame. J'appelle pour ma commande, le numéro 48213. J'ai reçu une lampe cassée, et personne n'a répondu à mon e-mail.
>
> Conseillère : Je suis désolée. Je regarde votre dossier… En effet, il y a eu un problème avec le transporteur. Comme le produit est cassé, nous allons le remplacer.
>
> Julien : D'accord, mais quand ? J'en ai besoin pour travailler.
>
> Conseillère : On vous livre une nouvelle lampe jeudi. Avant de signer, vérifiez bien le colis.
>
> Julien : Et la lampe cassée ?
>
> Conseillère : Gardez-la, ce n'est pas la peine de la renvoyer. Encore désolée pour cette erreur.
>
> Julien : Merci. Grâce à vous, le problème est réglé !

*Adviser: Customer service, hello! How can I help? — Julien: Hello. I'm calling about my order,
number 48213. I received a broken lamp, and nobody answered my e-mail. — Adviser: I'm sorry. I'm
looking at your file… Yes, indeed, there was a problem with the courier (le transporteur). As the
product is broken, we'll replace it. — Julien: OK, but when? I need it for work. — Adviser: We'll
deliver a new lamp on Thursday. Before signing, check the parcel carefully. — Julien: And the broken
lamp? — Adviser: Keep it, there's no need to send it back. Sorry again for this mistake. — Julien:
Thank you. Thanks to you, the problem is sorted out!*

## Pronunciation

- *car* "kar", like the English word; *comme* "kom".
- *grâce à* "grahs a"; *à cause de* "a kohz duh".
- *le colis* "ko-lee" (*s* silent, also in the plural).
- *la réclamation* "ray-kla-ma-syon"; *le remboursement* "rahn-boor-suh-mahn".
- *je me plains* "plan" (nasal), *nous nous plaignons* "play-nyon".
- *régler*: *je règle* "regl" (open *è*), *nous réglons* "ray-glon".

## Common mistakes

- *Car le colis est arrivé en retard, je vous écris.* *Car* can't put the cause first: use *Comme*:
  *Comme le colis est arrivé en retard, je vous écris.*
- *Pourquoi ? — Car …* Answer with *Parce que …*
- *parce que la grève*. Before a noun, use *à cause de*: *à cause de la grève*.
- *grâce à la neige, mon train est annulé*. For a bad cause: *à cause de la neige*.
- *à cause de le retard, grâce à les clients*. Contract: *à cause du retard, grâce aux clients*.
- *J'appelle pour je réserve.* *Pour* + infinitive: *J'appelle pour réserver.*
- *avant partir*, *avant de le départ*. *Avant de* + infinitive (*avant de partir*), *avant* + noun
  (*avant le départ*).
- *sans payant*. After a preposition, the infinitive: *sans payer*.
- *En effet* to mean "in effect". It means "indeed", "that's right".

## Key points

- Cause + sentence: *parce que* (everyday, answers *Pourquoi ?*), *car* (written, after what it explains),
  *comme* (at the start).
- Cause + noun: *à cause de* (bad), *grâce à* (good): *à cause du retard, grâce à toi*.
- *En effet* confirms or explains: "indeed".
- Consequence: *donc, alors, c'est pourquoi*.
- Purpose: *pour* + infinitive (same person), *pour* + noun; *pour que* + subjunctive is B1.
- *avant de, sans, au lieu de* + infinitive: *avant de signer, sans payer, au lieu de répondre*.
- Customer service: *la commande, la livraison, livrer, le colis, le client, le service client,
  l'erreur, se tromper (de), la faute, la réclamation, se plaindre, satisfait, mécontent, remplacer,
  le remboursement, régler*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: le CV et la lettre de motivation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 17 gave you the words of the job hunt: *l'offre d'emploi, le poste, postuler, le CV, la
candidature, l'entretien*. This honors lesson goes one step further and shows you how to write the
two documents a French employer usually expects: a CV and a **[[cover letter]]**, *la lettre de
motivation*. You'll see what goes in a French CV and in what order, what the law says you don't
have to put in it, and the set phrases of a formal letter.

The facts about the law in this lesson were checked on service-public.fr (the French government's
information site) and france-travail.fr (the public employment service) on 10 November 2026. Rules
and habits change: check them again before you apply. This is general information, not legal
advice. Everything in the sample CV and letter is invented.

The reader is *le recruteur* or *la recruteuse* (the recruiter), who works for *l'employeur* (the
employer, the company or person who hires). So the register is formal: the *vous* form, careful
words, set phrases. Don't use these phrases with friends.

## The French CV: what goes in

There is no law that says what a CV must contain. Service-public.fr even points out that sending a
CV isn't compulsory to apply for a job (though in practice most employers ask for one). But French
CVs follow strong habits. From top to bottom:

1. Your name and contact details (*les coordonnées*): first name, surname (often in capitals:
   Daniel WALSH), address, phone, e-mail. Many people add *permis B* (car driving licence) here.
   This top block is traditionally called *l'état civil* (personal details).
2. A title (*le titre du CV*) saying what you are looking for: *Stage en réception hôtelière*,
   *Vendeuse à temps partiel*. France Travail advises a precise title, not just "technician".
3. A short profile (*le profil*): one or two lines on who you are and what you want.
4. Work experience (*l'expérience professionnelle*), most recent first.
5. Education (*la formation*): your degrees and courses, also most recent first.
6. Languages (*les langues*): *anglais : langue maternelle ; français : courant (B2)*.
7. Skills (*les compétences*): software, techniques, *travail en équipe*.
8. Interests (*les centres d'intérêt*): sport, music, *le bénévolat* (voluntary work).

"Most recent first" is called **[[reverse chronological order]]** (*l'ordre antichronologique*): you
start with your current or last job and go back in time. It's the classic French layout.

![A one-page French CV with no photo. At the top, the name Daniel WALSH, an address in Lyon, an e-mail address, 24 ans and permis B. Under it, in a green band, the title: Stage en réception hôtelière, 6 mois, à partir de janvier 2027. Then the sections. Expérience professionnelle, most recent first: 2025–2026, serveur à temps partiel, Café du Parc, Lyon (accueil des clients, prise de commandes); 2024, stage de réceptionniste (3 mois) in a hotel in Ireland (gestion des réservations, réponse aux e-mails). Formation: 2026–2027, Master 1 Tourisme (en cours) at a university in Lyon; 2025, a bachelor's degree in tourism in Ireland (bac + 3). Langues: anglais, langue maternelle; français, courant (B2); espagnol, notions. Compétences: logiciels de réservation, Excel, travail en équipe. Centres d'intérêt: football in an amateur club, voluntary homework help for children, travel.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### What you don't have to put

- The photo is optional. Service-public.fr lists *une photo d'identité* among the things a CV
  *may* contain, not must. Many French CVs still have one; many don't. If you add one, use a
  plain, recent, serious photo.
- Age, family situation, nationality. Older French CVs often show *Âge : 24 ans, célibataire*
  (single). You may include your age, but nothing obliges you to give your family situation. The
  general rule (*Code du travail*, articles L1221-6 to L1221-9) is that an employer may only ask a
  candidate for information with a direct link to the job, and must not use information to
  discriminate. You never have to say anything about your health, a pregnancy, or your political,
  union or religious views.
- Honesty is required. You must act in good faith: knowingly false information (an invented
  degree, say) can later get you dismissed, and employers may check your diplomas.

### How CV lines are written

A CV isn't written in full sentences. Each line is short, usually built on a noun (or sometimes an
infinitive), with the date first:

| full sentence | CV line |
|---|---|
| *J'ai accueilli les clients.* | *Accueil des clients* |
| *J'ai géré les réservations.* (gérer, to manage) | *Gestion des réservations* |
| *J'ai répondu aux e-mails des clients.* | *Réponse aux e-mails des clients* |
| *J'ai pris les commandes.* | *Prise de commandes* |

France Travail's other tips: stay clear and brief, keep only what matters for the job, use
colours that are still readable when printed in black and white, and keep your CV up to date. Most
French advice says one page for a young candidate.

For languages, say your level honestly. *Langue maternelle* (mother tongue), *bilingue* (bilingual),
*courant* (fluent), *bon niveau* (good level), *notions* (basics), or a CEFR level: *français B2*.
The verb *maîtriser* (to master, to be good at) is common: *Je maîtrise Excel.*

### Example 1: turning notes into a CV entry

Sarah worked in a bookshop in Manchester last summer. Her notes in English: "July–August 2026,
bookshop, sales assistant, full-time; I served customers, put books on the shelves and did the till."

1. Date and job title first: *Juillet–août 2026 : vendeuse (à temps plein)*.
2. Where: *Librairie (bookshop) Northern Books, Manchester (Royaume-Uni)*. Say the country: the
   reader may not know the town.
3. The tasks as short noun lines: "served customers" → *Conseil aux clients* or *Accueil des
   clients*; "put books on the shelves" → *Mise en rayon* (a set expression for shelving);
   "did the till" → *Tenue de la caisse*.

Result:

> *Juillet–août 2026 — Vendeuse à temps plein, librairie Northern Books, Manchester (Royaume-Uni)*
>
> *Accueil et conseil des clients · Mise en rayon · Tenue de la caisse*

Don't translate the English job title word for word: a "shop assistant" is *un vendeur, une
vendeuse* (*assistant de magasin* is not the usual French title for a sales job; titles with
*assistant* or *adjoint* in French adverts often mean helping to run the shop).

## The cover letter: la lettre de motivation

The cover letter says why you want this job and why you are the right person. A French letter is
short (one page, France Travail insists) and follows the layout you met in French A1 (lesson 24h2):
your details top left, the employer's on the right, place and date, *Objet :*, then *Madame,
Monsieur,* and the body.

France Travail suggests three paragraphs, often summed up as *vous, moi, nous*:

1. *Vous* — the company: why it interests you, how you heard of the job.
2. *Moi* — you: your studies, your experience, your qualities, with an example.
3. *Nous* — working together: what you will bring, and a request for an interview.

It ends with a formal closing formula, as in A1. Here is a model for an internship.

> *Objet : Candidature pour un stage en réception (réf. ST-26)*
>
> *Madame, Monsieur,*
>
> *Votre hôtel accueille chaque année des clients du monde entier, et votre annonce pour un stage à la réception a retenu toute mon attention.*
>
> *Actuellement étudiant en tourisme, je cherche un stage de six mois à partir de janvier. En 2024, j'ai fait un stage de trois mois dans un hôtel en Irlande : j'y ai géré les réservations et accueilli des clients de nombreux pays. L'anglais est ma langue maternelle et je parle couramment français. Je suis rigoureux, dynamique, et j'aime travailler en équipe.*
>
> *Mon expérience et mes langues seront un atout pour votre équipe, en particulier avec vos clients anglophones. Je serais heureux de vous présenter mon parcours lors d'un entretien.*
>
> *Dans l'attente de votre réponse, je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.*
>
> *Daniel Walsh*

*Subject: Application for a reception internship (ref. ST-26). Dear Sir or Madam, Every year your
hotel welcomes guests from all over the world, and your advert for a reception internship caught my
attention. I am currently a tourism student, looking for a six-month internship from January. In
2024 I did a three-month internship in a hotel in Ireland, where I managed bookings and welcomed
guests from many countries. English is my mother tongue and I speak French fluently. I am thorough
and energetic, and I like working in a team. My experience and my languages will be an asset to your
team, especially with your English-speaking guests. I would be glad to present my background to you
in an interview. I look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully, Daniel Walsh*

### The set phrases

| purpose | formal French | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| opening | *Je me permets de vous adresser ma candidature pour le poste de …* | I am writing to apply for the position of … (lit. "I take the liberty of sending you …") |
| opening | *Votre annonce parue sur … a retenu toute mon attention.* | Your advert on … caught my attention. |
| who you are | *Actuellement étudiant(e) en …, je …* | I am currently studying … and I … |
| experience | *J'ai acquis une expérience de … en …* | I gained experience of … in … |
| interview | *Je serais heureux / heureuse de vous rencontrer lors d'un entretien.* | I would be glad to meet you for an interview. |
| attachments | *Vous trouverez ci-joint mon CV.* | Please find my CV attached. |
| closing | *Dans l'attente de votre réponse, je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.* | I look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully. |

Two traps for English speakers:

- *Actuellement* means "currently", not "actually" (that's *en fait*). *Actuellement étudiant* has
  no article: it describes you, like a job title after *être* (*je suis étudiant*).
- The conditionnel. You learned in lesson 14 that it makes requests polite, and *Je serais heureux
  de vous rencontrer* is a good use of it. But France Travail advises writing what you can do in
  the present or the futur, not the conditionnel: *Mon expérience sera un atout* sounds more
  confident than *Mon expérience pourrait être un atout*.

### Example 2: writing the "moi" paragraph

Amira, a nurse from Tunisia (*infirmière*), applies for a part-time job in a clinic in Marseille.
Her notes: nurse for five years; hospital in Sfax; speaks Arabic (mother tongue), French (fluent),
English (good level); calm, works well alone.

1. Start with who she is now: *Infirmière depuis cinq ans, …* (*depuis* + present, lesson 03).
2. Add where, with a concrete detail: *… je travaille actuellement aux urgences de l'hôpital de
   Sfax* (in the emergency department).
3. Languages, with the right words: *L'arabe est ma langue maternelle ; je parle couramment
   français et j'ai un bon niveau d'anglais.*
4. Qualities, as adjectives that agree with her: *Je suis calme, rigoureuse et autonome.*

Result: *Infirmière depuis cinq ans, je travaille actuellement aux urgences de l'hôpital de Sfax. L'arabe est ma langue maternelle ; je parle couramment français et j'ai un bon niveau
d'anglais. Je suis calme, rigoureuse et autonome.*

### Example 3: fixing the register

Tom wrote this first draft of the e-mail to send with his CV. It is understandable, but far too casual for an employer. What should change?

> *Salut ! Je veux le job de serveur. Mon CV est attaché. Bises, Tom*

1. *Salut !* → *Madame, Monsieur,* (an unknown employer).
2. *Je veux le job* → *Je me permets de vous adresser ma candidature pour le poste de serveur.*
   (*Je veux* is too direct; *le job* is informal.)
3. *Mon CV est attaché* → *Vous trouverez ci-joint mon CV et ma lettre de motivation.* (*Attaché*
   is an anglicism here.)
4. *Bises* → *Cordialement* (fine in an e-mail) or the full formula in a letter.
5. Add a subject line: *Objet : Candidature au poste de serveur.*

> *Objet : Candidature au poste de serveur*
>
> *Madame, Monsieur,*
>
> *Je me permets de vous adresser ma candidature pour le poste de serveur à temps partiel. Vous trouverez ci-joint mon CV et ma lettre de motivation.*
>
> *Cordialement,*
>
> *Tom Bradley*

## Common mistakes

- Starting the CV with your oldest job. The usual order is reverse chronological: the most recent
  first.
- Writing *Cher Monsieur Martin* to a recruiter you have never met. Use *Madame, Monsieur,* or
  *Madame,* / *Monsieur,* alone.
- *Actuellement* for "actually". It means "currently".
- *Je suis très motivé* and nothing else. Back up each quality with a fact from your experience.
- Translating "I am applying for" as ~~j'applique pour~~ (an anglicism; *appliquer* means to apply a
  rule or a cream). Use *je postule à / pour* or *je vous
  adresse ma candidature*.
- Two pages of CV for your first job, or a letter longer than one page.
- *Mon CV est attaché.* For an e-mail attachment, say *Vous trouverez ci-joint mon CV* or *mon CV
  en pièce jointe*.

## Key points

- CV order: *coordonnées / état civil* → title → profile → *expérience professionnelle* →
  *formation* → *langues* → *compétences* → *centres d'intérêt*, in reverse chronological order.
- The photo is optional; you don't have to give your family situation; an employer may only ask
  for information with a direct link to the job (Code du travail L1221-6). Checked on
  service-public.fr, 10 November 2026.
- CV lines: date first, short noun phrases: *Accueil des clients, Gestion des réservations.*
- Cover letter: one page, *vous / moi / nous*, formal set phrases: *Je me permets de …, Dans
  l'attente de votre réponse, je vous prie d'agréer …*
- *Actuellement* = currently. Write your strengths in the present or futur; keep the conditionnel
  for polite requests.
