lessons.title: Honors: la France administrative
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 19 gave you the words for offices and paperwork: *le dossier, la démarche, la demande,
l'accueil, le délai, la pièce d'identité*. This honors lesson is a map of the French offices that
anyone who lives in France meets sooner or later: *la mairie, la préfecture, la Sécurité sociale*
with its *carte Vitale*, *la mutuelle*, *la CAF*, and the bank document called *le RIB*. It ends with
how to read an official letter.

This is a simplified overview, checked on service-public.fr (the French government's official
information site) and the other sources in the course notes on 10 November 2026. It is not legal
or financial advice: rules change, and your own case may differ. For any real procedure, check
service-public.fr or ask the office itself.

## A country of acronyms

French administration loves the **[[acronym]]** (*le sigle*): a name made of initials. Some are read
letter by letter (*la CPAM* "say-pay-ah-em"); others are read as a word (*le RIB* "rib", *la CAF*
"kaf"). You'll hear them far more often than the full names, so this lesson gives
both.

| acronym | full name | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| *la CAF* | *Caisse d'allocations familiales* | the family benefits office |
| *la CPAM* | *Caisse primaire d'assurance maladie* | the local health insurance office |
| *le RIB* | *relevé d'identité bancaire* | a slip with your bank details |
| *l'ANTS* | *Agence nationale des titres sécurisés* | the agency for ID cards, passports and driving licences, renamed *France Titres* in 2024 (its website is still ants.gouv.fr) |

## The town hall: la mairie

Every *commune* (town or village) has *une mairie* (A1), run by the *maire* (mayor). For most
people it's the closest office. It deals with:

- *l'état civil*, the register of births, marriages and deaths: you ask the mairie for *un acte
  de naissance* (a birth certificate), and weddings take place there;
- enrolling a child in a state primary school, which usually starts at the mairie;
- the *carte d'identité* and the *passeport*. You can make an online pre-application (*une
  pré-demande*; optional, but it saves time) on the ANTS website, then go to a mairie that has the
  special equipment to take fingerprints, usually by appointment. Not every mairie has it, and it doesn't have to be the one in your own town; the
  card is then sent to the mairie where you applied.

## The State in the département: la préfecture

France is divided into *départements* (101 of them). In each one, *la préfecture* represents the
State. For foreign residents its best-known job is *le titre de séjour* (the residence permit). Many
procedures that used to need a visit to the counter are now done online: since 6 November 2017,
for example, driving licences and vehicle registration papers (*la carte grise*) are applied for
online, through the ANTS (now France Titres), and not at the préfecture.

## Health: la Sécurité sociale, la carte Vitale, la mutuelle

*La Sécurité sociale* (informally *la Sécu*) is the national system that covers health, family
benefits, pensions and accidents at work. Its health branch is *l'Assurance maladie*; its local
office is the CPAM, and its website is ameli.fr.

### Le numéro de Sécurité sociale

When you join, you get *un numéro de Sécurité sociale*: 15 digits, a 13-digit number plus a 2-digit
check key. The digits aren't random: the first one shows your sex, the next four your year and month
of birth, then come five for your place of birth and three to tell apart people born in the same
place at the same time.

### La carte Vitale

*La carte Vitale* is the green card with a chip that proves you are insured. You show it to the
doctor or the pharmacist, and the claim goes to the Assurance maladie electronically: no paper form,
and you are paid back faster (about a week). From age 16, young people get their own card (the
Assurance maladie sends them a form); parents can order one for a child from age 12 through their
online ameli account. Cards issued since 2007 have a photo. Since November 2025 everyone can also
use an official app (*l'appli carte Vitale*), but not every doctor or pharmacy can read it yet, so
carry the plastic card too.

### Le médecin traitant

From age 16, everyone is expected to choose *un médecin traitant*, a regular doctor (usually a GP)
whom they declare to the Assurance maladie. If you see doctors without having declared one, you are
usually paid back much less: it pays to choose one early.

### La mutuelle: complementary health insurance

The Assurance maladie doesn't pay everything back. The rest can be covered by
**[[complementary health insurance]]**, officially *la complémentaire santé* and in everyday French *la mutuelle* (strictly, a
*mutuelle* is one kind of insurer, but everyone uses the word). Since 1 January 2016, private-sector
employers in France must offer one to their employees and pay at least half of its cost.
*Ma mutuelle rembourse les lunettes* — my top-up insurance pays for glasses.

## Family and housing: la CAF

*La CAF* (*Caisse d'allocations familiales*) is the family branch of the Sécurité sociale. It pays
*les allocations* (benefits): family allowances, housing aid for many tenants and students, and,
on behalf of the State or the départements, income support and other means-tested benefits. Many
students in France apply to the CAF for help with their rent. The CAF decides, on your own
situation; this lesson can't say whether you qualify.

## Your bank details: le RIB

*Le RIB* (*relevé d'identité bancaire*) is a small document from your bank, usually downloaded from
its website. It gives your name, the bank's name, the account numbers, your *IBAN* (in France 27
characters, starting with FR) and the bank's *BIC* code. An employer asks for it to pay your salary;
the CAF, a landlord or a phone company ask for it to pay you or to take payments by direct debit.
The Banque de France explains that giving your RIB isn't risky in itself, because a direct debit
needs your signed agreement, but you should check who you are giving it to. Never confuse it with
your bank card number and code, which you never give out.

## Help with all of this: France services

If the procedures seem complicated, you are not alone. *Les espaces France services* are local
offices where staff help people with their procedures (tax, health insurance, the CAF, the
employment service, and more). The Cour des comptes counted more than 2,840 of them in 2024.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which office do I need?
  accDescr: A guide to five common needs. For a birth certificate, a wedding, or an identity card or passport, go to la mairie, an equipped one for ID cards and passports. For a residence permit, contact la préfecture, mostly online now. For your carte Vitale, a regular doctor or reimbursements, contact l'Assurance maladie, the CPAM, at ameli.fr. For family benefits or housing aid, contact la CAF. For top-up health insurance, contact your mutuelle, often chosen by your employer. If you need help with any of these, go to an espace France services.
  A{"What do you need?"} -- "birth certificate, wedding, ID card, passport" --> B["la mairie"]
  A -- "residence permit" --> C["la préfecture (mostly online)"]
  A -- "carte Vitale, doctor, reimbursements" --> D["l'Assurance maladie (CPAM, ameli.fr)"]
  A -- "family benefits, housing aid" --> E["la CAF"]
  A -- "top-up health insurance" --> F["la mutuelle"]
  B --> G["Need help? un espace France services"]
  C --> G
  D --> G
  E --> G
  F --> G
```

## Reading an official letter

Official letters (*le courrier*, A1) use a formal style full of set phrases. They are easier than
they look once you know them:

| official phrase | plain meaning |
|---|---|
| *Nous accusons réception de votre demande.* | We have received your application. |
| *Nous vous informons que …* | We are writing to tell you that … |
| *Nous vous prions de bien vouloir nous adresser …* | Please send us … |
| *les pièces justificatives suivantes* | the following supporting documents |
| *dans un délai de quinze jours* | within fifteen days |
| *à compter de la date de ce courrier* | from the date of this letter |
| *un justificatif de domicile de moins de trois mois* | a proof of address less than three months old (a recent bill, a rent receipt) |
| *Pour tout renseignement, adressez-vous à …* | For any information, contact … |
| *Veuillez agréer, Madame, l'expression de nos salutations distinguées.* | Yours sincerely. |

Then there are letters asking you to come in person, *une convocation* (a notice to attend), and
documents that certify something, *une attestation* (a certificate): *une attestation de droits*
from the Assurance maladie, *une attestation de travail* from an employer. *Les impôts* (taxes, from
*l'impôt*) send letters too.

### Example 1: what does this letter ask?

Here is an invented letter from an invented town hall.

![An official letter on a white page. Top left: Mairie de Saint-Aubin-les-Prés, Service Éducation. Top right: Madame Grace Okafor, 8 allée des Tilleuls, Saint-Aubin-les-Prés, then the date: le 2 novembre 2026. Objet : inscription scolaire de votre fils Samuel. Madame, Nous accusons réception de votre demande d'inscription à l'école primaire Jules-Ferry. Nous vous informons que votre dossier est incomplet. Afin de le compléter, nous vous prions de bien vouloir nous adresser les pièces justificatives suivantes, dans un délai de quinze jours à compter de la date de ce courrier : un justificatif de domicile de moins de trois mois ; l'acte de naissance de l'enfant ou le livret de famille. Pour tout renseignement, vous pouvez vous adresser au service Éducation, du lundi au vendredi, de 9 h à 12 h. Veuillez agréer, Madame, l'expression de nos salutations distinguées. Signed: Le service Éducation. At the bottom: Exemple inventé (invented example).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Read it in four questions:

1. Who writes, about what? The school service of the mairie, about enrolling Samuel in primary
   school (*Objet : inscription scolaire*).
2. What's the problem? *Votre dossier est incomplet*: the file is missing documents.
3. What must Grace do? Send *un justificatif de domicile de moins de trois mois* (a recent
   bill or rent receipt) and Samuel's *acte de naissance* or the *livret de famille* (the family
   record book French families are given at their wedding or at a first child's birth).
4. By when? *Dans un délai de quinze jours à compter de la date de ce courrier*: the letter is
   dated Monday 2 November 2026, so fifteen days take her to Tuesday 17 November. If in doubt, send
   the papers early.

### Example 2: replying by e-mail

Grace sends the documents by e-mail. She uses the formal register (lesson 20h1) and the links of
lesson 20:

> *Objet : Inscription scolaire de Samuel Okafor — pièces justificatives*
>
> *Madame, Monsieur,*
>
> *Suite à votre courrier du 2 novembre, vous trouverez ci-joint mon justificatif de domicile et l'acte de naissance de mon fils. Comme je travaille le matin, je ne peux pas venir au service Éducation avant midi : pourriez-vous me dire si un rendez-vous l'après-midi est possible ?*
>
> *Je vous remercie par avance.*
>
> *Cordialement,*
>
> *Grace Okafor*

*Suite à votre courrier* (following your letter) is a common opening. Notice the indirect question
of lesson 19 (*pourriez-vous me dire si …*) and *comme* + cause from lesson 20.

### Example 3: choosing the office

For each situation, which office?

1. Paul has just moved to France for a job and wants his doctor's bills paid back. → *l'Assurance
   maladie* (CPAM): he needs a social security number and then a *carte Vitale*.
2. Mei, a student, wants help paying her rent. → *la CAF*, for housing aid.
3. Karim needs a new identity card. → a mairie with the fingerprint equipment, ideally after a
   pre-application on the ANTS website.
4. Ana's new employer asks for her bank details. → She downloads *un RIB* from her bank's website.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking *la mutuelle* is the State system. The State system is the *Sécurité sociale /
  Assurance maladie*; the *mutuelle* is the private top-up.
- Going to the préfecture for a driving licence. That's done online now, through the ANTS.
- Going to any town hall for an ID card. Only mairies with the equipment take ID-card and passport
  applications.
- Giving your bank card number when someone asks for *un RIB*. A RIB gives your account details,
  never your card number or code.
- Reading *le délai* as a delay. *Dans un délai de quinze jours* = within fifteen days.
- Skipping the dates in an official letter. The deadline usually counts from the date of the
  letter (*à compter de la date de ce courrier*), not from the day you open it.

## Key points

- *la mairie*: *état civil* (birth certificates, weddings), school enrolment, ID cards and passports
  (equipped mairies only).
- *la préfecture*: the State in each département; residence permits (mostly online); driving
  licences and *carte grise* online since 6 November 2017.
- *la Sécurité sociale* → *l'Assurance maladie* (CPAM, ameli.fr); *le numéro de Sécurité sociale*
  (15 digits); *la carte Vitale* (own card from 16, app version too); *le médecin traitant*.
- *la mutuelle* (*complémentaire santé*): the private top-up; employers must offer one since 1 January
  2016 and pay at least half.
- *la CAF*: family benefits and housing aid. *le RIB*: your bank details (IBAN, BIC).
- Official letters: *Nous vous informons que …, pièces justificatives, dans un délai de …, à compter
  de …, adressez-vous à …*
- Simplified and dated (10 November 2026): always check service-public.fr for your own case.

lessons.title: In my opinion: opinions, agreeing and disagreeing
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At A1 you could say that you liked something: *J'aime ce film, c'était génial.* At A2 people
expect more: say what you think and why, ask someone else what they think, agree or disagree
politely, and weigh one side against the other ("the actors are good, but the story is weak").
That is what this lesson teaches, with television, the news and the press as the theme.
Opinions are also at the heart of the DELF A2 speaking test (lesson 24).

## Giving an opinion: je pense que, je trouve que, je crois que

Three **[[opinion verbs]]** introduce an opinion. Each is followed by *que* and a full sentence:

| French | English | when |
|---|---|---|
| *Je pense que …* | I think (that) … | the general, all-purpose opinion |
| *Je trouve que …* | I think, I find (that) … | a judgement from your own experience: you have seen, tasted or tried it |
| *Je crois que …* | I think, I believe (that) … | something you believe but aren't sure of |

- *Je pense que la télé est moins importante qu'avant.* — I think TV is less important than it used to be.
- *Je trouve que cette série est trop longue.* — I find this series too long. (I've watched it.)
- *Je crois que le documentaire commence à 21 heures.* — I think the documentary starts at 9 pm. (I'm not sure.)

*Trouver* (A1: to find) also takes a noun and an adjective with no *que*: *Je trouve ce
magazine intéressant. Cette émission ? Je la trouve nulle* (*nul, nulle* = rubbish, informal).
The difference between the three is a tendency, not a strict rule: *je pense que* and *je trouve
que* are often interchangeable, but *je crois que* sounds less certain.

### que is a conjunction, and it never disappears

This *que* is a **[[conjunction]]**: a word that joins two sentences (*je pense* + *il a raison*).
It is not the relative pronoun *que* of lesson 10 (*le site que j'utilise*), which stands for a
noun. In English you can drop "that" (*I think he's right*); in French you never drop *que*:

- *Je pense qu'il a raison.* — I think he's right. (not *Je pense il a raison*)

*Que* becomes *qu'* before a vowel: *qu'il, qu'elle, qu'on, qu'un*.

After these verbs you use the ordinary tenses you know, whatever time you mean: *Je pense que
c'était un bon film* (imparfait), *Je crois qu'il viendra* (futur, lesson 13), *Je pense que tu
devrais regarder ça* (conditionnel, lesson 14).

### Short openers: à mon avis, selon moi, pour moi, d'après moi

*L'avis* (masculine) is "opinion". These openers need no *que*; the sentence simply follows:

| opener | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *à mon avis* | in my opinion | *À mon avis, les infos sont trop négatives.* |
| *selon moi* | in my view | *Selon moi, cet article est faux.* |
| *pour moi* | for me, as far as I'm concerned | *Pour moi, la radio, c'est mieux le matin.* |
| *d'après moi* | in my view | *D'après moi, c'est une bonne idée.* |

*À mon avis* changes with the person: *à ton avis ?* (what do you think?), *à son avis, à notre
avis, à votre avis, à leur avis*. *Changer d'avis* = to change your mind.

*Selon* and *d'après* (according to) also introduce what someone else says, with a noun or a
stressed pronoun: *Selon la météo, il pleuvra demain. D'après les journalistes, le ministre va
partir. Selon elle, c'est faux.* *D'après* has a second meaning, "after": *un film d'après un
roman* (a film based on a novel), *le jour d'après* (the day after).

## Asking for someone's opinion

| question | meaning |
|---|---|
| *Qu'est-ce que tu en penses ?* | What do you think (of it)? |
| *Tu en penses quoi ?* | What do you think? (informal) |
| *Qu'est-ce que vous pensez de cette émission ?* | What do you think of this programme? |
| *Tu trouves ça comment ?* | What do you make of it? How do you find it? |
| *À ton avis, … ? / À votre avis, … ?* | In your opinion, …? |
| *Quel est ton point de vue ?* | What's your point of view? |
| *Et toi ? / Et vous ?* | And you? What about you? |

The *en* in *Qu'est-ce que tu en penses ?* is the pronoun *en* (lesson 7), replacing *de* + the
thing.

## penser à, penser de, penser que

*Penser* (lesson 6) has three constructions, each with a different meaning:

| construction | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *penser à* + person or thing | to think about, to have in mind | *Je pense à mes vacances. Je pense à toi.* |
| *penser de* + noun | to think of (have an opinion of), almost only in questions | *Qu'est-ce que tu penses de ce journal ?* |
| *penser que* + sentence | to think that (give an opinion) | *Je pense que ce journal est sérieux.* |

The trap: the question uses *de*, but the answer normally doesn't: *Je pense qu'il est trop long*
or *Je le trouve trop long*, not *Je pense de ce film …*. And *Je pense à ce film* means the film is on your
mind, not what you think of it.

## Saying "I don't think so"

| French | meaning |
|---|---|
| *Je pense que oui. / Je crois que oui.* | I think so. |
| *Je pense que non. / Je crois que non.* | I don't think so. |
| *Je ne pense pas. / Je ne crois pas.* | I don't think so. |

*Je ne pense pas* and *je ne crois pas* stand alone as answers. If you go on with a sentence
(*je ne pense pas que …*), standard French uses a new verb form, the subjunctive, which comes at
B1. (The honors lesson 16h3 shows what a subjunctive is, with *il faut que*; its use after *je
ne pense pas que* is for B1.) At A2 there is an easy way round it: make the opinion verb positive and
put the negative in the second half.

- *Je pense que ce n'est pas une bonne idée.* — I don't think it's a good idea.
- *À mon avis, il ne viendra pas.* — I don't think he'll come.

## Agreeing and disagreeing

![A horizontal scale with five faces from a big smile on the left to a frown on the right. Under them: tout à fait d'accord, d'accord, je ne sais pas trop, pas vraiment d'accord, pas du tout d'accord. An arrow along the bottom runs from "agree" to "disagree".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Être d'accord* (avec) is "to agree (with)". Alone, *d'accord* is A1's "OK".

- *Je suis d'accord avec toi.* — I agree with you.
- *Tu es d'accord avec cet article ?* — Do you agree with this article?
- *Je ne suis pas d'accord.* — I disagree.
- *Je suis tout à fait d'accord.* — I completely agree. (*tout à fait* = completely)
- *Je ne suis pas du tout d'accord.* — I don't agree at all. (*pas du tout* = not at all)

*Avoir raison* (to be right) and *avoir tort* (to be wrong) also use a different verb from
English: *avoir*, like *avoir faim* and *avoir froid* (A1).

- *Tu as raison, c'est un bon documentaire.* — You're right, it's a good documentary.
- *Il a tort : la série n'est pas finie.* — He's wrong: the series isn't over.

For a wrong answer, French usually says *c'est faux* or *je me suis trompé* (lesson 20).

*Au contraire* (on the contrary) rejects what someone has just said and says the opposite:

- *Le film était ennuyeux ? — Au contraire, il était passionnant !* — The film was boring? — On the contrary, it was gripping!

(*Ennuyeux* = boring, lesson 22.) A *point de vue* is a point of view: *de mon point de vue* (from
my point of view) works like *à mon avis*.

## Contrast: mais, pourtant, par contre, quand même

![A chart of four contrast words. mais: but, the everyday link, inside the sentence: Le film est long mais drôle. pourtant: yet, however, for a surprise, usually at the start of the second sentence: Il pleuvait. Pourtant, on est sortis. par contre: on the other hand, comparing two sides: Les acteurs sont bons. Par contre, l'histoire est faible. quand même: all the same, even so, after the verb: Il pleuvait, mais on est quand même sortis.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Mais* (A1) is the everyday "but". Three more words make the contrast clearer:

- *Pourtant* (yet, however) marks a surprise: the second fact is not what you expected after the
  first. *Il a beaucoup travaillé. Pourtant, il a raté l'examen.* — He worked a lot. Yet he
  failed the exam. It often starts the second sentence, or follows *et*: *C'est une série
  simple, et pourtant on ne s'ennuie pas.*
- *Par contre* (on the other hand) compares two sides or two things, often one good and one bad:
  *Les acteurs sont bons. Par contre, l'histoire est faible* (weak). It is very common in speech
  and in most writing; some style guides prefer *en revanche* in careful writing, which means
  the same.
- *Quand même* (all the same, even so) says that something happens in spite of a reason against
  it. It usually goes after the conjugated verb, or at the end: *Il pleuvait, mais on est quand
  même sortis. Il pleuvait, mais on est sortis quand même.* It also softens or strengthens an
  opinion: *C'était quand même un bon film* (it was a good film all the same). On its own,
  *Quand même !* is an exclamation of mild shock: "Really!", "Honestly!".

*Au contraire* and *par contre* are not the same: *au contraire* says the other person is wrong;
*par contre* adds a second, different side.

## Television, radio and the press

| French | English | note |
|---|---|---|
| *la télévision* (*la télé*) | television, TV | *à la télé* = on TV |
| *la radio* | radio | *à la radio* = on the radio |
| *l'émission* (feminine) | programme, show | *une émission de cuisine* |
| *la série* | series | *une série policière* = a crime series |
| *le documentaire* | documentary | |
| *les informations* (*les infos*) | the news (on TV or radio) | plural in this sense (*une information* = a piece of information) |
| *l'actualité* (feminine) | current events, the news in general | *l'actualité sportive*; *les actualités* = the news (a little old-fashioned) |
| *la publicité* (*la pub*) | advertising, an advert | *Il y a trop de pub !* |
| *le journaliste, la journaliste* | journalist | |
| *la presse* | the press (newspapers and magazines) | |
| *le magazine* | magazine | |
| *l'article* (masculine) | article; item (in a shop) | *un article sur l'environnement* |
| *la critique* | review; criticism | *une bonne critique* |
| *critiquer* | to criticise | regular -er verb |

Two A1 words have a new sense here. *Le journal* (A1: diary) is also "the newspaper" (*lire le
journal*), and *le journal télévisé* (*le JT*) is the TV news. *La nouvelle* (A1) is one piece of
news: *J'ai une bonne nouvelle !* The news on TV is *les informations* or *les infos*: *Tu as
vu les infos ce soir ?*

![A page from an evening TV guide for Thursday on an invented channel, Canal Nuage. 19 h 00, les informations: Le journal du soir, then the weather. 20 h 30, le documentaire: Les secrets des océans, with a fish symbol. 21 h 35, a short advert break, la publicité, with a megaphone. 21 h 40, la série: Rue des Lilas, season 2, episode 5. 22 h 30, l'émission de cuisine: À table !, with a chef's hat.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: what's on tonight?

Inès and Karim share a flat. Inès is reading the TV guide.

> Inès : Ce soir, il y a un documentaire sur les océans à 20 h 30. Qu'est-ce que tu en penses ?
>
> Karim : Bof. Je trouve que les documentaires, c'est souvent ennuyeux. Je préfère la série de 21 h 40.
>
> Inès : *Rue des Lilas* ? À mon avis, elle est nulle ! Les acteurs sont bons, par contre l'histoire est vraiment bête.
>
> Karim : Tu as tort ! Au contraire, l'histoire est super. Et la critique dans le magazine était très bonne.
>
> Inès : Selon les journalistes, tout est toujours génial… Je ne suis pas d'accord avec eux.
>
> Karim : Bon. On regarde les infos d'abord, et après on décide ?
>
> Inès : D'accord. Je crois qu'il y a un reportage sur l'environnement. Mais ta série, je l'ai vue une fois et je ne l'ai pas aimée.
>
> Karim : Pourtant, tu as regardé l'épisode jusqu'à la fin !
>
> Inès : C'est vrai… Bon, on la regarde quand même.

Translation:

> Inès: Tonight there's a documentary about the oceans at 8.30. What do you think?
>
> Karim: Meh. I find documentaries are often boring. I prefer the series at 9.40.
>
> Inès: *Rue des Lilas*? In my opinion it's rubbish! The actors are good, but on the other hand the story is really silly.
>
> Karim: You're wrong! On the contrary, the story's great. And the review in the magazine was very good.
>
> Inès: According to journalists, everything is always brilliant… I don't agree with them.
>
> Karim: OK. Shall we watch the news first and decide afterwards?
>
> Inès: All right. I think there's a report on the environment. But your series, I watched it once and I didn't like it.
>
> Karim: Yet you watched the episode right to the end!
>
> Inès: That's true… OK, we'll watch it all the same.

Notes: *Bof* is a shrug in a word: "meh, not really". *Bête* = silly, stupid. *Un reportage* is a
news report. *Je l'ai vue*: the participle agrees with *la* (*ta série*), as in lesson 8.
Karim's *Pourtant* points out a surprise: she didn't like the series, yet she watched to the end.

## Pronunciation

- *L'avis* [lavi] and *tort* [tɔʁ]: the final *-s* and *-t* are silent. *Raison* has a [z]: [ʁɛzɔ̃].
- *Quand même* [kɑ̃ mɛm]: the *d* of *quand* is silent here (no vowel follows).

## Common mistakes

- Leaving out *que*: not *Je pense il a raison* but *Je pense qu'il a raison*.
- Answering with *de*: to *Qu'est-ce que tu penses de ce film ?*, not *Je pense de ce film est
  bien* but *Je pense qu'il est bien* or *Je le trouve bien*.
- The wrong verb: not *Je suis raison* but *J'ai raison*; not *J'ai d'accord* but *Je suis
  d'accord*; not *d'accord à toi* but *d'accord avec toi*.
- *Les informations* in the singular for "the news": *les infos de 20 heures* (plural).
- Using *au contraire* to add a second side. *L'image est belle ; au contraire, le son est
  mauvais* is wrong: use *par contre* (or *mais*).

## Key points

- Give an opinion with *je pense que, je trouve que, je crois que* (+ the normal tenses) or with
  *à mon avis, selon moi, pour moi, d'après moi* (no *que*).
- *Que* (conjunction) is never left out; *qu'* before a vowel.
- Ask with *Qu'est-ce que tu en penses ?* or *Qu'est-ce que vous pensez de … ?*
- *Penser à* = to think about; *penser de* = opinion of (in questions); *penser que* = to think that.
- *Je ne pense pas* / *je pense que non*; to go on, use *je pense que … ne … pas*.
- *Être d'accord (avec)*, *avoir raison*, *avoir tort*, *au contraire*.
- Contrast: *mais* (but), *pourtant* (yet, a surprise), *par contre* (on the other hand),
  *quand même* (all the same).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Shall we go out? Suggestions, invitations and reactions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 21 was about saying what you think. This lesson is about doing things together: suggesting
an outing, accepting or turning it down politely with a reason, and reacting with feeling when it
goes well (or badly). These are everyday exchanges, and they are exactly what the DELF A2 asks for
in its writing and speaking tasks (an invitation and a reply; arranging something with the
examiner).

You will learn:

- the **[[suggestion]]** pattern *Si on allait … ?* and other ways to suggest (*Ça te dit de … ?, On
  pourrait …, Tu as envie de … ?*);
- how to say yes (*Volontiers !*) and no (*Désolé, je ne peux pas, je dois …*);
- **[[exclamations]]** with *Quel … !*, *Que … !* and *Comme … !*;
- feelings with *être* + adjective + *de* + infinitive (*Je suis ravi de venir*);
- the words for shows, exhibitions and nights out.

*La sortie* (A1: exit) also means "an outing, a night out": *une sortie au théâtre*, *On organise
une sortie samedi* (we're organising an outing on Saturday).

## Suggesting: Si on allait au cinéma ?

The friendliest way to suggest something is *si on* + the imparfait (lesson 1), said as a
question:

- *Si on allait au cinéma ce soir ?* — How about going to the cinema tonight?
- *Si on se retrouvait devant le théâtre ?* — Shall we meet in front of the theatre?
- *Et si on invitait Léa ?* — What if we invited Léa?

This is a set pattern. Even though the verb is in the imparfait, it is not about the past, and
there is no second half ("if we went…, then…"). It just means "how about…?". (The sentences with
*si* + imparfait + conditionnel, *Si j'avais le temps, je partirais*, are a different use,
previewed in the honors lesson 16h1.)

Other ways to suggest, from casual to polite:

| pattern | example | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *Ça te dit de* + infinitive ? | *Ça te dit d'aller à l'expo ?* | Do you fancy going to the exhibition? |
| *Ça te dit,* + noun ? | *Ça te dit, un concert samedi ?* | How about a concert on Saturday? |
| *Tu as envie de* + infinitive or noun ? | *Tu as envie de sortir ? Tu as envie d'une glace ?* | Do you feel like going out? Do you want an ice cream? |
| *On pourrait* + infinitive (lesson 14) | *On pourrait aller danser.* | We could go dancing. |
| *Tu veux* + infinitive ? (A1) | *Tu veux venir avec nous ?* | Do you want to come with us? |
| *Je te propose de* + infinitive | *Je vous propose de dîner ensemble.* | I suggest we have dinner together. |

- *Ça te dit ?* on its own means "How about it? Do you fancy it?". With *vous*: *Ça vous dit ?*
  The conditionnel softens it: *Ça te dirait de venir ?*
- *Avoir envie de* (to feel like, to want) is very common: *J'ai envie de rester à la maison.*
  *De* becomes *d'* before a vowel: *envie d'aller*. With a noun it takes *de* + the noun, often
  with an article: *envie d'une glace, envie de chocolat*.
- *Proposer* (to suggest, to offer) takes *à* + the person and *de* + infinitive: *Il a proposé à
  ses collègues de partir plus tôt.* The noun is *la proposition*: *Merci pour ta proposition !*

## Accepting and refusing

| accepting | refusing |
|---|---|
| *Volontiers !* — Gladly! (warm, a little polite) | *Désolé(e), je ne peux pas.* — Sorry, I can't. |
| *Avec plaisir !* (A1) — With pleasure! | *Je ne suis pas libre, je dois travailler.* — I'm not free, I have to work. |
| *Bonne idée ! / Quelle bonne idée !* — (What a) good idea! | *C'est dommage, j'ai déjà quelque chose.* — It's a pity, I've already got something on. |
| *Pourquoi pas ?* — Why not? (yes, without much excitement) | *Merci, mais ce n'est pas trop mon truc.* — Thanks, but it's not really my thing. |
| *D'accord ! Ça marche !* — OK! Sounds good! (casual) | *Une autre fois, peut-être ?* — Another time, maybe? |
| *Je suis ravi(e) de venir.* — I'm delighted to come. | *Ça dépend : c'est à quelle heure ?* — It depends: what time is it? |

A refusal in French nearly always comes with a reason, and often with an offer of another time.
A bare *Non, merci* to a friend's invitation sounds cold.

- *Dommage* (a pity, a shame) is used alone or in *C'est dommage !* and *Quel dommage !*
- *Ça dépend* (it depends) can stand alone, or take *de*: *Ça dépend du prix. Ça dépend de toi.*
  (*de + le = du*, A1.)
- *Pourquoi pas ?* can sound a little lukewarm. Add something to show you mean it: *Pourquoi
  pas ? J'adore le théâtre !*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How an invitation goes
  accDescr: Someone makes a suggestion, for example Si on allait au théâtre samedi? The other person either accepts, with Volontiers or Quelle bonne idée, and then they fix a time and a place with On se retrouve à 20 heures devant le théâtre; or refuses, with Désolé, je ne peux pas, gives a reason such as je dois travailler, and suggests another time, Une autre fois?
  A["Suggest: Si on allait au théâtre samedi ?"] --> B{"Answer"}
  B -- yes --> C["Accept: Volontiers ! Quelle bonne idée !"]
  C --> D["Fix the time and place: On se retrouve à 20 h devant le théâtre ?"]
  B -- no --> E["Refuse politely: Désolé, je ne peux pas…"]
  E --> F["Give a reason: je dois travailler."]
  F --> G["Suggest another time: Une autre fois ?"]
```

## Exclamations: Quel … !, Que … !, Comme … !

An **[[exclamation]]** expresses a strong feeling: surprise, delight, disappointment. French has two
main patterns.

![A chart of exclamations. Left box: quel, quelle, quels, quelles plus a noun, agreeing with it: Quel dommage ! Quelle bonne idée ! Quels beaux costumes ! Quelles belles photos ! Right box: que or comme plus a whole sentence, in normal word order: Que c'est beau ! Qu'il fait chaud ! Comme il est drôle ! A note says all four spellings of quel sound the same, kel.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Quel* + noun. *Quel* is the question word of A1 (*Quel âge … ?*), and it agrees with the noun
in the same way: *quel* (masculine), *quelle* (feminine), *quels*, *quelles* (plural). There is no
article after it, but there can be an adjective:

- *Quel dommage !* — What a pity!
- *Quelle bonne idée !* — What a good idea!
- *Quelle ambiance !* — What an atmosphere! (*l'ambiance* is feminine)
- *Quels beaux costumes !* — What beautiful costumes!

English says "What a good idea!"; French has no *une*: not *Quelle une bonne idée*.

*Que* or *comme* + sentence. To exclaim about a whole sentence, put *que* (*qu'* before a vowel)
or *comme* in front of it and keep the normal word order:

- *Que c'est beau !* — How beautiful it is!
- *Qu'il fait chaud ici !* — It's so hot in here!
- *Comme il est drôle !* — He's so funny!
- *Comme tu as grandi !* — How you've grown!

*Que* and *comme* mean the same here. In relaxed speech you will also hear *Qu'est-ce que c'est
beau !* (the same meaning) and simply *C'est trop beau !* (informal *trop* = really).

The English word order "How beautiful it is" doesn't work in French: not *Comme beau c'est !*
but *Comme c'est beau !*

## Feelings: être + adjective + de + infinitive

To say how you feel about doing something, use *être* + an adjective + *de* + infinitive. The
adjective agrees with the person, as always:

- *Je suis ravi de venir.* (a man) / *Je suis ravie de venir.* (a woman) — I'm delighted to come.
- *Nous sommes contents de vous voir.* — We're pleased to see you.
- *Elle est triste de partir.* — She's sad to leave.
- *Je suis désolé de ne pas pouvoir venir.* — I'm sorry I can't come.

In the last example the negative *ne pas* goes before the infinitive (lesson 17). *Ravi*
(delighted) is stronger and a little more polite than *content*.

## Going out: shows, exhibitions and nights out

| French | English | note |
|---|---|---|
| *le théâtre* | theatre | *aller au théâtre* |
| *la pièce de théâtre* (*la pièce*) | play | *une pièce de Molière* |
| *l'opéra* (masculine) | opera; opera house | *aller à l'opéra* |
| *l'exposition* (*l'expo*, feminine) | exhibition | *une expo de photos* |
| *la séance* | showing (of a film), session | *la séance de 20 heures* |
| *la boîte de nuit* (*la boîte*) | nightclub | 1990 spelling *boite* |
| *la danse* | dance, dancing | *un cours de danse* |
| *l'artiste* (masculine or feminine) | artist, performer | *un artiste, une artiste* |
| *le public* | audience; the public | *Le public a applaudi.* |
| *applaudir* | to clap, to applaud | a finir-type verb: *nous applaudissons* |
| *l'ambiance* (feminine) | atmosphere | *Il y avait une super ambiance.* |
| *s'amuser* | to have fun, to enjoy yourself | *On s'est bien amusés !* |
| *se retrouver* | to meet (up) | *On se retrouve où ?* |
| *ennuyeux* (feminine *ennuyeuse*) | boring | *une pièce ennuyeuse* |

Three A1 words take a new meaning when you go out. *L'entrée* (A1: starter) is also the entrance
and the admission: *L'entrée est gratuite* (admission is free). *La place* (A1: square) is also a
seat or a ticket: *Il reste des places ?* (Are there any tickets left?) And *complet* (lesson 14:
fully booked) is "sold out" for a show.

- *Se retrouver* (lesson 8 has *retrouver*, to find again) means "to meet up" with friends, by
  arrangement: *On se retrouve à 20 heures devant le cinéma.* For meeting someone for the first
  time, A1's *rencontrer* is the verb.
- *Amuse-toi bien !* / *Amusez-vous bien !* — Have fun! (to one friend / to several people). *Je
  me suis bien amusé(e)* = I had a great time.
- *Ennuyeux* means "boring" (it bores you). "I'm bored" is *je m'ennuie* (lesson 12): *Je suis
  ennuyeux* means "I am a boring person".

![A town street at night with five buildings, each with its sign: on the left le théâtre with two masks over the door, then l'opéra, a large building with columns and music notes, in the middle l'exposition, a gallery with framed pictures in the window and a banner, then le cinéma with a film reel, and on the right la boîte de nuit with a disco ball and music notes.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reading: a poster

![An original poster for an invented play, Le Voyage de Lou, at the Théâtre des Tilleuls in Rouvigny, with dance and music, from 4 to 13 December. Séances: Friday 20 h 30, marked COMPLET; Saturday 15 h and 20 h 30; Sunday 16 h. Tarifs: 18 euros, reduced price 12 euros, free under 12. A note: Réservation conseillée.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The poster gives the play (*la pièce*), the theatre, the showings (*les séances*), the prices (*les
tarifs*, lesson 14) and a note: *Réservation conseillée* (booking advised). Friday's showing is
*complet*: sold out. *Le tarif réduit* is the reduced price (students, the unemployed, and so on).

## Dialogue: planning Saturday

Chloé phones her friend Hugo.

> Chloé : Salut Hugo ! Dis, ça te dit d'aller au théâtre samedi ? Il y a une nouvelle pièce aux Tilleuls.
>
> Hugo : Le théâtre ? Bof… Je trouve ça souvent un peu ennuyeux.
>
> Chloé : Pas cette pièce ! Les critiques sont excellentes, et il y a de la danse et de la musique.
>
> Hugo : Bon, pourquoi pas ? C'est à quelle heure ?
>
> Chloé : Il y a deux séances, à 15 heures et à 20 h 30. Vendredi, c'est déjà complet.
>
> Hugo : Samedi après-midi, je ne peux pas, je dois aider mon frère à déménager. Le soir, volontiers !
>
> Chloé : Super ! Et après, si on allait danser ? Il y a une boîte sympa près du théâtre.
>
> Hugo : Quelle bonne idée ! Ça fait longtemps que je ne suis pas sorti. On se retrouve où ?
>
> Chloé : Devant le théâtre, à 20 heures. Je réserve les places tout de suite.
>
> Hugo : Parfait. Je suis vraiment content de te voir samedi !

Translation:

> Chloé: Hi Hugo! Listen, do you fancy going to the theatre on Saturday? There's a new play at the Tilleuls.
>
> Hugo: The theatre? Meh… I often find it a bit boring.
>
> Chloé: Not this play! The reviews are excellent, and there's dancing and music.
>
> Hugo: Well, why not? What time is it?
>
> Chloé: There are two showings, at 3 pm and at 8.30 pm. Friday is already sold out.
>
> Hugo: On Saturday afternoon I can't, I have to help my brother move. In the evening, gladly!
>
> Chloé: Great! And afterwards, how about going dancing? There's a nice club near the theatre.
>
> Hugo: What a good idea! I haven't been out for ages. Where shall we meet?
>
> Chloé: In front of the theatre, at 8 pm. I'll book the seats right away.
>
> Hugo: Perfect. I'm really pleased to be seeing you on Saturday!

Notes: Hugo refuses the afternoon with a reason (*je dois aider mon frère*) and accepts the
evening. *Ça fait longtemps que je ne suis pas sorti* uses *ça fait … que* from lesson 3, with a
negative: "it's been a long time since I went out". *Sympa* (A1) is "nice".

## Pronunciation

- *Quel, quelle, quels, quelles* all sound the same, [kɛl]. Before a vowel the plural has a
  liaison: *quels‿artistes* [kɛlzaʁtist].
- *Volontiers* [vɔlɔ̃tje]: the final *-rs* is silent.
- *Applaudir* [aplodiʁ]: *au* sounds like *o*.
- *Boîte* [bwat], *ambiance* [ɑ̃bjɑ̃s].

## Common mistakes

- Leaving out *de*: not *J'ai envie aller* but *J'ai envie d'aller*; not *Je suis ravi venir* but
  *Je suis ravi de venir*.
- *Quel* without a noun: not *Quel beau !* but *Que c'est beau !* (or *Quel beau spectacle !*).
- An article after *quel*: not *Quelle une bonne idée !* but *Quelle bonne idée !*
- The present in the suggestion pattern: *Si on va au cinéma ?* is heard in casual speech, but
  the standard pattern is the imparfait: *Si on allait au cinéma ?*
- *Je suis ennuyeux* for "I'm bored": that is *Je m'ennuie*.
- *Rencontrer* for meeting friends by arrangement: say *On se retrouve à 8 heures*.

## Key points

- Suggest with *Si on* + imparfait ? (*Si on allait … ?*), *Ça te dit de* + infinitive ?, *Tu as
  envie de … ?*, *On pourrait …*, *Je te propose de …*
- Accept: *Volontiers ! Avec plaisir ! Quelle bonne idée ! Pourquoi pas ?*
- Refuse with a reason: *Désolé(e), je ne peux pas, je dois …*; *Dommage !*; *Une autre fois ?*
- Exclaim with *Quel / Quelle / Quels / Quelles* + noun (no article), or *Que / Comme* + a
  sentence in normal order.
- Feelings: *être* + adjective + *de* + infinitive: *Je suis ravi(e) de venir.*
- *Se retrouver* = to meet up; *s'amuser* = to have fun; *ennuyeux* = boring.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Writing at A2: telling about an event; inviting, thanking, apologising
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At A1 you wrote postcards and short messages of a few sentences. At A2 you write short
connected texts: an account of something that happened, and a message that does a job
(inviting, accepting, declining, thanking, apologising, congratulating). These are the two texts of
the DELF A2 writing paper (lesson 24), and the two kinds of message you write most in real life.

You will learn:

- how to tell about an event with three tenses working together;
- more time **[[connectors]]**: *lorsque, au bout de, finalement, en attendant*, and *malgré*;
- the set phrases for social messages, and how to match their **[[register]]** (formal or informal)
  to the reader;
- a method for planning and checking a message of about 60 to 80 words.

## Telling about an event: three tenses together

An account of an event (a wedding, a trip, a party, a bad day) uses the tenses of this course,
each for its own job:

| job | tense | example |
|---|---|---|
| what happened, one event after another | passé composé | *On est allés au mariage de Léa. Elle est arrivée à 15 heures.* |
| the scene: weather, place, people, feelings, what was going on | imparfait (lessons 1 and 2) | *Il faisait beau. Tout le monde était content. Les enfants jouaient.* |
| what you will do next | futur simple (lesson 13) or futur proche | *On se reverra en juin. Je vais t'envoyer les photos.* |
| how you feel now | present | *Je suis encore fatiguée !* |

The passé composé moves the story forward; the imparfait stops to describe. A good A2 account has
both. A message with only the passé composé reads like a list; one with only the imparfait has no
story.

## Time connectors

You know *d'abord* (first), *ensuite* and *puis* (then), and *enfin* (finally) from A1. Four
more make a story clearer:

| connector | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *lorsque* | when (written; = *quand*) | *Lorsque nous sommes arrivés, tout le monde dansait.* |
| *au bout de* + length of time | after (a length of time) | *Au bout d'une heure, le bus est enfin arrivé.* |
| *finalement* | in the end | *On voulait aller à la plage. Finalement, on est restés à la maison.* |
| *en attendant* | in the meantime, meanwhile | *Le train avait du retard. En attendant, on a pris un café.* |

- *Lorsque* means exactly the same as *quand* in a time clause, but it is more written. It elides
  before *il, elle, on, un, une*: *lorsqu'il est parti*. It is not used for questions: "When are you
  coming?" is always *Quand est-ce que tu viens ?*
- *Au bout de* (literally "at the end of") also works with places: *au bout de la rue* (at the
  end of the street).
- *Finalement* and *enfin* are both "finally" in English, but they don't mean the same:
  - *finalement* = in the end, after all: the result was different from the plan, or came after a
    change. *Finalement, je ne suis pas venu.*
  - *enfin* = at last (after a long wait), or last in a list. *Enfin, le soleil !* — At last, the
    sun! *D'abord … ensuite … enfin …*
- *En attendant* is literally "while waiting". On its own it means "in the meantime": *Le
  dîner est à 8 heures. En attendant, on se promène ?*

### Despite: malgré

*Malgré* (despite, in spite of) is followed by a noun, not a verb:

- *Malgré la pluie, la fête était super.* — Despite the rain, the party was great.
- *Il est venu malgré sa fatigue.* — He came in spite of being tired.

It says the same thing as *quand même* (lesson 21), with a different structure: *Il pleuvait,
mais on est quand même sortis* = *Malgré la pluie, on est sortis.*

## A model account

Here is an original account of about 80 words, with its parts marked. Marc writes to a friend
about a wedding.

![An e-mail from Marc to Julie, with five coloured tags on the left naming its parts. Opening: Chère Julie,. The event: Samedi dernier, je suis allé au mariage de mon cousin Thomas, en Bretagne. Il faisait beau et tout le monde était très élégant. D'abord, il y a eu la cérémonie à la mairie, puis un grand repas dans une ferme. Lorsque les mariés sont arrivés, tout le monde a applaudi. Au bout d'une heure, on dansait déjà ! Feelings: C'était une journée inoubliable, j'étais très ému. Plans: Je te montrerai les photos quand on se verra en juin. Closing: Je t'embrasse, Marc.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> Chère Julie,
>
> Samedi dernier, je suis allé au mariage de mon cousin Thomas, en Bretagne. Il faisait beau et tout le monde était très élégant. D'abord, il y a eu la cérémonie à la mairie, puis un grand repas dans une ferme. Lorsque les mariés sont arrivés, tout le monde a applaudi. Au bout d'une heure, on dansait déjà ! C'était une journée inoubliable, j'étais très ému. Je te montrerai les photos quand on se verra en juin.
>
> Je t'embrasse,
>
> Marc

Translation:

> Dear Julie,
>
> Last Saturday I went to my cousin Thomas's wedding, in Brittany. The weather was lovely and everyone was very smart. First there was the ceremony at the town hall, then a big meal on a farm. When the bride and groom arrived, everyone clapped. After an hour, we were already dancing! It was an unforgettable day; I was very moved. I'll show you the photos when we see each other in June.
>
> Lots of love,
>
> Marc

Look at the tenses: the events (*je suis allé, il y a eu, sont arrivés, a applaudi*) are in the
passé composé; the scene and feelings (*il faisait beau, tout le monde était, on dansait, c'était,
j'étais*) in the imparfait; the plan (*je te montrerai … quand on se verra*) in the futur, with
the futur after *quand* (lesson 13). (*La mairie* = the town hall; *les mariés* = the bride and
groom; *ému* = moved, touched.)

## Messages that do a job: the set phrases

### Inviting, accepting, declining

| to … | informal (tu) | formal (vous) |
|---|---|---|
| invite | *Je t'invite à mon anniversaire samedi. Tu es libre ?* | *Nous avons le plaisir de vous inviter à …* |
| accept | *Merci pour ton invitation ! J'accepte avec plaisir.* | *J'accepte votre invitation avec plaisir.* |
| decline | *Désolé(e), je ne pourrai pas venir : je dois …* | *Je regrette de ne pas pouvoir venir.* |

- *L'invitation* (feminine) is the invitation; *inviter* (A1) is to invite: *inviter quelqu'un
  à* + noun or infinitive (*Je t'invite à dîner*).
- *Accepter* (to accept) and *refuser* (to refuse, to turn down) are regular -er verbs. *Refuser
  une invitation* is correct but blunt; in a message, *je ne pourrai pas venir* is kinder.
- *Regretter* (to be sorry, to regret) + *de* + infinitive: *Je regrette de ne pas pouvoir être
  avec vous.* (*Ne pas* before the infinitive, lesson 17.)

### Thanking

- *Merci pour* + noun: *Merci pour le cadeau ! Merci pour ton invitation.*
- *Merci de* + infinitive, to ask politely: *Merci de me répondre avant vendredi.* (Please reply
  by Friday.)
- To thank for something done, learn this chunk: *Merci de m'avoir invité(e)* (thank you for
  inviting me), *Merci de m'avoir aidé(e)*. (The form *avoir* + participle after *de* is the past
  infinitive; at A2 just learn the chunk.)
- *Remercier* (lesson 6) is a little more formal: *Je te remercie pour ton aide. Je vous remercie
  de votre réponse.*

### Apologising

- *Excuse-moi / Excusez-moi de* + infinitive: *Excuse-moi de répondre si tard.* (Sorry for
  replying so late.)
- *Excuse-moi / Excusez-moi pour* + noun: *Excusez-moi pour le retard.*
- *S'excuser* (to apologise): *Il s'est excusé.* In speech people say *Je m'excuse* all the time;
  some careful speakers prefer *Excusez-moi* or *Je vous prie de m'excuser* (please forgive me), so
  use those in a formal message.
- *L'excuse* (feminine) is an apology or an excuse: *Ce n'est pas une excuse !* *Je vous présente
  mes excuses* = please accept my apologies (formal).
- *Pardonner* (to forgive): *Tu me pardonnes ? Pardonne-moi !*

### Congratulating and wishing

- *Félicitations !* (Congratulations!) and *Bravo !* (Well done!): *Félicitations pour ton
  nouveau poste !* *Bravo pour ton examen !*
- *Féliciter* (to congratulate) + *pour* + noun: *Je te félicite pour ta réussite* (your success).
- *Bonne chance !* (Good luck!) before something that depends on luck, such as an exam or a
  match.
- *Bon courage !* is also "good luck", but for something long or hard: work, an exam you are
  revising for, moving house. It means "hang in there", "keep going".
- *Les vœux* (masculine, plural in this sense) are the good wishes people send at New Year and
  for special days: *Meilleurs vœux !* (Best wishes!), *Tous nos vœux de bonheur !* (to a newly
  married couple). In January people send *leurs vœux pour la nouvelle année*.

### Asking for news

- *Donne-moi de tes nouvelles.* — Let me know how you are. (*Donnez-moi de vos nouvelles* with
  *vous*.) *Les nouvelles* here is "news of you" (A1: *la nouvelle*, a piece of news).
- *Comment vas-tu ? Quoi de neuf ?* (What's new?, informal)

## Openings and closings: matching the register

**[[Register]]** is the level of formality of what you say or write: informal with friends and
family (*tu*), formal with people you don't know or in official situations (*vous*). Keep the same
register from the first line to the last (A1, lesson 23).

| | informal: family, close friends | friendly: friends, colleagues you know | formal |
|---|---|---|---|
| opening | *Coucou Léa ! Salut Tom !* | *Cher Paul, Chère Anne,* | *Madame, Monsieur,* |
| closing | *Bises ! Bisous ! Je t'embrasse.* | *Amicalement, À bientôt !* | *Cordialement, Bien cordialement,* |

- *Je t'embrasse* (literally "I kiss you") is a warm closing for family and close friends; with
  *vous* (to several people): *Je vous embrasse.* Not for colleagues or a teacher.
- *Amicalement* (in a friendly way) is friendly but not intimate: fine for a friend, a
  neighbour, a colleague you know well, a club.
- *Cher* (dear) agrees: *Cher Paul, Chère Anne, Chers amis.*

## Reading: a reply to an invitation

Lisa replies to her friend Nora, who has invited her to a party. About 65 words.

> Salut Nora,
>
> Merci beaucoup pour ton invitation ! Je suis vraiment désolée, mais je ne pourrai pas venir à ta fête samedi : je pars en Espagne avec mes parents pour l'anniversaire de ma grand-mère. Quel dommage ! Je regrette de ne pas pouvoir être avec vous. Est-ce qu'on pourrait se retrouver la semaine prochaine pour prendre un verre ? Je t'appelle à mon retour. Amuse-toi bien !
>
> Bises,
>
> Lisa

Translation:

> Hi Nora,
>
> Thank you very much for your invitation! I'm really sorry, but I won't be able to come to your party on Saturday: I'm going to Spain with my parents for my grandmother's birthday. What a pity! I'm sorry I can't be with you all. Could we meet up next week for a drink? I'll call you when I get back. Have fun!
>
> Love,
>
> Lisa

Lisa does everything a reply needs: she thanks, declines, gives a reason, says she is sorry,
suggests another time, and ends warmly. (*Prendre un verre* = to have a drink; *à mon retour* =
when I get back.)

## Planning and checking a message

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Planning and checking a short message
  accDescr: Six steps. One, read the task and underline every point you must cover. Two, decide tu or vous and choose a matching opening and closing. Three, write a short plan with one line per point. Four, write the message, linking sentences with connectors. Five, count the words: about 60 to 80, and at least the number the task asks for. Six, check verbs, agreements, accents and that every point is covered.
  A["1. Read the task: underline every point"] --> B["2. tu or vous? Choose the opening and closing"]
  B --> C["3. Plan: one line per point"]
  C --> D["4. Write, with connectors"]
  D --> E["5. Count the words: about 60–80"]
  E --> F["6. Check: tenses, agreements, accents, all points"]
```

- Cover every point. If the task says "thank, refuse, give a reason, suggest another day",
  each of the four must be there. A missing point costs more than a small grammar mistake.
- Length. The DELF A2 sample papers ask for at least 60 words for each text. Aim for about
  60 to 80, and check the number in the instructions on the day: it is printed in the task.
- Check. The participle with *être* agrees (*Nous sommes allés*); the imparfait for the scene,
  the passé composé for events; *tu* or *vous* all the way through; accents.

## Pronunciation

- *Lorsque* [lɔʁskə]: two syllables, the *s* is said.
- *Vœux* [vø], like *veux* (from *vouloir*). *Félicitations* [felisitasjɔ̃]: the *t* of *-tion*
  sounds like [s].
- *Amicalement* [amikalmɑ̃]: four syllables in speech, the *e* before *-ment* is silent.

## Common mistakes

- *Merci pour* + infinitive: not *Merci pour venir* but *Merci d'être venu(e)* (for the past) or
  *Merci de venir* (asking).
- *Excuse-moi pour* + infinitive: not *Excuse-moi pour être en retard* but *Excuse-moi d'être en
  retard*.
- *Enfin* for "in the end" after a change of plan: *Finalement, je ne suis pas venu.*
- *Malgré* + a verb: not *malgré il pleuvait* but *malgré la pluie*.
- Changing register halfway: *Madame, … Bisous !*
- Only one tense in an account: add the scene (imparfait) to the events (passé composé).

## Key points

- An account: passé composé for events, imparfait for the scene and feelings, futur for plans.
- Connectors: *d'abord, ensuite, puis, enfin*; *lorsque* (= *quand*, written), *au bout de* + time,
  *finalement* (in the end), *en attendant* (meanwhile); *malgré* + noun.
- *Merci pour* + noun, *merci de* + infinitive; *excuse-moi de* + infinitive / *pour* + noun.
- *Félicitations ! Bravo ! Bonne chance ! Bon courage ! Meilleurs vœux !*
- Match the register: *Bises / Je t'embrasse* (close), *Amicalement* (friendly), *Cordialement*
  (formal).
- Plan, cover every point, write about 60–80 words, check.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The DELF A2 exam and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This last core lesson explains what "A2" means, describes the **[[DELF]]** A2 with strategies for
each part, and reviews the grammar of the course with charts and pointers to the lessons. You
don't have to take an exam, but the free official sample papers are the best way to check that
you have reached A2.

## What A2 means

The six levels A1 to C2 come from the **[[CEFR]]** (Common European Framework of Reference for
Languages), published by the Council of Europe. A1 and A2 together are "basic user"; A2 is the
upper half. In plain words, someone at A2 can:

- understand sentences and common expressions about the things that matter most in daily life:
  themselves and their family, shopping, where they live, work;
- get the main point of short, clear messages and announcements;
- deal with simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar topics;
- describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings, what happened and what they
  plan to do;
- write short messages and simple personal letters, such as a thank-you note.

Lists like this one are **[[can-do statements]]**: descriptions of what a learner is able to do with
the language, not of the grammar they know. The big step from A1 is time (the past and the
future, not only now), linking (*parce que, qui, que, donc, pourtant*) and managing short
everyday exchanges on your own.

## The DELF A2

*DELF* stands for *Diplôme d'études en langue française*, the official French-language diplomas
of the French Ministry of Education, run by France Éducation international and taken at exam
centres in many countries. Each level is a separate diploma: you can take the A2 without having
taken the A1. The adult version is the *DELF tout public*; there are versions for school pupils
too.

The exam has four parts (*épreuves*), each marked out of 25 points:

| part | time | what it involves |
|---|---|---|
| *Compréhension de l'oral* (listening) | 25 minutes | short recordings about everyday life (announcements, messages, conversations), each heard twice, with questions |
| *Compréhension des écrits* (reading) | 30 minutes | short everyday documents (notices, messages, a letter or e-mail, a short article), with questions |
| *Production écrite* (writing) | 45 minutes | two short texts: an account of an event or a personal experience, and a message with a purpose (inviting, thanking, apologising, asking, informing, congratulating), often a reply |
| *Production orale* (speaking) | 6–8 minutes, after 10 minutes of preparation | three parts with an examiner: a guided interview about yourself, a short talk on a topic, and a conversation in an everyday situation in which the examiner plays a role |

![An overview chart of the DELF A2. A box for the written papers, 1 hour 40 minutes in total, holds three parts side by side: listening, 25 minutes, 25 points; reading, 30 minutes, 25 points; writing, 45 minutes, 25 points. A separate box for the speaking test: 10 minutes of preparation, then 6 to 8 minutes, 25 points. Below: total 100 points; pass with 50, and at least 5 out of 25 in every part.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The three written parts are taken together in one sitting of 1 hour 40 minutes. The speaking
test (its official name is *production et interaction orales*) is separate, often later the
same day or on another day. The honors lesson 24h2 goes through it part by part.

To pass, you need 50 points out of 100, and at least 5 out of 25 in each part. A mark below 5 in
any one part means you fail, even with a total of 50 or more. So never give up on your weakest
part: a few points there can decide the result.

### The newer format

The comprehension parts were revised a few years ago. According to France Éducation
international's description of the change, the new A2 papers were brought in from 2020, with
all levels from A1 to B2 due to use only the new format by 2023–24. They have more documents
(the recordings are also shorter) and only closed questions: mostly multiple choice with three options, some matching
(link each document to a situation) and some true/false, with no answers to write out in your own
words. The writing and speaking parts stay much the same. Older practice books may still show the
earlier format, so look at the official sample papers before you register.

France Éducation international publishes the official description and free sample papers with
audio and answers:

- [DELF A2 tout public: description of the exam](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/delf-tout-public/niveau-a2)
- [DELF A2 sample papers (exemples de sujets)](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/delf-tout-public/niveau-a2/exemples-sujets)
- [Advice for preparing the DELF A2 (entraînement)](https://www.france-education-international.fr/diplome/delf-tout-public/niveau-a2/entrainement)
- [The official regulation of the DELF and DALF (Bulletin officiel, 2009, PDF)](https://cache.media.education.gouv.fr/file/31/55/2/DELF-DALF_reglement-epreuve_101552.pdf)

Dates, fees and practical details are set by each exam centre, so always check with the centre
where you register.

## The words of exams and revision

| French | English | example |
|---|---|---|
| *l'épreuve* (feminine) | test (one part of an exam); ordeal | *l'épreuve de compréhension de l'oral* |
| *le candidat, la candidate* | candidate | *Chaque candidat a dix minutes de préparation.* |
| *l'examinateur, l'examinatrice* | examiner | *L'examinatrice pose des questions.* |
| *la compréhension* | understanding, comprehension | *la compréhension des écrits* |
| *l'oral* (masculine) | speaking test, oral | *J'ai passé l'oral ce matin.* |
| *l'écrit* (masculine) | written exam, writing | *à l'écrit* = in writing |
| *l'enregistrement* (masculine) | recording | *On entend chaque enregistrement deux fois.* |
| *le dialogue* | dialogue, conversation | |
| *le jeu de rôle* | role play | plural *les jeux de rôle* |
| *le sujet* | subject, topic | *Choisissez un sujet.* |
| *le point* | point; full stop | *50 points sur 100* |
| *le brouillon* | rough draft | *Écrivez d'abord au brouillon.* |
| *à voix haute* | aloud, out loud | *Lisez à voix haute.* |
| *le résumé, résumer* | summary, to summarise | |
| *la description, décrire* | description, to describe | *Décrivez votre ville.* |
| *la correction, corriger* | correction, to correct | |
| *la révision, réviser* | revision (for an exam), to revise | *Je révise pour le DELF.* |
| *se présenter* | to introduce yourself | *Présentez-vous, s'il vous plaît.* |
| *relire* | to read again, to check | *Relisez votre texte.* |
| *obtenir* | to get, to obtain | *obtenir son diplôme* |

- *Passer un examen* is "to take an exam"; *réussir* (A1) is "to pass": *J'ai passé l'écrit hier,
  et je crois que je l'ai réussi.* To get the diploma is *obtenir le diplôme*.
- *Réviser* is "to revise" in the British sense (study again for an exam), "to review" in
  American English. *La révision* is revision for an exam, and also a car's service.
- *Le point* is a point in a score and also the full stop at the end of a sentence. (*Le point de
  vue*, lesson 21, is a point of view.)

Four of these verbs are irregular or change their spelling:

| | décrire (like *écrire*) | relire (like *lire*) | obtenir (like *tenir*) | corriger |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| je | décris | relis | obtiens | corrige |
| tu | décris | relis | obtiens | corriges |
| il / elle / on | décrit | relit | obtient | corrige |
| nous | décrivons | relisons | obtenons | corrigeons |
| vous | décrivez | relisez | obtenez | corrigez |
| ils / elles | décrivent | relisent | obtiennent | corrigent |
| passé composé | j'ai décrit | j'ai relu | j'ai obtenu | j'ai corrigé |
| futur | je décrirai | je relirai | j'obtiendrai | je corrigerai |

*Obtenir* follows *venir* in the present and the futur (*j'obtiendrai*, like *je viendrai*), but
it takes *avoir*: *j'ai obtenu*. *Corriger* keeps the *e* before *-ons* like *manger*: *nous
corrigeons*, *je corrigeais*. *Se présenter* is a regular reflexive verb: *je me présente*.

## Strategies for each part

### Listening and reading: multiple choice with three options

- Read the questions and the three options before the recording starts or before you read the
  text. They tell you what to look for: a time, a price, a place, a reason.
- Expect traps. Wrong options often use words you hear or read in the document. The right option
  often says the same thing in other words (*il ne viendra pas* in the recording, *il est absent*
  in the option).
- Listen for corrections and contrasts: *Le rendez-vous est jeudi… non, pardon, vendredi.*
  *Le musée est ouvert, par contre la cafétéria est fermée.* The words after *non, pardon, mais,
  par contre, pourtant* usually carry the answer (lesson 21).
- You hear each recording twice: answer what you can the first time, check the second time.
- Preparation guides say that a wrong answer doesn't lose points, so never leave a question
  blank. Check the instructions on the day.

### Writing

- Two texts in 45 minutes: plan both quickly on your rough paper (*au brouillon*), then write.
- Cover every point the task asks for; give your opinion or feelings where it fits (lesson 21).
- In the account, mix the passé composé (events) and the imparfait (scene) (lessons 2 and 23).
  In the message, use the set phrases of lesson 23 and keep *tu* or *vous* all the way through.
- Write at least the number of words asked for (60 per text in the sample papers), then reread
  (*relisez*): agreements, participles, accents.

### Speaking

- Prepare a self-introduction in three tenses: now, the past (*Quand j'étais petit, j'habitais
  …*), a plan (*L'année prochaine, je voudrais …*).
- In the short talk, give an opinion, a reason and an example; in the role play, reach a result
  (buy, book, arrange) with the polite conditionnel (lesson 14). The honors lesson 24h2 has
  model answers.
- If you don't understand, ask: *Pardon, vous pouvez répéter ?*

## Review: the grammar of the course

### The past: imparfait or passé composé?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Imparfait or passé composé?
  accDescr: A decision chart for a verb in the past. If it describes the scene, such as weather, a place, a person, a feeling or a background, use the imparfait. If it was a habit or something repeated, such as every Saturday or when I was little, use the imparfait. If it was going on when something else happened, use the imparfait for it and the passé composé for the interruption. Otherwise, if it is a single finished event that moves the story on, use the passé composé.
  A["A verb in the past"] --> B{"Does it describe the scene: weather, place, person, feeling?"}
  B -- yes --> I["imparfait: il faisait beau, j'étais content"]
  B -- no --> C{"A habit or something repeated?"}
  C -- yes --> I2["imparfait: le samedi, je jouais au foot"]
  C -- no --> D{"Was it going on when something else happened?"}
  D -- yes --> I3["imparfait + passé composé: je dormais quand le téléphone a sonné"]
  D -- no --> P["passé composé: a finished event, je suis arrivé à 8 h"]
```

Lessons 1–4: the imparfait (*nous parlons → je parlais*; *être → j'étais*), the two past tenses
together, *depuis / il y a / pendant / en / dans*, *venir de* and *être en train de*.

### Pronouns

![A chart of French pronouns. Columns for je, tu, il, elle, nous, vous, ils, elles. Rows: subject (je, tu, il, elle, nous, vous, ils, elles); direct object, lesson 5 (me, te, le, la, nous, vous, les, les); indirect object, lesson 6 (me, te, lui, lui, nous, vous, leur, leur); stressed (moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles). Below: y replaces à plus a place or thing; en replaces de plus a thing, or a quantity (lesson 7). Position: before the conjugated verb, je le vois; before the infinitive, je vais le voir; before avoir or être in the passé composé, je l'ai vu (lesson 8); after the verb in a positive command, regarde-le.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Lessons 5–8: direct and indirect object pronouns, *y* and *en*, their position, and agreement of
the participle with a direct object before *avoir* (*la clé ? Je l'ai perdue*). Two pronouns
together are in 08h1.

### The future and the conditionnel

![A chart showing how the futur simple and the conditionnel share a stem. Stem: the infinitive (parler, finir; -re verbs drop the e: prendr-) or an irregular stem: être ser-, avoir aur-, aller ir-, faire fer-, venir viendr-, pouvoir pourr-, vouloir voudr-, devoir devr-, savoir saur-, voir verr-, envoyer enverr-, recevoir recevr-. Futur endings: -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. Conditionnel endings, the imparfait ones: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Example: je ferai, I will do; je ferais, I would do.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Lessons 13–16: the futur simple (predictions, promises, *quand* + futur), the conditionnel (polite
requests, wishes, advice: *tu devrais*), *si* + present (*S'il pleut, on restera à la maison*),
and the weather and impersonal expressions.

### The whole course at a glance

| topic | the core idea | lessons |
|---|---|---|
| imparfait and passé composé | scene and habits vs events | 1, 2 |
| time expressions | *depuis* + present; *il y a* = ago; *pendant, en, dans* | 3 |
| just done, doing now | *venir de, être en train de, être sur le point de* | 4 |
| object pronouns, *y, en* | *je le vois, je lui parle, j'y vais, j'en veux* | 5–8 |
| comparing | *plus … que, meilleur, mieux, le plus* | 9 |
| relative pronouns | *qui* (subject), *que* (object), *où* (place, time) | 10 |
| *celui, le mien* | demonstrative and possessive pronouns | 11 |
| adverbs | *-ment* from the feminine; *bien, mal, vite* | 12 |
| futur simple | infinitive + *-ai, -as, -a …*; irregular stems | 13 |
| conditionnel | future stem + imparfait endings: *je voudrais* | 14 |
| *si* + present, advice | *Si tu es fatigué, repose-toi. Il faut …* | 15 |
| impersonal expressions | *il est important de* + infinitive | 16 |
| negation | *ne … plus, jamais, rien, personne, aucun, que* | 17 |
| indefinites | *chaque, chacun, tout, plusieurs, quelques* | 18 |
| reported speech | *Il dit que …, Il demande si …* | 19 |
| cause and purpose | *car, comme, à cause de, grâce à, pour* + infinitive | 20 |
| opinions and contrast | *je pense que, à mon avis; pourtant, par contre* | 21 |
| suggestions, exclamations | *Si on allait … ? Quelle bonne idée !* | 22 |
| writing | three tenses in an account; social formulas | 23 |

If you had to remember only three things from this course, make them these: the imparfait
describes and the passé composé moves the story on; object pronouns go before the conjugated
verb (or the infinitive); and the future and the conditionnel share one stem.

## Dialogue: a practice role play

Sofia is preparing for the DELF A2. Her friend Paul plays the examiner. The situation: a friend
is visiting your town and you must organise the weekend together.

> Paul : Bon, on commence. Je suis ton ami, j'arrive vendredi. Qu'est-ce qu'on fait ce week-end ?
>
> Sofia : Alors, samedi matin, si on allait au marché ? Il est très animé, et après on pourrait visiter le musée.
>
> Paul : Le musée ? Bof, je trouve les musées un peu ennuyeux.
>
> Sofia : Je comprends. Par contre, il y a une super expo de photos en ce moment. Ça te dit ?
>
> Paul : Pourquoi pas. Et le soir ?
>
> Sofia : Je te propose d'aller au théâtre. Mais il faut réserver, c'est souvent complet.
>
> Paul : Pardon, je n'ai pas compris : il faut réserver où ?
>
> Sofia : Sur le site du théâtre. Je m'en occupe ce soir, si tu es d'accord.
>
> Paul : D'accord, volontiers. Bon, on arrête là. Tu as été très claire. Pourtant, tu disais que tu étais nulle à l'oral !
>
> Sofia : Merci ! Mais je vais quand même réviser les pronoms…

Translation:

> Paul: Right, let's start. I'm your friend, I arrive on Friday. What shall we do this weekend?
>
> Sofia: Well, on Saturday morning, how about going to the market? It's very lively, and afterwards we could visit the museum.
>
> Paul: The museum? Meh, I find museums a bit boring.
>
> Sofia: I understand. On the other hand, there's a great photo exhibition at the moment. Do you fancy it?
>
> Paul: Why not. And in the evening?
>
> Sofia: I suggest going to the theatre. But you have to book, it's often sold out.
>
> Paul: Sorry, I didn't understand: where do we have to book?
>
> Sofia: On the theatre's website. I'll take care of it this evening, if that's OK with you.
>
> Paul: OK, gladly. Right, let's stop there. You were very clear. And yet you said you were hopeless at speaking!
>
> Sofia: Thanks! But I'm still going to revise my pronouns…

Notes: Sofia reacts to Paul's objection with *par contre* and a new suggestion, as a role play
expects: she reaches a result (a plan for the weekend). *Je m'en occupe* (I'll take care of it)
uses *s'occuper de* (lesson 13) with *en* (lesson 7). *Tu disais que tu étais nulle* is reported
speech in the past, which you will learn at B1 (lesson 19 previews it).

## Pronunciation

- *L'épreuve* [lepʁœv]: the open *eu* of *peur*. *L'examinateur* [lɛɡzaminatœʁ]: *x* = "gz".
- *L'enregistrement* [lɑ̃ʁəʒistʁəmɑ̃]: *en-re-gis-tre-ment*. *Le brouillon* [bʁujɔ̃]: *ill* = [j].

## Common mistakes

- *Passer* for "to pass": *J'ai passé le DELF* means you took it. *J'ai réussi le DELF* means
  you passed. *J'ai obtenu le DELF A2* means you got the diploma.
- *J'ai obtenu* (avoir), not *je suis obtenu*, although *venir* takes *être*.
- *Nous corrigons*: keep the *e*, *nous corrigeons*.
- Leaving a part of the exam weak on purpose: every part needs at least 5/25.
- In the speaking test, answering with single words. Give a full sentence and a reason.

## What comes next

At B1 you will use the subjunctive (*il faut que tu viennes*), the plus-que-parfait (*il était
déjà parti*), *si* + imparfait + conditionnel (*si j'avais le temps, je voyagerais*), reported
speech in the past and *dont*, and follow longer conversations, films and articles. The honors
lessons preview several of these. Keep your vocabulary reviews going and read the graded readers
on the reading list.

## Key points

- A2: you manage short, routine everyday exchanges, and you can talk simply about the past and the
  future.
- The DELF A2 has four parts of 25 points: listening 25 min, reading 30 min, writing 45 min (1 h 40
  together), speaking 6–8 min after 10 min of preparation. Pass: 50/100, with at least 5/25 in
  each part.
- The comprehension parts use closed questions, mostly multiple choice with three options.
- Practise with the free sample papers from France Éducation international.
- *Passer* an exam = take it; *réussir* = pass it; *obtenir le diplôme* = get it.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. Félicitations : you have finished the core of French A2!

lessons.title: Honors: Lire la presse (reading the news)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 21 gave you the words for the media (*la presse, l'article, le journaliste, les infos*)
and taught you to give an opinion about them. This honors lesson takes you inside the news
itself: how French headlines are built, how a short news item is told, and a structure you meet
in almost every article, the **[[passive voice]]** (*Le voleur a été arrêté*). The passive is B1
grammar: here you learn to recognise and understand it, not to produce it.

Reading the press is the next step after graded readers. News items are short, they follow a
fixed pattern, and they repeat the same verbs and nouns, so a learner at A2 can read many of them
with a dictionary.

The texts in this lesson are original; the towns, streets and people in them are invented.

## Headlines: the nominal style

French headlines often have no verb. Instead of *Les prix augmentent* (prices are rising), the
paper prints *Hausse des prix* (rise of the prices). This is the **[[nominal style]]**: the action is
said with a noun, usually followed by *de* + who or what it concerns.

| headline (noun) | the same as a sentence | the verb behind the noun |
|---|---|---|
| *Hausse des prix* | *Les prix augmentent.* | *augmenter* (to rise); *la hausse* (a rise) |
| *Baisse du chômage* | *Le chômage baisse.* | *baisser* (to fall); *la baisse* (a fall) |
| *Grève des trains jeudi* | *Les conducteurs de train font grève jeudi.* | *faire grève* (to strike) |
| *Victoire du FC Rouvigny* | *Le FC Rouvigny a gagné.* | *gagner* (to win) |
| *Arrestation d'un voleur à Lille* | *Un voleur a été arrêté à Lille.* | *arrêter* (to arrest) |
| *Ouverture d'un nouveau musée* | *Un nouveau musée ouvre.* | *ouvrir* (to open) |
| *Élection du nouveau maire* | *On a élu le nouveau maire.* | *élire* (to elect) |

*Arrêter* (lesson 15: to stop) also means "to arrest": *La police a arrêté deux hommes.*

You can often guess the noun from the verb. The most common endings are:

- *-tion*, *-ation* (feminine): *arrêter → l'arrestation, réparer → la réparation, annuler →
  l'annulation, augmenter → l'augmentation* (another word for *la hausse*);
- *-ure* (feminine): *ouvrir → l'ouverture, fermer → la fermeture*;
- *-ée* (feminine): *arriver → l'arrivée*;
- *-ment* (masculine): *changer → le changement, déménager → le déménagement*;
- the bare stem + *-e* (feminine): *baisser → la baisse, hausser → la hausse*;
- an unrelated word: *gagner → la victoire, partir → le départ*.

Other features of headlines:

- A colon introduces the topic or a place: *Rouvigny : fermeture du pont pendant un mois.*
- Verbs, when there are any, are often in the present, even for the past or the future:
  *Le maire démissionne* (the mayor resigns, or has resigned). The article then tells the story in
  the passé composé.
- Abbreviations are everywhere: *la SNCF* (the national railway company), *l'UE* (the EU).

### Example 1: decoding headlines

Turn each headline into a full sentence.

1. *Hausse du prix de l'électricité en janvier* → *Le prix de l'électricité augmente en
   janvier.* *Hausse* is a rise; the verb is *augmenter*. *De + le = du*.
2. *Fermeture de la piscine municipale cet été* → *La piscine municipale ferme cet été.*
   *-ure* is the noun of *fermer*. (*Municipal* = run by the town.)
3. *Incendie dans un immeuble : deux blessés* → *Il y a eu un incendie dans un immeuble. Deux
   personnes ont été blessées.* *Un blessé* is an injured person (from *blessé*, lesson 2).
4. *Grève à la SNCF : un train sur deux jeudi* → *Les employés de la SNCF font grève : jeudi,
   seulement un train sur deux circulera.* (*Circuler* = to run, of trains and traffic.)

The trick: find the noun that carries the action, ask "which verb is this?", then ask "who or
what does it?" (the noun after *de*).

## The news item: le fait divers

*Un fait divers* is a short article about an incident: an accident, a fire, a theft, a rescue. It
answers the journalist's questions in the first sentence or two: what, where, when, who. Then it
gives details and, at the end, what will happen next.

The tenses are the ones of this course, each with its usual job:

- the passé composé for the events: *Les pompiers sont arrivés au bout de dix minutes.*
- the imparfait for the circumstances: *Il était 23 heures et il pleuvait.*
- the present for the situation now: *L'immeuble est fermé.*
- the futur for what comes next: *L'enquête dira pourquoi le feu a commencé.*
