- *selon* + a source (lesson 21) for information that the paper reports but doesn't state
  itself: *Selon la police, le voleur avait 20 ans.*

You will also meet the conditionnel used to report information that is not confirmed: *Le
voleur serait un homme de 30 ans* (the thief is said to be a man of 30). This journalistic
conditionnel is B1: just recognise that it means "reportedly", not "would".

### Example 2: reading a fait divers

> *Rouvigny : incendie rue des Peupliers*
>
> Mardi soir, un incendie a détruit un appartement au troisième étage d'un immeuble de la rue des Peupliers. Il était environ 23 heures et la plupart des habitants dormaient. Les pompiers sont arrivés au bout de dix minutes. Deux personnes ont été blessées et ont été transportées à l'hôpital. Selon les pompiers, le feu a commencé dans la cuisine. Une enquête a été ouverte. En attendant, les familles de l'immeuble ont été logées à l'hôtel par la mairie.

Translation:

> *Rouvigny: fire in Rue des Peupliers*
>
> On Tuesday evening a fire destroyed a flat on the third floor of a block in Rue des Peupliers. It was about 11 pm and most of the residents were asleep. The firefighters arrived after ten minutes. Two people were injured and were taken to hospital. According to the firefighters, the fire started in the kitchen. An investigation has been opened. In the meantime, the families from the building have been put up in a hotel by the town hall.

Step by step:

- What, where, when: the first sentence gives all three (*un incendie*, *rue des Peupliers*,
  *mardi soir*).
- The circumstances are in the imparfait: *il était, dormaient*.
- The events are in the passé composé: *a détruit, sont arrivés, a commencé*.
- Four verbs have the shape *a été / ont été* + participle: *ont été blessées, ont été
  transportées, a été ouverte, ont été logées*. These are passives, explained below.
- *Selon les pompiers* tells you where the information comes from.
- *La plupart des* = most of (+ plural verb); *loger* = to house, put up; *détruire* = to
  destroy.

## The passive voice (recognition: B1)

In an ordinary (active) sentence, the subject does the action: *La police a arrêté le voleur*
(the police arrested the thief). In a passive sentence, the subject undergoes the action: *Le
voleur a été arrêté (par la police)* (the thief was arrested by the police).

![A diagram of the passive. Top line, active: La police (subject) a arrêté (verb) le voleur (object). Two crossing arrows show le voleur moving to the front and la police moving to the end after par. Bottom line, passive: Le voleur (subject) a été arrêté (être plus participle) par la police (who did it). A note says the participle agrees with the new subject: La voleuse a été arrêtée.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The French passive is built just like the English one:

- *être* in the tense you need + the past participle;
- the participle agrees with the subject, like an adjective: *La voleuse a été arrêtée. Deux
  personnes ont été blessées.*
- *par* + whoever did it, if the paper says so: *par la police, par la mairie*.

| tense of être | passive | English |
|---|---|---|
| present: *est* | *Le courrier est distribué le matin.* | The post is delivered in the morning. |
| passé composé: *a été* | *Le voleur a été arrêté.* | The thief was (has been) arrested. |
| futur: *sera* | *Le résultat sera publié demain.* | The result will be published tomorrow. |
| imparfait: *était* | *La route était bloquée par la neige.* | The road was blocked by the snow. |

The key sign in news is *a été / ont été* + participle: it is almost always a passive. Don't confuse
it with the passé composé of the être verbs (A1): *Il est arrivé* (he arrived, active) has only
one auxiliary; *Il a été arrêté* (he was arrested, passive) has two.

Everyday French often avoids the passive with *on*: *On a arrêté le voleur* means the same as *Le
voleur a été arrêté*. That is what you should say yourself at A2.

### Example 3: from passive to active

Rewrite each passive sentence with *on* or with the person who acts.

1. *Le nouveau maire a été élu dimanche.* → *On a élu le nouveau maire dimanche.* (*élu* is the
   participle of *élire*.)
2. *L'article a été publié par un quotidien régional.* → *Un quotidien régional a publié
   l'article.* The noun after *par* becomes the subject.
3. *Les résultats du sondage seront publiés jeudi.* → *On publiera les résultats du sondage
   jeudi.* *Seront* is the futur of *être*, so the active verb goes in the futur.
4. *La manifestation a été annulée à cause de la pluie.* → *On a annulé la manifestation à
   cause de la pluie.* The agreement (*annulée*, feminine) disappears in the active sentence.

## Reading a front page

![The front page of an invented local daily, Le Courrier de Rouvigny, dated Wednesday 12 November. Under the paper's name, a large headline: Tramway : les habitants disent oui. A photo of a tram. Beside it, an article column with grey lines. In a box at the bottom left, a smaller headline: Incendie rue des Peupliers : deux blessés. At the bottom right, the weather with a sun and a cloud.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*La une* (the front page) is where the main stories go: *Ce sujet est à la une de tous les
journaux* (this story is on the front page of every paper). On it you find the paper's name,
the date, the main headline (*le titre*), a photo, the beginning of the main articles and often
the weather (*la météo*, lesson 13). *Un quotidien* is a daily paper; a weekly is *un
hebdomadaire*. The people who read it are *les lecteurs* (*la lectrice* for a woman).

A short article from that front page, with an opinion poll (*un sondage*):

> *Tramway : les habitants disent oui*
>
> Selon un sondage publié hier par notre journal, 62 % des habitants de Rouvigny sont pour le nouveau tramway. Le projet a été présenté au conseil municipal en septembre. Pourtant, les commerçants du centre-ville ne sont pas d'accord : ils ont peur d'une baisse du nombre de clients pendant les travaux. Une manifestation est prévue samedi devant la mairie. Le maire répondra aux questions des lecteurs jeudi soir.

Translation:

> *Tram: residents say yes*
>
> According to a poll published yesterday by our paper, 62% of the residents of Rouvigny are in favour of the new tram. The project was presented to the town council in September. Yet the shopkeepers in the town centre don't agree: they are afraid of a fall in the number of customers during the works. A demonstration is planned for Saturday in front of the town hall. The mayor will answer readers' questions on Thursday evening.

*Pourtant* (lesson 21) introduces the other side; *être pour / contre* = to be for / against;
*les commerçants* = shopkeepers; *les travaux* = building works. *Est prévue* (is planned) is a
passive in the present, from *prévoir* (lesson 13).

## Press vocabulary

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *la une*, *à la une* | the front page, on the front page |
| *le titre* | headline, title |
| *le quotidien* | daily newspaper |
| *le lecteur, la lectrice* | reader |
| *publier* | to publish |
| *le fait divers* (plural *les faits divers*) | news item (an incident) |
| *l'incendie* (masculine) | fire (in a building or forest) |
| *le pompier* | firefighter |
| *l'enquête* (feminine) | investigation; survey |
| *le sondage* | opinion poll |
| *la grève*, *faire grève* | strike, to go on strike |
| *la manifestation* (*la manif*) | demonstration (protest) |
| *la hausse, augmenter* | rise, to rise / increase |
| *la baisse, baisser* | fall, to fall / lower |
| *le gouvernement* | government |
| *le maire* | mayor |
| *l'élection* (feminine) | election |
| *la victoire* | victory, win |

*La grève* and *la manifestation* come from the honors lesson 04h2 (May 1968). *L'incendie* is a fire that destroys something (a building, a forest). *Le feu* is fire in general:
the fire in a fireplace, and also the flames of an *incendie* (*Le feu a commencé dans la cuisine*). *La manifestation* is also any organised event (*une
manifestation culturelle*), but in the news it usually means a protest march.

## Common mistakes

- Reading *a été* + participle as "has been" every time. In a story it usually translates as a
  simple past: *Il a été arrêté hier* = he was arrested yesterday.
- Forgetting the agreement in the passive: *Deux femmes ont été blessées* (the participle agrees
  with the subject, as with *être* verbs).
- Translating a headline word for word: *Hausse des prix* is not "the rise of the prices" but
  "prices are rising" or "prices up".
- Taking the journalistic conditionnel as a condition: *Le voleur serait parti en voiture* means
  "the thief reportedly left by car", not "would leave".
- *L'enquête* in a news story about a crime is an investigation, not a survey (*le sondage* is
  an opinion poll).

## Key points

- Headlines use the nominal style: a noun for the action (*hausse, baisse, grève, victoire,
  ouverture, arrestation*) + *de* + who or what.
- Nouns from verbs often end in *-tion, -ure, -ée, -ment*, or are the bare stem + *-e*.
- A *fait divers* gives what, where and when first; events in the passé composé, circumstances in
  the imparfait, sources with *selon*.
- The passive: *être* + participle (agreeing) + *par* … *A été / ont été* + participle is the
  sign. Recognise it; in your own French, use *on*.
- The conditionnel in news can mean "reportedly" (B1).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: L'oral du DELF A2 en pratique (the speaking test in practice)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 24 described the DELF A2 as a whole. This honors lesson goes through its speaking test
part by part, with original model answers, and teaches what good speakers do when they need time
to think or when communication breaks down: **[[fillers]]** (*euh, bon, en fait*) and
**[[repair strategies]]** (*Vous pouvez reformuler ?*). It ends with the features of everyday spoken French
you will hear from French speakers, and the mistakes examiners hear most often.

The model answers are written for this course; none of them comes from an exam paper. The
official sample papers from France Éducation international (linked in lesson 24) show real
tasks: use them for practice once you have worked through this lesson.

## How the speaking test runs

![A timeline of the DELF A2 speaking test. First, 10 minutes of preparation for parts 2 and 3. Then three parts with the examiner, 6 to 8 minutes in all: part 1, entretien dirigé, about 1 minute 30, no preparation, you talk about yourself; part 2, monologue suivi, about 2 minutes, you speak on one topic, then answer a few questions; part 3, exercice en interaction, about 3 to 4 minutes, a role play in which the examiner plays a part.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The test lasts 6 to 8 minutes, after 10 minutes of preparation. In the examiner's notes that come
with the official sample papers, the parts run like this (check the current sample papers, as
details can change):

1. *Entretien dirigé* (guided interview), about 1 minute 30, not prepared. The examiner asks
   you about yourself: your family, your work or studies, your hobbies, your town.
2. *Monologue suivi* (short talk), about 2 minutes. You choose a topic from two you have drawn
   (*tirer au sort* = to draw at random) and prepared, then speak about it on your own. The
   examiner may then ask two or three questions.
3. *Exercice en interaction* (interaction), about 3 to 4 minutes. Again you choose from two
   situations and prepare it. The examiner plays a role (a shop assistant, a friend, a
   receptionist), and together you must reach a result: buy something, arrange an outing, sort
   out a problem.

The examiner tells you when each part begins. Your *interlocuteur* (the person you are speaking
to) is the examiner: use *vous* unless the role is a friend and the examiner uses *tu*.

## Part 1: the guided interview

The examiner wants to hear you produce simple, correct sentences about your own life. The best
preparation is a self-introduction that you have practised until it comes naturally, using three
tenses: now, the past and the future.

### Example 1: a model self-introduction

> Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Daniel Ortiz, j'ai 34 ans et je suis mexicain. J'habite à Montréal depuis cinq ans avec ma femme et nos deux enfants. Je suis infirmier dans un grand hôpital. Quand j'étais petit, j'habitais à Puebla, et je ne parlais pas du tout français. J'ai commencé à l'apprendre il y a deux ans, parce que j'en avais besoin pour mon travail. Le week-end, j'aime faire du vélo et cuisiner pour mes amis. L'année prochaine, j'aimerais passer des vacances en France avec ma famille.

Translation:

> Hello! My name is Daniel Ortiz, I'm 34 and I'm Mexican. I've lived in Montreal for five years with my wife and our two children. I'm a nurse in a big hospital. When I was little, I lived in Puebla, and I didn't speak any French at all. I started learning it two years ago, because I needed it for my job. At the weekend I like cycling and cooking for my friends. Next year I'd like to spend a holiday in France with my family.

What makes it good at A2:

- *depuis* + present (*J'habite … depuis cinq ans*, lesson 3) and *il y a* + passé composé (*il y
  a deux ans*);
- the imparfait for the past (*j'habitais, je ne parlais pas*) and a reason with *parce que*;
- the pronoun *en* (*j'en avais besoin*, lesson 7) and a polite wish in the conditionnel
  (*j'aimerais*, lesson 14).

Be ready for follow-up questions: *Pourquoi est-ce que vous apprenez le français ? Qu'est-ce que
vous faites pendant vos vacances ? Comment est votre ville ?* Answer each with two or three
sentences, not one word.

## Part 2: the short talk

Here you speak on your own for about two minutes on an everyday topic: a place, a habit, an
event, a preference. A simple structure keeps you going:

1. Say what you are going to talk about: *Je vais vous parler de …*
2. Give two or three ideas, each with an example: *D'abord … Par exemple … Ensuite …*
3. Give your opinion and a reason: *À mon avis … parce que …*
4. Close: *Voilà, c'est pour ça que … / Pour finir, …*

Use *argument* in its French sense: *un argument* is a reason or a point in favour of an
opinion, not a quarrel (*une dispute*, lesson 5).

### Example 2: a model talk

The topic (an invented one): *Parlez d'une fête que vous aimez.*

> Je vais vous parler de la fête des Morts, une fête très importante au Mexique. Elle a lieu le 1er et le 2 novembre. D'abord, les familles préparent un autel dans la maison, avec des fleurs orange, des bougies et des photos des grands-parents. Ensuite, on mange un pain spécial, le *pan de muerto*. Quand j'étais petit, j'allais au cimetière avec ma grand-mère, et on restait là toute la soirée. Ce n'était pas triste, au contraire : on racontait des histoires et on riait. À mon avis, c'est une belle fête, parce qu'on pense à ceux qui sont partis. L'année prochaine, je vais la fêter avec mes enfants à Montréal. Voilà !

Translation:

> I'm going to talk to you about the Day of the Dead, a very important festival in Mexico. It takes place on 1 and 2 November. First, families make an altar in the house, with orange flowers, candles and photos of the grandparents. Then we eat a special bread, *pan de muerto*. When I was little, I went to the cemetery with my grandmother, and we stayed there all evening. It wasn't sad, on the contrary: we told stories and laughed. In my opinion, it's a beautiful festival, because we think of those who have gone. Next year I'm going to celebrate it with my children in Montreal. That's it!

Notes: *avoir lieu* = to take place; *l'autel* = altar; *la bougie* = candle; *le cimetière* =
cemetery; *ceux qui* (lesson 11) = those who. The talk uses the present for the custom, the
imparfait for childhood memories, *au contraire* and *à mon avis* (lesson 21), and the futur
proche for a plan. Speaking about your own culture is a good choice: you know the topic and
you can explain words the examiner may not know.

## Part 3: the interaction

The role play is a short everyday transaction. You need to: greet, explain what you want, ask
questions, react to what the examiner says (who will often raise a problem on purpose), and reach
an agreement. Polite conditionnels (*je voudrais, vous pourriez*), indirect questions (*Je
voudrais savoir si …*, lesson 19) and the suggestion patterns of lesson 22 are the tools.

### Example 3: a model interaction

The situation (invented): you want to sign up for a dance class; the examiner plays the
receptionist at the sports centre.

> Examinatrice : Bonjour, je peux vous aider ?
>
> Candidate : Bonjour, madame. Je voudrais m'inscrire à un cours de danse. Vous pourriez me donner des renseignements ?
>
> Examinatrice : Bien sûr. Nous avons un cours de salsa le mardi soir et un cours de danse moderne le samedi matin.
>
> Candidate : Le mardi, à quelle heure exactement ?
>
> Examinatrice : De 19 heures à 20 h 30. Mais attention, il est presque complet.
>
> Candidate : Ah, dommage. Et le samedi, il reste des places ?
>
> Examinatrice : Oui. C'est 120 euros le trimestre.
>
> Candidate : Pardon, je n'ai pas compris le mot « trimestre ». Vous pouvez préciser ?
>
> Examinatrice : C'est une période de trois mois.
>
> Candidate : D'accord, merci. C'est un peu cher… Est-ce qu'il y a un tarif réduit pour les étudiants ?
>
> Examinatrice : Oui, 90 euros.
>
> Candidate : Parfait, je suis étudiante. Alors je m'inscris au cours du samedi. Qu'est-ce que je dois apporter ?
>
> Examinatrice : Une pièce d'identité et votre carte d'étudiante.
>
> Candidate : Très bien. Je reviens demain avec mes papiers. Merci, au revoir !

Translation:

> Examiner: Hello, can I help you?
>
> Candidate: Hello. I'd like to sign up for a dance class. Could you give me some information?
>
> Examiner: Of course. We have a salsa class on Tuesday evenings and a modern dance class on Saturday mornings.
>
> Candidate: On Tuesdays, at what time exactly?
>
> Examiner: From 7 to 8.30 pm. But be careful, it's almost full.
>
> Candidate: Oh, a pity. And on Saturdays, are there places left?
>
> Examiner: Yes. It's 120 euros a term.
>
> Candidate: Sorry, I didn't understand the word "trimestre". Could you explain?
>
> Examiner: It's a period of three months.
>
> Candidate: OK, thank you. It's a bit expensive… Is there a reduced rate for students?
>
> Examiner: Yes, 90 euros.
>
> Candidate: Perfect, I'm a student. So I'll sign up for the Saturday class. What do I need to bring?
>
> Examiner: Proof of identity and your student card.
>
> Candidate: Very good. I'll come back tomorrow with my documents. Thank you, goodbye!

The candidate asks questions, reacts to the problem (*presque complet*), asks for an explanation
of an unknown word instead of pretending, negotiates the price and ends with a decision. That is
what the examiner listens for. (*S'inscrire*, *le renseignement*, *la pièce d'identité* and *les
papiers* come from lessons 8, 18 and 19.)

## Fillers: buying time

Everyone needs a second to think. A **[[filler]]** is a small word or sound that fills the silence
while you look for the next word. French ones (all informal, all heard constantly):

| filler | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *euh* | um, er | *Je suis allé, euh… à Lyon.* |
| *bon* | well, right (starting or closing) | *Bon, je vais vous parler de …* |
| *alors* | so, well | *Alors, le week-end, je …* |
| *en fait* | actually, in fact | *En fait, je préfère le samedi.* |
| *du coup* | so, as a result (very informal) | *Il pleuvait, du coup on est restés.* |
| *comment dire …* | how can I put it… | *C'est, comment dire, un peu bizarre.* |

- *Euh* is the French "um": use it instead of the English sound, which gives you away.
- *En fait* (actually) corrects or adds something unexpected. Don't confuse it with *en effet*
  (lesson 20), which confirms: "indeed".
- *Du coup* is everywhere in casual speech, but some people dislike it. With the examiner,
  *alors* or *donc* is safer.
- One or two fillers sound natural. One in every sentence sounds unprepared.

## Repair strategies: when communication breaks down

A **[[repair strategy]]** is what you do to get a conversation going again when you haven't understood
or can't find a word. Examiners expect them at A2: asking is a skill, not a failure.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: What to do when communication breaks down
  accDescr: If you didn't understand the examiner, ask them to repeat, Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît?, or to rephrase, Vous pouvez reformuler?, or ask about one word, Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire, trimestre? If you can't find a word, describe it, C'est un truc qui sert à…, or give an example. If you made a mistake, correct yourself: Pardon, je veux dire…. In every case, the conversation then goes on.
  A{"A problem"} -- "I didn't understand" --> B["Vous pouvez répéter ? / Vous pouvez reformuler ?"]
  A -- "one word I don't know" --> C["Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire, « … » ?"]
  A -- "I can't find my word" --> D["Describe it: c'est un truc qui sert à …"]
  A -- "I made a mistake" --> E["Correct it: pardon, je veux dire …"]
  B --> F["The conversation goes on"]
  C --> F
  D --> F
  E --> F
```

| you want to … | say |
|---|---|
| hear it again | *Pardon, vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?* |
| hear it in other words | *Vous pouvez reformuler ?* (*reformuler* = to rephrase) |
| hear it more slowly | *Vous pouvez parler plus lentement ?* |
| get more detail | *Vous pouvez préciser ?* (*préciser* = to be more precise, to explain exactly) |
| check you understood | *Vous voulez dire que … ? / Si je comprends bien, …* |
| describe a word you don't know | *C'est un truc qui sert à couper* (lesson 10); *C'est le contraire de …* |
| correct yourself | *Non, pardon, je veux dire …*; *c'est-à-dire …* (that is, I mean); *autrement dit …* (in other words) |

A *malentendu* is a misunderstanding. If one happens in the role play, clear it up in French:
*Ah non, je crois qu'il y a un malentendu : je voulais le cours du samedi.* (*Je voulais*, the
imparfait, is a polite way to say what you want, like *je voudrais*.)

*Hésiter* (to hesitate) is normal; long silences are not. If you are stuck, say so in French:
*J'hésite… Je ne sais pas comment dire ça en français.*

## Spoken French you will hear

French speakers, including friendly examiners, often speak in a relaxed way. These features are
normal speech, not mistakes; recognise them, but use the standard forms yourself in the exam.

| you hear | standard | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *T'as vu ?* | *Tu as vu ?* | Did you see? (*tu* shortened before a vowel) |
| *Y a du monde.* | *Il y a du monde.* | There are a lot of people. |
| *C'est pas grave.* | *Ce n'est pas grave.* | It doesn't matter. (*ne* dropped) |
| *J'sais pas* [ʃepa] | *Je ne sais pas.* | I don't know. |
| *Ouais.* | *Oui.* | Yeah. |
| *Chuis fatigué.* [ʃɥi] | *Je suis fatigué.* | I'm tired. (*je suis* run together) |

Dropping *ne* is the most common: in everyday speech most negatives lose it (lesson 17). In
writing and with the examiner, keep it.

## Common mistakes at the oral

- *Je suis 34 ans*: age takes *avoir*, *J'ai 34 ans* (A1, still heard at A2).
- Answering with one word. *Vous aimez votre ville ? — Oui.* Add a reason and an example.
- Reading your notes aloud. You may look at them, but speak to the examiner.
- Switching to English for a missing word. Describe it in French instead.
- Using *tu* with the examiner when the role doesn't call for it.
- Starting very long sentences you can't finish. Two short correct sentences are better.
- *Je suis fini* for "I've finished": say *J'ai fini* (*je suis fini* means "I'm done for").

## Key points

- Three parts in 6–8 minutes: a guided interview (about 1 min 30, not prepared), a short talk
  (about 2 min) and a role play (about 3–4 min), both prepared during the 10 minutes before.
- Prepare a self-introduction in three tenses, a structure for the talk (topic, ideas and
  examples, opinion, close), and polite phrases for the role play.
- Fillers (*euh, bon, alors, en fait*) buy time; use them sparingly. *Du coup* is very informal.
- Repair: *Vous pouvez répéter / reformuler / préciser ? Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ? C'est un
  truc qui … Pardon, je veux dire …*
- Recognise *t'as, y a* and dropped *ne*; use the standard forms yourself.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Un conte de Perrault: Le Petit Chaperon rouge
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lessons 01 and 02 you told stories with the imparfait (the background) and the passé composé
(the events). Written stories use another tense for their events: the **[[passé simple]]**, which you
met in French A1's fable lesson (*elle alla, il dit, il fut*). Here you read *Le Petit Chaperon
rouge* (Little Red Riding Hood) in the version that made it famous, Charles Perrault's of 1697, learn
many more passé simple forms, retell the story in A2 French, and see why Perrault's ending is not the
one most English speakers know.

## Charles Perrault and his tales

Charles Perrault (1628–1703) was a writer at the court of Louis XIV. In January 1697 the Paris
bookseller Claude Barbin published his *Histoires ou contes du temps passé, avec des moralités*
(tales of times past, with morals). Its frontispiece shows an old woman telling stories to
children under the words *Contes de ma mère l'Oye* (Mother Goose tales), the name the book is often
known by. Oddly, it was signed "P. Darmancour", the name of Perrault's teenage son Pierre; most
scholars think the father wrote it.

Its eight prose tales include *La Belle au bois dormant* (Sleeping Beauty), *La Barbe bleue*
(Bluebeard), *Le Chat botté* (Puss in Boots) and *Cendrillon* (Cinderella). A **[[conte]]** is a tale: a
short story, often with magic (*un conte de fées*, a fairy tale), told to children but not only to
them. Their characters (*les personnages*) include princesses, ogres, fairies (*les fées*) and clever
animals; other tales add witches (*les sorcières*). Each of Perrault's tales ends
with a **[[moralité]]**, a moral in verse.

## The text

The extracts keep the words of the 1697 first edition, as restored by Andrew Lang (*Perrault's
Popular Tales*, Oxford, 1888), in modern spelling (1697 printed *Il estoit* and *luy*) and
punctuation, following Georges Gérard's edition (*Le Cabinet des fées*, New York, 1859) where the
two agree.

![The path through the wood: the girl in her red hood walks along the long, winding path with her basket, past flowers and a butterfly; the wolf peeps from behind a tree and a woodcutter chops wood nearby. The short, straight path leads to the grandmother's cottage, whose door has a little peg on a string. Labels: le Petit Chaperon rouge, le loup, le bûcheron, le chemin le plus long, le chemin le plus court, la chevillette.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 1. The beginning

> Il était une fois une petite fille de village, la plus jolie qu'on eût su voir : sa mère en était folle, et sa mère-grand plus folle encore. Cette bonne femme lui fit faire un petit chaperon rouge, qui lui seyait si bien, que partout on l'appelait le Petit Chaperon rouge.

*Once upon a time there was a little village girl, the prettiest anyone had ever seen. Her mother was mad about her, and her grandmother even more. This good woman had a little red hood made for her, which suited her so well that everywhere people called her Little Red Riding Hood.*

*Qu'on eût su voir* = that anyone could ever have seen (an old tense: just read it); *la mère-grand*
= the grandmother (old; today *la grand-mère*); *fit faire* = had made; *un chaperon* = a hood;
*seyait* = suited.

### 2. The meeting

> Un jour, sa mère, ayant cuit et fait des galettes, lui dit : « Va voir comme se porte ta mère-grand, car on m'a dit qu'elle était malade. Porte-lui une galette et ce petit pot de beurre. » […] En passant dans un bois, elle rencontra compère le Loup, qui eut bien envie de la manger ; mais il n'osa, à cause de quelques bûcherons qui étaient dans la forêt.

*One day her mother, having baked some galettes, said to her: "Go and see how your grandmother is, because I've been told she's ill. Take her a galette and this little pot of butter." […] Passing through a wood, she met old Wolf, who very much wanted to eat her, but he didn't dare, because of some woodcutters who were in the forest.*

*Comme se porte* = how she is (*se porter* = to be in health; *comme* = *comment*, an old use); *une
galette* = a flat cake; *compère le Loup* = "old Wolf", a nickname; *il n'osa* = he didn't dare
(*oser*; *ne* without *pas* is literary with this verb). The cut sentence sends her off at once to her
grandmother's, in another village. She tells the wolf where she is going.

### 3. The race

> « Eh bien, dit le Loup, je veux l'aller voir aussi ; je m'y en vais par ce chemin ici, et toi par ce chemin-là, et nous verrons qui plus tôt y sera. » Le Loup se mit à courir de toute sa force par le chemin qui était le plus court, et la petite fille s'en alla par le chemin le plus long.

*"Well," said the Wolf, "I want to go and see her too. I'll go this way and you go that way, and we'll see who gets there first." The Wolf began to run as fast as he could along the shortest path, and the little girl went off along the longest one.*

On the way she picks hazelnuts (*des noisettes*) and chases butterflies. *Je veux l'aller voir* is the
old order for *je veux aller la voir*; *je m'y en vais* = I'm going there (old; today *j'y vais*);
*ce chemin ici* = this path (today *ce chemin-ci*, which Gérard prints); *qui plus tôt y sera* = who will
get there first.

### 4. At the grandmother's

> La bonne mère-grand, qui était dans son lit, à cause qu'elle se trouvait un peu mal, lui cria : « Tire la chevillette, la bobinette cherra. » Le Loup tira la chevillette, et la porte s'ouvrit. Il se jeta sur la bonne femme, et la dévora en moins de rien ; car il y avait plus de trois jours qu'il n'avait mangé.

*The good grandmother, who was in bed because she wasn't feeling well, called out to him: "Pull the little peg and the latch will fall." The Wolf pulled the peg and the door opened. He threw himself on the good woman and gobbled her up in no time, for he hadn't eaten for more than three days.*

*À cause qu'elle* = *parce qu'elle* (old). *La chevillette* is a small wooden peg, *la bobinette* a wooden latch, and *cherra* the future of the
old verb *choir* (to fall). French children know this line by heart. The wolf gets into the bed;
the girl arrives, and he tells her the same words.

### 5. The famous dialogue

> « Ma mère-grand, que vous avez de grands bras !
>
> — C'est pour mieux t'embrasser, ma fille.
>
> — Ma mère-grand, que vous avez de grandes jambes !
>
> — C'est pour mieux courir, mon enfant. […]
>
> — Ma mère-grand, que vous avez de grandes dents !
>
> — C'est pour te manger. »
>
> Et en disant ces mots, ce méchant Loup se jeta sur le Petit Chaperon rouge, et la mangea.

*Que vous avez de grands bras !* = What big arms you have! (an exclamation with *que*, lesson 22);
*C'est pour mieux…* = It's to better… ("All the better to…"); *t'embrasser* = to hug you (*em-bras-ser*,
to take in your arms: the wolf plays on *bras*); *en disant* = as he said. The cut lines
are the ears and the eyes. Gérard's 1859 edition has *grands pieds* (big feet) where 1697 has
*grandes jambes*: editions do differ.

### 6. The moral (lines 1–6 and the last two)

> On voit ici que de jeunes enfants,\
> Surtout de jeunes filles,\
> Belles, bien faites, et gentilles,\
> Font très mal d'écouter toute sorte de gens,\
> Et que ce n'est pas chose étrange,\
> S'il en est tant que le loup mange. […]\
> Mais hélas ! qui ne sait que ces loups doucereux,\
> De tous les loups sont les plus dangereux.

*Here we see that young children, especially young girls, pretty, shapely and kind, are very wrong to listen to all sorts of people, and that it's no wonder if the wolf eats so many of them. […] But alas! who doesn't know that these smooth-talking wolves are the most dangerous of all?*

The cut lines explain that not all wolves are alike: some are quiet, polite and gentle, and follow
young ladies right into their homes. *Doucereux* means sweet in a false way; *bien faites* = shapely (well made), not "well brought up".

## Reading the passé simple

The passé simple carries the events of a written story, as the passé composé does when you speak:
*elle rencontra* = *elle a rencontré* (she met). The imparfait keeps its job, the background
(lesson 02): *qui étaient dans la forêt, qui était dans son lit, se trouvait*. So a written story is
imparfait + passé simple; a spoken one, imparfait + passé composé.

Stories use it almost only in the *il/elle* and *ils/elles* forms:

| Type | il / elle | ils / elles | In the tale | Passé composé |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| all -er verbs (and *aller*) | -a | -èrent | *rencontra, se jeta, dévora, tira, cria, alla* | *elle a rencontré, elle est allée* |
| -ger, -cer verbs | -gea, -ça | -gèrent, -cèrent | *mangea* (and *commença*) | *il a mangé* |
| most -ir and -re verbs | -it | -irent | *dit, fit, s'ouvrit, se mit* (*mettre*); *prit* (*prendre*) | *il a dit, elle s'est ouverte* |
| u-type verbs | -ut | -urent | *eut, fut*; *voulut, put, sut* | *il a eu, il a été* |
| *venir*, *tenir* | *vint, tint* | *vinrent, tinrent* | *vint heurter* (came knocking) | *elle est venue* |

- *-ger* verbs keep their *e* before *a* (*il mangea*), as in *nous mangeons*; *-cer* verbs take *ç*.
- *Il dit* and *il finit* look exactly like the present, and *il fit* or *il mit* are easy to take for
  *fait* or *mis*. Next to other passé simple forms in a past story, they are passé simple.

Recognise it; your own stories use the passé composé.

### Example 1: From the tale to spoken French

Rewrite each sentence in the passé composé.

1. *Elle rencontra le Loup.* An -er verb (-a): *rencontrer*, with *avoir*: *Elle a rencontré le loup.*
2. *Il se jeta sur la bonne femme.* Pronominal, so *être*, agreeing with *il*: *Il s'est jeté sur la
   grand-mère.*
3. *Il la dévora.* *La* is a direct object pronoun (lesson 05); it goes before *avoir*, and the
   participle agrees with it because it comes first (lesson 08): *Il l'a dévorée.*
4. *Le Petit Chaperon rouge vint heurter à la porte.* *Venir* takes *être*, and the girl is feminine;
   *heurter* is old, today's verb is *frapper*: *Elle est venue frapper à la porte.*

### Example 2: Background or event?

Sort the verbs of passage 4.

1. Background (imparfait): *était* and *se trouvait* (her state), *il y avait* (the reason).
2. Events (passé simple): *cria, tira, s'ouvrit, se jeta, dévora*, one after another.
3. Told aloud: *Le loup l'a tirée, la porte s'est ouverte et il a dévoré la grand-mère.*

## The story in A2 French

> Il était une fois une petite fille que tout le monde appelait le Petit Chaperon rouge. Un jour, sa mère lui a donné une galette pour sa grand-mère, qui était malade. Dans le bois, elle a rencontré un loup. Il voulait la manger, mais il n'a pas osé, parce que des bûcherons travaillaient tout près. Il a pris le chemin le plus court ; elle, elle a pris le plus long et elle s'est amusée à cueillir des fleurs.
>
> Le loup est arrivé le premier et il a mangé la grand-mère. Puis il s'est couché dans son lit. Quand la petite fille est arrivée, elle a trouvé sa grand-mère bizarre : elle avait de très grands bras, de très grandes dents… « C'est pour te manger ! » a dit le loup, et il l'a mangée.

Every form here is from lessons 01–08: imparfait for the background (*était, voulait, travaillaient,
avait*), passé composé for the events, pronouns before *avoir* (*il l'a mangée*). *Tout près* = close
by; *bizarre* = strange.

## Perrault and the Grimms

The happier ending comes from the brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, who published *Rotkäppchen*
(Little Red Cap) in the first edition of their *Kinder- und Hausmärchen* (Children's and Household
Tales) in 1812. Its first part follows Perrault closely (one of their storytellers came from a French
Huguenot family), but a hunter (*un chasseur*) cuts the sleeping wolf open, the girl and her
grandmother, whom he had swallowed whole (*avalées*), come out alive, and they fill the wolf's belly
with stones.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Two endings of Little Red Riding Hood
  accDescr: In both versions the wolf meets the girl in the wood and eats the grandmother, then the girl. Perrault's story of 1697 ends there, with a moral in verse about smooth-talking wolves. In the Grimms' version of 1812 a hunter opens the wolf's belly and the girl and her grandmother are saved.
  A["Le loup rencontre la fille dans le bois"] --> B["Il mange la grand-mère, puis la fille"]
  B --> C["Perrault, 1697 : fin de l'histoire"]
  C --> D["Moralité : attention aux loups doucereux"]
  B --> E["Grimm, 1812 : un chasseur ouvre le ventre du loup"]
  E --> F["La fille et la grand-mère sont sauvées"]
```

Perrault saves (*sauver*) nobody. His heroine is naive (*naïve*): she talks to a stranger (*un
inconnu*), and the cunning (*rusé*) wolf uses what she tells him. His moral says who the "wolves" are:
charming, gentle men who follow girls home, so *méfiez-vous* (be wary). The Grimms made it a children's story
about obeying (*obéir à*) your mother: their girl disobeys (*désobéit*) by leaving the path. Neither
ending is the "right" one: tales were told in many versions before anyone printed them, and
folklorists have collected oral versions of this one in the French countryside.

## Common mistakes

- Writing the passé simple in your own messages. Read it; write the passé composé.
- Taking *il dit* or *il fit* in a past story for the present or a participle.
- Reading *mangea* as an imparfait. The imparfait is *mangeait*; *mangea* is one event.
- Using *heurter à la porte* or *la mère-grand* today: say *frapper à la porte*, *la grand-mère*.

## Key points

- Perrault's *Histoires ou contes du temps passé* (Paris, Claude Barbin, 1697), also called *Contes de
  ma mère l'Oye*, has eight prose tales, each with a moral in verse.
- In Perrault the wolf eats the grandmother and the girl, and the story ends; the Grimms (1812) add
  a hunter who saves them.
- Written stories: imparfait for the background, passé simple for the events: *-a / -èrent, -it /
  -irent, -ut / -urent, vint / vinrent; mangea, commença*.
- To retell, use the passé composé, with the pronoun before *avoir* and agreement when the direct
  object comes first (*il l'a mangée*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Chansons françaises
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Songs are one of the best ways to remember French: the words come back with the tune. This lesson
reads three songs that are old enough to be free for everyone (their authors died long ago, or
nobody knows who they were), with a gloss. You'll find grammar from this course inside them: the
imperative with a pronoun (*Prête-moi*, lessons 05–06), *y* (lesson 07), *ne … plus* (lesson 17) and
the futur simple (lesson 13). Then you'll meet four great singers of the twentieth century, in a
description: their songs are still under copyright, so we name them and talk about them, but don't
quote them.

## What is a chanson?

*Une chanson* is simply a song. But *la chanson française* also names a tradition in which the words
matter as much as the tune: the **[[chanson à texte]]**, a song you listen to like a short poem. Most
songs are built from **[[couplets]]** (verses: the words change each time) and a **[[refrain]]** (the
chorus: the same words come back). *Les paroles* are the words (lyrics), *la mélodie* the tune.

![A song map. At the top, the title Au clair de la lune above a music staff with eleven notes, with the words under the notes: Au clair de la lu-ne, mon a-mi Pier-rot. At the bottom, the shape of Sur le pont d'Avignon in five boxes: the refrain Sur le pont d'Avignon three times, with the couplets Les beaux messieurs and Les belles dames between them. Labels: le titre, la mélodie, les paroles, le refrain, le couplet.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Au clair de la lune

A folk song from the eighteenth century, sung to French children for generations. Pierrot is a
character from the old Italian comedy (*la commedia dell'arte*), a sad clown dressed in white.

> Au clair de la lune,\
> Mon ami Pierrot,\
> Prête-moi ta plume\
> Pour écrire un mot.\
> Ma chandelle est morte,\
> Je n'ai plus de feu.\
> Ouvre-moi ta porte\
> Pour l'amour de Dieu.

*By the light of the moon, my friend Pierrot, lend me your pen so I can write a word. My candle has gone out, I have no fire any more. Open your door to me, for the love of God.*

- *Au clair de la lune* = in the moonlight (*la lune* = the moon).
- *Prête-moi, Ouvre-moi*: the affirmative imperative with the pronoun after it and *me → moi*
  (lesson 05). In the negative it would be *Ne me prête pas ta plume*.
- *La plume* is a feather, and so a quill pen. *La chandelle* is an old word for a candle (today *la
  bougie*); *Ma chandelle est morte* = my candle has gone out.
- *Je n'ai plus de feu*: *ne … plus* = no longer, with *de* after the negative (lesson 17).

In the next verse Pierrot says no: he has no pen and he's in bed, so go next door. A curiosity: on 9
April 1860 a Frenchman, Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville, recorded someone singing *Au clair de la
lune* as a wavy line on sooty paper with his phonautograph. Nobody could play it back until American
researchers turned the line into sound in 2008: about ten seconds, often called the oldest recording
of a song you can recognise.

## Sur le pont d'Avignon

Here the shape is clear: a refrain, then a short couplet with a new group of people each time (the
fine gentlemen, the fine ladies, and so on), then the refrain again. Words vary a little from one
version to another; this is a common one.

> Sur le pont d'Avignon,\
> L'on y danse, l'on y danse,\
> Sur le pont d'Avignon,\
> L'on y danse tous en rond.
>
> Les beaux messieurs font comme ça,\
> Et puis encore comme ça.

*On the bridge of Avignon, people dance there, people dance there, on the bridge of Avignon, everyone dances there in a ring. The fine gentlemen go like this, and then again like this.*

- *L'on y danse* = *on y danse*: people dance there. *Y* stands for *sur le pont* (lesson 07: *y*
  replaces a place). *L'on* is an older, more elegant form of *on* (many versions just sing *On y
  danse*).
- *Tous en rond* = all in a ring; *comme ça* = like this (children copy a bow or a curtsy).

The bridge is real: the pont Saint-Bénézet, built across the Rhône in the twelfth century. Floods
broke it again and again, and since the seventeenth century it has stopped in the middle of the
river; four of its original twenty-two arches are left. Nobody knows who wrote the song. It became
famous in 1853, when the composer Adolphe Adam used it in a comic opera. Many people say that the
dancing really took place *sous le pont* (under the bridge), on the river banks: a story often told,
hard to prove.

## Le Temps des cerises

Jean-Baptiste Clément wrote the words in 1866, and Antoine Renard set them to music in 1868. The song
is older than the Paris Commune, the uprising crushed by the government's army in May 1871 (the
*Semaine sanglante*, the "bloody week"), but it has been tied to it ever since: Clément, who had fought
on the barricades, later dedicated it to a nurse, "Louise", whom he met on the last day, Sunday 28 May
1871 (the dedication appears in 1882). Since then it has been both a love song and a song of hope for a better world. Clément died in
1903 and Renard in 1872, so words and music are in the public domain. Here is the first verse, as
Clément printed it in his *Chansons* of 1882:

> Quand nous en serons au temps des cerises,\
> Et gai rossignol et merle moqueur\
> Seront tous en fête.\
> Les belles auront la folie en tête\
> Et les amoureux du soleil au cœur.\
> Quand nous en serons au temps des cerises,\
> Sifflera bien mieux le merle moqueur.

*When we get to cherry time, the merry nightingale and the mocking blackbird will all be celebrating. Pretty girls will have madness in their heads, and lovers sunshine in their hearts. When we get to cherry time, the mocking blackbird will whistle much better.*

- *Quand nous en serons à* = when we have reached (*en être à* = to have got to a point). Most singers
  today start *Quand nous chanterons le temps des cerises* (when we sing of cherry time), a later
  change; Clément's books keep *en serons au*.
- *La cerise* = cherry; *le rossignol* = nightingale; *le merle* = blackbird; *moqueur* = mocking.
- *Sifflera bien mieux le merle moqueur*: the subject comes after the verb, as poems and songs allow:
  *le merle moqueur sifflera bien mieux*.

The other verses turn sad: cherry time is short, and love hurts. The last verse begins *J'aimerai
toujours le temps des cerises* (I will always love cherry time).

## Tenses in songs

Look at the verbs of the first verse: *serons, seront, auront, sifflera*. They are all futur simple
(lesson 13), and they all follow *quand*: *Quand nous en serons…* — French uses the future after
*quand* when the time is in the future, where English uses the present ("when we get to"). The song
looks forward to a happier time.

Many other songs look back instead, and then the imparfait sets the scene: how things were, what we
used to do (lesson 01). A rough rule for songs: the imparfait for memories and nostalgia (*la
nostalgie*), the futur for promises and hopes.

### Example 1: Find the tense and say why

Name the tense of each verb and why the song uses it.

1. *Seront tous en fête* (*être*, stem *ser-*): futur simple, a prediction of cherry time.
2. *Les belles auront la folie en tête* (*avoir*, stem *aur-*): futur simple, another prediction.
3. *Ma chandelle est morte* (from *Au clair de la lune*): present of *être* + the adjective *morte*;
   it describes the situation now.
4. *J'aimerai toujours*: futur simple of *aimer* (infinitive + *-ai*), a promise.

### Example 2: Write a couplet of your own

Here is an original couplet, written for this lesson, that looks back and then forward: four lines
of about seven syllables.

> Quand j'étais petit, l'été,\
> On dansait au bord de l'eau.\
> Quand je serai vieux, un jour,\
> Je chanterai ce rondeau.

*When I was little, in summer, we used to dance by the water. When I'm old, one day, I'll sing this rondeau.*

1. Lines 1–2 look back: imparfait for the scene and the habit (*j'étais, on dansait*).
2. Lines 3–4 look forward: *quand* + futur, then futur (*je serai, je chanterai*).
3. The sounds match at the end of lines 2 and 4 (*eau / rondeau*): a **[[rime]]**, or in English a rhyme.
   *Un rondeau* is an old kind of short poem or song.

Now write your own four lines: two in the imparfait about a childhood memory, two in the futur about
a hope.

## Four great names of the chanson

These singers made the *chanson française* famous around the world. Their songs are protected by
copyright, so listen to them on a music service and read their lyrics there.

- Édith Piaf (1915–1963), from Paris: a tiny woman with an enormous voice, nicknamed *la Môme
  Piaf* (the kid sparrow; *un piaf* is an informal word for a sparrow). She wrote the words of *La Vie
  en rose* (1945) and *Hymne à l'amour* (1950), and in 1960 she recorded *Non, je ne regrette rien*,
  whose title says it all: no regrets.
- Georges Brassens (1921–1981), from Sète on the Mediterranean: a man alone with his guitar,
  singing witty, tender and sometimes rude songs that mock self-important people. He started in 1952
  in the singer Patachou's cabaret, and in 1967 the Académie française gave him its poetry prize.
- Jacques Brel (1929–1978), born in Brussels, Belgian: a singer who threw his whole body into
  each song. *Ne me quitte pas* (1959) is one of the best-known love songs in French; *Amsterdam*
  (1964) and *Le Plat Pays* (1962) are others. He gave up concerts in the late 1960s and is buried on
  Hiva Oa, in French Polynesia.
- Barbara (1930–1997), born Monique Serf in Paris: a pianist and singer known for dressing in black.
  After a concert in the German town of Göttingen on 4 July 1964, she wrote the song *Göttingen*,
  which is still remembered as a symbol of friendship between France and Germany after the war.

### Talking about a song

Here is how a fan might describe a concert, in a text written for this lesson:

> Hier soir, l'interprète est monté sur scène avec sa guitare, sans micro au début. Le public chantait le refrain avec lui. Ses chansons ressemblent à des poèmes : c'est un vrai poète. Le rythme de son dernier tube est plus rapide que celui des autres, mais la chanson que je préfère, c'est une ballade pleine de nostalgie. Depuis, je la fredonne et je la siffle toute la journée !

*Last night the performer came on stage with his guitar, without a mic at first. The audience sang the chorus with him. His songs are like poems: he's a real poet. The rhythm of his latest hit is faster than the others', but the song I like best is a ballad full of nostalgia. Since then I've been humming it and whistling it all day!*

*Le tube* (a hit) is informal; *la poésie* is poetry, and *un poème* a poem. Notice the grammar: *que
je préfère* (relative, lesson 10), *plus rapide que celui des autres* (lessons 09 and 11), *je la
fredonne* (pronoun, lesson 05), *depuis* + present (lesson 03).

## Common mistakes

- Quoting the lyrics of a modern song in your own work: you may name a song and talk about it, but its
  words belong to its authors.
- *Le couplet* is not "a couplet" (two lines) in the English sense: it's a whole verse.
- After *quand* about the future, using the present: *Quand je serai grand*, not *Quand je suis grand*
  (lesson 13).
- *Prête-moi*, not *Prête-me*: after the verb, *me* becomes *moi*.
- *Une chanson* is a song; *le chant* is singing (*un chant de Noël* is a carol).

## Key points

- A song has **[[couplets]]** (verses) and a **[[refrain]]** (chorus); *les paroles* are the lyrics.
- *Au clair de la lune* (eighteenth century) and *Sur le pont d'Avignon* (author unknown; famous from
  1853) are traditional; the bridge is the pont Saint-Bénézet.
- *Le Temps des cerises*: words by Jean-Baptiste Clément (1866), music by Antoine Renard (1868),
  tied to the Paris Commune (1871); its first verse is in the futur simple after *quand*.
- In songs, as in stories: the imparfait looks back, the futur looks forward.
- Piaf, Brassens, Brel and Barbara: describe and discuss their songs, but don't copy their lyrics.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Le cinéma français
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

France calls cinema *le septième art* (the seventh art), and the screening usually taken as its birth
took place in Paris. This lesson tells that history in a few dates, shows you how
French cinemas list films, has you read a synopsis, and then puts the grammar of the course to work
in a short film review: relatives (lesson 10), comparisons and superlatives (lesson 09), adverbs
(lesson 12) and opinions (lesson 21).

## A short history in five dates

![A timeline of French cinema from 1890 to today with five events: 1895, les frères Lumière; 1902, Méliès: Le Voyage dans la Lune; 1946, le premier festival de Cannes; 1959, la Nouvelle Vague; 1976, les premiers César.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 1895: the Lumière brothers

On Saturday 28 December 1895, in the *Salon indien*, a basement room
of the Grand Café on the boulevard des Capucines in Paris, Louis and Auguste Lumière gave the first
public screening of their *cinématographe* for a paying audience. A ticket cost one franc, and the
spectators (*les spectateurs*) saw ten short films, each under a minute, starting with *La Sortie de l'usine Lumière à
Lyon* (workers leaving the Lumière factory in Lyon). Their most famous film, the train arriving at
La Ciotat station, was shown in the following weeks, not on the first evening.

### 1902: Georges Méliès

Méliès ran a magic theatre in Paris, the Théâtre Robert-Houdin. He was at
the Grand Café in 1895 and wanted to buy the Lumières' machine; they refused. So he made his own
films, in a studio he built at Montreuil, near Paris, in 1897, and used camera tricks, some of the first *effets spéciaux* (special effects), to make
people appear and disappear. In *Le Voyage dans la Lune* (A Trip to the Moon, 1902) a space shell lands in
the eye of the Man in the Moon. He made about five hundred films, but he was ruined, and for some years he sold
toys in a shop at the Gare Montparnasse.

### 1946: the Cannes festival

The first festival was planned for September 1939 in Cannes, but the
Second World War broke out just as it was about to open. The first one finally opened on 20 September 1946. It has been held
in May since 1952. Its top prize (*la récompense* that every director dreams of), *la Palme d'or*,
was first given in 1955.

### 1959: the Nouvelle Vague

At the end of the 1950s, young filmmakers, several of them critics for
the magazine *Les Cahiers du cinéma*, began to make their own films. For *le tournage* (the shoot) they left the studios for the streets, with light cameras,
small teams and small budgets, and told personal stories in a free, new way: the **[[Nouvelle Vague]]**
(New Wave). In 1959 François Truffaut won the prize for best director at Cannes with *Les Quatre Cents
Coups*; Jean-Luc Godard's *À bout de souffle* came out in 1960, and Agnès Varda's *Cléo de 5 à 7* in
1962.

### 1976: the César

France's national film awards, modelled on the Oscars, were created by Georges
Cravenne. The first ceremony took place on 3 April 1976; every year since, the César have rewarded (*récompensent*)
the best films, actors and directors. The trophy, a block of compressed metal,
was designed by the sculptor César (César Baldaccini), and the awards are named after him.

## At the cinema: VO, VF and sous-titres

A French cinema programme tells you the language of each *séance* (showing, lesson 22):

| You see | It means |
|---|---|
| **[[VO]]** or *VOST* | *version originale (sous-titrée)*: the original language, with French subtitles |
| *VF* | *version française*: dubbed into French (*doublé*) |
| *1 h 45* | the length (*la durée*, lesson 03) of a *long métrage* (feature film); a *court métrage* is a short film |
| *Comédie dramatique* | the type of film: *une comédie, un drame*, or *un documentaire* (lesson 21) |

Many French people watch foreign films in VO, especially in big cities; dubbed versions are common
too. Before you choose, watch *la bande-annonce* (the trailer).

Some words you know take on a cinema meaning: *tourner un film* = to shoot a film (A1 *tourner* = to
turn), *réaliser un film* = to direct it (lesson 13: *réaliser un rêve*), *le prix* = the prize (A1:
the price), *un film muet* = a silent film. *Un acteur joue un rôle*: an actor plays a part.

## Reading a synopsis

A **[[synopsis]]** is a short summary of a film's plot (*l'intrigue*), written in the present, which stops
before the end. This one is for an invented film.

> **Les Cerises de juillet** — comédie dramatique, France, 1 h 45
>
> Lucie, une jeune pianiste qui vit à Paris, perd son travail le jour de ses trente ans. Elle retourne dans le village du Jura où elle a passé son enfance et où sa grand-mère tient toujours un petit café. Là, elle retrouve Malik, un ami d'enfance qui rêve de devenir réalisateur. Ensemble, ils décident de tourner un court métrage avec les habitants du village… mais rien ne se passe comme prévu.

*Cherries in July — comedy-drama, France, 1 h 45. Lucie, a young pianist who lives in Paris, loses her job on her thirtieth birthday. She goes back to the village in the Jura where she spent her childhood and where her grandmother still runs a little café. There she meets up again with Malik, a childhood friend who dreams of becoming a director. Together they decide to shoot a short film with the people of the village… but nothing goes as planned.*

*Perd* = loses (*perdre*); *tient* = runs (a café); *les habitants* = the people who live there;
*comme prévu* = as planned. Notice the relatives: *qui vit à Paris* (*qui*, subject), *où elle a
passé son enfance* (*où*, place).

## Writing a review

*Une critique* is a review, and a good short one has the same parts as a DELF message: facts, a short
summary, your opinion with reasons, and a recommendation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The parts of a short film review
  accDescr: Five steps from top to bottom. First the title and the facts (type of film, director, actors). Then a short summary in the present that doesn't give away the ending. Then what you liked, with reasons. Then what you liked less. Finally your recommendation and a mark.
  A["Le titre et les faits : genre, réalisateur, acteurs"] --> B["Un court résumé au présent, sans la fin"]
  B --> C["Les points forts, avec des raisons"]
  C --> D["Les points faibles"]
  D --> E["Je le recommande ou pas ? Ma note"]
```

The tools:

- Relatives to describe without repeating: *un film qui fait du bien* (a feel-good film), *l'actrice
  que je préfère*, *le village où se passe l'histoire*.
- Comparisons: *plus drôle que le premier, moins long que …, aussi beau que …, le meilleur film de
  l'année*.
- Opinions (lesson 21): *Je trouve que …, À mon avis, …, J'ai adoré …, Par contre, …*.
- Adverbs (lesson 12): *vraiment émouvant, complètement raté, très bien joué*.

### Example 1: Join the sentences

Join each pair with *qui*, *que* or *où*.

1. *C'est une comédie. Elle fait rire toute la salle.* The second sentence's subject is *elle* (the
   comedy), so *qui*: *C'est une comédie qui fait rire toute la salle.*
2. *Malik est le personnage. Je préfère ce personnage.* *Ce personnage* is the object of *je préfère*,
   so *que*: *Malik est le personnage que je préfère.*
3. *Le café est magnifique. Une grande partie du film se passe dans ce café.* A place, so *où*: *Le
   café où se passe une grande partie du film est magnifique.* (After *où*, the subject often comes
   after a short verb: *où se passe le film*.)

### Example 2: A model review

> **Les Cerises de juillet : un film qui fait du bien**
>
> J'ai vu *Les Cerises de juillet* samedi dernier. C'est une comédie dramatique qui raconte l'histoire de Lucie, une pianiste qui retourne dans le village où elle a grandi.
>
> J'ai surtout aimé les acteurs : l'actrice qui joue Lucie est vraiment émouvante. Le scénario est plus original que celui de la plupart des comédies, et la musique est la meilleure partie du film. Par contre, la fin est un peu décevante : elle arrive trop vite.
>
> À mon avis, c'est quand même un des meilleurs films de l'année. Je le recommande à tous ceux qui aiment les histoires simples. Ma note : 4 sur 5.

*Cherries in July: a feel-good film. I saw Cherries in July last Saturday. It's a comedy-drama that tells the story of Lucie, a pianist who goes back to the village where she grew up. Above all I liked the actors: the actress who plays Lucie is really moving. The screenplay is more original than that of most comedies, and the music is the best part of the film. On the other hand, the ending is a bit disappointing: it comes too quickly. In my opinion it's still one of the best films of the year. I recommend it to everyone who likes simple stories. My mark: 4 out of 5.*

How it's built:

1. Facts and summary: the passé composé for what you did (*J'ai vu*), the present for the story
   (*qui raconte, qui retourne*).
2. Points for and against: *qui joue Lucie* (relative), *plus original que celui de …* (comparison +
   *celui*, lesson 11), *la meilleure partie* (superlative), *par contre* (contrast).
3. Verdict: *un des meilleurs films de l'année* (superlative + *de*), *Je le recommande à …*
   (direct object pronoun before the verb), and a mark.

About 100 words: a little more than a DELF A2 writing task asks for (about 60–80; lesson 23).

## Common mistakes

- *Le film est très ému.* *Ému* means moved (a person is moved); the film is *émouvant* (moving).
  Same pair: *déçu* (disappointed, a person) / *décevant* (disappointing, a thing).
- *Le directeur* runs a company or a school; a film's director is *le réalisateur* (*réaliser un film*
  = to direct a film).
- *Faire un rôle*: say *jouer un rôle*.
- Telling the end in a synopsis or review: stop before it.
- *Une critique* is a review, and also criticism; *le critique* is the person who writes it.

## Key points

- 28 December 1895: the Lumière brothers' first paying public screening, at the Grand Café in Paris.
- Méliès (*Le Voyage dans la Lune*, 1902) invented film tricks; the Nouvelle Vague (from 1959:
  Truffaut, Godard, Varda) took cinema into the streets; Cannes began in 1946 (planned for 1939), the
  César in 1976.
- **[[VO]]** = original language (with subtitles: VOST); *VF* = dubbed into French.
- A synopsis is in the present and keeps the ending secret.
- A short review: facts, summary, points for and against with reasons, recommendation, using *qui,
  que, où*, comparisons, superlatives and opinions.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Une année en France
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last lesson of French A2, and it puts the whole course together. You'll follow Kate, a
young Irish woman from Cork, through one year in Lyon, told in the messages she writes and receives:
e-mails to a friend, a formal e-mail, text messages, a complaint, an invitation. Every text uses the
grammar of the course, and after each one you'll see where it comes from. At the end you'll write
your own year, in 150 to 200 words, with a model and a checklist.

```map
base: world
title: L'année de Kate
view: Ireland, France
point: Cork | 51.90, -8.47 | Kate's home
point: Lyon | 45.76, 4.84 | Kate's year
point: Annecy | 45.90, 6.13 | Kate's year
point: Nantes | 47.22, -1.55 | Léa's town
route: Le voyage de Kate | 51.90, -8.47; 45.76, 4.84 | Kate's year
caption: Kate flies from Cork to Lyon in September, spends a weekend in Annecy in May, and writes all year to her friend Léa in Nantes.
```

![Kate's year as a strip of twelve months from September to August, September to June in Lyon (blue), July and August, after the internship, in green. Six months have a picture: a suitcase in September (l'arrivée), a key in October (la colocation), a bank card in February (la carte avalée), mountains and a lake in May (le week-end à Annecy), an open book in June (le dernier jour de stage) and a plane in August (le retour à Cork).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The year in eight documents

Kate is 23. She has an internship (*un stage*) in a bookshop (*une librairie*, not a library) in Lyon
from September to June. Her
friend Léa, whom she met when Léa was a student in Ireland, lives in Nantes.

### 1. Septembre: an e-mail to Léa

> Salut Léa,
>
> Ça y est, je suis arrivée à Lyon il y a dix jours ! Pour l'instant, je dors dans une auberge de jeunesse, mais je cherche une chambre. La ville est magnifique : elle est plus grande que Cork, mais moins stressante que Paris. Le premier jour, il pleuvait et je ne comprenais rien quand les gens parlaient vite. Mais hier, à la librairie, une cliente m'a demandé un livre et j'ai tout compris ! Mon stage a commencé lundi. J'ai encore un peu peur, mais je suis contente, et je commence à m'habituer à la ville.
>
> Je t'embrasse, Kate

*Ça y est* = that's it, I've done it; *pour l'instant* = for now; *stressant* = stressful;
*s'habituer à* = to get used to. Grammar:
*il y a dix jours* (ago, lesson 03), comparisons (09), imparfait for the background and passé composé
for the events (01–02).

### 2. Octobre: a formal e-mail about a room

> Madame, Monsieur,
>
> J'ai vu votre annonce pour une chambre dans une colocation à la Croix-Rousse. Je suis irlandaise, j'ai 23 ans et je fais un stage dans une librairie jusqu'en juin. Pourriez-vous me dire si la chambre est encore disponible ? Je voudrais aussi savoir combien coûtent les charges et quand je pourrais la visiter. Je suis libre tous les soirs après 18 heures.
>
> Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.
>
> Kate O'Neill

*La Croix-Rousse* is a district of Lyon; *une colocation* = a flat-share; the closing line is the
formal "Yours faithfully". Grammar: the polite conditionnel (*Pourriez-vous, Je voudrais, je
pourrais*, lesson 14), indirect questions with *si, combien, quand* (19), *la* = the room (05).

### 3. Novembre: texts with Hugo, her flatmate

> Hugo : Tu peux acheter du pain en rentrant ?
>
> Kate : J'en ai déjà acheté ce matin !
>
> Hugo : Génial. Et du lait, il y en a encore ?
>
> Kate : Non, il n'y en a plus. Je vais en prendre.
>
> Hugo : Merci ! Au fait, Mathilde fait une fête samedi. Je lui ai parlé de toi. Tu viens ?
>
> Kate : Avec plaisir ! Je lui apporterai un gâteau irlandais.

*En rentrant* = on your way home (a gérondif, 12h3); *au fait* = by the way. Grammar: *en* for a
quantity and with *il y a* (07), *en* before *avoir* in the passé composé (08), *ne … plus* (17),
*lui* (06), futur (13).

### 4. Décembre: missing home

> Coucou Léa !
>
> Ici, il fait froid et il fait nuit à cinq heures. Je travaille beaucoup : avant Noël, tout le monde achète des livres ! Hugo et Mathilde m'ont très bien accueillie, mais parfois j'ai le mal du pays : ma famille me manque. Je rentrerai à Cork le 22 décembre et je reviendrai le 3 janvier. Si tu as le temps en janvier, viens me voir ! On mangera dans un bouchon.
>
> Bises, Kate

*Le mal du pays* = homesickness; *un bouchon* = a small traditional Lyon restaurant; *m'ont accueillie*
= welcomed me (the participle agrees with *m'*, Kate, lesson 08). *Ma famille me
manque* = I miss my family: with *manquer*, what you miss is the subject (literally "my family is
missing to me"). Grammar: *tout le monde* + singular verb (18), futur (13), *si* + present →
imperative (15).

### 5. Février: a problem, then a solution

> Madame,
>
> Samedi soir, vers 22 heures, le distributeur de l'agence de la place Bellecour a avalé ma carte bancaire. Comme l'agence était fermée, je n'ai pas pu la récupérer. Je n'ai donc plus de carte, et je dois payer mon loyer avant le 10. Pourriez-vous me dire ce que je dois faire ?
>
> Cordialement, Kate O'Neill

Three days later, thanks to her adviser, Kate has a new card: *Grâce à ma conseillère, j'ai eu une
nouvelle carte en trois jours.* Grammar: *comme* first for the cause, *donc* for the consequence,
*grâce à* for a good result (20); *ce que* in an indirect question (19); *avaler* (lesson 90).

### 6. Avril: an invitation

> Salut Léa,
>
> Bonne nouvelle : ma patronne m'a donné quatre jours de congé en mai ! Si on allait à Annecy ? Ça te dit ? Ce n'est pas très loin de Lyon, et Hugo dit que c'est le plus beau lac de France. On pourrait louer des vélos et faire le tour du lac. Dis-moi vite !
>
> Kate

> Trop bien ! J'arriverai jeudi soir. J'apporterai mon maillot de bain, même si l'eau est sûrement froide !
>
> Léa

*Trop bien !* = brilliant! (informal); *même si* = even if (like *si*, it takes the present here, not the
futur). Grammar: *si on* + imparfait and *Ça te
dit ?* (22), *on pourrait* (14), reported speech in the present (*Hugo dit que …*, 19), superlative +
*de* (09).

### 7. Juin: the last day

> Aujourd'hui, c'était mon dernier jour à la librairie. Ma patronne dit que je parle couramment. Ce n'est pas vrai, mais je n'ai plus peur de téléphoner en français et je ne cherche plus mes mots tout le temps. J'ai fait beaucoup de progrès. Je n'oublierai jamais les clients du samedi matin, qui venaient toujours avec leur chien. Ce soir, j'ai fait mes adieux à mes collègues, et ils m'ont offert un livre de chansons de Brassens.

*Faire des progrès* = to make progress; *faire ses adieux* = to say goodbye. Grammar: *ne … plus,
ne … jamais* (17), relative *qui* (10), imparfait for a habit (*venaient
toujours*, 01), *couramment* (12), *m'ont offert* (06).

### 8. Août: back in Cork

> Chère Léa,
>
> Me voilà de retour à Cork. Ici, tout est pareil, mais moi, j'ai changé. Quel bilan ! Au début, le dépaysement était dur et j'ai eu du mal à m'adapter, mais cette année a été une vraie aventure, pleine de découvertes. Il y a un an, je n'osais pas commander un café en français ; aujourd'hui, je lis des romans ! J'ai vraiment progressé, et je suis reconnaissante à Hugo et à toi. Lyon me manque déjà : les marchés, les bouchons, nos soirées… L'année prochaine, je finirai mes études, et après, j'aimerais bien revenir en France. Si je trouve du travail à Nantes, on sera voisines !
>
> Je t'embrasse très fort, Kate

*Me voilà de retour* = here I am, back; *pareil* = the same; *le bilan* = the review, taking stock;
*le dépaysement* = the feeling of being far from home and your habits; *avoir du mal à* = to find it
hard to; *reconnaissant à* = grateful to; *oser* = to dare (lesson 90). Grammar:
then and now (*il y a un an* + imparfait, *aujourd'hui* + present), futur, a wish in the conditionnel
(*j'aimerais bien*, 14), *si* + present → futur (15).

## Spotting the grammar

### Example 1: Why this tense?

Take Kate's sentence from September: *Le premier jour, il pleuvait et je ne comprenais rien quand les
gens parlaient vite. Mais hier, une cliente m'a demandé un livre et j'ai tout compris !*

1. *pleuvait, comprenais, parlaient*: imparfait, the background of that first day (lesson 02).
2. *m'a demandé, ai compris*: passé composé, two events, one after the other.
3. *m'a demandé*: *me* is an indirect object (*demander à quelqu'un*), so no agreement (lesson 08).
4. *tout* goes between *ai* and *compris*, like *bien* and *déjà*: *j'ai tout compris*.

### Example 2: Planning your own year

The final task: write about a year of your life (real or imagined) in 150 to 200 words. Here is a
plan, then a model written for this lesson.

1. Where and when: *L'année dernière, j'ai passé six mois à …*
2. The start, with background: *Au début, je ne connaissais personne et …*
3. Two or three events, with feelings: *Un jour, … Heureusement, grâce à …*
4. Then and now: *Avant, je … ; maintenant, je …*
5. The future: *L'année prochaine, je … ; j'aimerais … ; si …, je …*

> Il y a deux ans, j'ai passé une année à Bordeaux pour mes études. Au début, c'était difficile : je ne connaissais personne et je n'osais pas parler en cours. Mon studio était petit et sombre, mais il était tout près de la fac. En octobre, je me suis inscrit à un club de randonnée. C'est là que j'ai rencontré Inès et Paul, qui sont devenus mes meilleurs amis. Chaque dimanche, on partait marcher au bord de l'océan ou dans les vignes. En mars, je suis tombé malade et j'ai raté deux examens. Heureusement, grâce à mes amis, j'ai pu les repasser en juin, et je les ai réussis ! Avant, j'avais peur de faire des fautes ; maintenant, je parle sans réfléchir. Bordeaux me manque souvent. L'année prochaine, je ferai un master, et si je peux, je retournerai en France pour un stage. J'aimerais bien travailler dans le monde du vin !

*Sombre* = dark; *la randonnée* = hiking; *les vignes* = vineyards; *repasser un examen* = to retake
an exam; *réussir un examen* = to pass it; *le monde du vin* = the wine business. The model has just over 150 words. The writer is a man
(*inscrit, tombé*): a woman would write *inscrite, tombée*.

### Your checklist

Before you finish, check your text:

- 150–200 words, in paragraphs, with a beginning, a middle and an end.
- Imparfait for descriptions and habits, passé composé for events (01–02).
- At least one time expression: *il y a, pendant, depuis, en* (03).
- Pronouns instead of repeated nouns: *le, la, lui, y, en* (05–08), with agreement where needed.
- A comparison or a superlative (09) and a relative *qui, que* or *où* (10).
- The futur for plans (13) and the conditionnel for a wish (14); *si* + present (15).
- A negation beyond *ne … pas* (17) and a connector of cause or consequence (20).
- A past participle with *être* agrees with its subject (a few reflexive verbs are exceptions: *ils se
  sont parlé*).

## Common mistakes

- *Je manque ma famille.* With *manquer*, turn it round: *Ma famille me manque* (my family is missing
  to me). *Tu me manques* = I miss you.
- The futur for a memory: *Quand j'étais petit* (01) looks back; *Quand je serai grand* (13) looks
  forward.
- Mixing *tu* and *vous* in one message. Kate writes *tu* to Léa and Hugo, *vous* to the landlord and
  the bank.
- Starting a formal e-mail with *Salut* or ending it with *Bises*: use *Madame, Monsieur* and
  *Cordialement* (23).

## Key points

- A year abroad uses every part of the course: the past (01–08), description and comparison
  (09–12), plans (13–16), everyday services (17–20) and messages (21–23).
- *Manquer* turns round: *Lyon me manque* = I miss Lyon.
- Choose the register for each reader: informal to friends, formal to offices.
- Your final text: 150–200 words, then check it against the list.

Félicitations : you have finished French A2! At B1 you'll learn to use the forms you have so far
only met as previews, such as the plus-que-parfait and the subjunctive, while the passé simple stays
a tense you read.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

sections.name: Opinions, messages and the DELF A2
Honors: Contes, chansons et cinéma (stories, songs and film)

questions.stem: Where and when did Perrault's Histoires ou contes du temps passé, with Le Petit Chaperon rouge, first appear?
questions.explanation: The Paris bookseller Claude Barbin published the book in January 1697, under Louis XIV. 1812 is the Grimms' first edition (in German), and 1668 is La Fontaine's first Fables.

questions.stem: How does Perrault's version of Le Petit Chaperon rouge end?
choices: A hunter cuts the wolf open and saves the girl and her grandmother.
The girl runs away through the window.
The wolf eats the girl, and a moral in verse follows.
The grandmother hides the girl in a cupboard.
questions.explanation: In Perrault (1697) the wolf eats the grandmother and then the girl, and the story stops; the moralité in verse warns young girls about smooth-talking "wolves". The hunter comes from the Grimms' version of 1812.

questions.stem: In "Le Loup tira la chevillette, et la porte s'ouvrit", what tense are "tira" and "s'ouvrit"?
questions.explanation: Tira (-er verb: -a) and s'ouvrit (-it) are passé simple: two events, one after the other. Spoken, you'd say "le loup a tiré la chevillette et la porte s'est ouverte". The imparfait would be tirait, s'ouvrait.

questions.stem: Match each passé simple form to its passé composé.
questions.explanation: -er verbs end in -a (mangea keeps its e, like nous mangeons); fit is faire; vint is venir, an être verb; eurent is avoir in the ils form (-urent). Il a mis would be il mit, ils sont allés would be ils allèrent.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this picture of the tale.

image.alt: The path through the wood with no labels: a girl in a red hood with a basket on a long winding path, a wolf behind a tree, a woodcutter with an axe, a short straight path to a cottage, and a little peg on the cottage door. Six parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 the girl in her red hood, 2 the wolf behind the tree, 3 the woodcutter (le bûcheron) whose presence stops the wolf, 4 the long winding path the girl takes, 5 the short path the wolf takes, 6 the little peg on the door (la chevillette). The hunter belongs to the Grimms' version, and the grandmother is inside the house.

questions.stem: In "elle rencontra compère le Loup […] à cause de quelques bûcherons qui étaient dans la forêt", why is "étaient" in the imparfait?
choices: It describes the background: where the woodcutters were.
It is a single event that moves the story on.
It is the passé simple of être.
It is a future seen from the past.
questions.explanation: The imparfait gives the background (lesson 02): the woodcutters were there all along. The events are in the passé simple (rencontra, eut, n'osa). The passé simple of être is fut / furent.

questions.stem: Which of these are passé simple forms? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Dévora and cria are -er verbs in -a, and rencontrèrent is the ils form (-èrent). Dévorait is the imparfait, and a tiré the passé composé.

questions.stem: Retell "Il la dévora" (la = the grandmother) in the passé composé: Il ___.
questions.explanation: The pronoun goes before avoir (l'a), and because the direct object la comes before the verb, the participle agrees with it: dévorée (lesson 08).

questions.stem: "Le Petit Chaperon rouge vint heurter à la porte." How would you say this in everyday spoken French today?
choices: Elle venait frapper à la porte.
Elle est venue frapper à la porte.
Elle a venu frapper à la porte.
Elle vint frapper à la porte.
questions.explanation: Vint is the passé simple of venir, which takes être in the passé composé, and the girl is feminine: elle est venue. Heurter is old; today we say frapper. Venait is the imparfait (a background), "a venu" uses the wrong auxiliary, and vint is still the written tense.

questions.stem: Put the events of Perrault's tale in order.
choices: La mère envoie sa fille chez la grand-mère.
Dans le bois, la fille rencontre le loup.
Le loup prend le chemin le plus court.
La fille arrive et parle au loup, qui est dans le lit.
questions.explanation: The errand, the meeting in the wood, the race (the wolf takes the short path), the grandmother eaten, the famous dialogue in the bed, and the end: the wolf eats the girl.

questions.stem: What does "Ma mère-grand, que vous avez de grands bras !" mean?
choices: Grandmother, do you have big arms?
Grandmother, your arms are bigger than mine.
Grandmother, what big arms you have!
Grandmother, what do you have in your big arms?
questions.explanation: Que + a sentence is an exclamation (lesson 22): what big arms you have! Mère-grand is the old word for grand-mère. The wolf answers: "C'est pour mieux t'embrasser, ma fille."

questions.stem: According to Perrault's moral, which wolves are the most dangerous?
choices: the ones that live deep in the forest
the ones that hunt in packs
the gentle, smooth-talking ones who follow girls home
questions.explanation: The moral ends: "qui ne sait que ces loups doucereux, / De tous les loups sont les plus dangereux". Doucereux means falsely sweet: the quiet, polite wolves who follow young ladies right into their homes.

questions.stem: On the long path, the girl "s'amusait à ___ des noisettes" (to pick hazelnuts). Which verb fits?
questions.explanation: Cueillir is to pick flowers or fruit: elle cueille, elle a cueilli. Couper is to cut, manger to eat, chercher to look for.

questions.stem: In the wood, the wolf wanted to eat the girl but didn't dare. Build: "He didn't eat her."
questions.explanation: Il ne l'a pas mangée: ne before the pronoun, pas after the auxiliary, and the participle agrees with l' (the girl, feminine) because the direct object comes first (lesson 08).

questions.stem: In a song, what is "le refrain"?
choices: A verse whose words change each time
The chorus: the lines that come back with the same words
questions.explanation: Le refrain is the chorus. A verse whose words change is le couplet, the tune is la mélodie, and the words are les paroles.

questions.stem: Why does Au clair de la lune say "Prête-moi ta plume" and not "Prête-me ta plume"?
choices: Because moi is the subject of the sentence.
